paras.en: The birth and circumcision of the Forerunner having been described, now the birth and circumcision of Christ are described. [[2:1|And it came to pass that in those days|Factum est autem in diebus illis]], that is, at the time when John was growing and being strengthened, or thereabouts, [[2:1|there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus|exiit edictum a Cæsare Augusto]], that is, Octavian the emperor commanded: which Octavian was the successor of Julius, the first emperor, who seized the empire, gaining it by battles after he had put Pompey to flight. Julius was called Caesar either because, his mother having died, he was taken out by the cutting of his mother's womb, according to Isidore, or because he was born with a full head of hair [*cæsaries*], or because he was a victorious slayer [*cæsor*] of his enemies [Isidore's etymologies of *Caesar*, from *cædere*, “to cut”, *cæsaries*, “hair”, and *cæsor*, “one who cuts down”]. Now the daughter of Julius was the wife of Octavian, who kept this name, Caesar, from his predecessor, and was besides surnamed Augustus, because he greatly increased [*auxit*] the commonwealth, the Roman empire and all the wealth of Rome. [[2:1|that the whole world should be enrolled|Ut describeretur universus orbis]], that is, that the names of the regions, cities, towns and villages, and of all their inhabitants, should be put down in writing and brought to Rome and made known to him. For this emperor wished to know the greatness of his power from the number of his subjects, namely over how many provinces, cities, villages and towns, and indeed over how many men, he ruled; and also to know the amount and worth of the tribute paid him in each province of his dominion, and how he might best keep the provinces in peace, providing each with governors, judges or rulers.

paras.t: Interea, secundum Ambrosium et Glossam, Octavianus non imperavit universo orbi, imo nec Gothis, neque Armeniis, secundum Ambrosium; nec videtur possibile, quod ad omnes mundi provincias potuerit potestatem suam extendere aut venire: idcirco, quod totus orbis dicitur ad ejus jussionem descriptus, hyperbolica locutio est, qua aliquid dicitur per excessum, ad insinuandum magnitudinem rei, quemadmodum apud Joannem Pharisæi dicunt de Christo et populo eum in die Palmarum sequente: Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum. Ad innuendum ergo quod Augustus latissime imperavit, dicitur toti orbi dominatus, illumque describi jussisse.
paras.en: However, according to Ambrose and the Gloss, Octavian did not rule the whole world, nor even the Goths or the Armenians, according to Ambrose; nor does it seem possible that he could have extended his power to, or reached, all the provinces of the world. So when the whole world is said to have been enrolled at his command, it is a hyperbolic way of speaking [hyperbole], in which something is said by excess, to suggest the greatness of the thing: as in John the Pharisees say of Christ and of the people following Him on Palm Sunday: [[John 12:19|Behold, the whole world is gone after him|Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum]]. To convey, then, that Augustus ruled very widely, he is said to have ruled the whole world and to have ordered it to be enrolled.

paras.t: Revera namque latissime imperavit, nec aliqua ei regio quivit resistere, sed victoriosissimus ac fortunatissimus fuit. Propter quod in senatu postea, scilicet tempore Trajani imperatoris, fuit acclamatum: Nullus felicior Octaviano, nullus melior Trajano.
paras.en: For in truth he ruled very widely, and no region could withstand him, but he was most victorious and most fortunate. Wherefore in the senate afterwards, namely in the time of the emperor Trajan, the acclamation was made: None more fortunate than Octavian, none better than Trajan.

paras.t: Denique, quinquaginta septem annis et medio Octavianus legitur imperasse, et quadragesimo secundo sui imperii anno edictum istud constituisse: ita quod sub ejus imperio inaudita pax fuit in sæculo, omnibus uni homini subditis, ad præfigurandum quod Christus tunc veniens, veram pectoris æternitatisque pacem omnibus in se credentibus esset daturus, eosque in patria æternæ felicitatis collocaturus. Unde tunc litteraliter fuit impletum, quod in primo Christi adventu esse implendum prædictum fuit per Isaiam atque Michæam: Conflabunt gladios suos in vomeres, et lanceas suas in falces; non levabit gens contra gentem gladium.
paras.en: Lastly, Octavian is read to have reigned fifty-seven and a half years, and to have issued this edict in the forty-second year of his reign: so that under his rule there was an unheard-of peace in the world, all men being subject to one man, to prefigure that Christ, coming then, would give to all who believe in Him the true peace of the heart and of eternity, and would set them in the fatherland of eternal happiness. Hence there was then literally fulfilled what was foretold by Isaias and Micheas as to be fulfilled at Christ's first coming: [[Is 2:4|they shall turn their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles: nation shall not lift up sword against nation|Conflabunt gladios suos in vomeres, et lanceas suas in falces; non levabit gens contra gentem gladium]][[Mich 4:3||]].

paras.t: Hæc descriptio prima facta est a præside Syriæ Cyrino. Ante hanc generalem mundi descriptionem, præcesserant particulares certarum regionum descriptiones, sicut in libro Regum legitur David jussisse Joab, ut populum regni sui numeraret atque in scriptis redigeret; sed ista quam Octavianus fieri jussit, fuit prima, loquendo de generali orbis descriptione. Itaque hæc descriptio prima, scilicet universalis quam alia similis non præcessit, facta est a præside Syriæ. Vel hæc descriptio ab Augusto præcepta, facta est prima, hoc est, primo exsecutioni mandata est, seu fieri cœpit, a præside Syriæ nomine Cyrino. Quem Cyrinum Augustus præfecit Syris et Judæis, secundum Græcum expositorem: sed Cyrinus in Syria orsus est exsequi imperatoris edictum, eo quod Syria, ut dicitur, sit umbilicus seu medium terræ habitabilis, in cujus medio dicunt fuisse Judæam.
paras.en: [[2:2|This enrolling was first made by Cyrinus, the governor of Syria|Hæc descriptio prima facta est a præside Syriæ Cyrino]]. Before this general enrolment of the world there had been particular enrolments of certain regions, as we read in the book of Kings that David ordered Joab to number the people of his kingdom and put them down in writing[[2 Kings 24:2||]]; but this one which Octavian ordered was the first, speaking of a general enrolment of the world. So *this enrolling* was *first*, that is, universal, with no other like it before it, and was made by the governor of Syria. Or: this enrolment commanded by Augustus was first made, that is, was first put into execution, or began to be made, by the governor of Syria named Cyrinus. Augustus set this Cyrinus over the Syrians and the Jews, according to the Greek expositor [probably Theophylact]; but Cyrinus began to carry out the emperor's edict in Syria because Syria, as is said, is the navel or middle of the habitable earth, and in the middle of it, they say, was Judea.

paras.t: Et ibant omnes, videlicet principales de qualibet domo, vel etiam ceteri qui ire valebant, ut profiterentur, hoc est, verbo et facto protestarentur subjectos se Romano imperio, singuli in suam civitatem, hoc est in urbem de qua nati fuerunt, vel ad quam amplius pertinebant. Ascendit autem et Joseph a Galilæa de civitate Nazareth, in qua Christus fuit conceptus; et ibidem Virgo beatissima cum Joseph suo ministro, sponso et viro, tunc habitavit. Fertur quoque Joseph ascendisse, quoniam civitas illa inferior fuit loco quem adiit. De qua subditur: In Judæam civitatem, hoc est in urbem ad tribum Juda spectantem: ut Judæa adjective sumatur, quemadmodum in Joanne, quo dicitur, In Judæam terram: civitatem, inquam, David, quæ vocatur Bethlehem, id est, de qua exstitit oriundus. Ibi enim pater suus moratus est, et ipse cum illo, ut in libris Regum habetur. Sion quoque dicitur civitas David, quoniam ibi specialem sibi constituit mansionem, puta palatium, et quia Jerusalem fuit metropolis regni David. Sion autem quandoque pro Jerusalem, quandoque pro illa parte Jerusalem ubi palatium fuit ac templum, accipitur.
paras.en: [[2:3|And all went|Et ibant omnes]], namely the chief men of each house, or also the others who were able to go, [[2:3|to be enrolled|ut profiterentur]], that is, to declare by word and deed that they were subject to the Roman empire, [[2:3|every one into his own city|singuli in suam civitatem]], that is, into the city in which they were born, or to which they chiefly belonged. [[2:4|And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth|Ascendit autem et Joseph a Galilæa de civitate Nazareth]], in which Christ was conceived; and there the most blessed Virgin was then living with Joseph, her minister, spouse and husband. Joseph is said to have *gone up* because that city lay lower than the place he went to. Of which it follows: [[2:4|into Judea, to the city|In Judæam civitatem]] [so Denis reads the words, as one phrase], that is, into a city belonging to the tribe of Juda: so that *Judæa* is taken as an adjective, as in John, where it is said, [[John 3:22|into the land of Judea|In Judæam terram]]: the city, I say, [[2:4|of David, which is called Bethlehem|David, quæ vocatur Bethlehem]], that is, from which he sprang. For his father lived there, and he with him, as we have it in the books of Kings[[1 Kings 16:1||]][[1 Kings 17:12||]]. Sion too is called the city of David[[2 Kings 5:7||]], because there he set up a special dwelling for himself, namely his palace, and because Jerusalem was the capital of David's kingdom. Now Sion is taken sometimes for Jerusalem, sometimes for that part of Jerusalem where the palace and the temple were.

paras.t: Eo quod esset de domo, et, pro id est, familia David, ut patet in Matthæo, et infra capitulo tertio. Vel per domum intelligitur genus seu cognatio in communi; per familiam, pars cognationis. Multæ namque familiæ de eodem patre prodibant, quando multos filios habuit. Circa quod ait Græcus: Per hoc quod Evangelista ostendit Joseph fuisse de cognatione David, contentus fuit ipsam quoque Virginem de eadem fuisse cognatione promulgare, quum divina lex præciperet conjugales copulas ex eadem progenie contrahi.
paras.en: [[2:4|because he was of the house and family of David|Eo quod esset de domo, et, pro id est, familia David]], where *and* stands for *that is*: as is clear in Matthew[[Matt 1:16||]], and below in the third chapter[[3:23||]]. Or by *house* is understood the race or kindred in general; by *family*, a part of the kindred. For many families came from the same father, when he had many sons. On which the Greek says: By showing that Joseph was of the kindred of David, the Evangelist was content to make known that the Virgin herself was also of the same kindred, since the divine law commanded that marriages be contracted within the same stock [the margin reads Deut. xxv; the law of marrying within one's tribe is at Num 36:6–8].

paras.t: Ut profiteretur cum Maria desponsata sibi antequam illa conciperet Christum. Missus est enim Gabriel angelus ad virginem desponsatam viro, cui nomen Joseph, ut dictum est. Uxore prægnante, hoc est partui jam propinqua. Veraciter enim uxor ipsius fuit, quamvis eam nunquam cognoverit. Unde apud Matthæum, angelus ait ad eum, ante Christi nativitatem ex Virgine: Noli timere accipere Mariam conjugem tuam. Siquidem verum inter eos matrimonium fuit, quamvis non sit carnali copula consummatum.
paras.en: [[2:5|To be enrolled with Mary his espoused|Ut profiteretur cum Maria desponsata sibi]], espoused before she conceived Christ. For the angel Gabriel was sent[[Luke 1:26||]] [[Luke 1:27|To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph|ad virginem desponsatam viro, cui nomen Joseph]], as was said. [[2:5|wife, who was with child|Uxore prægnante]], that is, now near her delivery. For she was truly his wife, though he never knew her. Hence in Matthew the angel says to him before Christ's birth from the Virgin: [[Matt 1:20|fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife|Noli timere accipere Mariam conjugem tuam]]. For there was a true marriage between them, though it was not consummated by carnal union.

paras.t: Porro, professio illa fiebat verbo et facto, quia dicebant se imperatori subjectos, atque in signum veritatis, ponebant denarium imperatoris imagine insignitum super proprium caput, quem statim porrigebant imperatoris ministro, qui nomina profitentium mox descripsit. Estque dubium apud quosdam, an solus vir profitebatur. Quod si dicatur, tunc quod ait Evangelista, Cum Maria, refertur ad verbum, Ascendit, non ad verbum, Profitebatur.
paras.en: Further, that enrolment [*professio*: a declaration of allegiance] was made by word and deed: for they said that they were subject to the emperor, and in token of the truth they placed on their own heads a penny stamped with the emperor's image, which they at once handed to the emperor's officer, who straightway wrote down the names of those enrolling. And some are in doubt whether the husband alone was enrolled. If that is said, then the Evangelist's words *with Mary* refer to the word *went up*, not to the word *be enrolled*.

paras.t: Factum est autem, quum essent ibi, puta in Bethlehem, impleti sunt dies ut pareret Virgo benedicta, novem mensibus jam elapsis: quæ revelante Spiritu Sancto noverat se in Bethlehem parituram, ut illud Michææ impleretur, quo Dominus ait: Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata, ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel; et magnificabitur in medio universæ terræ. De quo fertur in Psalmo: Et dominabitur a mari usque ad mare; et a flumine usque ad terminos orbis terrarum. Et Daniel ait: Omnes populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei. Et peperit filium suum primogenitum, scilicet Jesum Christum, qui dicitur primogenitus per exclusionem prioris, non per respectum sequentis seu posterioris: ut dicatur primogenitus, ante quem alius non est natus, etiam si nullus post eum nascatur. Sic enim primogenitus in lege accipitur, dum omne primogenitum Domino offerri jubetur. Certum est enim, quod multi tunc unigeniti erant in populo Judæorum, qui tamen Deo offerebantur propter illud præceptum.
paras.en: [[2:6|And it came to pass that when they were there|Factum est autem, quum essent ibi]], namely in Bethlehem, [[2:6|her days were accomplished that she should be delivered|impleti sunt dies ut pareret]], the blessed Virgin, nine months having now passed: who knew, by the revelation of the Holy Ghost, that she would give birth in Bethlehem, so that the word of Micheas might be fulfilled, in which the Lord says: [[Mich 5:2|And thou Bethlehem Ephrata|Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata]], [[Mich 5:2|out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be the ruler in Israel|ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel]]; and he shall be magnified in the midst of the whole earth[[Mich 5:4||]] [these last words are Denis's summary of Mich 5:4, “now shall he be magnified even to the ends of the earth”]. Of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:8|And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.|Et dominabitur a mari usque ad mare, et a flumine usque ad terminos orbis terrarum.]] And Daniel says: [[Dan 7:14|all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him|Omnes populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei]] [the margin reads Dan. vii, 14, misread as vii, 1–4]. [[2:7|And she brought forth her first born son|Et peperit filium suum primogenitum]], namely Jesus Christ, who is called *firstborn* by the exclusion of anyone before Him, not with regard to anyone following or after: so that he is called firstborn before whom no other was born, even if none is born after him. For so is *firstborn* taken in the Law, where every firstborn is commanded to be offered to the Lord[[Ex 13:2||]]. For it is certain that many in the Jewish people were then only sons, who were nevertheless offered to God because of that precept.

paras.t: Denique, quoniam Christus nasci dignatus est ex Virgine, ut per spiritualem regenerationem fratres multos acquireret, hinc, ut sic, aptius dictus est primogenitus, quam unigenitus. Hinc Beda affirmat: Unigenitus est in substantia deitatis, primogenitus in substantia humanitatis; primogenitus in gratia, unigenitus in natura. Excellentissimam namque gratiam secundum assumptam humanitatem accepit, ita quod de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes, ut Joannes habet. Iterum Christus dicitur primogenitus, quoniam dignior universis. Unde in Apocalypsi vocatur primogenitus mortuorum; et ad Colossenses de eo scribit Apostolus: Qui est principium, primogenitus ex mortuis. Rursus vocatur primogenitus omnis creaturæ, quia secundum divinam suam naturam, natus est ante omnia sæcula, ab æterno. Secundum humanitatem quoque prælatus est omni creato, non solum per hypostaticam suæ humanitatis unionem cum Verbo, sed et per excellentissimam gratiæ et gloriæ plenitudinem, quam a primo incarnationis instanti suscepit.
paras.en: Again, since Christ deigned to be born of a Virgin so as to gain many brethren by spiritual regeneration, He is for this reason, as it were, more aptly called *firstborn* than *only-begotten*. Hence Bede declares: He is only-begotten in the substance of the Godhead, firstborn in the substance of the manhood; firstborn in grace, only-begotten in nature. For according to the manhood He assumed He received the most excellent grace, so that [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes]], as John has it. Christ is called firstborn, again, because He is worthier than all. Hence in the Apocalypse He is called [[Apoc 1:5|the first begotten of the dead|primogenitus mortuorum]]; and the Apostle writes of Him to the Colossians: [[Col 1:18|who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead|Qui est principium, primogenitus ex mortuis]]. Again, He is called [[Col 1:15|the firstborn of every creature|primogenitus omnis creaturæ]], because according to His divine nature He was born before all ages, from eternity. According to His manhood too He is set above every created thing, not only by the hypostatic union of His manhood with the Word [that is, the union of the two natures in the one Person of the Word], but also by the most excellent fulness of grace and glory which He received from the first instant of the incarnation.

paras.t: Itaque, Peperit filium suum, Deique Patris unicum natum, quem sicut sine carnali delectatione, cum ingenti spirituali lætitia, in alta exsistens contemplatione concepit, ita sine corporali dolore, cum interno dulcore, in sublimi exsistens contemplatione, quasi in ictu oculi, peperit, natumque protinus ut Deum verum atque altissimum humillime fortis ac jucundissima adoravit; et pannis eum involvit, propriis manibus, nec utens nec indigens auxilio obstetricum, dicente Hieronymo: Nulla ibi obstetrix, nulla muliercularum sedulitas intercessit; ipsa pannis involvit infantem, ipsa mater et obstetrix fuit. Itaque, si alicubi hujus oppositum inveniatur, tanquam mendacium respuatur. Communiter autem asseritur, quod pannis, id est vilibus atque veteribus panniculis, eum involvit. Verumtamen in Revelationibus beatissimæ Brigittæ, virgo Maria inducitur loqui ad Brigittam, quod scivit se parituram in Bethlehem, ut impleretur Scriptura, idcirco de mundissimis et decentissimis lineis panniculis sibi providit, quibus et filium suum mox reverenter involvit. Nempe, ut legitur ibi, credibiliter utique, sacratissima Virgo mox paritura genua devotissime flexit, et mente ad Deum erecta, velut in momento puerum est enixa, viditque eum ante se in terra jacentem, et paulo post præ frigore palpitantem: cui illa tenerrime condolens, susceptum et amplexatum, deosculabatur, stringens eum ad pectus suum et calefaciens ipsum; deinde candidissimis involvit panniculis, agens quod subditur:
paras.en: So, [[2:7|she brought forth her first born son|Peperit filium suum]], the only Son of God the Father; whom, as she conceived Him without carnal pleasure, with immense spiritual joy, being in lofty contemplation, so she brought Him forth without bodily pain, with inward sweetness, being in sublime contemplation, as it were in the twinkling of an eye; and as soon as He was born, she, strong and most joyful, most humbly adored Him as the true and most high God; [[2:7|and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes|et pannis eum involvit]] with her own hands, neither using nor needing the help of midwives, as Jerome says: No midwife was there, no busy care of women came between; she herself wrapped the infant in swaddling clothes, she herself was mother and midwife. So if the contrary of this is found anywhere, let it be rejected as a lie. It is commonly asserted that she wrapped Him in *swaddling clothes*, that is, in poor and old bits of cloth. Yet in the Revelations of the most blessed Bridget the Virgin Mary is brought in saying to Bridget that she knew she would give birth in Bethlehem, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, and therefore provided herself with the cleanest and most seemly little linen cloths, in which she soon reverently wrapped her Son. Indeed, as we read there (and it is surely to be believed), the most holy Virgin, about to give birth, most devoutly knelt down, and with her mind raised to God brought forth the Child as in a moment, and saw Him lying on the ground before her, and a little after trembling with the cold: and she, most tenderly pitying Him, took Him up and embraced Him and kissed Him, pressing Him to her breast and warming Him; then she wrapped Him in the whitest of little cloths, doing what follows:

paras.t: Et reclinavit in præsepio juxta se posito: quod vel Joseph faber lignarius ibi tunc fecit (propter bovem et asinum quos secum fertur duxisse, vehens Virginem super asinum, et bovem pro necessariis in itinere vendere volens, quamvis aliqui putent animalia illa, aut saltem bovem, aliunde fuisse adducta); vel præsepe jamdudum fuit ibi constructum in loco, de quo subditur: quia non erat ei locus in diversorio, hoc est, alium aptiorem locum, quo puerum poneret, ibi Virgo sancta non reperit.
paras.en: [[2:7|and laid him in a manger|Et reclinavit in præsepio]] placed beside her: which either Joseph the carpenter made there at that time (because of the ox and the ass which he is said to have brought with him, carrying the Virgin on the ass, and meaning to sell the ox for necessaries on the journey; though some think those animals, or at least the ox, were brought from elsewhere); or else the manger had long been built there in the place of which it is added: [[2:7|because there was no room for them in the inn|quia non erat ei locus in diversorio]] [Denis reads *ei*, “for him”, where the Vulgate has *eis*, “for them”], that is, the holy Virgin found there no other, fitter place to lay the Child.

paras.t: Porro, diversorium, secundum Isidorum, dicitur, quia diversi ibi conveniunt; atque, ut asserit Beda, fuit domus seu spatium inter duos vicos, ex utroque latere habens murum, et ex utraque parte portam, desuper quoque ob aeris intemperiem coopertum: quo festis diebus cives ad conferendum et solatiandum convenerant, quo etiam urbem ingredientes animalia sua ad tempus locare solebant: sicque a divertendo diversorium est vocatum, quoniam illic homines divertebant. Alii dicunt, quod fuit hospitalaria, ad quam ab extra venientes divertebant ad hospitandum, præsertim egeni. Unde, quia tunc Bethlehem fuit hominibus plena, et ditiores hospitia occupaverant meliora, Joseph ut verecundus, simplex et pauper, cum Virgine divertit ad locum præfatum. Quod utique non casualiter factum est, sed Deo præordinante ac moderante, propter multiplicem rationem, videlicet ad commendandam paupertatem ac humilitatem, mundique contemptum edocendum, quia ad hæc instruenda verbo ac opere, ipsemet Filius Dei advenit; item ad implendam Scripturam, quoniam per Habacuc de Christo prædictum est, secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum: In medio duorum animalium cognosceris.
paras.en: Now *diversorium* [the inn], according to Isidore, is so called because diverse people come together there; and, as Bede asserts, it was a house or space between two streets, with a wall on either side and a gate at either end, roofed over against bad weather: where on feast days the townsfolk gathered to talk and take their ease, and where those entering the town used to lodge their animals for a time: and so it was called *diversorium* from *divertere* [to turn aside], because men turned aside there. Others say that it was a hostel, to which those coming from outside, especially the poor, turned aside for lodging. Hence, because Bethlehem was then full of people and the richer had taken the better lodgings, Joseph, being modest, simple and poor, turned aside with the Virgin to the said place. This surely did not happen by chance, but by God's foreordaining and governing, for many reasons: namely, to commend poverty and humility and to teach contempt of the world, since the Son of God Himself came to teach these things by word and deed; and also to fulfil the Scripture, for it was foretold of Christ by Habacuc, according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters: In the midst of two living creatures thou shalt be known[[Hab 3:2||]] [the Septuagint reading of Hab 3:2, where the Vulgate has “in the midst of the years”; the margin's Habac. iii, 2 is misread as iv, 2].

paras.t: Itaque Dominus virtutum, Rex gloriæ, Deus majestatis immensæ, assumpturus et redempturus naturam humanam, in cunctis elegit, quæ secundum mundum abjectiora sunt et corpori graviora. Pauperem etenim elegit matrem, in alieno, anguste vilique loco natus et reclinatus est, tempore hiemali et media nocte voluit nasci, ut mundi damnaret superbiam, reprobaret lasciviam, penuriam vero in se decoraret et pauperes consolaretur: quatenus ejus exemplo carnem nostram cum vitiis et concupiscentiis crucifigamus, aspera et ardua viriliter aggrediamur. Væ ergo vanissimis sæculi dilectoribus, qui de sua nobilitate et opulentia stultissime gloriantur et jactant se: qui tandem sero et infructuose dicturi sunt illud Sapientis: Quid profuit nobis superbia? aut divitiarum jactantia quid contulit nobis? Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra. Ubi jam qui lectorum gaudent mollitie, qui ibi satisfaciunt desideriis carnis? Quibus dicitur per Amos prophetam: Væ qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris. Ecce qui sedet super Cherubim, et in cœlestibus Thronis quiescit, duri præsepis propter nos continetur angustia.
paras.en: So the [[Ps 23:10|Lord of hosts, he is the King of Glory|Dominus virtutum, Rex gloriæ]], the God of immense majesty, being about to take and redeem human nature, chose in all things what is more abject in the world's eyes and harder for the body[[1 Cor 1:27||]]. For He chose a poor mother; He was born and laid down in a place not His own, narrow and mean; He willed to be born in winter time and at midnight, to condemn the pride of the world, to reprove wantonness, to adorn want in Himself and comfort the poor: so that by His example we may crucify our flesh with its vices and concupiscences[[Gal 5:24||]], and manfully take up what is rough and hard. Woe, then, to the most vain lovers of the world, who most foolishly glory and boast of their nobility and wealth: who at last, too late and to no profit, will say that word of the Wise man: [[Wis 5:8|What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?|Quid profuit nobis superbia? aut divitiarum jactantia quid contulit nobis?]] [[Wis 5:9|All those things are passed away like a shadow|Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra]]. Where now are those who delight in soft beds, who there satisfy the desires of the flesh? To whom it is said by Amos the prophet: Woe [[Amos 6:4|You that sleep upon beds of ivory, and are wanton on your couches|qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris]]. Behold, [[Ps 98:1|he that sitteth on the cherubims|qui sedet super Cherubim]], and rests on the heavenly Thrones, is held for our sakes in the narrowness of a hard manger.

paras.t: Denique, quoniam homo comparatur jumento, vel divinæ legis jugum pie ac obedienter ferendo (juxta illud Psalmi, Ut jumentum factus sum apud te, et ego semper tecum; quod in persona justi dicitur ibi); vel irrationabiliter seu bestialiter conversando, quemadmodum scriptum est, Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit, comparatus est jumentis insipientibus: hinc Christus ut fieret horum refectio jumentorum, factus est fœnum, eo modo quo in Isaia scribitur, Omnis caro fœnum, voluitque eis in præsepe primo proponi.
paras.en: Again, since man is compared to a beast of burden, either by bearing the yoke of the divine law devoutly and obediently (according to that word of the Psalm, [[Ps 72:23|I am become as a beast before thee: and I am always with thee.|ut jumentum factus sum apud te, et ego semper tecum.]], which is said there in the person of the just man), or by living unreasonably and like a beast, as it is written: [[Ps 48:21|Man when he was in honour did not understand: he hath been compared to senseless beasts|Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit, comparatus est jumentis insipientibus]]: therefore Christ, to become the food of these beasts, became hay, in the sense in which it is written in Isaias, [[Is 40:6|All flesh is grass|Omnis caro fœnum]][[1 Pet 1:24||]] [*fœnum* is “hay” as well as “grass”: the food of the beasts in the manger], and willed to be first set before them in a manger.

paras.t: Postremo, ut aliqui dicunt, præfatum diversorium fuit intra urbem Bethlehem in fine, juxta unam portarum, sub concava rupe, non habens desuper tectum nisi rupem ex monte dependentem.
paras.en: Lastly, as some say, the said inn was within the town of Bethlehem at its edge, beside one of the gates, under a hollow rock, having no roof above it but the rock hanging from the hill.

paras.t: Et pastores erant in regione eadem, scilicet in Judæa. Hic autem Evangelista ostendit, quomodo Christi nativitas cœpit hominibus revelari. Vigilantes et custodientes vigilias noctis, hoc est, consuetas nocturnas vigilationes sollicite conservabant, super gregem suum, id est circa pecora quæ alebant in rure, etiam tempore noctis, sicut in locis illis fieri consuevit. Dicitur quoque, quod tunc erant juxta turrim quamdam inter Bethlehem atque Jerusalem, ubi Jacob de Mesopotamia rediens cum suis moratus est gregibus, ubi mortua et sepulta est Rachel, ut patet in Genesi: quæ dicebatur, turris Gregis. De qua illud Michææ exponitur: Et tu, turris Gregis nebulosa filiæ Sion, ad te veniet potestas prima, regnum Jerusalem, hoc est Christus, virtus prima, summa, omnipotens: quem ibidem angelus nuntiavit pastoribus, qui tres fuisse dicuntur; et ibi postea fuit constructa ecclesia, ubi illorum monstrantur (ut fertur) sepulcra. Ad quem etiam locum Christum postea venisse non irrationabiliter creditur.
paras.en: [[2:8|And there were in the same country shepherds|Et pastores erant in regione eadem]], namely in Judea. Here the Evangelist shows how the birth of Christ began to be revealed to men. [[2:8|watching and keeping the night watches|Vigilantes et custodientes vigilias noctis]], that is, they carefully kept their accustomed watches by night, [[2:8|over their flock|super gregem suum]], that is, about the cattle which they kept in the country, even in the night-time, as is the custom in those places. It is said too that they were then near a certain tower between Bethlehem and Jerusalem, where Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia, stayed with his flocks[[Gen 35:21||]], and where Rachel died and was buried[[Gen 35:19||]], as is plain in Genesis: which was called the Tower of the Flock. Of it that saying of Micheas is expounded: [[Mich 4:8|And thou, O cloudy tower of the flock, of the daughter of Sion, unto thee shall it come|Et tu, turris Gregis nebulosa filiæ Sion, ad te veniet]]: [[Mich 4:8|the first power shall come, the kingdom to the daughter of Jerusalem|potestas prima, regnum Jerusalem]], that is, Christ, the first, highest and almighty Power: whom the angel announced there to the shepherds, who are said to have been three; and a church was afterwards built there, where (as is reported) their tombs are shown. And it is not unreasonably believed that Christ afterwards came to that place.

paras.t: Et ecce angelus Domini stetit juxta illos: assumpsit enim corporis humani effigiem, et visibiliter eis apparuit; et claritas Dei circumfulsit illos, id est, lux quædam divinitus missa, aerem prope pastores sic clarificavit, quod ipsi luce illa undique operiebantur, secundum quod paulo post interius spirituali luce perfusi sunt, ad cognoscendum veritatem de Christo: quemadmodum in Actibus de Paulo habetur, Subito circumfulsit eum lux de cœlo. Denique angelus forte tanti fuit splendoris in corpore quod assumpsit, quod ab ipso tanta lux diffundebatur; vel præter claritatem ab ipso diffusam, etiam lux desuper Deo agente dispergebatur: per quam copiosam lucis diffusionem figurabatur, quod Christus sol sapientiæ atque justitiæ esset in mundo hoc natus. Unde in veteri Testamento non leguntur angeli cum tanta claritate apparuisse. Et timuerunt timore magno, propter tam grandem inconsuetamque visionem, et ne forte illusio esset, vel quid prætenderit visio ignorantes. De causis quippe hujuscemodi timoris dictum est plenius in expositione primi capituli. Unde et in Judicum libro, Manue viso angelo, dixit conjugi suæ: Morte moriemur, quia vidimus Dominum.
paras.en: [[2:9|And behold an angel of the Lord stood by them|Et ecce angelus Domini stetit juxta illos]]: for he took on the likeness of a human body and appeared to them visibly; [[2:9|and the brightness of God shone round about them|et claritas Dei circumfulsit illos]], that is, a certain light sent from God so brightened the air about the shepherds that they were covered all round by that light, as shortly afterwards they were inwardly flooded with a spiritual light, so as to know the truth about Christ: as we have it of Paul in the Acts: [[Acts 9:3|suddenly a light from heaven shined round about him|Subito circumfulsit eum lux de cœlo]]. Again, perhaps the angel was of such splendour in the body he had taken that so great a light poured out from him; or, besides the brightness that poured out from him, a light was also spread from above by God's working: and by this copious outpouring of light it was figured that Christ, the sun of wisdom and of justice, had been born into this world. Hence we do not read in the Old Testament that angels appeared with so great a brightness. [[2:9|and they feared with a great fear|Et timuerunt timore magno]], because of so great and unaccustomed a vision, and lest perhaps it were an illusion, or not knowing what the vision portended. Of the causes of fear of this kind more has been said in the exposition of the first chapter[[1:12||]]. So too in the book of Judges, Manue, having seen the angel, said to his wife: [[Judg 13:22|We shall certainly die, because we have seen God|Morte moriemur, quia vidimus Dominum]] [Denis has *Dominum*, “the Lord”, where the Vulgate has *Deum*].

paras.t: Et dixit illis angelus, qui sua visione territos consolari solet et confortare, ut dictum est: Nolite timere, id est immoderato ac dejiciente timore, qui usum impedit rationis, estque passio inordinata, quia per rationem et fiduciam seu fortitudinem est frenanda ac moderanda. Cur autem timere non debeant, sed gaudere, adjecit: Ecce enim evangelizo, id est, bonum denuntio, vobis gaudium magnum, id est causam atque materiam spiritualis boni ac præcipui gaudii, seu multum esse gaudendum, quod erit omni populo: id est, tam Judæis quam gentilibus inerit gaudium istud, cunctis videlicet fidelibus et electis: ut sit distributio accommoda pro generibus singulorum, quia de omni genere seu natione hominum aliqui inde gavisi sunt. Juxta quem sensum loquitur Christus apud Joannem: Omnia traham ad me ipsum.
paras.en: [[2:10|And the angel said to them|Et dixit illis angelus]], who is wont to console and strengthen those terrified by his appearing, as has been said: [[2:10|Fear not|Nolite timere]], that is, with an immoderate and dejecting fear, which hinders the use of reason and is a disordered passion, since it must be bridled and moderated by reason and confidence, or fortitude. And why they should not fear but rejoice, he adds: [[2:10|for, behold, I bring you good tidings|Ecce enim evangelizo]], that is, I announce good, [[2:10|you good tidings of great joy|vobis gaudium magnum]], that is, the cause and matter of a spiritual good and of a special joy, or that there is great cause to rejoice, [[2:10|that shall be to all the people|quod erit omni populo]]: that is, this joy will be in Jews and Gentiles alike, namely in all the faithful and the elect: so that the distribution is to be taken “for the kinds of individual things” [that is, *all* means some of every kind], since some of every kind or nation of men have rejoiced in it. In which sense Christ says in John: [[John 12:32|will draw all things to myself|Omnia traham ad me ipsum]].

paras.t: Quia natus est vobis, id est ad veram vestram salutem, hodie, id est die hoc naturali, scilicet in hac nocte (quæ est pars naturalis diei, qui dicitur viginti quatuor horas habere: sicque hebdomada dicitur spatium septem dierum), Salvator, utpote unigenitus Filius Dei: qui secundum naturam suam divinam, est Salvator per auctoritatem et efficientiam principalem, tanquam creator et dator salutis et gratiæ, prima ac omnipotente virtute. Qui in Isaia testatur: Deus justus et salvans non est præter me; atque per Osee ait, Ego Dominus Deus tuus, et salvator non est præter me. Porro, secundum humanitatem assumptam, est ipse salvator per efficientiam instrumentalem, et velut meritoria causa gratiæ ac salutis. Sicque in Actibus ait de Christo Apostolus: Acquisivit Ecclesiam sanguine suo. De quo in Isaia prædictum est: Ecce Deus vester, ipse veniet et salvabit vos. Sua enim passione nostra abstersit peccata, et gratiam et salutem nobis promeruit: quod etiam suæ sanctissimæ conversationis meritis fecit.
paras.en: [[2:11|For, this day is born to you|Quia natus est vobis]], that is, for your true salvation, [[2:11|this day|hodie]], that is, on this natural day, namely in this night (which is part of the natural day, which is said to have twenty-four hours: as a week is called the space of seven days), [[2:11|a Saviour|Salvator]], namely the only-begotten Son of God: who according to His divine nature is Saviour by authority and principal efficiency, as the creator and giver of salvation and grace, by first and almighty power. He testifies in Isaias: [[Is 45:21|A just God and a saviour, there is none besides me|Deus justus et salvans non est præter me]]; and says by Osee: [[Osee 13:4|I am the Lord thy God|Ego Dominus Deus tuus]] … [[Osee 13:4|and there is no saviour beside me|et salvator non est præter me]]. Further, according to the humanity He assumed, He is Saviour by instrumental efficiency, and as it were the meritorious cause of grace and salvation. So the Apostle says of Christ in the Acts: [[Acts 20:28|which he hath purchased with his own blood|Acquisivit Ecclesiam sanguine suo]]. Of whom it was foretold in Isaias: [[Is 35:4|behold your God|Ecce Deus vester]] … [[Is 35:4|God himself will come and will save you|ipse veniet et salvabit vos]]. For by His passion He wiped away our sins, and merited grace and salvation for us: which He did also by the merits of His most holy life.

paras.t: Qui est Christus. Christus Græce, Latine dicitur unctus. Christus autem unctus est, non corporali oleo, aut humana unctione, sicut olim in lege in ejus figuram ungebantur reges atque pontifices, quum ipse sit summus rex ac pontifex, finis et consummator legis, secundum Apostolum; sed unctus est, secundum humanitatem, divina et spirituali unctione, hoc est plenitudine gratiæ, omnique gratiarum charismate, virtute, dono, ac sanctitate, imo et lumine gloriæ, ac beatifica fruitione a primo incarnationis instanti, juxta illud Psalmi: Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis. Quæ unctio facta est a tota superbenedicta Trinitate, cujus indivisa est actio ad extra. Hinc per Isaiam loquitur Christus secundum naturam assumptam: Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxit me. Denique Christus, prout in novo Testamento communiter utimur nomine isto, significat seu supponit increatam Personam in duplici natura, videlicet divina et humana, subsistentem, hoc est Unigenitum Dei incarnatum. Dominus. Christus secundum utramque naturam dicitur Dominus, sed diversimode: quia ut Deus, est Dominus per independentem auctoritatem, primamque potestatem, et universalem præsidentiam prorsus perfectam; sed secundum naturam humanam, est Dominus etiam omnium creaturarum per potestatem et gratiam temporaliter datam, creatam, instrumentalem, atque finitam seu limitatam, secundum quod in Matthæo ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. De quo in Actibus Petrus inquit: Hic est omnium Dominus.
paras.en: [[2:11|who is Christ|Qui est Christus]]. *Christus* in Greek is in Latin *unctus*, “anointed”. Now Christ was anointed not with bodily oil or human anointing, as of old under the law kings and high priests were anointed as figures of Him, since He is Himself the supreme king[[1 Tim 6:15||]] and high priest[[Heb 4:14||]], the end[[Rom 10:4||]] and finisher[[Heb 12:2||]] of the law, according to the Apostle; but He was anointed, according to His humanity, with a divine and spiritual anointing, that is, with the fulness of grace, and with every gift of graces, virtue, endowment and holiness, nay with the light of glory also and the beatific enjoyment, from the first instant of the Incarnation: according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis]]. This anointing was done by the whole superblessed Trinity, whose action outward is undivided. Hence Christ speaks by Isaias according to the nature He assumed: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me|Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxit me]]. Lastly, *Christ*, as we commonly use this name in the New Testament, signifies or stands for the uncreated Person subsisting in a twofold nature, divine and human, that is, the incarnate Only-begotten of God. [[2:11|the Lord|Dominus]]. Christ is called Lord according to both natures, but in different ways: for as God He is Lord by independent authority, first power, and wholly perfect universal rule; but according to His human nature He is Lord also of all creatures by a power and grace given in time, created, instrumental, and finite or limited: according to what He says in Matthew: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]. Of whom Peter says in the Acts: [[Acts 10:36|He is Lord of all|Hic est omnium Dominus]].

paras.t: In civitate David, scilicet Bethlehem. Ecce quomodo, juxta Apostolum, infirma et contemptibilia seu abjecta, stultaque mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat magnos, fortes et sapientes in oculis suis. Siquidem non pontificibus et sacerdotibus templi in mollibus stratis jacentibus, non Scribis de legis scientia tumidis, non Pharisæis de sanctitate præsumentibus, non nobilibus, divitibusque superbis, sed pastoribus, idiotis, egenis, humilibus, angelus, deinde angelicus apparet exercitus. Illis angelus Christum denuntiat: quod angelicus exercitus jubilando confirmat. Per quod etiam figurabatur, quod non otiosis, sed studiosis verisque dominici gregis custodibus, seu dignis et virtuosis pastoribus, præcipue his qui nocturnis temporibus laudibus vacant divinis, supernæ illuminationes, angelicæ visitationes, cœlestes consolationes præstantur. Nam et per hoc quod pastores illi taliter vigilabant super pecora sua, insinuatur quod pastores ovium Christi, utpote Christianorum, jugi sollicitudine atque custodia debent intendere sibi commissis, easque pascere oratione, doctrina, exemplo, ut illud Isaiæ dicere possint: Super speculam Domini ego sum, stans jugiter per diem; et super custodiam meam ego sum, stans totis noctibus. Oportet namque pastores sic intendere aliis, ut se ipsos custodire ab omni peccato non negligant. Propterea in Actibus loquitur eis Apostolus: Attendite vobis et universo gregi in quo posuit vos Spiritus Sanctus pastores.
paras.en: [[2:11|in the city of David|In civitate David]], namely Bethlehem. See how, according to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 1:27|the foolish things of the world hath God chosen|stultaque mundi elegit Deus]] [[1 Cor 1:28||]], the weak and contemptible or despised things, to confound those who are great, strong and wise in their own eyes. For not to the high priests and priests of the temple lying on soft couches, not to the Scribes puffed up with their knowledge of the law, not to the Pharisees presuming on their holiness, not to the nobles and the proud rich, but to shepherds, simple, needy and lowly men, the angel appears, and then the angelic host. To them the angel announces Christ: which the angelic host confirms with jubilation. By this it was figured also that heavenly enlightenments, angelic visits and celestial consolations are granted not to the idle, but to zealous and true keepers of the Lord's flock, or worthy and virtuous pastors, above all those who give themselves to the divine praises in the night-time. For by the fact that those shepherds kept such watch over their cattle it is hinted that the shepherds of Christ's sheep, that is of Christians, ought with constant care and watchfulness to attend to those committed to them, and feed them by prayer, teaching and example, so as to be able to say that of Isaias: [[Is 21:8|I am upon the watchtower of the Lord, standing continually by day: and I am upon my ward, standing whole nights|Super speculam Domini ego sum, stans jugiter per diem; et super custodiam meam ego sum, stans totis noctibus]]. For pastors must so attend to others as not to neglect to keep themselves from all sin. Therefore the Apostle says to them in the Acts: [[Acts 20:28|Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, wherein the Holy Ghost hath placed you|Attendite vobis et universo gregi in quo posuit vos Spiritus Sanctus]] shepherds [Denis has *pastores* where the Vulgate has *episcopos*, “bishops”].

paras.t: Præterea contemplandum, quod sicut in Christo est natura summa, puta divinitas, et infima in ordine intellectualium creaturarum, hoc est humanitas, sic in omnibus quæ de Christo leguntur, est quædam venustissima decentissimaque permixtio sublimium et declivium, cœlestium et terrestrium, divinorum et humanorum, altissimorum et infimorum. Nempe, quod a puella concipitur, in stabulo nascitur, pannis involvitur, in præsepio ponitur, circumciditur, et in Ægyptum fugatur, et cetera quæ in Evangelio scripta sunt, patitur: nonne hæc omnia ad parvitatem inferioritatemque pertinent? Verum, quod ab angelo nuntiatur, a virgine generatur, ab angelico exercitu commendatur, et cetera quæ in Evangelio scripta sunt, supernaturalia operatur, excellentia est divina. Præterea aliqui sic legunt, Natus est nobis, non, Vobis, ut angelus fateatur Christum natum, non solum ob hominum salvationem, sed ob angelicæ quoque reparationem ruinæ.
paras.en: We should consider, besides, that as in Christ there is the highest nature, namely the Godhead, and the lowest in the order of intellectual creatures, that is, the manhood, so in everything we read of Christ there is a most lovely and most fitting mingling of the lofty and the lowly, the heavenly and the earthly, the divine and the human, the highest and the lowest. For that He is conceived by a girl, born in a stable, wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger, circumcised, driven into Egypt, and suffers the other things written in the Gospel: do not all these belong to littleness and lowliness? But that He is announced by an angel, begotten of a virgin, extolled by the angelic host, and works the other supernatural things written in the Gospel: this is divine excellence. Moreover, some read *is born to us*, not *to you*, so that the angel declares Christ born not only for the salvation of men, but also for the repairing of the angels' fall.

paras.t: Et hoc vobis signum. Juxta Apostolum, Judæi signa quærunt: idcirco pastoribus tanquam Judæis dat angelus signum, non utique propter illorum incredulitatem, sed potius propter illorum et omnium saluberrimam instructionem. Nam subditur: Invenietis infantem pannis involutum, et positum in præsepio. Tanquam dicat: Quamvis Christus natus sit omnium rex et princeps altissimus, attamen, quod admirabilissimum est, in maxima paupertate et humilitate nasci et conversari elegit, non in opulentia temporalique regno, ut præstolabantur Judæi: sicut usque in præsens exspectant regem Messiam in primo suo adventu temporaliter regnaturum, et totum mundum sibi ac populo Judæorum potentissime subjecturum, secundum exteriorem atque terrenam dominationem; quum tamen sancti Prophetæ primum Christi adventum in paupertate et humilitate futurum descripserint, ut judicaretur et pateretur, hominesque sua passione salvaret. Hoc igitur signo angelus docuit quod Christus advenit ut omnium terrenorum verbo et opere edoceret contemptum, et ad divinorum amorem corda fidelium prorsus transferret. Hoc quoque signo angelus ipsos pastores egenos, omnesque pauperes, vehementissime consolabatur. Itaque, juxta Bernardum: Panni Christi positi sunt in signum, sed in signum cui quotidie a multis contradicitur. Qui enim pretiositate, superfluitate, seu multitudine et cultura atque mollitie vestium gloriantur, contradicunt huic signo. Itaque scripta sunt hæc ad eruditionem nostram, ut Christi paupertatem humilitatemque cognoscentes, eum in paupertate et humilitate sectemur, saltem sic, ut divitiæ si affluant, cor non apponamus.
paras.en: [[2:12|And this shall be a sign unto you|Et hoc vobis signum]]. According to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 1:22|the Jews require signs|Judæi signa quærunt]]: therefore the angel gives a sign to the shepherds as to Jews, not indeed because of their unbelief, but rather for their own and everyone's most wholesome instruction. For there follows: [[2:12|You shall find the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger|Invenietis infantem pannis involutum, et positum in præsepio]]. As if to say: Although Christ was born King of all and Prince most high, yet, what is most wonderful, He chose to be born and to live in the utmost poverty and lowliness, not in wealth and a temporal kingdom, as the Jews were waiting for: as even to the present day they expect a King Messias who at His first coming will reign temporally, and subject the whole world most mightily to himself and to the Jewish people, by an outward and earthly rule; though the holy Prophets described Christ's first coming as to be in poverty and lowliness[[Jer 14:8||]][[Zach 9:9||]], so that He might be judged and suffer, and save men by His passion. By this sign, then, the angel taught that Christ came to teach by word and work the contempt of all earthly things, and to carry the hearts of the faithful wholly over to the love of divine things. By this sign too the angel most powerfully consoled the needy shepherds themselves and all the poor. So, according to Bernard: The swaddling clothes of Christ have been set for a sign, but for a sign that is contradicted daily by many. For those who glory in costliness, superfluity, or number, finery and softness of clothing, contradict this sign. These things, then, were written for our learning[[Rom 15:4||]], that, knowing Christ's poverty and lowliness, we may follow Him in poverty and lowliness, at least so far that, [[Ps 61:11|if riches abound, set not your heart upon them|divitiæ si affluant, cor non apponamus]].

paras.t: Et subito, id est præfato angelo cum pastoribus adhuc loquente, secundum Origenem, vel repente post hoc, facta, id est exhibita, est et in aere apparuit, cum angelo pastores docente (quem aliqui putant Gabrielem fuisse, et ceteris tunc apparentibus principaliorem, ideo tantum mysterium nuntiantem), multitudo cælestis exercitus, id est copiosum agmen angelicorum spirituum: qui milites summi Regis consistunt, quoniam contra ejus adversarios, puta aereas potestates, victorialiter dimicant, eosque vincunt et arcent, et ad omne æternæ majestatis prosequendum imperium promptissime, repente feruntur. Insuper, Christo duci, qui ad superandas aereas potestates advenit, humiliter serviebant. Itaque ad veritatis certificationem, et ad nati pueri dignitatem insinuandam, tam multi, imo secundum Origenem, tam innumerabiles angeli apparuerunt. Laudantium Deum ardentissima, devotissima atque lætissima mente, et dicentium consona voce ac suavissima melodia per ora corporum assumptorum:
paras.en: [[2:13|And suddenly|Et subito]], that is, while the said angel was still speaking with the shepherds, according to Origen, or suddenly after this, [[2:13|there was|facta]], that is, there was shown and appeared in the air, [[2:13|with the angel|cum angelo]] who was teaching the shepherds (whom some think to have been Gabriel, more eminent than the others who then appeared, and therefore announcing so great a mystery), [[2:13|a multitude of the heavenly army|multitudo cælestis exercitus]], that is, a great host of angelic spirits: who are the soldiers of the supreme King, since they fight victoriously against His adversaries, the powers of the air, and overcome them and hold them off, and are borne swiftly and most promptly to carry out every command of the eternal Majesty. Moreover, they humbly served Christ their leader, who had come to overcome the powers of the air. So, to make the truth certain and to make known the dignity of the Child born, so many angels appeared, nay, according to Origen, angels without number, [[2:13|praising God|Laudantium Deum]] with most ardent, most devout and most joyful minds, [[2:13|and saying|et dicentium]], with one accord and the sweetest melody, through the mouths of the bodies they had assumed:

paras.t: Gloria, id est summa excellentia, seu clara cum laude notitia, seu beatitudo atque lætitia, proprie autem gloria, hoc est clarificatio divinæ majestatis in cordibus intellectualium creaturarum cum debita laude, sit in altissimis Deo, id est Deo qui in cælis est. Præsertim in cælo empyreo esse et habitare asseritur, in quantum ibi evidentius ac magnificentius operatur, clariusque conspicitur, quamvis secundum se sit penitus supersimplicissimus, incircumscriptus, immensus, nullam ad locum habitudinem habens. Vel, Gloria, id est præfata clarificatio divinæ dignitatis, sit in altissimis, id est mentibus Beatorum, Deo, ut ipsi in omnibus honorem et gloriam Deo exhibeant. Unde secundum hoc, verbum istud est verbum congratulationis magis quam exhortationis, quemadmodum illud, Laudate Deum, omnes angeli ejus: juxta illud Apostoli, Soli Deo honor et gloria.
paras.en: [[2:14|Glory|Gloria]], that is, supreme excellence, or knowledge that is bright with praise, or beatitude and joy; but properly glory, that is, the glorifying of the divine majesty in the hearts of intellectual creatures with due praise, be [[2:14|to God in the highest|in altissimis Deo]], that is, to God who is in the heavens. He is said to be and to dwell above all in the empyrean heaven [the highest heaven, the dwelling of the blessed], inasmuch as there He works more evidently and magnificently and is more clearly seen, though in Himself He is wholly beyond all simplicity, uncircumscribed, immense, having no relation to place. Or: *Glory*, that is, the said glorifying of the divine dignity, be *in the highest*, that is, in the minds of the Blessed, *to God*, so that they in all things may render honour and glory to God. So, on this reading, the phrase is one of rejoicing with Him rather than of exhortation, like the words: [[Ps 148:2|Praise ye him, all his angels|Laudate Deum, omnes angeli ejus]]; according to that saying of the Apostle: To [[1 Tim 1:17|the only God, be honour and glory|Soli Deo honor et gloria]].

paras.t: In hoc ergo conformemus nos angelis sanctis ac Deo, ut soli Deo gloriam adscribamus, itemque ab omnibus tribui cupiamus. Nam ipsemet ait per Isaiam: Gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Et sic cum Psalmographo digne cantabimus: Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam. Sed nonne et nos gloriam desiderare possumus et debemus, præsertim quum propter felicitatem seu gloriam sempiternam omnia finaliter sint agenda? Et respondendum, quod gloriam optare debemus in Deo, secundum Deum, et propter Deum: in Deo, ut in objecto, datore et causa; secundum Deum, hoc est secundum voluntatem ipsius, non secundum propriam cupiditatem, videlicet ordinate, ut competit menti creatæ; propter Deum, id est finaliter ad laudem et honorationem ejus, ad quem et ad cujus honorificentiam nos ipsos et quidquid in nobis aut nostrum est, referre debemus. Ideo dicit Apostolus: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur; et Psalmista, In Domino laudabitur anima mea. Sed vani, vitiosi et frivoli homines, in se et propter se volunt laudari, gloriamque sortiri, furtum Domino facientes, quia quod ejus est, sibi usurpant.
paras.en: In this, then, let us conform ourselves to the holy angels and to God, ascribing glory to God alone and desiring that it be given Him by all. For He Himself says by Isaias: [[Is 48:11|and I will not give my glory to another|Gloriam meam alteri non dabo]]. And so we shall worthily sing with the Psalmist: [[Ps 113:9|Not to us, O Lord, not to us; but to thy name give glory.|Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam]] But may we not, and ought we not, desire glory ourselves, especially since everything is to be done in the end for the sake of happiness, or everlasting glory? The answer is that we ought to desire glory in God, according to God, and for God: in God, as its object, giver and cause; according to God, that is, according to His will, not according to our own desire, namely in an orderly way, as befits a created mind; for God, that is, with His praise and honour as our end, to whom and to whose honour we ought to refer ourselves and whatever is in us or is ours. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 1:31|He that glorieth may glory in the Lord|Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:3|In the Lord shall my soul be praised|In Domino laudabitur anima mea]]. But vain, vicious and frivolous men wish to be praised in themselves and for themselves, and to win glory, committing theft against the Lord, since they usurp for themselves what is His.

paras.t: Et in terra pax vera et spiritualis: quæ est tranquillitas mentis in bono honesto, præsertim in Deo fonte totius boni honesti seu virtuosi, de qua circa expositionem primi capituli plenius dictum est; hominibus bonæ voluntatis: loquendo de voluntate non optativa tantum, quæ est velleitas imperfecta, de qua Salomon loquitur, Vult et non vult piger; sed de voluntate imperativa et efficaci, quæ dum opportunitas adest seu exigit, procedit in opus. Talem autem voluntatem bonam habentes, sunt boni, et in statu salutis seu in caritate et gratia, quoniam talis voluntas seu volitio, reputatur a Deo pro opere. Sumitur equidem nunc voluntas pro actu interiori voluntatis qui est volitio, non pro potentia tantum, vel pro potentia tali actu formata. Denique a voluntate potissimum dicitur homo bonus vel malus, quoniam prima radix merendi ac demerendi consistit in voluntate, secundum quod libertas primo, directe ac proprie competit voluntati. Peccatum autem in tantum est voluntarium, quod si non esset voluntarium, non esset peccatum, secundum Augustinum. Et similiter dicendum est de actu virtutis. Hinc bonum et malum dicuntur esse in voluntate, verum et falsum in intellectu. Hinc congrue pax annuntiatur hominibus bonæ voluntatis. Insuper pax ista non competit malis, juxta illud in Isaia: Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus. — Potest quoque hic pax accipi pro reconciliatione generis humani facta cum Deo per Christum, quam angeli tunc instare dicebant. Unde ad Romanos inquit Apostolus: Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus. Patet autem ex verbis his, quia de spirituali pace intelligenda sunt, quam Prophetæ denuntiaverunt de futura pace in Christi adventu, quæ est pax bonæ voluntatis. Per bonitatem enim voluntatis dicitur homo simpliciter bonus, potius quam per aliarum animæ virium bonitatem. Voluntatis namque est, alias potentias ad actus suos movere: ideoque bonitas et malitia ejus in illas redundant, quemadmodum virtus seu influentia causæ moventis, in ea quæ ab ipsa moventur.
paras.en: [[2:14|and on earth peace|Et in terra pax]], true and spiritual peace: which is tranquillity of mind in the good that is honourable [*bonum honestum*: good in itself, as distinct from the useful or the pleasant], above all in God, the fountain of all honourable or virtuous good; of which more was said in the exposition of the first chapter[[1:79||]]; [[2:14|to men of good will|hominibus bonæ voluntatis]]: speaking not of a will that only wishes, which is imperfect velleity, of which Solomon says, [[Prov 13:4|The sluggard willeth, and willeth not|Vult et non vult piger]]; but of a will that commands and is effective, which goes forward into the deed when occasion offers or requires. Those who have such a good will are good, and in the state of salvation, that is, in charity and grace, since such a will, or willing, is counted by God as the deed. For *will* is taken here for the inner act of the will, which is willing, not only for the power, or for the power formed by such an act. Further, a man is called good or bad chiefly from his will, since the first root of merit and demerit lies in the will, inasmuch as freedom belongs first, directly and properly to the will. Sin, indeed, is so far voluntary that if it were not voluntary it would not be sin, according to Augustine. And the same must be said of an act of virtue. Hence good and evil are said to be in the will, true and false in the intellect. Hence peace is fittingly announced *to men of good will*. Moreover this peace does not belong to the wicked, according to that saying in Isaias: [[Is 48:22|There is no peace to the wicked, saith the Lord.|Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus.]] — Peace can also be taken here for the reconciliation of mankind with God, made through Christ, which the angels then said was at hand. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 5:10|we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son|Reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus]]. It is plain, then, from these words, that they are to be understood of the spiritual peace which the Prophets foretold of the peace to come at Christ's coming, which is the peace of good will. For it is by goodness of will that a man is called good simply, rather than by the goodness of the other powers of the soul. For it belongs to the will to move the other powers to their acts: and so its goodness and its malice overflow into them, as the power or influence of a moving cause overflows into the things that are moved by it.

paras.t: Porro pax temporalis quæ fuit in mundo in Christi adventu, figura exstitit hujus principaliter intentæ spiritualisque pacis, de qua ad Colossenses ait Apostolus: Pax Christi exsultet semper in cordibus vestris. De qua etiam per Michæam prædictum est: Pax erit in terra nostra, dum venerit, et quando calcaverit in domibus nostris; atque in Psalmo, Orietur in diebus ejus justitia et abundantia pacis. Hæc est pax interna justorum vere christianorum, quæ eis per exteriores inquietudines seu tribulationes auferri non valet, dicente in Proverbiis Salomone: Justus quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit; et rursus, Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit. Hinc de primitiva Ecclesia Deus per Isaiam prædixit: Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta. Hæc est vera ac sancta securitas, qua perfecti pro Deo omnia adversantia pati parati, non timent eos qui corpus occidunt. Propter quod per Jeremiam scriptum est: In diebus illis salvabitur Juda, et Israel habitabit confidenter. Unde in Actibus Apostolorum Paulus et alii quidam fiducialiter egisse leguntur. Et iterum: Discipuli replebantur gaudio et Spiritu Sancto. Itaque, si Deo placere appetimus, veram cum omnibus, quantum possibile est, pacem et concordiam habeamus, præsertimque mentem in Deo quietam, fixam et imperturbatam servemus: quod fieri poterit, si vere mites, patientes, humilesque fuerimus, et cunctis terrenis contemptis, Deum ferventer amemus. Postremo, inquiritur a quo residuum hujus angelici cantici editum sit. Ad quod Albertus et aliqui alii dicunt, quod a Symmacho Papa; alii credibilius asserunt, quod ab Hilario sancto episcopo. Legitur nempe in gestis Romanorum Pontificum, quod Telesphorus Papa instituit, ut solis episcopis liceret canticum istud incipere. Postea vero Symmachus Papa instituit, ut etiam ceteri sacerdotes possent illud incipere in festis diebus, quia de sacerdote scriptum est apud Malachiam: Angelus Domini exercituum est.
paras.en: Now the temporal peace that was in the world at Christ's coming was a figure of this spiritual peace, which is the one chiefly intended; of which the Apostle says to the Colossians: [[Col 3:15|let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts|Pax Christi exsultet semper in cordibus vestris]]. Of which it was also foretold through Micheas: There shall be peace in our land when He comes, and when He shall set His foot in our houses[[Mich 5:5||]] [Denis quotes freely; in Micheas the one who sets his foot in our houses is the Assyrian]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:7|In his days shall justice spring up, and abundance of peace|Orietur in diebus ejus justitia et abundantia pacis]]. This is the inward peace of the just, of true Christians, which cannot be taken from them by outward disquiet or tribulation, as Solomon says in the Proverbs: [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Justus quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]; and again: [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]]. Hence God foretold of the primitive Church through Isaias: [[Is 32:18|my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest|Sedebit populus meus in pulchritudine pacis, et in tabernaculis fiduciæ, et in requie opulenta]]. This is the true and holy security by which the perfect, ready to suffer every adversity for God, do not fear [[Matt 10:28|them that kill the body|eos qui corpus occidunt]]. Wherefore it is written through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:6|In those days shall Juda be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently|In diebus illis salvabitur Juda, et Israel habitabit confidenter]]. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles we read that Paul and certain others dealt confidently[[Acts 9:27||]][[Acts 14:3||]]. And again: [[Acts 13:52|the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Ghost|Discipuli replebantur gaudio et Spiritu Sancto]]. So, if we desire to please God, let us have true peace and concord with all, as far as is possible[[Rom 12:18||]], and above all keep our mind quiet in God, fixed and undisturbed: which can be done if we are truly meek, patient and humble, and, despising all earthly things, love God fervently. Lastly, it is asked by whom the rest of this angelic canticle [the *Gloria in excelsis* of the Mass] was composed. To which Albert and some others say: by Pope Symmachus; others, more credibly, say: by the holy bishop Hilary. For we read in the deeds of the Roman Pontiffs that Pope Telesphorus ordained that only bishops might intone this canticle. But afterwards Pope Symmachus ordained that the other priests too might intone it on feast days, since of the priest it is written in Malachias: [[Mal 2:7|he is the angel of the Lord of hosts|Angelus Domini exercituum est]].

paras.t: Et factum est, ut discesserunt ab eis angeli in cælum, id est, quum abstraxissent se adspectibus pastorum, et rediissent in cælum, quo solent reverti, ministerio propter quod missi sunt consummato, quemadmodum Tobiæ Raphael ait: Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit; pastores loquebantur ad invicem. Quamvis enim primo territi ac stupore repleti fuissent, tamen ex consolatione angelica ac dulcissima perceptione rei tam gaudiosæ confortati fuerunt, et læti alacresque effecti, dixerunt: Transeamus usque Bethlehem: quæ, ut dicitur, per milliare distabat a loco quo ista viderunt pastores; et videamus corporaliter, quod nunc oculis fidei credimus, hoc verbum quod factum est, id est rem verbis ad nos dictis significatam, scilicet puerum natum, qui est Christus Dominus, rex Messias. Verbum quippe in Scripturis, interdum pro verbo mentali, interdum pro verbo vocali seu scripto, quandoque pro re significata, accipitur, quemadmodum in libris Regum loquitur Ezechias: Non fuit verbum in domo mea quod non ostenderim eis. Quod Dominus fecit, id est, per angelos ad nos locutus est; vel, quam rem fecit: qui Dominus Pater seu Trinitas tota, fecit Christum secundum humanitatem assumptam, secundum quam Christus dicitur creatura, quamvis simpliciter loquendo dici non debeat creatura, sed Deus verus, omniumque Creator. Ait namque Apostolus: Factus est ex semine David secundum carnem. Verumtamen ista particula, Quod Dominus fecit, in Græcis et antiquis correctisque codicibus non habetur, nec est de textu. Quod Dominus ostendit nobis, id est, quem puerum manifestavit nobis per angelum natum esse. — Potest quoque de increato Verbo exponi, ut sit sensus: Videamus hoc Verbum, id est Dei Unigenitum, de quo dicitur, In principio erat Verbum; quod factum est, id est incarnatum, juxta illud, Verbum caro factum est; quod Dominus fecit: quia Verbum hoc factum est homo a Deo Trinitate, quamvis absolute loquendo non sit factum, sed genitum et æternum. Unde expositio ista videtur impropria, nec certum est quod ex præinductis angelicis verbis intellexerunt pastores rudes ac simplices, quod Christus diceretur et esset Verbum Dei. Quod Dominus ostendit nobis, id est, natum esse jam notificavit.
paras.en: [[2:15|And it came to pass, after the angels departed from them into heaven|Et factum est, ut discesserunt ab eis angeli in cælum]], that is, when they had withdrawn themselves from the shepherds' sight and gone back to heaven, whither they are wont to return when the ministry for which they were sent is accomplished, as Raphael says to Tobias: [[Tob 12:20|It is time therefore that I return to him that sent me|Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit]]; [[2:15|the shepherds said one to another|pastores loquebantur ad invicem]]. For though at first they had been terrified and filled with amazement, yet they were strengthened by the angels' comfort and by the sweetest perception of so joyful a thing, and, made glad and eager, they said: [[2:15|Let us go over to Bethlehem|Transeamus usque Bethlehem]], which, as is said, was a mile from the place where the shepherds saw these things; [[2:15|and let us see|et videamus]] with our bodily eyes what we now believe with the eyes of faith, [[2:15|this word that is come to pass|hoc verbum quod factum est]], that is, the thing signified by the words spoken to us, namely the Child born, who is Christ the Lord, the King Messias. For *word* in the Scriptures is taken sometimes for the word of the mind, sometimes for the spoken or written word, and sometimes for the thing signified, as when Ezechias says in the books of Kings: There was not a *word* [that is, a thing] in my house which I have not shewn them[[Is 39:4||]] [the margin gives Is. xxxix, 2, 4, as in Art. II]. *Which the Lord hath made*, that is, which He has spoken to us by the angels; or, which thing He has made: for the Lord, the Father, or the whole Trinity, made Christ according to the humanity He assumed, according to which Christ is called a creature, though speaking simply He ought not to be called a creature, but true God and Creator of all. For the Apostle says: [[Rom 1:3|who was made to him of the seed of David, according to the flesh|Factus est ex semine David secundum carnem]]. However, this phrase, *which the Lord hath made*, is not found in the Greek manuscripts nor in the old and corrected ones, and is not part of the text [the Douay-Rheims, like the Vulgate, has only “which the Lord hath shewed to us”]. [[2:15|which the Lord hath shewed to us|Quod Dominus ostendit nobis]], that is, the Child whom He has made known to us, by the angel, to have been born. — It can also be expounded of the uncreated Word, so that the sense is: Let us see this Word, that is, the Only-begotten of God, of whom it is said, [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word|In principio erat Verbum]]; *that is come to pass* [*quod factum est*, “that is made”], that is, incarnate, according to the saying, [[John 1:14|And the Word was made flesh|Verbum caro factum est]]; *which the Lord hath made*: because this Word was made man by God the Trinity, though absolutely speaking He was not made, but begotten and eternal. Hence this exposition seems improper; nor is it certain that the shepherds, rude and simple men, understood from the angel's words recorded above that Christ was called, and was, the Word of God. *Which the Lord hath shewed to us*, that is, has now made known to have been born.

paras.t: Et venerunt festinantes: quia ferventes erant in Dei et pueri nati amore; desiderabantque fervide tam magnum novum, videlicet Christum natum, conspicere, cujus majestatem ex angelici exercitus apparitione et testificatione et gratulatione pensabant. Gaudebant quoque de totius mundi salvatione jam imminente, et Scripturarum impletione. Sed et ad greges suos, quos sine custode reliquerant, redire velociter satagebant: ideo festinabant. Itaque et nos Christum cum festinatione, id est diligenter ac ferventer, quæramus: quem nemo cum torpore et desidia digne quærit. Siquidem ad Deum festinare et currere, est ardenter diligere, et ex spirituali amore quæ bona sunt alacriter agere; et quo amamus ferventius, eo properamus currimusque celerius.
paras.en: [[2:16|And they came with haste|Et venerunt festinantes]]: because they were fervent in the love of God and of the Child that was born; and they fervently desired to see so great a new thing, namely Christ born, whose majesty they weighed from the appearing, the testimony and the rejoicing of the angelic host. They rejoiced, too, at the salvation of the whole world now at hand, and at the fulfilment of the Scriptures. And they were anxious, besides, to go back quickly to their flocks, which they had left without a keeper: and so they made haste. Let us also, then, seek Christ with haste, that is, diligently and fervently: for no one seeks Him worthily with sluggishness and sloth. For to make haste and run to God is to love ardently, and out of spiritual love to do eagerly what is good; and the more fervently we love, the more quickly we hasten and run.

paras.t: Et invenerunt Mariam: quam divinus Ignatius in suis ad eam epistolis toties vocat Christiferam; et Joseph, Virginis sponsum, custodem, ministrum, ejusque integerrimæ virginitatis verissimum testem, et infantem, id est parvulum: qui licet more aliorum parvulorum, infans, quasi non fans, seu loqui non valens, vocatus sit; tamen a prima suæ nativitatis hora disertissime ac sapientissime loqui valebat, non Hebræa dumtaxat, sed et omnium gentium lingua: nam et dona gratiæ gratis datæ, ut prophetiam, genera linguarum, scientiam, interpretationemque sermonum, a primo incarnationis instanti accepit; positum in præsepio: in quo, secundum Gorram, impletum est spiritualiter illud admirabile in Job scriptum: Numquid volet rhinoceros servire tibi, aut morabitur ad præsepe tuum? Rhinoceros quippe est animal fortissimum, quod unum in fronte fert cornu, propter quod unicornis vocatur, et capitur in gremio virginis, in quo caput reclinat quando fugatur: et Christum designat, qui in virginalis uteri gremio captus, atque in nostrum redactus servitium dicitur.
paras.en: [[2:16|and they found Mary|et invenerunt Mariam]], whom the divine Ignatius in his letters to her so often calls *Christifera* [“Christ-bearer”]; [[2:16|and Joseph|et Joseph]], the Virgin's spouse, guardian and servant, and the truest witness of her most perfect virginity, [[2:16|and the infant|et infantem]], that is, the little one: who, though after the manner of other little ones He was called *infans*, as it were *non fans*, that is, not able to speak [*infans* from *in-* “not” and *fari* “to speak”], yet from the first hour of His birth was able to speak most eloquently and most wisely, not only in the Hebrew tongue but in the tongue of every nation: for He received the gifts of grace freely given, such as prophecy, kinds of tongues, knowledge and the interpretation of speeches[[1 Cor 12:10||]] [the margin gives I Cor. xii, 8–10], from the first instant of the incarnation; [[2:16|lying in the manger|positum in præsepio]]: in which, according to Gorran, was fulfilled spiritually that wonderful saying written in Job: [[Job 39:9|Shall the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee, or will he stay at thy crib?|Numquid volet rhinoceros servire tibi, aut morabitur ad præsepe tuum?]] For the rhinoceros is a very strong animal, which bears one horn on its forehead, for which reason it is called the unicorn; and it is caught in the lap of a virgin, in which it lays its head when it is hunted: and it signifies Christ, who is said to have been caught in the lap of the virginal womb and brought into our service.

paras.t: Videntes autem puerum involutum et collocatum ut prædixerat angelus, cognoverunt de verbo quod dictum erat illis de puero hoc, id est, consideraverunt sermonem eis ab angelo de infante isto prolatum esse veracem; vel, Cognoverunt de Verbo increato, quod dictum erat illis de puero hoc, id est, quod angelus prædicavit eis esse hunc puerum. Verbum enim factum, fuit infans unius diei, et angelus dixit quod puer ille esset Christus Dominus, unigenitus Dei Filius: sicque corporalibus oculis corpus Christi videntes, interioribus oculis ejus divinitatem per fidem noverunt. Nam, ut Ambrosius asserit, dum caro videbatur, Verbum videbatur, videlicet Christus, qui in una persona est Deus et homo.
paras.en: [[2:17|And seeing|Videntes autem]] the Child wrapped up and laid as the angel had foretold, [[2:17|they understood of the word that had been spoken to them concerning this child|cognoverunt de verbo quod dictum erat illis de puero hoc]]: that is, they considered that the message spoken to them by the angel about this Infant was true; or, they came to know of the uncreated Word, *that had been spoken to them concerning this child*, that is, what the angel had preached to them that this Child was. For the Word made flesh was an infant of one day, and the angel had said that this Child was Christ the Lord, the only-begotten Son of God: and so, seeing the body of Christ with the eyes of the body, they knew His divinity with the inner eyes by faith. For, as Ambrose says, while the flesh was seen, the Word was seen, namely Christ, who in one person is God and man.

paras.t: Et omnes qui audierant, mirati sunt. Hoc quidam exponunt sic: Omnes qui audierant ab angelo ista Christi mysteria, scilicet quomodo natus esset, mirati sunt, quod Christus omnium Dominus in tam vili stabulo esset natus et in præsepio reclinatus, et tamen ab angelico exercitu tam solenniter prædicatus. Ex quo sequeretur, quod non pastoribus tantum angeli præfati apparuerunt, nec angelica illa laus a solis pastoribus sit audita.
