Or this *salvation* would be the salvation or redemption then to be wrought by Christ, which Simeon foresaw by the spirit of prophecy.

paras.t: Postremo, de hac Christi in templo præsentatione prædictum fuit in Psalmo: Suscepimus, Deus, misericordiam tuam in medio templi tui. Sed et apud Malachiam, quum de Christi præcursore Dominus protulisset, Ecce (inquiens) mitto angelum meum, protinus de Christo adjecit: Et statim veniet ad templum suum Dominator quem vos quæritis, et Angelus testamenti quem vos vultis. — Hoc quoque sciendum, quod duplex est benedictio, videlicet consecrationis vel donationis, et laudis. Benedictione consecrationis seu donationis, major benedicit minori et Deus creaturæ, juxta illud Apostoli ad Hebræos: Sine ulla contradictione, quod minus est a majore benedicitur. Unde benedictio qua Deus benedicit creaturæ, est collatio munerum ejus, et multiplicatio eorumdem. Benedictione autem laudis, minor benedicit majori, quamvis sæpe etiam et econtra: sicque Simeon benedixit Deo; et in Psalmo cantamus, Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore.
paras.en: Lastly, of this presentation of Christ in the temple it was foretold in the Psalm: [[Ps 47:10|We have received thy mercy, O God, in the midst of thy temple|Suscepimus, Deus, misericordiam tuam in medio templi tui]]. And in Malachias too, when the Lord had spoken of Christ's forerunner, saying: [[Mal 3:1|Behold I send my angel|Ecce (inquiens) mitto angelum meum]], He at once added of Christ: [[Mal 3:1|And presently the Lord, whom you seek, and the angel of the testament, whom you desire|Et statim veniet ad templum suum Dominator quem vos quæritis, et Angelus testamenti quem vos vultis]]. — This too should be known: that blessing is twofold, namely of consecration or bestowal, and of praise. By the blessing of consecration or bestowal the greater blesses the less, and God the creature, according to that of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 7:7|And without all contradiction, that which is less is blessed by the better|Sine ulla contradictione, quod minus est a majore benedicitur]]. Hence the blessing with which God blesses a creature is the bestowal of His gifts and their multiplying. But by the blessing of praise the less blesses the greater, though often also the other way about: and thus Simeon [[2:28|blessed God|benedixit Deo]]; and in the Psalm we sing: [[Ps 33:2|I will bless the Lord at all times|Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore]].

paras.t: Et erant pater ejus, videlicet Joseph, qui dicitur pater Christi, quia nutricius, et quia ob famam Virginis Matris conservandam, permissus est æstimari pater Christi. Circa quod loquitur Origenes: Qui altius aliquid inquirit, potest dicere quoniam generationis ordo a David usque Joseph deducitur, ne videretur ipse Joseph frustra nominari, quia non fuit pater Salvatoris; attamen, ut generationis ordo locum haberet, pater Domini appellatus est. Rursus, quoniam Joseph vere fuit vir Mariæ, cujus Christus fuit veraciter filius, Christus magis proprie dicitur filius Joseph, quam si esset aliunde, seu ex alia conjuge adoptatus. Et mater ejus qui cum Patre et Spiritu Sancto unus est Deus æternus, omnipotens et immensus, Mater ejus qui omnium est Creator, quem universi angelicorum spirituum ordines incessanter adorant. Mirantes, non admiratione dubitationis, sed reverentiæ et congratulationis, super his quæ dicebantur de illo, hoc est de magnalibus atque magnificis laudibus de puero Jesu prolatis, a parentibus Præcursoris, ab angelo exercituque angelico, a pastoribus quoque et Simeone. Itaque, mirabantur quod de eo qui in tanta paupertate ac humilitate advenit, tam altissima dicebantur, quod scilicet esset salutare Dei Patris, et omnium Dominus, lumen gentium, gloria Judæorum, mundi Salvator, Unigenitus Dei, verusque Deus. Mirabantur quoque non parum se electos ad tantum mysterium, et quod mundi thesaurus eis esset commissus.
paras.en: [[2:33|And his father|Et erant pater ejus]], namely Joseph, who is called the father of Christ because he was His foster-father, and because, to keep the good name of the Virgin Mother, he was allowed to be thought Christ's father. On which Origen says: One who inquires more deeply can say that the order of the generation is drawn down from David to Joseph lest Joseph should seem to be named for nothing, since he was not the father of the Saviour; yet, that the order of the generation might stand, he was called the Lord's father. Again, since Joseph was truly the husband of Mary, whose son Christ truly was, Christ is more properly called the son of Joseph than if He had come from elsewhere, or been adopted from another wife. [[2:33|and mother|Et mater]]: mother of Him who, with the Father and the Holy Ghost, is one God, eternal, almighty and boundless; Mother of Him who is the Creator of all, whom all the orders of angelic spirits ceaselessly adore. [[2:33|were wondering|Mirantes]], not with the wonder of doubt but of reverence and rejoicing, [[2:33|at those things which were spoken concerning him|super his quæ dicebantur de illo]]: that is, at the great things and the magnificent praises uttered of the child Jesus by the parents of the Forerunner, by the angel and the angelic host, by the shepherds also and Simeon. So they wondered that such lofty things were said of Him who came in such poverty and lowliness: namely, that He was the salvation of God the Father, and Lord of all[[Acts 10:36||]], the light of the Gentiles, the glory of the Jews, the Saviour of the world, the Only-begotten of God and true God. They wondered too, not a little, that they had been chosen for so great a mystery, and that the treasure of the world had been entrusted to them.

paras.t: Et benedixit illis, scilicet parentibus Jesu Christi, Simeon. Consuetudo enim fuit sacerdotibus legis, benedicere parentibus infantem in templo offerentibus cum hostiis debitis: et benedictio illa videtur fuisse imprecatio boni, qua sacerdos expetebat seu imprecabatur eis bona a Deo. Formam tamen benedictionis illius non habemus expressam, ut dicitur; sed forte fuit illa, aut similis illi, de qua in Numeris habetur: Locutus est Dominus ad Moysen et Aaron, dicens: Sic benedicetis filiis Israel: Benedicat tibi Dominus et custodiat te; ostendat Dominus faciem suam tibi, et misereatur tui; convertat Dominus vultum suum ad te, et det tibi pacem. Verumtamen, reor quod Simeon speciali omnino benedictione benedixerit Mariæ et Joseph, utpote benedictione laudis, beatos et benedictos eos dicendo. Dignitatem namque, electionem, et gratiam illorum etiam ipsemet vehementissime mirabatur. Nihilo minus eis benedixit, quia major fuit sacerdotali officio, quamvis non sanctitate et merito, saltem quoad Mariam. Major autem officio, benedictionem largitur. Vere equidem beatus fuit ille Joseph qui ad tantum secretum fuit admissus: qui sponsus et custos virgineæ Matris Genitricisque Dei esse, electus fuit ac meruit; qui Dei Patris Filium, Deum incarnatum, nutrire, tractare, deferre, cohabitantem, imo et obedientem ac ministrantem habere, fuit præordinatus: nempe, ut infra habetur, Jesus fuit subditus illis, haud dubium quin Mariæ et Joseph.
paras.en: And [[2:34|Simeon blessed them|benedixit illis]], namely the parents of Jesus Christ. For it was the custom for the priests of the law to bless the parents who offered an infant in the temple with the due victims: and that blessing seems to have been a calling down of good, by which the priest asked or called down good things upon them from God. Yet we do not have the form of that blessing set down, as is said; but perhaps it was that one, or one like it, of which we read in Numbers: The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: [[Num 6:23|Thus shall you bless the children of Israel|Sic benedicetis filiis Israel]]: [[Num 6:24|The Lord bless thee, and keep thee.|Benedicat tibi Dominus et custodiat te]] [[Num 6:25|The Lord shew his face to thee, and have mercy on thee.|ostendat Dominus faciem suam tibi, et misereatur tui]] [[Num 6:26|The Lord turn his countenance to thee, and give thee peace.|convertat Dominus vultum suum ad te, et det tibi pacem]] [the margin reads Num. vi, 23–26; Denis writes “to Moses and Aaron”, where the Vulgate has the Lord speak to Moses, bidding him speak to Aaron]. Nevertheless I think that Simeon blessed Mary and Joseph with an altogether special blessing, namely the blessing of praise, calling them blessed and happy. For he himself wondered exceedingly at their dignity, their election and their grace. Still, he blessed them because he was greater by his priestly office, though not in holiness and merit, at least as regards Mary; and one greater by office bestows the blessing. Truly blessed indeed was that Joseph who was admitted to so great a secret: who was chosen and was found worthy to be the spouse and guardian of the virgin Mother and Mother of God; who was foreordained to nourish, handle and carry the Son of God the Father, God incarnate, and to have Him living with him, nay obedient and ministering to him: for, as we read further on, Jesus [[2:51|was subject to them|subditus illis]], doubtless to Mary and Joseph.

paras.t: Et dixit ad Mariam matrem ejus. Ad quam prophetico spiritu loquitur de futuris potius quam ad Joseph, quia sciebat quod vera esset Genitrix Christi, Joseph autem nutricius et minister dumtaxat. Ecce positus est hic, hoc est, puer iste quem brachiis stringo, per assumptam humanitatem datus, situs atque a Deo statutus est, in ruinam, id est perditionem, et in resurrectionem, hoc est salvationem, multorum in Israel, hoc est plurium Israelitarum. Christus namque per suam incarnationem, prædicationem, vitam ac passionem, fuit multis Judæis causa salutis: de quibus in Joanne ipse ait, Ego scio quos elegerim. Multis quoque et pluribus Judæis per præfata fuit occasio excæcationis, et transgressionis, et damnationis: quibus in Joanne loquitur, Vos non estis ex ovibus meis. Hinc denuo: In judicium (inquit) ego in hunc mundum veni, ut qui non vident, videant, et qui vident, cæci fiant. Ubi per videntes, intelliguntur illi qui sapientes et magni fuerunt in oculis suis, sæculariterque prudentes: quales præcipue fuerunt sacerdotes et Scribæ, quos constat pro maxima parte obtenebratos esse atque damnatos. Porro, per non videntes, intelliguntur idiotæ, humiles, et simplices: quorum multos Christus illuminavit, ut fuerunt Apostoli, ceterique discipuli, quibus et Spiritum Sanctum infudit. Hinc quoque in Matthæo ait cum gaudio: Confiteor tibi, Pater, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis.
paras.en: [[2:34|and said to Mary his mother|Et dixit ad Mariam matrem ejus]]. To her rather than to Joseph he speaks of things to come in the spirit of prophecy, because he knew that she was truly the Mother of Christ, while Joseph was only His foster-father and servant. [[2:34|Behold this child is set|Ecce positus est hic]], that is, this child whom I hold in my arms, given through the humanity He has taken, is placed and appointed by God [[2:34|for the fall|in ruinam]], that is, the perdition, [[2:34|and for the resurrection|et in resurrectionem]], that is, the salvation, [[2:34|of many in Israel|multorum in Israel]], that is, of a great number of Israelites. For Christ by His incarnation, preaching, life and passion was the cause of salvation to many Jews, of whom He Himself says in John: [[John 13:18|I know whom I have chosen|Ego scio quos elegerim]]. And to many, indeed more, of the Jews these same things were the occasion of blinding, of transgression and of damnation; to whom He says in John: [[John 10:26|you are not of my sheep|Vos non estis ex ovibus meis]]. Hence again: [[John 9:39|For judgment I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind|In judicium (inquit) ego in hunc mundum veni, ut qui non vident, videant, et qui vident, cæci fiant]]. Where by *they who see* are understood those who were wise and great in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]] [the margin seems to read Is. v, 24; “wise in their own eyes” is Is 5:21], and prudent after the manner of the world: such as were above all the priests and Scribes, who, it is plain, were for the most part darkened and damned. And by *they who see not* are understood the unlearned, the lowly and the simple, many of whom Christ enlightened, as were the Apostles and the other disciples, into whom He also poured the Holy Ghost. Hence too in Matthew He says with joy: [[Matt 11:25|I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of Heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones|Confiteor tibi, Pater, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis]] [Denis leaves out “Lord of heaven and earth”].

paras.t: Generaliter autem loquendo, Christus venit in ruinam omnium reproborum seu incredulorum, et resurrectionem electorum fidelium. Verumtamen non uniformiter venit, seu positus est, in ruinam et resurrectionem: quia in ruinam reproborum est positus occasionaliter et indirecte; in resurrectionem vero electorum, causaliter et directe. Sic namque positus est in ruinam, quomodo Deus dicitur hominem indurare. Nunc itaque sermo est de ruina peccati, quæ est ipsamet culpa, et de damnatione æterna, quæ est effectus culpæ et incredulitatis, secundum illud Salvatoris: Qui non credit, jam judicatus est, quia non credit in nomine unigeniti Filii Dei. Nunc etiam sermo est de resurrectione spirituali, qua homo per Baptismum et pœnitentiam ac gratiam Dei, a peccato resurgit. Unde ait Apostolus: Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis. Item Psalmista, Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio: quod de resurrectione a peccato in judicio discretionis rite exponitur, quanquam et de futura resurrectione corporali felicis immutationis accipi possit, quæ erit effectus dominicæ passionis, seu meriti Christi, dicente Apostolo: Quoniam quidem per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Sic ergo in illorum ruinam Christus est positus, de quibus Paulus testatur: Prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Judæis quidem scandalum, gentibus autem stultitiam. In illorum vero resurrectionem est positus, de quibus Paulus adjecit: Ipsis vero vocatis, hoc est electis, Judæis et Græcis, prædicamus Christum Dei virtutem et Dei sapientiam.
paras.en: Speaking generally, Christ came for the fall of all the reprobate, or unbelievers, and for the resurrection of the elect faithful. Yet He did not come, or was not set, in the same way for the fall and for the resurrection: for He is set for the fall of the reprobate occasionally and indirectly [that is, as the occasion of it, not its cause], but for the resurrection of the elect causally and directly. For He is set for the fall in the way in which God is said to harden a man. Here, then, the speech is of the fall of sin, which is the fault itself, and of eternal damnation, which is the effect of fault and unbelief, according to that saying of the Saviour: [[John 3:18|he that doth not believe is already judged: because he believeth not in the name of the only begotten Son of God|Qui non credit, jam judicatus est, quia non credit in nomine unigeniti Filii Dei]]. Here the speech is also of the spiritual resurrection, by which a man rises again from sin through Baptism and penance and the grace of God. Hence the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 1:5|Therefore the wicked shall not rise again in judgment|Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio]]: which is rightly expounded of rising from sin in the judgment of discernment, though it can also be taken of the future bodily resurrection of happy change, which will be the effect of the Lord's passion, or of Christ's merit, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:21|For by a man came death: and by a man the resurrection of the dead|Quoniam quidem per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum]]. Thus, then, Christ is set for the fall of those of whom Paul testifies: [[1 Cor 1:23|But we preach Christ crucified: unto the Jews indeed a stumblingblock, and unto the Gentiles foolishness:|Prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Judæis quidem scandalum, gentibus autem stultitiam]] And He is set for the resurrection of those of whom Paul adds: [[1 Cor 1:24|But unto them that are called|Ipsis vero vocatis]], that is, the elect, [[1 Cor 1:24|both Jews and Greeks, Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God|Judæis et Græcis, prædicamus Christum Dei virtutem et Dei sapientiam]].

paras.t: Et in signum cui contradicetur. Signum tripliciter sumitur: primo, pro indicio alicujus significativo, ut circulus designat potum venalem; secundo, pro miraculo, secundum quod in Joanne loquitur Christus, Nisi signa et prodigia videritis, non creditis; tertio, pro vexillo quo in bello milites unius partis ab alterius partis militibus discernuntur, sicut in Psalmo, Posuerunt signa sua, signa, et non cognoverunt. Itaque, juxta primam signi acceptionem, sensus est: Positus est Christus in signum, id est ad evangelicæ veritatis doctrinam insinuandam seu proponendam, cui a multis contradicetur, vel verbo, vel opere, vel modo utroque. Inobedientes namque Christiani opere contradicunt. Juxta secundam acceptionem, sensus est: Positus est in signum, id est miraculum, quia et ipso Christo homine de Virgine nato, mirabilius quid est? Omnia quæ de Christo narrat Scriptura, signum est, hoc est miraculum, cui contradicetur a perfidis universis, ut quod Mater virgo est, quod in unitate personæ sit Deus et homo, quod veraciter resurrexit. Ita Origenes exponit. Juxta tertiam acceptionem, per signum intelligitur crux Christi seu fides crucis: quo signo distinguuntur servi Christi a servis diaboli, dum signum istud ab illis honoratur ac fronti imprimitur, ab illis contemnitur. — Postremo, exponi potest de signo pacificationis, ut sit sensus: Positus est in signum fœderis, et reconciliationis seu pacis inter Deum et homines: quia videlicet factus est mediator Dei et hominum, et figurabatur per arcum de quo loquitur Dominus in Genesi: Arcum meum ponam in nubibus, et erit signum fœderis inter me et terram. Christus autem signum est fœderis memorati, non significative solum, sed et causaliter, dicente Apostolo: Ipse est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum; et denuo, Pacificans per sanguinem crucis suæ, sive quæ in cœlo, sive quæ in terra.
paras.en: [[2:34|and for a sign which shall be contradicted|Et in signum cui contradicetur]]. *Sign* is taken in three ways: first, for a token that signifies something, as a hoop [hung out at a tavern] marks drink for sale; secondly, for a miracle, in the sense in which Christ says in John: [[John 4:48|Unless you see signs and wonders, you believe not|Nisi signa et prodigia videritis, non creditis]]; thirdly, for a standard, by which in war the soldiers of one side are told apart from the soldiers of the other, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 73:4|They have set up their ensigns for signs|Posuerunt signa sua, signa]], and they knew not [Denis joins the end of Ps 73:4 to the start of 73:5, *et non cognoverunt*]. So according to the first meaning of *sign* the sense is: Christ is set for a sign, that is, to make known or set forth the teaching of the gospel truth, which will be contradicted by many, by word, or by deed, or in both ways; for disobedient Christians contradict it by their deeds. According to the second meaning the sense is: He is set for a sign, that is, a miracle; for what is more wonderful than Christ Himself, a man born of a Virgin? All that Scripture tells of Christ is a sign, that is, a miracle, which will be contradicted by all the faithless: as that His Mother is a virgin, that in unity of person He is God and man, that He truly rose again. So Origen expounds it. According to the third meaning, by *sign* is understood the cross of Christ, or faith in the cross: by which sign the servants of Christ are told apart from the servants of the devil, since this sign is honoured by the one and marked on the forehead, and despised by the other. — Lastly, it can be expounded of the sign of peace-making, so that the sense is: He is set for a sign of covenant, and of reconciliation or peace between God and men; for He was made the [[1 Tim 2:5|mediator of God and men|mediator Dei et hominum]], and was prefigured by the bow of which the Lord speaks in Genesis: [[Gen 9:13|I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me and between the earth|Arcum meum ponam in nubibus, et erit signum fœderis inter me et terram]]. And Christ is the sign of that covenant not only by signifying it but also by causing it, as the Apostle says: [[Eph 2:14|For he is our peace, who hath made both one|Ipse est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum]]; and again: [[Col 1:20|making peace through the blood of his cross|Pacificans per sanguinem crucis suæ]], both the things in heaven and the things on earth.

paras.t: Et tuam ipsius, o Maria, animam pertransibit gladius, hoc est amarissimus dolor compassionis, quo anima tua implebitur, quum videris Filium tuum occidi, et persecutiones pati. Imo Virgo beata frequenter ante Christi passionem, præcogitando quanta ille esset passurus, amarissime affligebatur: qui dolor cœpit in ea in Christi infantia. De qua re in revelationibus S. Brigittæ multa credibiliter scripta sunt. Iste est gladius spiritualis de quo fertur in Psalmo: Lingua eorum gladius acutus; et, Gladius in labiis eorum. Ibi tamen accipitur gladius pro causa doloris. Sic ergo gladius pertransiit animam Virginis gloriosæ, quomodo de Joseph in Psalmo cantatur: Ferrum pertransiit animam ejus, hoc est dura afflictio. — Ambrosius per gladium intelligit verbum seu sapientiam. Unde et Paulus ad Ephesios: Accipite, ait, gladium spiritus, quod est verbum Dei. Itaque sensus est: Tui ipsius animam pertransibit gladius, id est, intellectum tuum intime illustrabit verbum vel sapientia mysterii crucis, ita quod illud non ignorabis, sed præcognitio passionis Filii tui tua intima penetrabit. Hanc quoque interpretationem tangit vir illustrissimus S. Paulinus episcopus, in sermone seu epistola ad B. Augustinum. Et allegant ad hoc Ambrosius et Paulinus illud Apostoli ad Hebræos: Vivus est sermo Dei, et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ et spiritus. Verumtamen hoc ad litteram de increato sermone, Verbo æterno, Unigenito Patris, inducitur, ut textum intuenti patescit.
paras.en: [[2:35|And thy own soul a sword shall pierce|Et tuam ipsius, o Maria, animam pertransibit gladius]], O Mary: that is, the most bitter sorrow of compassion, with which thy soul will be filled when thou seest thy Son slain and suffering persecutions. Indeed the blessed Virgin was often most bitterly afflicted before Christ's passion, in thinking beforehand how much He was to suffer: and this sorrow began in her in Christ's infancy. Of this many things are written, worthy of belief, in the revelations of St Bridget. This is the spiritual sword of which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 56:5|their tongue a sharp sword|Lingua eorum gladius acutus]]; and: [[Ps 58:8|a sword is in their lips|Gladius in labiis eorum]]. There, however, *sword* is taken for the cause of sorrow. So, then, the sword pierced the soul of the glorious Virgin in the way in which it is sung of Joseph in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:18|the iron pierced his soul|Ferrum pertransiit animam ejus]], that is, hard affliction. — Ambrose understands by the sword the word, or wisdom. Hence Paul too says to the Ephesians: Take, he says, [[Eph 6:17|the sword of the Spirit (which is the word of God)|gladium spiritus, quod est verbum Dei]]. So the sense is: A sword shall pierce thy own soul, that is, the word or wisdom of the mystery of the cross will enlighten thy understanding inwardly, so that thou wilt not be ignorant of it, but the foreknowledge of thy Son's passion will pierce thy inmost being. This interpretation is touched on also by that most illustrious man St Paulinus the bishop, in a sermon or letter to blessed Augustine. And Ambrose and Paulinus cite for it that of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|For the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword; and reaching unto the division of the soul and the spirit|Vivus est sermo Dei, et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ et spiritus]]. Yet this, in its literal sense, is brought in of the uncreated Word, the eternal Word, the Only-begotten of the Father, as is plain to one who looks at the text.

paras.t: Ut revelentur ex multis cordibus cogitationes. Verbum istud intricatum est, referrique potest ad particulam immediate præhabitam, vel ad id quod dixerat Simeon, Positus est hic in ruinam, etc. Ex hoc ergo quod Christus venit in quorumdam salutem, et ad aliquorum majorem damnationem occasionaliter, ut dictum est, item ex passione ipsius compassioneque Matris ejus, factum est ut multorum hominum cogitationes quæ ante latebant, revelarentur, id est, per quosdam effectus aliis proderentur ac declararentur. Ex dictis enim ostensum est, quis bonis cogitationibus Deum quæsierit, quis in Christum crediderit, quis ejus adventum sincere optaverit, quis etiam temporalia quærens, promissaque putans in Christi adventu, in eum tam pauperem, tam humilem et abjectum credere spreverit. Denique tempore passionis, Judæi cogitationes suas quas de Christo habebant, manifestaverunt, dum pro maxima parte negando ipsum, dicebant verba quæ in Evangelio scripta sunt, aliqui vero manebant ei adstantes, sicque suas de Christo cogitationes pandentes. Secundum hunc sensum, dictio Ut tenetur concomitanter, non causaliter: quia non ideo venit, et passus est Christus modo præfato, ut talis cogitationum manifestatio fieret, sed illa secuta est per modum eventus.
paras.en: [[2:35|that, out of many hearts thoughts may be revealed|Ut revelentur ex multis cordibus cogitationes]]. This saying is involved, and can be referred to the phrase just before it, or to what Simeon had said: *this child is set for the fall*, etc. From this, then, that Christ came for the salvation of some and, as was said, occasionally for the greater damnation of others, and also from His passion and the compassion of His Mother, it came about that the thoughts of many men, which before were hidden, were revealed: that is, were brought to light and made known to others by certain effects. For by the things said it was shown who had sought God with good thoughts, who had believed in Christ, who had sincerely longed for His coming; and who also, seeking temporal things and supposing them promised at Christ's coming, scorned to believe in Him, so poor, so lowly and so cast down. Lastly, at the time of the passion the Jews showed the thoughts they had of Christ: for the most part denying Him and saying the words that are written in the Gospel, while some stayed standing by Him, and so laid open their thoughts of Christ. In this sense the word *that* is taken as concomitant, not causal [that is, as marking what followed, not the purpose]: for Christ did not come and suffer in the way described in order that such a showing of thoughts should take place; but it followed as an outcome.

paras.t: Vel sic: Ut revelentur, hoc est, in confessione seu humili sui ipsius accusatione aperiantur, ex multis cordibus peccatorum cogitationes iniquæ: quæ ante confessionem latebant, sed merito passionis Christi data est, et datur hominibus gratia confitendi salubriter. Sicque dictio illa, Ut, teneri potest causaliter aliquo modo: nam ideo passus est Christus, ut hominibus hanc gratiam mereretur. Ita exponit Origenes, dicens: Cogitationes malæ in hominibus erant, quæ propterea revelatæ sunt, ut occideret eas ille qui pro nobis mortuus est. Postremo, fideles passionem Christi et compassionem Mariæ cordialiter intendentes, mox se de suis vanis cogitationibus reprehendunt, easque promunt modis prætactis.
paras.en: Or thus: *that … may be revealed*, that is, opened in confession, or in the humble accusing of oneself, *out of many hearts* of sinners, their wicked *thoughts*, which were hidden before confession; but by the merit of Christ's passion the grace of confessing to salvation was given, and is given, to men. And so that word *that* can in some way be taken causally: for Christ suffered for this end, to merit this grace for men. So Origen expounds it, saying: Evil thoughts were in men, and they were revealed for this reason, that He who died for us might slay them. Lastly, the faithful, heartily attending to the passion of Christ and the compassion of Mary, soon reproach themselves for their vain thoughts, and bring them out in the ways mentioned.

paras.t: Consequenter recitatur testimonium Christo impertitum a femina sancta. Et erat Anna prophetissa, filia Phanuel, de tribu Aser. Tam determinate describitur, propter veritatis certificationem, et ut ab aliis quæ simili nomine vocabantur, distinguatur. Aser autem fuit unus duodecim Patriarcharum filiorum Jacob. Hæc processerat in diebus multis, hoc est, diu vixit, et virtutibus magis processit quam annis, quotidie augens merita sua; et vixerat cum viro suo annis septem a virginitate sua, id est a tempore quo eam adhuc virginem sumpsit in conjugem. Et hæc vidua fuit et mansit usque ad annos octoginta quatuor. Unde propter senium suum honorabilior, fideque dignior fuit. Scriptum est enim in Levitico: Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis. Job quoque ait: In antiquis est sapientia, et in multo tempore prudentia.
paras.en: Next is recounted the testimony given to Christ by a holy woman. [[2:36|And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser|Et erat Anna prophetissa, filia Phanuel, de tribu Aser]]. She is described so precisely to make the truth certain, and to distinguish her from others who were called by the same name. Now Aser was one of the twelve Patriarchs, the sons of Jacob[[Gen 30:13||]]. [[2:36|She was far advanced in years|Hæc processerat in diebus multis]], that is, she lived long, and advanced in virtues more than in years, increasing her merits daily; [[2:36|and had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity|et vixerat cum viro suo annis septem a virginitate sua]], that is, from the time when he took her to wife while she was still a virgin. [[2:37|And she was a widow until fourscore and four years|Et hæc vidua fuit et mansit usque ad annos octoginta quatuor]]: she was a widow and remained so. Hence on account of her great age she was the more honourable and the more worthy of belief. For it is written in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:32|Rise up before the hoary head, and honour the person of the aged man|Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis]]. And Job says: [[Job 12:12|In the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days prudence.|In antiquis est sapientia, et in multo tempore prudentia.]]

paras.t: Quæ non discedebat de templo: non quod ibi sine interruptione permanserit, et omnia corpori necessaria egerit, quum statim subdatur, Hæc ipsa hora superveniens. Itaque dicitur non discessisse de templo, quia omni hora opportuna, imo frequenter præ ceteris ibi fuit: sicut de homine multum devoto et diu in ecclesia perdurante dicimus, quod semper est in ecclesia. Sic et Christus testatur: Oportet semper orare. Jejuniis et obsecrationibus serviens Deo, cui soli latriæ servitus est reddenda, nocte ac die, hoc est competentibus, imo et diuturnis atque frequentibus vicibus diei noctisque. Porro, obsecratio proprie ponitur species orationis qua Deum invocamus per commemorationem alicujus sacri, ut quum dicimus: Per passionem tuam libera nos, Christe; vel, Per bonitatem tuam me adjuva. Jejunium autem ad orationem disponit, sobriam ac vigilem mentem præstando, vitia carnis, somnolentiam, loquacitatem, pigritiamque pellendo: quæ omnia ex edacitate nascuntur. Ad illuminationem quoque, omnisque gratiæ incrementum jejunium confert. Quanta autem sit virtus orationis atque jejunii, constat ex eo quod de pessimo genere dæmoniorum asserit Christus: Hoc genus in nullo potest exire, nisi in oratione et jejunio.
paras.en: [[2:37|who departed not from the temple|Quæ non discedebat de templo]]: not that she stayed there without interruption and did there everything the body needs, since straight after it is added, *at the same hour, coming in*. She is said, then, not to have departed from the temple because she was there at every fitting hour, indeed more often than others: as we say of a very devout man who stays long in church that he is always in church. So too Christ declares: [[Luke 18:1|we ought always to pray|oportet semper orare]]. [[2:37|by fastings and prayers serving|Jejuniis et obsecrationibus serviens]] God, to whom alone the service of *latria* [the worship due to God alone] is to be rendered, [[2:37|night and day|nocte ac die]], that is, at fitting times, and indeed at long and frequent times of the day and night. Now *obsecratio* [here rendered “prayers”; more exactly “supplication”] properly means the kind of prayer in which we call upon God by recalling some sacred thing, as when we say: By Thy passion deliver us, O Christ; or, By Thy goodness help me. Fasting disposes to prayer, making the mind sober and watchful and driving out the vices of the flesh, drowsiness, talkativeness and sloth, all of which are born of gluttony. Fasting also helps towards enlightenment and every increase of grace. And how great is the power of prayer and fasting is plain from what Christ says of the worst kind of devils: [[Mark 9:28|This kind can go out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting|Hoc genus in nullo potest exire, nisi in oratione et jejunio]].

paras.t: Insuper, vidua ista plena fuit omni virtute; sed ideo de istis duobus virtutum actibus specialiter commendatur, quia in eis magis excrevit ac fulsit, sicut de Simeone habitum est cur specialiter timoratus ac justus vocetur. Unde per longa jejunia et frequentes ac fervidas orationes, ad gratiam prophetiæ ascendit. Nam per utrumque mens elevatur ad Deum: per jejunium quidem, dispositive ac mediate; per orationem autem, directe, formaliter et immediate. Per quæ duo etiam peccata præcipue auferuntur: sicque anima purificatur et sanctificatur, instarque speculi tersi, pervii et politi, capax fit sapientiæ copiosæ et illustrationis propheticæ, tanquam amica et consiliaria Creatoris, cui Deus incerta et occulta sapientiæ suæ revelat, juxta illud Sapientis: Sapientia in animas sanctas se transfert, amicos Dei et Prophetas constituit.
paras.en: Moreover, this widow was full of every virtue; but she is praised especially for these two acts of virtue because in them she most grew and shone, just as was said of Simeon why he in particular is called devout and just[[2:25||]]. Hence by long fasts and frequent, fervent prayers she rose to the grace of prophecy. For by both the mind is raised up to God: by fasting, as a disposition and mediately; by prayer, directly, formally and immediately. By these two also sins above all are taken away: and so the soul is purified and sanctified, and like a mirror wiped clean, clear and polished, it becomes capable of abundant wisdom and of prophetic enlightenment, as the friend and counsellor of the Creator, to whom God reveals the uncertain and hidden things of His wisdom[[Ps 50:8||]] [the margin reads Ps. …, 8, the psalm number unreadable; the words are those of Ps 50:8]; according to that saying of the Wise man: [[Wis 7:27|into holy souls, she maketh the friends of God and prophets|in animas sanctas se transfert, amicos Dei et Prophetas constituit]] [Denis has *Sapientia* for the Vulgate's opening words].

paras.t: Si ergo et nos a vitiis emundari, concupiscentias refrenare, in gratia et virtutibus crescere, dæmonibus prævalere, desuper illustrari et sanctificari optamus, jejuniis et orationibus indesinenter et fervide insistamus, a templo Dei non recedamus, quantum ratio id permittit, vel mente non abeamus. Obsecratio autem est ferventior, potior, magisque impetrativa species orationis: ideo obsecrationi instandum est, sicut est illud Psalmistæ: Secundum misericordiam tuam memento mei tu, propter bonitatem tuam, Domine.
paras.en: If, then, we too desire to be cleansed of vices, to bridle our desires, to grow in grace and virtues, to prevail over the devils, to be enlightened and sanctified from above, let us give ourselves unceasingly and fervently to fasts and prayers; let us not depart from the temple of God, as far as reason allows, or at least not go from it in mind. And *obsecratio* is the more fervent, the stronger, and the more effective kind of prayer: so we must be instant in supplication, such as that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 24:7|According to thy mercy remember thou me: for thy goodness' sake, O Lord|Secundum misericordiam tuam memento mei tu, propter bonitatem tuam, Domine]].

paras.t: Et hæc beatissima Anna, ipsa hora diei purgationis Mariæ, qua Simeon tenebat puerulum Jesum in ulnis, superveniens, id est, templum Spiritu Sancto monente ingrediens, quoniam Spiritu Sancto revelante cognovit quis esset, et quid ageretur in templo, confitebatur Domino, id est, Christum quem vidit præsentem laudavit, eique gratias retulit, quod juxta Prophetarum oracula ad mundi redemptionem jam descendisset. Est autem duplex confessio, scilicet laudis, et culpæ. Prima confessione confitemur Dei bonitatem et beneficia ejus: de qua loquitur Christus, Confiteor tibi, Pater. Secunda vero confitemur propria mala. Denique verba Annæ non sunt seriatim descripta, forte quia quantum ad sensum satis coincidebant cum verbis Simeonis ac Zachariæ supra descriptis. Nam et ipsa felicissima Anna tantæ exstitit senectutis, quod cum Simeone non immerito optavit dissolvi viso jam Christo, ejusque adventum exspectare cum patribus sanctis in limbo. Et loquebatur de illo, scilicet de Christo et ejus adventu, beneficiis atque mysteriis. Unde patet, quod paulo ante, per Dominum intelligatur ad litteram Christus. Omnibus qui exspectabant redemptionem Jerusalem. Per Jerusalem Judææ metropolim, tota regio vel plebs Israelitica designatur. Omnibus ergo qui devote optabant ac præstolabantur liberationem populi Israel a jugo peccati et potestate diaboli, Anna hæc testabatur Christum jam advenisse, et populum Israel totumque sæculum liberaturum nunc esse: intelligendumque est de omnibus quibus opportune seu convenienter poterat loqui.
paras.en: [[2:38|Now she|Et hæc]], this most blessed Anna, [[2:38|at the same hour|ipsa hora]] of the day of Mary's purification at which Simeon was holding the little child Jesus in his arms, [[2:38|coming in|superveniens]], that is, entering the temple at the prompting of the Holy Ghost, since by the Holy Ghost's revelation she knew who He was and what was being done in the temple, [[2:38|confessed to the Lord|confitebatur Domino]], that is, praised Christ, whom she saw present, and gave Him thanks that, according to the oracles of the Prophets, He had now come down to redeem the world. Now confession is twofold: of praise, and of guilt. By the first we confess the goodness of God and His benefits; of this Christ speaks: [[Matt 11:25|I confess to thee, O Father|Confiteor tibi, Pater]]. By the second we confess our own sins. The words of Anna are not written out in order, perhaps because in sense they agreed closely enough with the words of Simeon and Zachary written above. For this most happy Anna too was of so great an age that, with Simeon, she not unfittingly wished to be dissolved, now that she had seen Christ, and to await His coming with the holy fathers in limbo. [[2:38|and spoke of him|Et loquebatur de illo]], namely of Christ and of His coming, His benefits and mysteries. Hence it is plain that just before, by *the Lord* is meant, literally, Christ. [[2:38|to all that looked for the redemption of Israel|Omnibus qui exspectabant redemptionem Jerusalem]] [Denis reads *Jerusalem* where the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have *Israel*]. By Jerusalem, the chief city of Judea, the whole region or people of Israel is meant. To all, then, who devoutly longed for and awaited the deliverance of the people of Israel from the yoke of sin and the power of the devil, this Anna bore witness that Christ had now come and would now set free the people of Israel and the whole world: and this is to be understood of all to whom she could fittingly or suitably speak.

paras.t: Et ut perfecerunt omnia secundum legem Domini, id est, postquam Maria et Joseph omnia peregerunt quæ secundum præcepta legis ad ritum purificationis spectabant, videlicet Filium in templo offerendo, eumque quinque siclis redimendo, hostias quoque immolando legales, quamvis ad nullum istorum (ut dictum est) tenerentur, reversi sunt in Galilæam, videlicet in civitatem suam Nazareth: quæ dicitur urbs eorum, quia habitaverunt ibidem antequam venirent ad Bethlehem. Christus quoque in Nazareth fuit conceptus.
paras.en: [[2:39|And after they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord|Et ut perfecerunt omnia secundum legem Domini]], that is, after Mary and Joseph had done all that belonged by the precepts of the law to the rite of purification, namely by offering the Son in the temple and redeeming Him with five shekels, and by sacrificing the legal victims, though (as was said) they were bound to none of these, [[2:39|they returned into Galilee|reversi sunt in Galilæam]], namely [[2:39|to their city Nazareth|in civitatem suam Nazareth]]: which is called their city because they lived there before they came to Bethlehem. Christ too was conceived in Nazareth.

paras.t: Præterea, secundum Origenem, Bedam, multosque alios, prætermittit hoc loco Lucas quædam, quæ a Matthæo evangelista novit descripta, quomodo scilicet Jesus post hæc sit in Ægyptum translatus, ne ab Herode occideretur, et post mortem Herodis reductus sit, tuncque cœperit Nazareth habitare. Itaque secundum istos, antequam Maria et Joseph cum Jesu venirent in Nazareth, in Ægyptum profecti sunt. Dicuntque aliqui, quod in Bethlehem a Jerusalem redierunt, et a Bethlehem in Ægyptum progressi sint. Alii probabiliter dicunt, quod a Jerusalem non redierunt in Bethlehem, quia ob nullam causam a Nazareth venerunt ad Bethlehem, nisi propter descriptionem, ut patuit: idcirco expedito illo negotio, revertentes a Jerusalem, non ad Bethlehem, sed ad Nazareth redierunt, in qua velut in civitate patriæ mansionisque suæ, libentius morabantur; et postea, ex illa urbe angelo nuntiante in Ægyptum fugerunt. Ceteri quasi mediam viam tenentes, affirmant quod a Jerusalem cœperunt reverti in Nazareth, atque in via angelus locutus est ipsi Joseph, ut cum matre et puero fugeret in Ægyptum. Verum quidquid horum dicatur, verum est quod Evangelistæ singuli aliqua hinc inde omittunt, quæ ab aliis noverunt jam scripta, vel Spiritu revelante describenda viderunt: sic tamen, ut narrationis seu descriptionis suæ serie continuata, quasi nulla prætermisisse videantur, quæ alterius Evangelistæ pensata descriptione, quo loco transilita sint, diligens lector inveniet.
paras.en: Further, according to Origen, Bede and many others, Luke here passes over certain things which he knew to have been described by Matthew the evangelist: namely how after this Jesus was taken into Egypt, so as not to be killed by Herod[[Matt 2:13||]][[Matt 2:14||]], and after Herod's death was brought back[[Matt 2:15||]], and then began to live at Nazareth. According to these, then, Mary and Joseph went into Egypt with Jesus before they came to Nazareth. And some say that they went back from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, and from Bethlehem went on into Egypt. Others say, with probability, that they did not go back from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, since they had come from Nazareth to Bethlehem for no other reason than the enrolment, as was shown: so that, that business done, they returned from Jerusalem not to Bethlehem but to Nazareth, where they preferred to stay, as in the city of their home and dwelling; and afterwards, at the angel's word, they fled from that city into Egypt. Others again, keeping as it were a middle way, affirm that they began to return from Jerusalem to Nazareth, and on the way the angel spoke to Joseph, that he should flee into Egypt with the mother and the child. But whichever of these is said, it is true that each of the Evangelists leaves out here and there some things which he knew to have been written already by others, or saw by the Spirit's revelation were to be described by them: yet in such a way that, the course of his narrative or description running on unbroken, he seems to have left nothing out; and the careful reader, weighing the account of another Evangelist, will find at what place things have been passed over.

paras.t: Puer autem, secundum quod homo, crescebat ætate et corporis quantitate: qui secundum quod Deus, æternus est atque immensus; et confortabatur robore corporali, secundum incrementi mensuram: quamvis omni momento poterat tantam corporis fortitudinem assumere et habere, quantum jussisset seu voluisset ut Deus, vel etiam ut homo comprehensor secundum superiorem suæ animæ portionem, ut Deitate fruentem. Tanta enim exstitit beatitudo animæ Christi, quod redundasset in corpus ipsius, dando illi quatuor dotes corporis glorificati, nisi dispensative Deus hoc distulisset, ut in epistola ad Dioscorum asserit Augustinus. Insuper, Christus ut homo, confortabatur spiritu, id est in anima sua a Spiritu Sancto, non per gratiæ vel virtutum aut donorum augmentum sive profectum, sed quantum ad ostensionem, qua secundum ætatis incrementum perfectionem suam magis ac magis monstravit, seu aliis per effectum ostendit. Iterum, confortabatur a Spiritu Sancto, imo a tota Trinitate, in anima, in quantum indesinenter anima ejus conservabatur in fortitudine gratiæ ac virtutum a Deo, quam in primo suæ creationis instanti suscepit ab eo. De hac autem re plenius in fine hujus articuli erit dicendum.
paras.en: [[2:40|And the child|Puer autem]], as man, [[2:40|grew|crescebat]] in age and in size of body: He who as God is eternal and immeasurable; [[2:40|and waxed strong|et confortabatur]] in bodily strength, according to the measure of growth: although at any moment He could have taken and had as much bodily strength as He commanded or willed as God, or even as man, a comprehensor [one who already enjoys the vision of God] in the higher part of His soul, which enjoyed the Godhead. For so great was the blessedness of Christ's soul that it would have overflowed into His body, giving it the four endowments of a glorified body [impassibility, clarity, agility and subtlety], had not God by dispensation deferred this, as Augustine says in his letter to Dioscorus. Moreover Christ as man *waxed strong* in spirit, that is, in His soul, by the Holy Ghost: not by any increase or progress of grace, virtues or gifts, but as to their showing, in that as He grew in age He showed His perfection more and more, or showed it to others by its effects. Again, He waxed strong by the Holy Ghost, indeed by the whole Trinity, in soul, inasmuch as His soul was unceasingly kept by God in the strength of grace and virtues which it received from Him in the first instant of its creation. Of this, however, more will be said at the end of this article.

paras.t: Plenus sapientia, quia secundum divinitatem, fuit substantialiter ipsa Sapientia increata. Porro secundum humanitatem, repletus fuit multiplici sapientia creata, ut post pauca dicetur; fuitque sapientia illa creata in ipso perfecta ab incarnationis principio: propter quod dicit Apostolus, quod in ipso sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi. Et gratia Dei erat in illo. Tanta enim fuit plenitudo gratiæ in eo secundum naturam humanam, quantum valet capere mens creata, ita quod tota capacitas animæ ejus fuit gratia Dei repleta in suæ creationis exordio. De multiplici autem gratia quæ in Christo ponitur, statim patebit.
paras.en: [[2:40|full of wisdom|Plenus sapientia]], since as God He was in substance the uncreated Wisdom itself. And as man He was filled with manifold created wisdom, as will be said a little later; and that created wisdom was perfect in Him from the beginning of the incarnation: for which reason the Apostle says that in Him [[Col 2:3|are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge|sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi]]. [[2:40|and the grace of God was in him|Et gratia Dei erat in illo]]. For the fulness of grace in Him according to His human nature was as great as a created mind can hold, so that the whole capacity of His soul was filled with the grace of God at the outset of its creation. Of the manifold grace that is placed in Christ we shall see presently.

paras.t: Et ibant parentes ejus per omnes annos in Jerusalem in die solenni Paschæ. Si Maria et Joseph cum puero Jesu septem annis in Ægypto morati sunt, quomodo singulis annis pueritiæ Jesu in Jerusalem circa Pascha profecti sunt? Præterea in Matthæo habetur, quod Joseph angelo præcipiente rediens de Ægypto in terram Israel, audito quod in Judæa, cujus metropolis fuit Jerusalem, regnaret Archelaus filius Herodis, timuit illo ire, ideoque in Galilæam reversus est, atque in Nazareth habitavit. Quomodo ergo quolibet anno ivit Jerusalem, si timore Archelai non audebat illuc accedere? Insuper lex præcepit, ut tribus vicibus in quolibet anno, omne masculinum Judæorum appareret coram Domino in loco ad hoc electo, hoc est in loco præcipuo cultus divini, qui fuit Jerusalem, præsertim postquam ibidem constructum est templum. Ergo, qua ratione semel ascenderunt Jerusalem? Videtur quod ter ascendere debuerunt.
paras.en: [[2:41|And his parents went every year to Jerusalem, at the solemn day of the pasch|Et ibant parentes ejus per omnes annos in Jerusalem in die solenni Paschæ]]. If Mary and Joseph stayed seven years in Egypt with the child Jesus, how did they go to Jerusalem about the Pasch in every year of Jesus' childhood? Besides, we have it in Matthew that Joseph, returning from Egypt into the land of Israel at the angel's bidding, on hearing that Archelaus the son of Herod reigned in Judea, whose capital was Jerusalem, [[Matt 2:22|was afraid to go thither|timuit illo ire]], and so went back into Galilee and dwelt in Nazareth[[Matt 2:23||]]. How then did he go to Jerusalem every year, if for fear of Archelaus he did not dare go there? Moreover the law commanded that three times in each year all the males of the Jews should appear before the Lord in the place chosen for this[[Ex 23:17||]][[Deut 16:16||]], that is, in the chief place of divine worship, which was Jerusalem, above all after the temple was built there. For what reason, then, did they go up to Jerusalem once? It seems they ought to have gone up three times.

paras.t: Et respondendum ad primum, quod Lucas loquitur de tempore quo Maria et Joseph in Galilæa seu Nazareth sunt morati. Ad secundum respondet Augustinus in libro de Consensu Evangelistarum dupliciter: primo, quod licet Joseph timuerit in Judæa morari, Archelao regnante, ne esset conspicuus inter turbam, tamen in gentem in qua facile quivit latere, secrete ascendere potuit, ne esset irreligiosus; secundo, quod Lucas loquitur pro tempore quo Archelaus non timebatur, defunctusve erat. Ad tertium respondetur, quod lex in Exodo jussit, ut omnis masculus Judæorum in tribus solennitatibus, scilicet Pascha, Pentecostes, et Tabernaculorum, coram Domino appareret; sed cum his qui habitabant multum remote a loco præfato, dispensabatur quoad duas solennitates, videlicet Pentecostes et Tabernaculorum. Maria autem et Joseph a Jerusalem remote manebant: idcirco ad principalem dumtaxat solennitatem venerunt, legi obedientes, et obediendi exemplum præstantes. De mulieribus tamen præceptum non fuit ita venire; sed si comitabantur viros, ex devotione vel consuetudine fuit.
paras.en: To the first the answer is that Luke speaks of the time when Mary and Joseph dwelt in Galilee, or Nazareth. To the second Augustine, in his book *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, answers in two ways: first, that although Joseph was afraid to stay in Judea while Archelaus reigned, he could still go up secretly among the crowd, in which he could easily lie hidden, so as not to fail in religion [the Latin, *in gentem*, seems corrupt; the sense is “among the people”, so as not to be conspicuous]; secondly, that Luke speaks of the time when Archelaus was no longer feared, or was dead. To the third it is answered that the law in Exodus ordered every male of the Jews to appear before the Lord at three solemnities, namely the Pasch, Pentecost and Tabernacles[[Deut 16:16||]]; but those who lived very far from the said place were dispensed for two of the solemnities, namely Pentecost and Tabernacles. Now Mary and Joseph lived far from Jerusalem, and so they came only to the chief solemnity, obeying the law and giving an example of obedience. As for women, however, there was no command to come in this way; but if they accompanied their husbands, it was out of devotion or custom.

paras.t: Postremo quod ait, Ibant Jerusalem in die solenni Paschæ, non est intelligendum quod in die illo tam celebri ibant, sed quod iter sic arripiebant, ut in illo die in Jerusalem essent: imo in vigilia Paschæ, quando agnus seu phase immolabatur, ibi esse curabant, ut manducarent de agno paschali.
paras.en: Lastly, when he says *they went to Jerusalem at the solemn day of the pasch*, it is not to be understood that they travelled on that so festal day, but that they set out on the journey in such a way as to be in Jerusalem on that day: nay, they took care to be there on the eve of the Pasch, when the lamb, or *phase* [the paschal victim], was sacrificed, so as to eat of the paschal lamb.

paras.t: Deinceps recitat Evangelista quomodo puer Jesus primo sapientiam suam declarare seu manifestare incepit. Et quum factus esset Jesus annorum duodecim, secundum quod homo: qui secundum divinitatem idem ipse æternaliter et invariabiliter permanet; ascendentibus illis, videlicet Maria et Joseph, Jerosolymam. Sic enim appellavit eam Salomon, quæ communiter Jerusalem nuncupatur; situque altior fuit quam Galilæa, ideo ascendisse dicuntur; secundum consuetudinem diei festi, id est, prout solitum fuit circa festivitatem paschalem. Bona quippe et laudabilis consuetudo vim legis habet, ideo sine idonea causa omittenda non est.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist relates how the child Jesus first began to show or make known His wisdom. [[2:42|And when he was twelve years old|Et quum factus esset Jesus annorum duodecim]], that is, according as He is man: for according to the Godhead He remains the selfsame eternally and unchangeably; [[2:42|they going up into Jerusalem|ascendentibus illis Jerosolymam]], namely Mary and Joseph. For so Solomon called the city which is commonly named *Jerusalem* [Denis comments on the form *Jerosolyma* in his text]; and it lay higher than Galilee, so they are said to have gone up; [[2:42|according to the custom of the feast|secundum consuetudinem diei festi]], that is, as was usual about the paschal festival. For a good and praiseworthy custom has the force of law, and so is not to be left off without fitting cause.

paras.t: Consummatisque diebus, id est expletis seu transactis diebus ad solennitatem illam spectantibus: qui septem diebus durabat, juxta illud Deuteronomii, Septem diebus comedes absque fermento. Verumtamen aliqui dicunt, quod octo diebus duraverit, quia et Glossa testatur: Octo prolongabatur diebus. Quod verum est cum præfatis septem integris diebus de quibus ait Scriptura, computando diem eos immediate præcedentem, in cujus vespera immolabatur phase, luna quartadecima, prout in Exodo fuit præceptum. Quum redirent, id est, a Jerusalem reverti ad Galilæam inciperent, remansit puer Jesus in Jerusalem, non absque multiplici causa, rationabilissimisque motivis, videlicet: ut suam sapientiam tunc monstrare ad gloriam Patris inciperet; ut pueris, imo et cunctis, exemplum persistendi in templo et in cultu ac opere Dei præberet; ut zelum suum circa divina ac Patris honorem a pueritia declararet; ut amore spiritualis profectus in sapientia, scientiis atque virtutibus, carnales parentes ostenderet relinquendos. Et non cognoverunt parentes ejus, quod ibi remansit: quia ut Beda fatetur, ad solennitates præfatas venientes atque ad propria redeuntes, viri et feminæ incedebant seorsum, infantes autem ac pueri cum quolibet parente poterant ire: ideo Maria putavit puerum esse cum Joseph, et vice versa. Sic namque seorsum tendebant viri ac feminæ, ut continendo, devotius solennitatibus interessent. Verumtamen Origenes subtilius aliquid tangit, nescio tamen si verius. Imaginabatur equidem, quod supernaturaliter imperceptibiliterque elapsus sit manus parentum, quemadmodum in Evangelio secundum Joannem legitur sæpe elapsus manus Judæorum cum lapidare volentium: quod qualiter factum sit, infra dicetur.
paras.en: [[2:43|And having fulfilled the days|Consummatisque diebus]], that is, when the days belonging to that solemnity were completed or past: which lasted seven days, according to that of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 16:3|seven days shalt thou eat without leaven|Septem diebus comedes absque fermento]]. Some, however, say that it lasted eight days, for the Gloss too testifies: It was prolonged for eight days. This is true if, with the said seven full days of which Scripture speaks, one counts the day immediately before them, in the evening of which the *phase* was sacrificed, on the fourteenth day of the moon, as was commanded in Exodus[[Ex 12:18||]]. [[2:43|when they returned|Quum redirent]], that is, when they began to go back from Jerusalem to Galilee, [[2:43|the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem|remansit puer Jesus in Jerusalem]]: not without manifold cause and most reasonable motives, namely, that He might then begin to show His wisdom to the glory of the Father; that He might give to children, nay to all, an example of abiding in the temple and in the worship and work of God; that He might declare from His childhood His zeal for divine things and for His Father's honour; that He might show that for love of spiritual progress in wisdom, knowledge and virtue one's parents according to the flesh are to be left. [[2:43|And his parents knew it not|Et non cognoverunt parentes ejus]] that He had stayed there: because, as Bede declares, when they came to the said solemnities and went back home, the men and the women walked apart, while infants and children could go with either parent: so Mary thought the boy was with Joseph, and the other way about. For men and women went apart in this way so that, by keeping continence, they might take part in the solemnities more devoutly. Origen, however, touches on something more subtle, though I do not know whether it is truer. For he imagined that He slipped from His parents' hands supernaturally and imperceptibly, as we read in the Gospel according to John that He often slipped out of the hands of the Jews who wished to stone Him[[John 8:59||]][[John 10:39||]]: how this was done will be said below.

paras.t: Existimantes autem illum esse in comitatu, id est inter eos qui pariter incedebant, ita quod Maria putavit quod esset in comitatu virorum, Joseph autem, quod esset in comitatu mulierum, venerunt iter diei, id est, unius diei iter confecerunt a Jerusalem recedendo, et requirebant eum inter cognatos et notos. Quum enim in fine primi diei, tam Maria quam Joseph adverterent quod cum nullo ipsorum esset vel redisset Jesus, non mediocriter sollicitabantur: idcirco die sequenti eum in utroque comitatu, præsertim inter cognatos et vicinos seu notos et familiares, diligentissime requirebant. Et non invenientes eum inter illos: ad insinuandum quod carnalis amor atque propinquitas, societasque humana plurimum impedit a vacatione divina inventioneque Christi; regressi sunt in Jerusalem tertia die, requirentes eum in ea, ubicumque putabant spem esse quod inveniretur. Quo enim plus diligebant, eo vigilantius et abundantius quærebant dilectum: quia ut ait Gregorius, vis amoris multiplicat intentionem et studium inquisitionis.
paras.en: [[2:44|And thinking that he was in the company|Existimantes autem illum esse in comitatu]], that is, among those who were travelling together, so that Mary thought He was in the company of the men, and Joseph that He was in the company of the women, [[2:44|they came a day's journey|venerunt iter diei]], that is, they made one day's journey going away from Jerusalem, [[2:44|and sought him among their kinsfolks and acquaintance|et requirebant eum inter cognatos et notos]]. For when at the end of the first day both Mary and Joseph noticed that Jesus was not, and had not come back, with either of them, they were not a little anxious: and so on the following day they sought Him most diligently in both companies, above all among their kinsfolk and neighbours, or acquaintances and friends. [[2:45|And not finding him|Et non invenientes eum]] among them: to suggest that carnal love and kinship, and human company, greatly hinder us from giving ourselves to God and from finding Christ; [[2:45|they returned into Jerusalem|regressi sunt in Jerusalem]] on the third day, [[2:45|seeking him|requirentes eum]] in it, wherever they thought there was hope that He might be found. For the more they loved, the more watchfully and abundantly they sought the beloved: since, as Gregory says, the force of love multiplies the effort and eagerness of the search.

paras.t: Et factum est, post triduum, utpote quarto die, invenerunt illum in templo, non in theatro, foro, ludorumve loco, ut pueri solent inveniri: ad innuendum quod Filium Dei quærere et invenire optantes, templum, oratorium, ecclesiam, seu locum cultui Dei contemplationique aptum ingredi debent, non spectaculorum aut tumultuum loca. Imo, sicut qui libenter est in ecclesia propter divina, filius Dei creditur adoptivus, tanquam libenter consistens in domo Patris cœlestis; sic qui in tabernis et locis vanitatum libenter est, diaboli filius reputatur. Sedentem in medio doctorum: ad designandum quod pueri, imo et ceteri, debent se doctoribus applicare, a quibus in virtutibus atque scientiis valeant informari, secundum illud Ecclesiastici: Si videris sensatum, statim evigila ad illum; et iterum, In multitudine presbyterorum sapientium sta, et sapientiæ illorum ex corde conjungere. Audientem illos, et interrogantem. Audivit doctrinam illorum, non ut aliquid disceret sive proficeret, sed ut juxta prolata ab illis congruenter, non extranee, interrogaret, et quia inter homines conversans, humano decentique modo habere se debuit; itemque, ut exemplum præstaret simplicibus, præsertim pueris et minoribus, quamvis peritis, ut magistros et seniores audire potius curent, quam docere præsumant, nec vana ostentatione se jactent, præsertim quum scriptum sit: Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum; et iterum, Nolite plures magistri fieri, fratres mei, scientes quia majus judicium accipitis.
paras.en: [[2:46|And it came to pass, that, after three days, they found him in the temple|Et factum est, post triduum, utpote quarto die, invenerunt illum in templo]]: that is, on the fourth day; not in the theatre, the market-place or a place of games, where boys are usually found: to hint that those who long to seek and find the Son of God must go into the temple, the oratory, the church, or a place fit for the worship and contemplation of God, not into places of shows and tumults. Nay, as he who gladly stays in church for the sake of divine things is held to be an adopted son of God, as one who gladly abides in the house of his heavenly Father; so he who gladly stays in taverns and places of vanity is reckoned a son of the devil. [[2:46|sitting in the midst of the doctors|Sedentem in medio doctorum]]: to signify that children, and indeed others too, ought to attach themselves to teachers by whom they may be formed in virtue and learning, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:36|if thou see a man of understanding, go to him early in the morning|Si videris sensatum, statim evigila ad illum]] [*evigila*: literally “wake up and go”]; and again, [[Ecclus 6:35|Stand in the multitude of ancients that are wise, and join thyself from thy heart to their wisdom|In multitudine presbyterorum sapientium sta, et sapientiæ illorum ex corde conjungere]]. [[2:46|hearing them and asking them questions|Audientem illos, et interrogantem]]. He heard their teaching, not so as to learn or gain anything, but so as to ask questions fittingly, and not beside the point, according to what they had said; and because, living among men, He ought to behave in a human and seemly way; and also to give an example to the simple, above all to children and juniors, however learned, that they should take care rather to listen to their masters and elders than presume to teach, and not boast themselves with vain display; above all since it is written: [[Jas 1:19|let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak|Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum]]; and again: [[Jas 3:1|Be ye not many masters, my brethren, knowing that you receive the greater judgment.|Nolite plures magistri fieri, fratres mei, scientes quia majus judicium accipitis]]

paras.t: Itaque, postquam illos audivit, quæstiones Christus proposuit, ut illos instrueret, atque ad Dei laudationem induceret. Denique hic disciplinæ rectus est ordo: primo, diligenter audire, deinde circa audita pertinenter inquirere, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Audi tacens simul et quærens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi bona gratia. Quo contra nonnulli non exspectata responsione tentant objicere, seu non audita ad plenum objectione incipiunt respondere, non attendentes illud Proverbiorum: Qui prius respondet antequam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat et confusione dignum. Propterea in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Priusquam audias, non respondeas verbum. Quæ autem fuerint Christi quæstiones atque responsa, Evangelista non exprimit. Arbitror tamen, quod aliqua circa sua mysteria atque adventum suum spectantia fuerit sciscitatus, ut daret eis agnoscendæ veritatis occasionem. Stupebant autem, id est, vehementer mirabantur, omnes qui eum audiebant, quod scilicet in puero tantulæ ætatis esset sapientia, eloquentia, maturitas, constantia tanta: præsertim tamen de sapientiæ ejus eminentia. Nam subditur: super prudentia ejus intus manente: et sumitur hic prudentia pro sapientia, vel notitia Scripturarum; et responsis ejus, per quæ sua interior prudentia patefiebat. Unde elicitur, quod sicut Christus proposuit eis quæstiones, sic vice versa; sed ipsi ei tam prompte ac sapienter respondere nequibant, ut eis ipse. Ex eodem equidem sapientiæ fonte procedit, apte interrogare, convenienterque respondere.
paras.en: So, after He had heard them, Christ put questions, so as to instruct them and lead them to the praise of God. And here is the right order of learning: first to listen diligently, then to inquire pertinently about what has been heard, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 32:9|Hear in silence, and for thy reverence good grace shall come to thee|Audi tacens simul et quærens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi bona gratia]] [Denis adds *simul et quærens*, “and asking too”]. Contrariwise some try to object without waiting for the answer, or begin to answer before they have fully heard the objection, not heeding that of Proverbs: [[Prov 18:13|He that answereth before he heareth, sheweth himself to be a fool, and worthy of confusion.|Qui prius respondet antequam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat et confusione dignum]] Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:8|Before thou hear, answer not a word|Priusquam audias, non respondeas verbum]] [the margin's numerals are unreadable; the words are those of Ecclus 11:8]. What Christ's questions and answers were the Evangelist does not say. I think, however, that He asked about some things concerning His own mysteries and His coming, so as to give them occasion to know the truth. [[2:47|And all that heard him were astonished|Stupebant autem omnes qui eum audiebant]], that is, they wondered greatly that in a boy of so tender an age there should be such wisdom, eloquence, maturity and steadiness: above all, however, at the eminence of His wisdom. For there follows: [[2:47|at his wisdom|super prudentia ejus]], abiding within; and *prudentia* is taken here for wisdom, or knowledge of the Scriptures; [[2:47|and his answers|et responsis ejus]], through which His inner wisdom was made plain. From this we gather that, as Christ put questions to them, so they did to Him; but they could not answer Him as readily and wisely as He answered them. For it comes from the same fountain of wisdom to ask aptly and to answer fittingly.

paras.t: Et videntes admirati sunt: id est, cuncti qui aderant huic disputationi, et corporaliter puerum illum intuebantur, quam facete, modeste, reverenter se habuit, intellectualiter quoque videbant quam sapiens esset, admiratione repleti sunt, quod puer ille doctores ætate, studio, atque humana instructione provectos, tam incomparabiliter superaret: cujus simile nunquam viderunt et forte nec audierunt, quum sit contra vel supra cursum et ordinem rerum. — Præterea quæritur, cur Christus duodecimo ætatis suæ anno sapientiam suam sic orsus est declarare. Ad quod Græcus respondet, quia duodecimo anno penes homines discretionis ratio perfici solet: unde non antea fecit hoc, ne phantasticum aut diabolicum putaretur. Potest quoque dici, ut tangit Ambrosius, quoniam duodenarius Apostolorum numerus fuit ad prædicationem Evangelii eligendus.
paras.en: [[2:48|And seeing him, they wondered|Et videntes admirati sunt]]: that is, all who were present at this disputation, and who looked with their bodily eyes on that boy, how gracefully, modestly and reverently He bore Himself, and saw with their minds too how wise He was, were filled with wonder that this boy so incomparably surpassed doctors advanced in age, study and human instruction: the like of which they had never seen, and perhaps never heard of, since it is against or above the course and order of things. — It is asked besides why Christ began to show His wisdom in this way in the twelfth year of His age. To which the Greek [that is, Theophylact] answers that in the twelfth year the power of discernment is usually brought to completion in men: so He did not do this earlier, lest it should be thought illusory or devilish. It can also be said, as Ambrose touches on, that it was because the number of the Apostles to be chosen for preaching the Gospel was twelve.

paras.t: At vero affectuosissima atque piissima Mater, viso unico ac supercarissimo Filio suo, tanto amplius est gavisa, quo de ejus amissione plus fuit tristata; verumtamen eum alloqui non præsumpsit, quamdiu vidit eum cum doctoribus occupatum. Sed Puer Matrem adesse conspiciens, actu illo completo, venit ad eam. Quæ mox maternis concussis visceribus et præ gaudio lacrimans, fiducialiter, humiliter, dulciter et affectuose, tanquam mater ait ad ipsum: Fili, quid fecisti nobis sic? Et est verbum hoc non quasi increpatio, sed quasi pia et amorosa conquestio, seu avida inquisitio, exponendum. Noverat nempe beatissima Virgo Filium suum esse Deum et hominem, nec posse peccare, nec sine rationabili causa quidpiam agere. Ideo sciscitatur: O fili, quid, id est cur, fecisti nobis sic, nobis ignorantibus in Jerusalem remanendo, ac per hoc tantam nobis tristitiam ingerendo, quos noveras de tua absentia taliter affligendos? O felicissima incomparabilisque Maria, quæ Unigenitum Patris æterni tam vere ac confidenter filium vocat!
paras.en: But the most loving and most tender Mother, on seeing her only and most dearly beloved Son, rejoiced the more, the more she had grieved at losing Him; yet she did not presume to speak to Him so long as she saw Him busy with the doctors. But the Boy, seeing His Mother there, came to her when that business was finished. And she at once, her mother's heart deeply stirred and weeping for joy, said to Him trustfully, humbly, sweetly and lovingly, as a mother: [[2:48|And his mother said to him: Son, why hast thou done so to us?|Fili, quid fecisti nobis sic?]] And this word is to be expounded not as a rebuke, but as a tender and loving complaint, or an eager question. For the most blessed Virgin knew that her Son was God and man, and could not sin, nor do anything without reasonable cause. So she asks: O Son, what, that is, why, hast thou done so to us, staying in Jerusalem without our knowing, and so bringing such sorrow upon us, who, as Thou knewest, would be so afflicted by Thy absence? O most happy and incomparable Mary, who so truly and so confidently calls the Only-begotten of the eternal Father her son!

paras.t: Ecce ego et pater tuus putativus, dolentes de tua absentia, quærebamus te cum grandi dolore. Cujus doloris causam Glossa assignat, quia timebant ne quod puero in infantia facere molitus fuit Herodes, alii puero jam provectioris ætatis inferrent, videlicet Archelaus et alii. Sed nonne sapiens Virgo cognovit, quod puer ideo venit, ut in virili ætate pro mundi salute crucifigeretur? Et respondendum, quod utique: nihilo minus metuere potuit ne puero qui ad patiendum venit, aliquid adversitatis accideret, quamvis sciret sibi hoc contra ipsius voluntatem non posse accidere. Denique Origenes circa hoc subtiliter scribit: Cur, inquiens, quærebant puerum cum dolore? An ideo, ne forte perierit sive erraverit? Absit. Nunquam enim fieri potuit, ut perditum formidarent, quem Dominum esse cognoverant, et quem Maria se de Spiritu Sancto concepisse perpendit. Sed quomodo tu, dum Scripturas legis, quæris in eis sensum cum dolore et quodam tormento, non quod Scripturas errasse arbitreris, sed quoniam veritatem quam continent nescis, et invenire quæris; sic illi quærebant Jesum, ne forte eos relinquens ad alia demigrasset, et quod magis puto, ne forte reversus esset ad cœlos, quum ei placuisset iterum descensurus.
paras.en: [[2:48|Behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing|Ecce ego et pater tuus putativus, dolentes de tua absentia, quærebamus te]]: thy father, that is, thy supposed father, grieving at thy absence, with great sorrow. The cause of this sorrow the Gloss gives: they feared lest what Herod tried to do to the child in His infancy[[Matt 2:13||]], others, namely Archelaus and the rest, might do to the boy now that He was older. But did not the wise Virgin know that the boy had come for this, to be crucified in His manhood for the salvation of the world? The answer is: certainly; nevertheless she could fear lest some harm should befall the boy who had come to suffer, though she knew that this could not happen to Him against His will. Origen, finally, writes subtly on this: Why, he says, did they seek the boy sorrowing? Was it lest perhaps He had perished or gone astray? God forbid. For it could never be that they should fear Him lost whom they knew to be the Lord, and whom Mary knew she had conceived of the Holy Ghost. But as thou, when thou readest the Scriptures, seekest their meaning with sorrow and a kind of torment, not because thou thinkest the Scriptures have erred, but because thou knowest not the truth they contain and seekest to find it; so they sought Jesus, lest perhaps He had left them and gone elsewhere, and, as I rather think, lest perhaps He had gone back to heaven, to come down again when it should please Him.

paras.t: Itaque et nos, dum peccando amiserimus Jesum, protinus cordialiter doleamus, et cum sollicitudine ac mœrore eum quæramus, nec dissolute et negligenter pertranseamus, ut illi qui quærunt nec tamen eum inveniunt. Unde in Deuteronomio habetur: Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; si tamen toto corde quæsieris eum, et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ. Tanto enim plus de perpetratione peccati et Christi amissione dolere debemus, quam de temporalium et corporalium perditione, quanto malum culpæ pejus est malo pœnæ, et quanto salus æterna seu incommutabile bonum majoris est bonitatis ac dignitatis quam transitoria universa. Nihilo minus multi cæca et misera mente plus de transitoriorum ablatione, quam de gratiæ ac salutis perditione tristantur.
paras.en: So we too, when by sinning we have lost Jesus, should grieve at once from the heart, and seek Him with care and mourning, and not pass on carelessly and negligently, like those who seek and yet do not find Him. Hence we have in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 4:29|when thou shalt seek there the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him: yet so, if thou seek him with all thy heart, and all the affliction of thy soul|Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; si tamen toto corde quæsieris eum, et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ]]. For we ought to grieve more over committing sin and losing Christ than over the loss of temporal and bodily things, by so much as the evil of guilt is worse than the evil of punishment, and as eternal salvation, the unchangeable good, is greater in goodness and dignity than all passing things. Nevertheless many, with blind and wretched minds, are more saddened by the taking away of passing things than by the loss of grace and salvation.

paras.t: Et ait ad illos: Quid est quod me quærebatis? quasi dicat: Necesse non fuit me taliter quæri cum tanta mœstitia. Quibus verbis non increpat eos quasi culpabiles, quia nec male egerunt quærendo; sed caritative et pie insinuat, quod aliter quærendus potius fuit, et quod melius ac sapientius facere potuissent, quam fecerunt ita quærendo inter cognatos ac notos: quemadmodum Christi voluntas de qua dixit, Pater, non quod ego volo, bona fuit; et tamen quæ dixit, Sed quod tu, melior fuit. Hinc subditur: Nesciebatis (quasi dicat: Utique perpendere potuistis) quia in his quæ Patris mei sunt, id est in cultu et templo Patris æterni, oportet me esse, qui veni ad hoc, ut secundum formam servi quam accepi, Patrem meum cœlestem indesinenter honorem? Unde apud Joannem Christus ait de Patre: Quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper. Tanquam dicat: Primo fui a vobis in templo, non inter cognatos quærendus, ceteris paribus; vel advertere poteratis, quod non nisi in divinis essem moratus. Hoc tamen pro tunc non tenebantur considerare, sed paulatim proficere debuerunt. Et Christus his verbis interrogat eos, non ut reprehendat quasi peccantes, sed ut instruat aliqua ignorantes, ut moris est his qui ex præcipua caritate loquuntur.
paras.en: [[2:49|And he said to them: How is it that you sought me?|Et ait ad illos: Quid est quod me quærebatis?]] As if to say: There was no need for Me to be sought so, with such sadness. By these words He does not rebuke them as blameworthy, for they did no wrong in seeking; but in charity and tenderness He hints that He should rather have been sought in another way, and that they could have done better and more wisely than they did in seeking Him so among kinsfolk and acquaintance: just as Christ's will, of which He said, [[Mark 14:36|Father, all things are possible to thee: remove this chalice from me; but not what I will|Pater, non quod ego volo]], was good; and yet that of which He said, [[Mark 14:36|but what thou wilt|Sed quod tu]], was better. Hence there follows: [[2:49|Did you not know|Nesciebatis]] (as if to say: you could surely have weighed it) [[2:49|that I must be about my father's business|quia in his quæ Patris mei sunt, oportet me esse?]], that is, in the worship and the temple of the eternal Father: I who came for this, that according to the form of a servant which I have taken[[Phil 2:7||]] I might ceaselessly honour My heavenly Father? Hence in John Christ says of the Father: [[John 8:29|I do always the things that please him|Quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper]].
