As if He said: I was to be sought by you first in the temple, not among kinsfolk, other things being equal; or you could have noticed that I would not be staying anywhere but in divine things. Yet at that time they were not bound to consider this, but were to advance little by little. And by these words Christ questions them, not to reproach them as sinners, but to instruct them as ignorant of some things, as is the way of those who speak out of special charity.

paras.t: Et ipsi non intellexerunt verbum quod locutus est ad eos. Non est putandum ignorasse eos, præsertim Mariam, quod per patrem intellexerit Deum Patrem æternum; sed plene non intellexerunt quid Christus per ista verba prætenderet, hoc est, per quem modum assereret se esse oportere in his quæ Patris sunt, utpote quantum ad locum et tempus, aliasque circumstantias, et quoad actus determinatos: quia et verbum hoc multipliciter intelligi potuit; et Maria non ignoravit Filium suum indesinenter Deo Patri actibusque divinis intentum, sed quando, qualiter, quoties oporteret eum esse in templo, non ita prævidit distincte.
paras.en: [[2:50|And they understood not the word that he spoke unto them.|Et ipsi non intellexerunt verbum quod locutus est ad eos.]] We must not think that they were ignorant, Mary above all, that by *Father* He meant God the eternal Father; but they did not fully understand what Christ intended by these words, that is, in what way He declared that He must be about the things that are His Father's: as to place and time, namely, and the other circumstances, and as to particular acts. For this saying could be understood in many ways; and Mary was not ignorant that her Son was ceaselessly intent on God the Father and on divine acts, but when, how and how often He would need to be in the temple she did not foresee so distinctly.

paras.t: Et descendit cum eis, et venit Nazareth, a qua cum illis ascendit Jerusalem. De qua ascensione sua ad festivitatem legalem, per Zachariam de se ipso prædixit, dicens: Vadam etiam ego. Nam paulo ante ibidem habetur: Hæc dicit Dominus exercituum: Usquequo veniant populi et habitent in civitatibus multis, et vadant habitatores unusquisque ad alterum, dicentes, Eamus et deprecemur faciem Domini. Quibus mox subditur: Vadam etiam ego, scilicet Dominus exercituum qui loquitur ista. Non enim Zacharias de se ipso hoc ait: quod super Zachariam clarius demonstravi. Et erat subditus illis: quoniam sicut in se ipso humillimus fuit ut homo, sic usque perfectum in exterioribus humiliavit se ipsum, non solum Matri, sed et nutricio et ministro se subdens, secundum naturam assumptam; et legem quam de honoratione parentum dedit, implevit, non necessitate, sed dignatione et pietate. Non enim communi legi fuit adstrictus, aut de necessitate præcepti subjectus, sed supra legem, non solum secundum divinitatem, sed et secundum humanitatem, ut a Verbo æterno assumptam et toti creaturæ prælatam.
paras.en: [[2:51|And he went down with them and came to Nazareth|Et descendit cum eis, et venit Nazareth]], from which He had gone up with them to Jerusalem. Of this going up of His to the feast of the law He foretold of Himself through Zacharias, saying: [[Zach 8:21|I also will go|Vadam etiam ego]]. For a little before, in the same place, we have: [[Zach 8:20|Thus saith the Lord of hosts, until people come and dwell in many cities|Hæc dicit Dominus exercituum: Usquequo veniant populi et habitent in civitatibus multis]], [[Zach 8:21|And the inhabitants go one to another, saying: Let us go, and entreat the face of the Lord|et vadant habitatores unusquisque ad alterum, dicentes, Eamus et deprecemur faciem Domini]]. To which is presently added: *I also will go*, that is, the Lord of hosts who says these things. For Zacharias does not say this of himself: as I have shown more clearly in the commentary on Zacharias. [[2:51|and was subject to them|Et erat subditus illis]]: for as in Himself He was most humble as man, so in outward things He humbled Himself to the full[[Phil 2:8||]], subjecting Himself, according to the nature He had taken, not only to His Mother but also to His foster-father and servant; and He fulfilled the law He had given on honouring parents[[Matt 15:4||]], not of necessity but of condescension and love. For He was not bound by the common law, nor subject to it by the necessity of a precept, but was above the law, not only according to His divinity but according to His humanity too, as taken up by the eternal Word and set above the whole creation.

paras.t: Denique, secundum gradus diversos potestatis altioris, determinandus est obedientiæ gradus. Ideo potestati in spiritualibus præsidenti, in illis est obediendum; præsidenti autem in regimine rei publicæ, in talibus est obediendum; similiter præsidenti in regimine domus atque familiæ, in talibus obediendum est a domesticis. Christus autem simpliciter superior fuit suis parentibus: quibus tamen parebat et humillime atque promptissime serviebat, dans omnibus nobis, præsertim junioribus, obedientiæ ac humilitatis exemplum, et ut non solum carnalibus, sed et spiritualibus patribus ac senioribus obediamus, dicente Apostolo: Filioli, obedite parentibus vestris per omnia. Debent autem filii parentibus honorem reverentiæ, sicut in assurgendo; honorem obedientiæ, in omittendo seu faciendo, dummodo non sit impeditivum salutis; itemque honorem subventionis necessariæ, pro loco et tempore. Hac ergo Christi humilitate vehementissime superbia nostra confunditur, rebellio nostra damnatur, dum superioribus nostris non obtemperamus: quia Dominus universorum, qui etiam secundum naturam assumptam et Verbo unitam dignior Deoque carior est toto universo, non solum pauperi Matri, sed et fabro obedivit lignario.
paras.en: Further, the degree of obedience must be fixed according to the different degrees of higher authority. So to an authority set over spiritual things we must obey in those things; to one set over the government of the commonwealth we must obey in such things; likewise to one set over the government of a house and family, the household must obey in such things. Now Christ was simply superior to His parents: yet He obeyed them and served them most humbly and most promptly, giving to all of us, and above all to the young, an example of obedience and humility, that we may obey not only our fathers in the flesh but also our spiritual fathers and elders, as the Apostle says: [[Eph 6:1|Children, obey your parents|Filioli, obedite parentibus vestris]] in all things [the margin gives Ephes. vi; *per omnia*, “in all things”, is from the parallel Col 3:20]. Now children owe their parents the honour of reverence, as in rising before them; the honour of obedience, in leaving undone or doing, so long as it is no hindrance to salvation; and also the honour of needful support, as place and time require. By this humility of Christ, then, our pride is most vehemently put to shame, and our rebellion condemned when we do not obey our superiors: for the Lord of all things, who even according to the nature He took, united to the Word, is worthier and dearer to God than the whole universe, obeyed not only a poor Mother but also a carpenter.

paras.t: Et Mater ejus conservabat omnia verba hæc, scilicet verba et facta Filii sui, in corde suo, tanquam optima ac docillima sapientiæ æternæ discipula, sapientiæ capacissima ac avidissima; et quidquid Filius ejus de cetero fecit aut dixit, cum summa veneratione pensavit, ac inde eminenter profecit, non ut puerum vel virum dumtaxat, sed ut Deum illum attendens. Unde nec ipsa, nec Joseph, sine debita reverentia ei aliquid injungere consueverunt.
paras.en: [[2:51|And his mother kept all these words|Et Mater ejus conservabat omnia verba hæc]], that is, the words and deeds of her Son, [[2:51|in her heart|in corde suo]], as the best and most teachable disciple of the eternal Wisdom, most capable of wisdom and most eager for it; and whatever her Son did or said thereafter she pondered with the highest veneration, and profited from it eminently, regarding Him not as a boy or a man only, but as God. Hence neither she nor Joseph were wont to bid Him do anything without due reverence.

paras.t: Et Jesus proficiebat ætate, quia tempus quod sibi accrevit, fructuosissime expendebat, et sapientia et gratia apud Deum et homines, id est veraciter coram Deo et hominibus, Deum in omnibus pura conscientia honorando, et proximos ædificando, suam sapientiam, perfectionem et gratiam eis paulatim manifestando, secundum quod ætate processit; ut per hoc ad Dei honorem et gloriam provocarentur. Denique quoad Deum, sufficit bona conscientia; sed propter homines exigitur bona fama, exemplarisque vita: quam qui negligit, secundum Augustinum, crudelis est. Propter quod in Ecclesiaste legitur: Melius est nomen bonum, quam unguenta pretiosa; et alibi, Curam habe de bono nomine. Apostolus quoque: Provideamus (inquit) bona non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram hominibus; et alibi, Honeste ambuletis ad eos qui foris sunt.
paras.en: [[2:52|And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age|Et Jesus proficiebat ætate]], for He spent most fruitfully the time that was added to Him, [[2:52|in wisdom|et sapientia]] [[2:52|and grace with God and men|et gratia apud Deum et homines]], that is, truly before God and men: honouring God in all things with a pure conscience, and edifying His neighbours, showing them His wisdom, perfection and grace little by little as He went forward in age, that they might be stirred by this to the honour and glory of God. Now as regards God a good conscience suffices; but for the sake of men a good name is required, and a life that gives example: and he who neglects it, according to Augustine, is cruel. Wherefore we read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:2|A good name is better than precious ointments|Melius est nomen bonum, quam unguenta pretiosa]]; and elsewhere: [[Ecclus 41:15|Take care of a good name|Curam habe de bono nomine]]. The Apostle too: [[2 Cor 8:21|we forecast what may be good, not only before God but also before men|Provideamus (inquit) bona non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram hominibus]]; and elsewhere: [[1 Thess 4:11|that you walk honestly towards them that are without|Honeste ambuletis ad eos qui foris sunt]].

paras.t: Postremo jam diligentius intuendum, quomodo Christus profecit sapientia et gratia. Ad quod intelligendum, oportet advertere, quod quum Christus sit Deus et homo in unitate personæ, duplex fuit in eo sapientia, scilicet increata, quæ est ipsummet Verbum æternum ac divina essentia, et creata. Et ista sapientia Christi creata multiplex fuit. Una dicitur Beatorum, qua a principio creationis animæ suæ, ipse secundum animam ut Deo fruentem omnia cognovit in Verbo seu in divina essentia, sicut Beati in patria, imo multo excellentius eis. Insuper fuit in anima Christi a suæ creationis principio, sapientia indita seu infusa, qua cognoscit res per proprias earum species sibi concreatas, suæque animæ connaturales et proportionatas. Nulla enim naturalis perfectio defuit animæ Christi. Unde, quemadmodum, secundum Augustinum, Verbum æternum seu Deus a principio indidit mentibus angelicis intelligibiles rerum species, per quas cognoscunt res cognitione vespertina, præter cognitionem matutinam qua res cognoscuntur in Verbo, sic Verbum animæ Christi sibi unitæ indidit species intelligibiles naturales.
paras.en: Lastly, we must now consider more carefully how Christ advanced in wisdom and grace. To understand this we must observe that, since Christ is God and man in unity of person, there was a twofold wisdom in Him: the uncreated, which is the eternal Word itself and the divine essence; and the created. And this created wisdom of Christ was manifold. One is called the wisdom of the Blessed, by which from the beginning of the creation of His soul He knew, according to His soul as enjoying God, all things in the Word, that is, in the divine essence, as the Blessed do in their fatherland [that is, in heaven], indeed far more excellently than they. Besides, there was in the soul of Christ from the beginning of its creation an implanted or infused wisdom, by which it knows things through their own species [that is, the intelligible likenesses of things by which the mind knows them], created together with it, connatural and proportioned to His soul. For no natural perfection was lacking to the soul of Christ. Hence, as according to Augustine the eternal Word, or God, from the beginning implanted in the angelic minds intelligible species of things, through which they know things by evening knowledge, besides the morning knowledge by which things are known in the Word [Augustine's terms: knowledge of things in themselves, and knowledge of them in God], so the Word implanted natural intelligible species in the soul of Christ united to Him.

paras.t: Præter has sapientias seu scientias, ponunt quidam theologi in anima Christi scientiam acquisitam seu experimentalem; quam S. Thomas primo negavit esse in anima Christi; sed postea in tertia parte retractat hoc, et asserit talem scientiam in Christo ponendam: quia ut ait, nihil eorum defuit Christo quæ Deus in natura humana plantavit, ideo Christus habuit intellectum agentem, ejusque operationem. Operatio autem intellectus agentis est, a phantasmatibus intelligibiles species abstrahere, atque in intellectu eas possibili ponere, ut tertio de Anima dicitur. Itaque in intellectu possibili animæ Christi fuerunt species intelligibiles ab intellectu agente illi impressæ: quod est scientiam acquisitam, quam quidam vocant experimentalem, in Christo consistere, quæ habetur per modum humanum, naturaleque lumen. De qua ad Hebræos ait Apostolus, loquens de Christo: Didicit ex his quæ passus est obedientiam. Et sumitur ibi Discere, pro Experiri. Christus namque non didicit ab aliis scientiam acquisitam, sed per propriam adinventionem eam adeptus est. Hæc secundum Thomam in tertia parte inducta sunt.
paras.en: Besides these wisdoms or kinds of knowledge, certain theologians place in the soul of Christ an acquired or experimental knowledge. St Thomas at first denied that this was in the soul of Christ; but afterwards, in the Third Part [of the *Summa theologiae*, q. 9, as the margin indicates], he retracts this and asserts that such knowledge must be placed in Christ: because, as he says, nothing was lacking to Christ of what God planted in human nature, and so Christ had the agent intellect and its operation. Now the operation of the agent intellect is to abstract intelligible species from the phantasms [the images of the senses] and to set them in the possible intellect, as is said in the third book *On the Soul* [Aristotle]. So in the possible intellect of Christ's soul there were intelligible species impressed on it by the agent intellect: which is to say that there was in Christ acquired knowledge, which some call experimental, had in the human manner and by natural light. Of this the Apostle says to the Hebrews, speaking of Christ: [[Heb 5:8|he learned obedience by the things which he suffered|Didicit ex his quæ passus est obedientiam]]. And there *to learn* is taken for *to experience*. For Christ did not learn acquired knowledge from others, but gained it by His own discovery. These things are brought forward following Thomas in the Third Part.

paras.t: Ex quibus ostenditur, quod Christus in nulla sapientia seu scientia prænominata profecit, quantum ad habitum illius, nisi in scientia acquisita. Fuit quoque anima Christi indesinenter quæque perfecta in actu sapientiæ Beatorum, ac sapientiæ inditæ seu infusæ: unde in nulla earum profecit, nisi quantum ad manifestationem; sed in actu ac habitu sapientiæ acquisitæ profecit, secundum ponentes illam in ipso. Insuper fuit in anima Christi ab incarnationis exordio gratia habitualis, tanta, tamque perfecta, ut per ipsam, et de plenitudine ejus universis fidelibus, qui membra ejus vocantur, influere possit spiritualem sensum ac motum virtutum vivificum, quemadmodum caput influit membris motum naturalem ac sensum. Hinc gratia habitualis et gratia capitis ponitur, secundum rem, una eademque Christo: in qua etiam, secundum rem, nunquam profecit, sed secundum manifestationem dumtaxat; imo gratia illa tanta fuit et est in Christo, quod mens creata majoris gratiæ capax non est. Ponitur quoque in Christo gratia unionis, quæ secundum quosdam est ipsum esse increatum Verbi, humanitati Christi communicatum. Aliqui tamen affirmant, quod gratia unionis in Christo sit quid creatum; sed illi gratiam unionis aliter sumunt. Unde diversitas horum consistit in verbis. Itaque, quoniam humanitati Christi a principio suæ creationis communicata est hypostatica unio cum Verbo æterno, quod est super omne donum creatum, etiam ex tunc ei data est plenitudo gratiæ et donorum sapientiæ ac virtutum, beatitudinum quoque et fructuum, imperfectionem in sua ratione non includentium.
paras.en: From this it is shown that Christ did not advance, as to the habit, in any of the wisdoms or kinds of knowledge named above, except in acquired knowledge. And the soul of Christ was ceaselessly and wholly perfect in the act of the wisdom of the Blessed and of the implanted or infused wisdom: hence He advanced in none of these except as to their showing forth; but in the act and habit of acquired wisdom He did advance, according to those who place it in Him. Moreover there was in the soul of Christ from the beginning of the incarnation habitual grace, so great and so perfect that through it, and of its fulness[[John 1:16||]], He can pour into all the faithful, who are called His members[[1 Cor 6:15||]][[Eph 5:30||]], spiritual sense and the life-giving movement of the virtues, as the head pours into the members natural movement and sense. Hence habitual grace and the grace of headship [*gratia capitis*: the grace by which Christ, as Head of the Church, gives grace to its members] are held to be in reality one and the same in Christ: and in this too He never advanced in reality, but only in its showing forth; indeed that grace was and is so great in Christ that a created mind is not capable of greater grace. There is also held to be in Christ the grace of union, which according to some is the uncreated being itself of the Word, communicated to the humanity of Christ. Others, however, affirm that the grace of union in Christ is something created; but they take *grace of union* in another sense. So the difference between them lies in words. Therefore, since from the beginning of its creation there was communicated to the humanity of Christ the hypostatic union with the eternal Word, which is above every created gift, from then also there was given to it the fulness of grace and of the gifts of wisdom and of the virtues, of the beatitudes too and of the fruits [of the Holy Ghost], such as do not include imperfection in their nature.

3.title: Enarratio capituli tertii: Anno autem quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris
3.title_en: Exposition of the third chapter: “Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar”

paras.t: Quemadmodum Christi annuntiationem, conceptionem, nativitatem, circumcisionem, nominationem, pueritiam descripturus Evangelista, præmisit de Præcursoris annuntiatione, conceptione, ceterisque prædictis; ita nunc de Christi prædicatione, Baptismo et gestis scripturus, præmittit de prædicatione, baptismate factisque Præcursoris, quia præambula et accessoria sunt ad Christi documenta et gesta. Anno autem quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris: qui Octaviano imperatori, cujus et filiam habuit conjugem, in imperio immediate successit. Octavianus autem annis quinquaginta septem regnavit, et anno quadragesimo secundo imperii ejus nati sunt Christus et præcursor ejus: sicque quindecim annis sub Octaviano in mundo hoc conversati sunt, et quintusdecimus annus imperii Tiberii fuit tricesimus annus ætatis Christi ac Præcursoris: quo anno gesta sunt, quæ paulo post describuntur. Procurante, id est, per modum procuratoris regente, Pontio Pilato Judæam. Dicuntque aliqui, quod Pontius fuit proprium nomen ejus, Pilatus vero agnomen. Alii probabilius asserunt, quod proprium ejus nomen fuit, Pilatus; Pontius autem vocatus sit a Pontia insula, in qua stetit: qui, secundum Bedam, duodecimo anno imperii Tiberii ad regendam Judæam ab imperatore hoc missus est. Judæa quoque hic sumitur, non pro toto regno Judæorum, sed pro ea parte Judææ quæ fuit Archelai, ut statim dicetur. Tetrarcha autem Galilææ exsistente Herode Antipa: qui decollavit Joannem, fuitque filius Herodis qui occidit infantes. Porro, tetrarchia dicitur quarta pars regni, a tetra, quod est quatuor, et archos, quod est princeps: unde tetrarcha vocatur princeps quartæ partis regni. Philippo autem fratre ejus exsistente tetrarcha Iturææ et Trachonitidis regionis: quæ duæ provinciæ reputabantur quarta pars regni totius Judææ, quod fuit regnum Herodis Ascalonitæ patris fratrum istorum. Denique iste est Philippus, cujus uxorem, puta Herodiadem, abstulit ei frater suus Herodes Antipas, quem ob hoc increpavit Joannes. Et Lysania exsistente Abilinæ, id est provinciæ sic vocatæ, tetrarcha. Lysanias, secundum Bedam, fuit filius Herodis Ascalonitæ. Josephus vero affirmat, quod fuit nepos ipsius, utpote filius Ptolomæi cujusdam ex Alexandria sorore præfati Herodis: quod verius creditur. Beda autem nomen filii forsitan extense accepit, prout nepotes alicujus, filii ejus dicuntur.
paras.en: As the Evangelist, about to describe the annunciation, conception, nativity, circumcision, naming and childhood of Christ, first set down the annunciation, conception and the rest of these things concerning the Forerunner; so now, about to write of the preaching, Baptism and deeds of Christ, he first sets down the preaching, baptism and deeds of the Forerunner, because they are the preamble and accessories to Christ's teachings and deeds. [[3:1|Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar|Anno autem quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris]]: who succeeded immediately to the empire after the emperor Octavian, whose daughter he had as his wife. Now Octavian reigned fifty-seven years, and in the forty-second year of his reign Christ and His forerunner were born: and so they lived in this world fifteen years under Octavian, and the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius was the thirtieth year of the age of Christ and of the Forerunner: in which year were done the things described a little later. [[3:1|Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea|procurante Pontio Pilato Judæam]], that is, ruling it as procurator. And some say that Pontius was his proper name, and Pilate a surname. Others assert more probably that his proper name was Pilate, and that he was called Pontius from the island of Pontia, where he had lived; and according to Bede he was sent by the emperor to rule Judea in the twelfth year of the reign of Tiberius. *Judea*, too, is taken here not for the whole kingdom of the Jews, but for that part of Judea which had been Archelaus's, as will be said presently. [[3:1|and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee|Tetrarcha autem Galilææ exsistente Herode]], Herod Antipas: who beheaded John[[Mark 6:27||]], and was the son of the Herod who slew the infants[[Matt 2:16||]]. Now a tetrarchy is the fourth part of a kingdom, from *tetra*, which is “four”, and *archos*, which is “prince”: whence a tetrarch is called the prince of the fourth part of a kingdom. [[3:1|and Philip his brother tetrarch of Iturea and the country of Trachonitis|Philippo autem fratre ejus exsistente tetrarcha Iturææ et Trachonitidis regionis]]: these two provinces were reckoned the fourth part of the whole kingdom of Judea, which was the kingdom of Herod the Ascalonite, the father of these brothers. This is the Philip whose wife, Herodias, his brother Herod Antipas took from him, for which John rebuked him[[Mark 6:17||]][[Mark 6:18||]]. [[3:1|and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilina|Et Lysania exsistente Abilinæ, id est provinciæ sic vocatæ, tetrarcha]], that is, of the province so called. Lysanias, according to Bede, was the son of Herod the Ascalonite. Josephus, however, affirms that he was his grandson, namely the son of a certain Ptolemy of Alexandria by the sister of the said Herod: which is believed to be truer. Bede perhaps took the name *son* in a broad sense, as the grandsons of a man are called his sons.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod Herodes Ascalonita sex habuit filios, quorum tres ipse adhuc vivens occidit; ipsoque mortuo, tres reliqui filii ejus, videlicet Archelaus, Herodes Antipas, et Philippus contendebant de regno patris habendo. Tandem Octavianus imperator de senatus consilio, regnum Herodis Ascalonitæ defuncti divisit in quatuor partes, dans duas Archelao, puta Judæam et Idumæam, tertiam vero Herodi Antipæ, videlicet Galilæam, quartam Philippo, utputa Ituræam et Trachonitidem regionem. Archelaus demum decimo sui dominii anno apud imperatorem de tyrannide accusatus, a principatu depositus est, atque in exsilium relegatus; et tunc una pars principatus sui, scilicet Judæa, cœpit per procuratores et officiales Romanorum administrari, quorum quintus legitur fuisse Pilatus.
paras.en: Further, note that Herod the Ascalonite had six sons, three of whom he slew himself while still alive; and when he was dead his three remaining sons, namely Archelaus, Herod Antipas and Philip, contended over the possession of their father's kingdom. At length the emperor Octavian, on the advice of the senate, divided the kingdom of the dead Herod the Ascalonite into four parts, giving two to Archelaus, namely Judea and Idumea, the third to Herod Antipas, namely Galilee, and the fourth to Philip, namely Iturea and the country of Trachonitis. Archelaus, at last, in the tenth year of his rule, was accused of tyranny before the emperor, deposed from his principality and banished into exile; and then one part of his principality, namely Judea, began to be administered by procurators and officials of the Romans, of whom Pilate is said to have been the fifth.

paras.t: Sub principibus sacerdotum Anna et Caipha: non quod isti duo simul pontifices fuerunt; sed Annas pontifex fuit anno quo Præcursor orsus est prædicare, Caiphas autem anno quo passus est Dominus. Tempore autem intermedio inter hos duos pontifices, fuerunt et alii tres sibi invicem succedentes, videlicet Ismael, Eleazarus, et Simon. Refert equidem Josephus, quod tunc sub imperio Romanorum, sacerdotium fuit irreverenter venale, ita quod præceptis legis de successione pontificum per vim et ambitionem cessantibus, nulli honor pontificatus, vitæ vel generis merito præstabatur. Unde Valerius Gratus, Anna a pontificatu remoto, Ismaelem filium Baphi designavit pontificem: quo post modicum temporis abjecto, Eleazarum Ananiæ pontificis filium subrogavit, quem post annum amovit, et Simoni Caiphæ filio episcopatum tradebat: qui non plus quam per annum pontifex exsistens, successorem accepit Josephum, qui et Caiphas dictus est. Itaque de his duobus facit Evangelista, aliis omissis, mentionem, quia ad Christi magis pertinent passionem ac persecutionem. Frequentius quoque dicuntur sibi in pontificio successisse, et quod affinitate conjuncti fuerunt. Factum est verbum Domini super Joannem Zachariæ filium, in deserto.
paras.en: [[3:2|Under the high priests Anna and Caiphas|Sub principibus sacerdotum Anna et Caipha]]: not that these two were high priests at the same time; but Annas was high priest in the year in which the Forerunner began to preach, and Caiphas in the year in which the Lord suffered. In the time between these two high priests there were also three others, succeeding one another, namely Ismael, Eleazar and Simon. For Josephus relates that at that time, under the rule of the Romans, the priesthood was irreverently put up for sale, so that, the precepts of the law about the succession of high priests having ceased through force and ambition, the honour of the high priesthood was given to no one for the merit of his life or of his birth. Hence Valerius Gratus, having removed Annas from the high priesthood, appointed as high priest Ismael the son of Baphus [the edition's footnote reads *alias Phabi*]: and having cast him out after a short time, put in his place Eleazar the son of the high priest Ananias, whom he removed after a year, and handed over the office of bishop [that is, of high priest] to Simon the son of Caiphas: who, having been high priest for no more than a year, had as his successor Joseph, who was also called Caiphas. So the Evangelist makes mention of these two, passing over the others, because they belong more to Christ's passion and persecution. And they are more frequently said to have succeeded one another in the high priesthood, and because they were joined by affinity [Caiphas was Annas's son-in-law]. [[3:2|the word of the Lord was made unto John, the son of Zachary, in the desert|Factum est verbum Domini super Joannem Zachariæ filium, in deserto]].

paras.t: Ecce quam solenniter describit Evangelista tempus quo divina revelatio facta est Præcursori de prædicando ac baptizando. Et cur hoc? nisi propter reverentiam et magnificentiam ejus cujus ille fuit annuntiator, videlicet Christi. Denique, juxta Origenem, in libris Prophetarum, ubi commemoratur tempus revelationum eis factarum, solum Judæorum describitur regnum, quoniam sermones Prophetarum ad solos fiebant Judæos. In descriptione vero evangelicæ revelationis ac prædicationis, quæ toti mundo fuerat nuntianda, imperium Romani dominatoris, qui toti orbi videbatur dominari, describitur. Quia tamen et Judæis fuerat Evangelium prædicandum, describuntur et tetrarchiæ eorum: imo, quoniam Christus quem Joannes prædicaturus fuit, rex et sacerdos seu pontifex est, tempus prædicationis Joannis recte per regnum et pontifices est descriptum.
paras.en: See how solemnly the Evangelist describes the time at which the divine revelation was made to the Forerunner about preaching and baptizing. And why this, unless for the reverence and greatness of Him whose herald he was, namely Christ? Further, according to Origen, in the books of the Prophets, where the time of the revelations made to them is recorded, only the kingdom of the Jews is described, since the words of the Prophets were addressed to the Jews alone. But in the description of the gospel revelation and preaching, which was to be announced to the whole world, the empire of the Roman ruler, who seemed to rule the whole world, is described. Yet because the Gospel was to be preached to the Jews too, their tetrarchies also are described: nay, since Christ, whom John was to preach, is King and Priest or High Priest, the time of John's preaching is rightly described by the kingdom and the high priests.

paras.t: Itaque, Factum est verbum Domini super Joannem, id est, divina jussio facta est Joanni, sive per solam inspirationem internam, angelicam vel divinam, sive per exteriorem angelicam apparitionem et allocutionem, vel per imaginariam visionem. Non enim determinat Evangelista quomodo factum sit verbum Domini istud super Joannem, nec exprimit an in vigilia vel in somno. Nec dubium quin ante hoc tempus divinæ illuminationes, inspirationes et allocutiones frequenter sint factæ beatissimo Præcursori; sed nunc primo facta est sibi præceptio exeundi de deserti secreto, et veniendi in publicum, ad prædicandum ac baptizandum. Et venit in omnem regionem Jordanis, id est ad loca Judææ circa fluenta Jordanis. Quoniam enim gratia baptizandi advenit, loca aquis propinqua accedere debuit.
paras.en: So: *the word of the Lord was made unto John*, that is, the divine command was given to John, whether by inward inspiration alone, from an angel or from God, or by an outward appearance and address of an angel, or by an imaginary vision [that is, one seen in the imagination]. For the Evangelist does not determine how this word of the Lord was made unto John, nor does he say whether it was waking or sleeping. Nor is there any doubt that before this time divine enlightenments, inspirations and addresses were often given to the most blessed Forerunner; but now for the first time he received the command to come out of the hiddenness of the desert into public, to preach and to baptize. [[3:3|And he came into all the country about the Jordan|Et venit in omnem regionem Jordanis]], that is, to the places of Judea along the waters of the Jordan. For since he came for the sake of baptizing, he had to go to places near the waters.

paras.t: Prædicans baptismum pœnitentiæ in remissionem peccatorum. Hoc dupliciter explanatur: primo, de Baptismo Christi; secundo, de baptismo Joannis. Primo modo iste est sensus: Prædicans, id est, de proximo futurum ac dandum annuntians suscipiendumque hortans Christi Baptismum, quem Christus per Apostolos et ceteros discipulos suos dedit. Non enim personaliter baptizavit, sed discipuli ejus eo jubente, ut patet in Joanne. Dicitur quoque Baptismus Christi, quoniam eum instituit, et a merito ejus efficaciam habet, gratiamque sortitus est, sicut et cetera legis evangelicæ sacramenta. Itaque Joannes auditoribus suis prædixit instare Christi Baptismum, ut infra in isto habetur capitulo, et in Matthæo et Marco. Dicitur autem Baptismus Christi, baptismus pœnitentiæ, quia adultis non datur nec prodest, nisi pœniteant. Propter quod in Actibus Petrus ait Judæis: Pœnitentiam agite, et baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Christi Jesu in remissionem peccatorum. Nec obest quod ait Ambrosius, Baptismalis gratia non requirit gemitum, neque planctum, quia vel de infantibus loquitur, vel de pœnitentia exteriori, quæ dicitur punitio mali vel satisfactio pro peccato, non de pœnitentia interiori, quæ est displicentia seu detestatio culpæ. Insuper Baptismum istum prædicavit in remissionem peccatorum, docendo quod Christi Baptismus peccata deleret, gratiamque conferret. — Secundo, exponitur de baptismo Joannis, hoc est de baptismo quem dedit: quem prædicavit, quia ad eum accipiendum plebem admonuit. Qui baptismus pœnitentiæ dicitur, quia quos baptizavit ad pœnitentiam hortabatur; et qui baptismum illum accipiebant, sua peccata confitebantur, sicque se pœnitere monstrabant. Rursus, ad hoc baptizavit, ut baptismum suum suscipientes, per illam lotionem in aqua, ad cordialem contritionem et humiliationem provocarentur, sicque ad suscipiendum devote Baptismum Christi et gratiam ejus disponerentur. Sic quoque baptismus Joannis fuit in remissionem peccatorum, non causaliter aut directe, sed dispositive seu præparatorie, quia per modum prætactum baptismus Joannis aptavit præparavitque homines ad Christi Baptismum, ut infra dicetur. — Primo modo exponit Gregorius, dicens: Baptisma quod peccata solveret, quia dare non potuit, prædicabat: ut sicut incarnatum Patris Verbum præcurrebat verbo prædicationis, ita baptismum pœnitentiæ quo peccata solvuntur, præcurreret suo baptismate, quo peccata solvi non possunt.
paras.en: [[3:3|preaching the baptism of penance for the remission of sins|Prædicans baptismum pœnitentiæ in remissionem peccatorum]]. This is explained in two ways: first, of the Baptism of Christ; secondly, of the baptism of John. In the first way the sense is this: *preaching*, that is, announcing as soon to come and to be given, and urging men to receive, the Baptism of Christ, which Christ gave through the Apostles and His other disciples. For He did not baptize in person, but His disciples did at His command, as is plain in John[[John 4:2||]]. And it is called the Baptism of Christ because He instituted it, and it has its efficacy from His merit and has received grace from it, as have the other sacraments of the gospel law. So John foretold to his hearers that the Baptism of Christ was at hand, as we have it below in this chapter[[3:16||]], and in Matthew[[Matt 3:11||]] and Mark[[Mark 1:8||]]. And the Baptism of Christ is called the baptism of penance because it is not given to adults, nor does it profit them, unless they repent. Wherefore in the Acts Peter says to the Jews: [[Acts 2:38|Do penance: and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins|Pœnitentiam agite, et baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Christi Jesu in remissionem peccatorum]]. Nor does it stand in the way that Ambrose says, Baptismal grace does not require groaning or lamentation; for he speaks either of infants, or of outward penance, which is called the punishment of evil or satisfaction for sin, not of inward penance, which is displeasure at or detestation of the fault. Moreover he preached this Baptism *for the remission of sins*, teaching that the Baptism of Christ would blot out sins and confer grace. — Secondly, it is expounded of the baptism of John, that is, of the baptism which he gave: which he preached because he exhorted the people to receive it. It is called the baptism of penance because he exhorted those whom he baptized to penance; and those who received that baptism confessed their sins, and so showed that they repented. Again, he baptized to this end: that those receiving his baptism might be moved, by that washing in water, to heartfelt contrition and humility, and so be disposed to receive devoutly the Baptism of Christ and His grace. Thus too the baptism of John was *for the remission of sins*, not causally or directly, but dispositively or by way of preparation [that is, it did not itself remit sins, but prepared men for the sacrament that does], because in the way touched on above the baptism of John fitted and prepared men for the Baptism of Christ, as will be said below. — Gregory expounds it in the first way, saying: Because he could not give the baptism that would loose sins, he preached it: so that as he ran before the incarnate Word of the Father with the word of preaching, so he might run before the baptism of penance, by which sins are loosed, with his own baptism, by which sins cannot be loosed.

paras.t: Consequenter prædicatio et doctrina Joannis testimonio confirmatur prophetico, ut credibilior comprobetur. Sicut scriptum est in libro sermonum Isaiæ prophetæ, id est, sicut Isaias de Joanne prædixit. Quia beatissimus Isaias tam luculenter ac plene Christi atque Ecclesiæ mysteria prænuntiavit, sed et de Christi præcursore vaticinatus est tam aperte, ut non solum Propheta, sed et Evangelista dicendus sit: cujus librum Lucas rite appellat librum sermonum, propter eloquentiam ejus et sententiarum majestatem, item ob libri illius magnitudinem, qui numero capitulorum ceteros excedit Prophetas. Quid autem ibi scriptum sit, subditur:
paras.en: Next, John's preaching and teaching is confirmed by the testimony of a prophet, so that it may be shown to be the more credible. [[3:4|As it was written in the book of the sayings of Isaias the prophet|Sicut scriptum est in libro sermonum Isaiæ prophetæ]], that is, as Isaias foretold of John[[Is 40:3||]]. For the most blessed Isaias foretold the mysteries of Christ and of the Church so clearly and fully, and prophesied of Christ's forerunner too so openly, that he should be called not only a Prophet but also an Evangelist: and Luke rightly calls his book *the book of the sayings*, because of his eloquence and the majesty of his thoughts, and also because of the size of that book, which exceeds the other Prophets in the number of its chapters. What is written there follows:

paras.t: Vox clamantis in deserto. Per vocem intelligi potest sermo Joannis, vel ipsemet S. Joannes. Primo igitur sensus est: Vox clamantis, id est doctrina, prædicatio, seu sermo Joannis in eremo prædicantis, est iste qui subditur: Parate viam Domini, id est, Christo omnium Domino disponite, facite, parate, præbete medium veniendi ad vos per fidei ac gratiæ infusionem: hoc est, obstacula gratiæ, impedimenta virtutum, videlicet obliquitates vitiorum, seu peccata cuncta abjicite, ad fidem et gratiam vos parate, pœnitentiam agite, quod in vobis est facite; rectas facite semitas ejus, id est, præcepta consiliaque divina, per quorum observationem itur ad Deum, pure et irreprehensibiliter adimplete. Istæ sunt viæ Domini ex parte nostri, id est viæ per quas aptamus nos ad Dei adventum, videlicet ad suscipiendam gratiosam inhabitationem ipsius, vel virtutes et gratiam ejus: a peccato recedere, et bona peragere. De quibus duabus viis fertur in Psalmo, Declina a malo, et fac bonum. Porro, viæ Domini ex parte ipsius, per quas venit ad nos, sunt misericordia et justitia, de quibus cantamus, Universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas; item caritas et liberalitas ejus, quæ ad misericordiam reducuntur. Semitæ autem proprie nominantur itinera secretiora et compendiosiora; viæ vero, itinera apertiora et magis communia. Idcirco, per vias intelligi possunt præcepta, per semitas autem consilia, quæ directius ducunt ad Deum. De quibus in Proverbiis scriptum est: Viæ ejus, scilicet Dei, viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ; atque in Psalmo, Vias tuas, Domine, demonstra mihi, et semitas tuas edoce me. Insuper, sicut corporalis via paratur, quando corporale medium fit, seu perficitur, per quod de uno loco ad alium procedatur; sic spiritualis hæc via Dei paratur, dum per contritionem a malo receditur, et actioni virtuosæ insistitur: sic enim Deus venit ad nos dona gratiæ infundendo, aut infusa perficiendo.
paras.en: [[3:4|A voice of one crying in the wilderness|Vox clamantis in deserto]][[Is 40:3||]] [Denis's lemma is the prophecy as Luke cites it from Isaias]. By *voice* may be understood John's discourse, or St John himself. The first sense, then, is: *The voice of one crying*, that is, the teaching, preaching or discourse of John preaching in the desert, is this which follows: [[3:4|Prepare ye the way of the Lord|Parate viam Domini]], that is, make ready, make, prepare and offer to Christ, the Lord of all, the means of coming to you by the infusion of faith and grace: that is, cast away the obstacles to grace, the hindrances to virtue, namely the crookedness of vices, or all sins; prepare yourselves for faith and grace, do penance, do what lies in you; [[3:4|make straight his paths|rectas facite semitas ejus]], that is, fulfil purely and blamelessly the divine precepts and counsels, by the keeping of which one goes to God. These are the ways of the Lord on our side, that is, the ways by which we make ourselves fit for God's coming, namely for receiving His gracious indwelling, or His virtues and grace: to depart from sin, and to do good. Of these two ways it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 36:27|Decline from evil and do good|Declina a malo, et fac bonum]]. But the ways of the Lord on His side, by which He comes to us, are mercy and justice, of which we sing: [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|Universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas]]; and also His charity and liberality, which come under mercy. Now *paths* are properly the more hidden and shorter routes; *ways*, the more open and common ones. So by the ways may be understood the precepts, by the paths the counsels, which lead more directly to God. Of which it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable|Viæ ejus … viæ pulchræ … pacificæ]] [Denis applies to God what Proverbs says of wisdom]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 24:4|Shew, O Lord, thy ways to me, and teach me thy paths|Vias tuas, Domine, demonstra mihi, et semitas tuas edoce me]]. Moreover, as a bodily way is prepared when a bodily means is made or finished by which one may go from one place to another, so this spiritual way of God is prepared when by contrition one departs from evil and applies oneself to virtuous action: for so God comes to us, pouring in the gifts of grace, or perfecting those poured in.

paras.t: Secundo, per vocem intelligitur ipse Præcursor: quemadmodum apud Joannem quærentibus Judæis, Tu quis es? respondit: Ego vox clamantis in deserto. Dicitur enim vox per similitudinem, ratione sui officii: quia ut vox ordine naturæ prior est verbo, sic Joannes Christum præcessit. Iterum, sicut vox rem significatam notificat, sic Christum Joannes monstravit. Rursus, sicut vox sonat et transit, et verbum in audientium corde relinquit; ita Joannes prædicando sonuit, et per martyrium ad patres descendit, sed Christum in terra atque in credentium corde dereliquit. Postremo, sicut verbum et vox simul sunt tempore, et tamen vox præfato modo prior est verbo; sic Christus et Joannes simul in mundo vixerunt, et tamen Joannes modico tempore Christum præcessit nativitate, prædicatione, baptizatione ac passione. Verumtamen, sicut verbum mentale prius est voce in eo qui loquitur, sic Christus secundum quod est Verbum Patris æterni, fuit et est prior Joanne. Dicitur quoque Joannes vox clamantis, id est Christi, seu Spiritus Sancti per ipsum loquentis. Deus enim loquebatur per ipsum, sicut et Paulus ait: An experimentum quæritis ejus qui in me loquitur Christus?
paras.en: Secondly, by *voice* is understood the Forerunner himself: as in John, when the Jews asked him, Who art thou? he answered: [[John 1:23|I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness|Ego vox clamantis in deserto]]. For he is called a voice by a likeness, by reason of his office: because as the voice is prior to the word in the order of nature [that is, the spoken sound reaches the hearer before the meaning it carries], so John went before Christ. Again, as the voice makes known the thing signified, so John pointed out Christ. Again, as the voice sounds and passes, and leaves the word in the hearers' heart, so John sounded by preaching, and by martyrdom went down to the fathers, but left Christ on earth and in the heart of believers. Lastly, as the word and the voice are together in time, and yet the voice is prior to the word in the way described, so Christ and John lived in the world together, and yet John went before Christ by a little time in his birth, preaching, baptizing and passion. Yet as the word in the mind is prior to the voice in him who speaks, so Christ, as He is the Word of the eternal Father, was and is prior to John. John is also called the voice *of one crying*, that is, of Christ, or of the Holy Ghost speaking through him. For God spoke through him, as Paul too says: [[2 Cor 13:3|Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me|An experimentum quæritis ejus qui in me loquitur Christus?]]?

paras.t: Omnis vallis implebitur, id est, omne cor humile donis gratiæ copiose ditabitur: humilitas enim ad omnem virtutem et gratiam præparat mentem, sicut superbia ad omne peccatum. Et sicut stillicidia a cacuminibus montium descendunt ad bassitudinem vallium, imo quo valles sunt profundiores, eo abundantior in eis colligitur aqua; sic charismata Spiritus Sancti relictis superbis, ad humilium corda descendunt, atque in eis quiescunt, et tanto exuberantius colliguntur, quo Deo profundius substernuntur. Et omnis mons, id est superbus et aliis eminens, et collis, hoc est superbus minor sive inferior, humiliabitur, id est, a Deo spernetur, deprimetur, damnabitur. Hoc est quod loquitur Christus: Omnis qui se humiliat, exaltabitur; et qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Hinc Petrus: Humiliamini, inquit, sub potenti manu Dei, ut vos exaltet in tempore visitationis. In Job quoque legitur: Qui humiliatus fuerit, erit in gloria; et in Proverbiis: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Et erunt prava, hoc est, corda vitiosa convertentur et fient, in directa, hoc est justa, et secundum rectitudinem æquitatis dirigentur; et aspera in vias planas, id est, feroces, rebelles, distortique moribus, erunt obedientes et simplices, ita quod verbum Dei ingrediatur ad eos faciliter, et indurati per gratiam mollificabuntur. Hæc per prædicationem Joannis fieri inceperunt, quia multos convertit; deinde per Christi discipulorumque ejus evangelizationem completa sunt. — Insuper, per valles intelligi queunt corda carnalium per terrenam affectionem depressa, quæ per divinorum amorem impleta sunt; per montes vero et colles, corda vanorum per mundanam vanitatem erecta, quæ per propriæ defectuositatis illuminatam recognitionem humiliata sunt, in primo Salvatoris adventu.
paras.en: [[3:5|Every valley shall be filled|Omnis vallis implebitur]], that is, every humble heart shall be copiously enriched with the gifts of grace: for humility prepares the mind for every virtue and grace, as pride does for every sin. And as the drops of rain run down from the tops of the mountains to the low places of the valleys, and indeed the deeper the valleys, the more abundantly the water gathers in them, so the gifts of the Holy Ghost leave the proud and come down into the hearts of the humble, and rest in them, and gather the more abundantly, the more deeply these lie low before God. [[3:5|and every mountain|Et omnis mons]], that is, the proud man who stands above others, [[3:5|and hill|et collis]], that is, the lesser or lower proud man, [[3:5|shall be brought low|humiliabitur]], that is, shall be scorned, cast down and condemned by God. This is what Christ says: [[Luke 14:11|he that humbleth himself shall be exalted|Omnis qui se humiliat, exaltabitur]]; and [[Luke 14:11|every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled|qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]]. Hence Peter: [[1 Pet 5:6|Be you humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation|Humiliamini, inquit, sub potenti manu Dei, ut vos exaltet in tempore visitationis]]. In Job too we read: [[Job 22:29|he that hath been humbled, shall be in glory|Qui humiliatus fuerit, erit in gloria]]; and in Proverbs[[Prov 3:34||]]: [[Jas 4:6|God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble|Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam]] [these are the words of James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5, which quote Prov 3:34 in the Septuagint's form; the margin gives all three]. [[3:5|and the crooked shall be made|Et erunt prava]], that is, vicious hearts shall be converted and become [[3:5|straight|in directa]], that is, just, and shall be directed according to the rightness of equity; [[3:5|and the rough ways plain|et aspera in vias planas]], that is, the fierce, the rebellious and those crooked in their ways shall be obedient and simple, so that the word of God may easily enter into them, and the hardened shall be softened by grace. These things began to be done through the preaching of John, for he converted many; and then they were completed through the preaching of the gospel by Christ and His disciples. — Further, by the valleys may be understood the hearts of the carnal, sunk low by earthly affection, which were filled by the love of divine things; and by the mountains and hills, the hearts of the vain, lifted up by worldly vanity, which were humbled by the enlightened recognition of their own defects, at the first coming of the Saviour.

paras.t: Porro, offuscati quidam Judæi inductam Isaiæ auctoritatem de vallium impletione, etc., corporaliter nimis ruditerque exponunt, affirmantes in adventu Messiæ, terram penitus complanandam, ut Judæi per orbem dispersi, sine difficultate itineris expeditius confluant ad Judæam: quod super Isaiam plenius reprobavi. Rabbi Moyses quoque hoc reprobat. Verumtamen, quidam Catholici ita exponunt ad litteram de terræ complanatione per montium depressionem, et vallium elevationem seu impletionem, referendo scripturam hanc ad secundum Christi adventum, circa quem terra dicitur complananda.
paras.en: Now certain benighted Jews expound this text of Isaias that is brought in, about the filling of the valleys, etc., in too bodily and crude a way, affirming that at the coming of the Messias the earth is to be levelled completely, so that the Jews scattered through the world may flock to Judea more readily, without hardship on the road: which I refuted more fully on Isaias. Rabbi Moses [that is, Maimonides] also refutes it. Some Catholics, however, expound it literally of the levelling of the earth by the lowering of the mountains and the raising or filling of the valleys, referring this scripture to the second coming of Christ, at which the earth is said to be levelled.

paras.t: Et videbit omnis caro, id est omnis homo, salutare Dei, hoc est Christum, per quem secundum quod homo est, Deus Pater seu Trinitas genus humanum salvavit, dicente Apostolo: Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. Denique, Christum in mundo hoc conversantem omnis homo, id est aliqui de omni genere hominum, corporaliter adspexerunt, quia et multi gentiles sic eum intuiti sunt, præsertim in die Palmarum, quando Pharisæi dixerunt: Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum. Sicque est hic distributio pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum, sicut in Joele Dominus ait: Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem; et Isaias inquit, Cadavera virorum prævaricatorum erunt ad satietatem visionis omni carni. Ex quibus locis id etiam innotescit, quod in Scripturis frequenter ponitur pars pro toto, et caro pro homine. Spiritualiter vero, per fidem et sapientiæ donum multo plures in toto mundo viderunt et contemplati sunt Salvatorem, quemadmodum de gentilibus conversis vaticinatus est Isaias: Quibus non est annuntiatum, viderunt; et qui non audierunt, contemplati sunt. De qua visione ad Hebræos scribit Apostolus: Videmus Jesum propter passionem mortis, gloria et honore coronatum.
paras.en: [[3:6|And all flesh shall see|Et videbit omnis caro]], that is, every man, [[3:6|the salvation of God|salutare Dei]], that is, Christ, through whom, as He is man, God the Father, or the Trinity, saved mankind, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:19|God indeed was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself|Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi]]. Further, every man, that is, some of every kind of men, saw Christ with bodily eyes as He went about in this world, for many gentiles too beheld Him so, above all on Palm Sunday, when the Pharisees said: [[John 12:19|Behold, the whole world is gone after him|Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum]]. And so the distribution here is “for the kinds of individual things, not for the individuals of each kind” [*all* means some of every sort, not every single one], as the Lord says in Joel: [[Joel 2:28|I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh|Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem]]; and Isaias says: The carcasses of the men that have transgressed [[Is 66:24|shall be a loathsome sight to all flesh|erunt ad satietatem visionis omni carni]] [literally “shall be to all flesh a sight to the full”]. From these places it is also made known that in the Scriptures the part is often put for the whole, and *flesh* for man. Spiritually, however, far more throughout the whole world saw and contemplated the Saviour by faith and the gift of wisdom, as Isaias prophesied of the converted gentiles: [[Is 52:15|they to whom it was not told of him, have seen: and they that heard not, have beheld|Quibus non est annuntiatum, viderunt; et qui non audierunt, contemplati sunt]]. Of which sight the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:9|we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour|Videmus Jesum propter passionem mortis, gloria et honore coronatum]].

paras.t: Aliqui autem referunt verbum istud ad secundum Christi adventum, in quo omnis caro, id est electi et reprobi, Christum videbunt in solio majestatis, ac sede judicii, juxta illud Apocalypsis: Ecce venit cum nubibus, et videbit eum omnis oculus. Sic exponit Beda sequens Gregorium, sumens distributionem ejus quod dicitur, Omnis caro, pro singulis generum. Verumtamen ultima particula auctoritatis hic ab Evangelista allegatæ, videlicet, Videbit omnis caro salutare Dei, in Isaia cum præcedentibus verbis quæ in Isaia scripta sunt, secundum translationem Hieronymi non habetur, quantum ad formam verborum; tamen quoad sensum satis ibi includitur, quum dicitur, Et revelabitur gloria Domini: cujus sensus est, Filius Dei ostendetur. Etenim filius gloria patris vocatur, quemadmodum scriptum est: Filius sapiens gloria patris.
paras.en: Some, however, refer this saying to the second coming of Christ, at which all flesh, that is, the elect and the reprobate, shall see Christ on the throne of majesty and the seat of judgement, according to that of the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:7|Behold, he cometh with the clouds, and every eye shall see him|Ecce venit cum nubibus, et videbit eum omnis oculus]]. So Bede expounds it, following Gregory, taking the distribution in *all flesh* “for the individuals of each kind” [that is, every single man]. Yet the last part of the text cited here by the Evangelist, namely *all flesh shall see the salvation of God*, is not found in Isaias, together with the preceding words written in Isaias, in Jerome's translation, as to the form of the words; but as to the sense it is sufficiently included there, where it says: [[Is 40:5|And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed|Et revelabitur gloria Domini]]; the sense of which is, the Son of God shall be shown. For a son is called the glory of his father, as it is written: A wise son is the glory of his father[[Prov 10:1||]] [the words are not those of Prov 10:1, which the margin gives; the thought is nearer Prov 17:6, *gloria filiorum patres eorum*, reversed].

paras.t: Dicebat autem ad turbas quæ exibant ut baptizarentur ab eo. De quibus in Matthæo legitur: Tunc exibat ad eum Jerosolyma, et omnis Judæa, et omnis regio circa Jordanem. Genimina viperarum, hoc est, filii serpentium, videlicet hominum venenatorum, calliditate criminibusque plenorum: de quibus seu qualibus Dominus ait Ezechieli, Subversores et increduli sunt tecum, et cum scorpionibus habitas. Homines quippe nominibus bestiarum exprimuntur, quia illarum proprietatem sequuntur: idcirco astuti et callidi, pungitivi, nocivi, recte serpentes seu viperæ nominantur. Quis ostendit vobis fugere a ventura ira, id est a districto Dei judicio et damnatione æterna? tanquam dicat: Ita impie vixistis et secure peccastis, quasi divinam possetis effugere ultionem.
paras.en: [[3:7|He said therefore to the multitudes that went forth to be baptized by him|Dicebat autem ad turbas quæ exibant ut baptizarentur ab eo]]. Of whom we read in Matthew: [[Matt 3:5|Then went out to him Jerusalem and all Judea, and all the country about Jordan:|Tunc exibat ad eum Jerosolyma, et omnis Judæa, et omnis regio circa Jordanem]] [[3:7|Ye offspring of vipers|Genimina viperarum]], that is, sons of serpents, namely of venomous men, full of cunning and crimes: of whom, or of such as whom, the Lord says to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 2:6|thou art among unbelievers and destroyers, and thou dwellest with scorpions|Subversores et increduli sunt tecum, et cum scorpionibus habitas]]. For men are expressed by the names of beasts, because they follow their properties: and so the astute and cunning, the stinging and harmful, are rightly called serpents or vipers. [[3:7|who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?|Quis ostendit vobis fugere a ventura ira]], that is, from the strict judgment of God and eternal damnation? as though he said: You have lived so impiously and sinned so securely, as though you could escape the divine vengeance.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod in turba illa fuerunt aliqui boni ac pœnitentes, præsertim vulgares, qui recta intentione venerunt ut baptizarentur; aliqui quoque perversi et ficti, qui non ex devotione, sed malignitate venerunt. Quantum ergo ad primos, possunt hæc verba esse commendatio pœnitentium: quos nominat genimina viperarum, non quod patrum suorum sequantur malitiam, sed in laudem filiorum proferatur, quod quum sint filii iniquorum, nihilo minus bene se habeant. Quibus et dicitur: Quis ostendit vobis fugere a ventura ira? id est, quis docuit vos pœnitere, et vitam corrigere, atque ad baptismum venire, per quæ æterna vitatur damnatio? quasi dicat: Non a vobis ipsis nec a patribus vestris, sed a pietate et gratia Dei, hoc accepistis. Ita exponit Ambrosius. Quantum vero ad malos, sunt verba hæc increpatio impœnitentium, secundum sensum prætactum: et illi fuerunt Pharisæi et aliqui Sadducæi. Unde in Matthæo legitur: Videns Joannes multos Pharisæorum et Sadducæorum venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit eis: Progenies viperarum, quis demonstravit vobis fugere a ventura ira?
paras.en: It is to be noted besides that in that crowd there were some good and penitent men, especially common folk, who came with right intention to be baptized; and some also perverse and feigned, who came not from devotion but from malice. As regards the first, then, these words can be a commendation of the penitent: he calls them *offspring of vipers*, not because they follow the malice of their fathers, but it is said in praise of the sons that, though they are sons of the wicked, they nevertheless bear themselves well. And to them it is said: *who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?* that is, who taught you to repent and amend your life and come to baptism, by which eternal damnation is avoided? as though he said: Not from yourselves nor from your fathers, but from the loving-kindness and grace of God have you received this. So Ambrose expounds it. As regards the wicked, these words are a rebuke of the impenitent, in the sense touched on above: and these were the Pharisees and some Sadducees. Hence we read in Matthew: [[Matt 3:7|And seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: Ye brood of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come?|Videns Joannes multos Pharisæorum et Sadducæorum venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit eis: Progenies viperarum, quis demonstravit vobis fugere a ventura ira?]]

paras.t: Denique, secundum Origenem: Vipera, ut fertur, marem coeundo necat, fetusque viperæ exeundo matrem occidit, scisso utero ejus, in vindictam quodammodo genitoris sui perempti. Itaque parricida est proles viperea: talesque erant Judæi qui patres suos spirituales atque doctores interficiebant.
paras.en: Lastly, according to Origen: The viper, as is said, kills the male in mating, and the young of the viper kill the mother in coming forth, tearing open her womb, as if in vengeance for their slain father. So the brood of the viper is parricidal: and such were the Jews, who killed their spiritual fathers and teachers.

paras.t: Consequenter, increpatis et in periculo damnationis constitutis proponit compendiosum consilium. Facite ergo fructus dignos pœnitentiæ, hoc est, actus pœnitentiales interiores et exteriores peragite, secundum exigentiam seu mensuram multitudinis magnitudinisque culparum vestrarum, videlicet intus cordialiter de peccatis dolendo, ore plenarie confitendo, et opera satisfactoria perpetrando: tanto utique amplius atque perfectius, quo plura et majora exstant peccata. Contritio quippe, secundum Hieronymum, debet æquari peccato, ut secundum mensuram gravitatis et numerositatis peccati, ac magnitudinem delectationis seu complacentiæ illicitæ, sit mensura interni doloris seu displicentiæ de peccato, operum quoque pœnitentialium et afflictionis spontaneæ, si adsit opportunitas seu facultas. Itaque pœnitentia debet esse fructuosa, ut veniat ex caritate: aliter enim nihil meretur. Propter quod Antiochus rex frustra pœnituit, nec veniam impetravit, quoniam ex solo servili timore Deum oravit atque pœnituit, ut in libro Machabæorum habetur. De Esau quoque ait ad Hebræos Apostolus, quod non invenit pœnitentiæ locum, quanquam cum lacrimis inquisisset eam. Insuper debet esse operosa, quantum ad opera satisfactoria, laboriosa et afflictiva; item condigna, ut commensuretur quantitati qualitatique culpæ.
paras.en: Next, to those he has rebuked and placed in danger of damnation he puts forward a short counsel: [[3:8|Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of penance|Facite ergo fructus dignos pœnitentiæ]], that is, perform acts of penance, inward and outward, according to the requirement or measure of the number and greatness of your sins: namely, by grieving for your sins from the heart within, by confessing them fully with the mouth, and by doing works of satisfaction; and so much the more fully and perfectly, the more and the greater the sins are. For contrition, according to Jerome, must be equal to the sin, so that according to the measure of the gravity and number of the sin, and the greatness of the unlawful delight or complacency, there may be the measure of inward sorrow or displeasure at the sin, and also of works of penance and voluntary affliction, if there is opportunity or means. So penance must be fruitful, so as to come from charity: otherwise it merits nothing. Therefore King Antiochus repented in vain and did not obtain pardon, since he prayed to God and repented from servile fear alone, as we have it in the book of Machabees[[1 Mach 6:13||]][[2 Mach 9:13||]] [the margin gives I Mach. vi, 12 et seq. and II Mach. ix, 11 et seq.]. Of Esau too the Apostle says to the Hebrews that [[Heb 12:17|he found no place of repentance, although with tears he had sought it|non invenit pœnitentiæ locum, quanquam cum lacrimis inquisisset eam]]. Moreover it must be laborious, as regards works of satisfaction, toilsome and afflictive; and also condign [that is, proportioned to what is owed], so as to be measured to the quantity and quality of the sin.

paras.t: Sed quum peccatum, ex ea parte qua fit contra Deum majestatis et sanctitatis immensæ, sit enormitatis quodammodo infinitæ, quomodo valet quis condigne pœnitere aut satisfacere pro peccato? Et respondendum, quod propria hoc potestate non potest, nec in quantum actus sui ex libero procedunt arbitrio; sed adjutorio Christi, in quantum meritum ejus suis membris per caritatem et sacramentum pœnitentiæ communicatur, sicque in virtute meriti Christi actus pœnitentiales Domino offeruntur; itemque in quantum actus tales procedunt ex caritate infusa, et actuali motione Spiritus Sancti in omni actu meritorio concurrente, qui Spiritus Sanctus est motor dignitatis immensæ. Sicque actio pœnitentiæ virtuosa, ex parte hujus principii cooperantis habet proportionatam efficaciam, et adæquationem bonitatis, contra pravitatem peccati. Iterum dici potest, quod contritio et satisfactio æquari debent offensæ seu culpæ, æqualitate proportionis, utpote per respectum ad hominis possibilitatem, non æqualitate æquiparentiæ. Propter quod dici solet, quod totus mundus pro uno peccato mortali de condigno satisfacere nequeat, propter infinitam ejus qui peccato offenditur dignitatem. Sed Deus ultra posse hominis non requirit; quumque homo debitam diligentiam facit, Deus quasi condignum quid reputat factum: tam infinita est pietas atque dignatio ejus.
paras.en: But since sin, on the side by which it is committed against God of immense majesty and holiness, is of a kind of infinite enormity, how can anyone do condign penance or make satisfaction for sin? The answer is that he cannot do so by his own power, nor inasmuch as his acts proceed from free will; but by the help of Christ, inasmuch as His merit is communicated to His members through charity and the sacrament of penance, and so acts of penance are offered to the Lord in the power of Christ's merit; and again inasmuch as such acts proceed from infused charity and from the actual motion of the Holy Ghost concurring in every meritorious act, the Holy Ghost being a mover of immense dignity. And so the virtuous act of penance, on the side of this co-operating principle, has a proportionate efficacy and an equalling of goodness against the wickedness of sin. Again, it can be said that contrition and satisfaction must equal the offence or sin by an equality of proportion, namely with respect to what man can do, not by an equality of strict parity. Wherefore it is commonly said that the whole world could not make condign satisfaction [*de condigno*: in strict justice] for one mortal sin, because of the infinite dignity of Him who is offended by sin. But God does not require beyond what man can do; and when man uses due diligence, God reckons what is done as though it were condign: so infinite is His loving-kindness and condescension.

paras.t: Et ne cœperitis dicere, Patrem habemus Abraham, hoc est, de carnalis propaginis nobilitate nolite frustra confidere, inaniter superbire, stulte vos jactare, quasi hoc sufficiat ad salutem, quia de viri sancti ac magni Patriarchæ semine nati estis. Noverat S. Joannes, quod carnales illi Judæi de carnis propagine tumuerunt, quod scilicet de Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum semine descendissent: quum tamen ex hoc eorum peccata plus gravarentur, quia quo de sanctioribus patribus descenderunt, eo gravius peccaverunt, illorum virtutes non imitando nec Deo gratias referendo. Unde nil confert carnalis generositas, nisi consimilibus studiis fulciatur, ut ait Cyrillus: idcirco vanum est extolli de bonis prædecessoribus, et deficere ab eorum virtutibus. Denique, secundum Scripturas, imitatores fidei atque justitiæ Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum, potius appellantur illorum filii, quam filii solum carnales; imo tales censentur indigni vocari filii illorum Sanctorum, dicente Apostolo: Non qui semen sunt Abrahæ, hi omnes filii. Unde carnalibus Judæis loquitur Christus apud Joannem: Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite. Quod quia non impleverunt, adjecit: Vos ex patre diabolo estis.
paras.en: [[3:8|and do not begin to say, We have Abraham for our father|Et ne cœperitis dicere, Patrem habemus Abraham]]: that is, do not trust in vain in the nobility of your fleshly descent, do not be proud for nothing or boast foolishly, as though it sufficed for salvation that you were born of the seed of a holy man and great Patriarch. St John knew that those carnal Jews were puffed up by their fleshly descent, namely that they came down from the seed of the Patriarchs and Prophets: though their sins were made the heavier by this, since the holier the fathers they came down from, the more gravely they sinned, by not imitating their virtues nor giving thanks to God. Hence nobility of the flesh avails nothing unless it is supported by like pursuits, as Cyril says: and so it is vain to be lifted up over good forebears and to fall short of their virtues. Lastly, according to the Scriptures, the imitators of the faith and justice of the Patriarchs and Prophets are called their sons rather than those who are only their sons according to the flesh; nay, such are judged unworthy to be called sons of those Saints, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 9:7|Neither are all they that are the seed of Abraham, children|Non qui semen sunt Abrahæ, hi omnes filii]]. Hence Christ says to the carnal Jews in John: [[John 8:39|If you be the children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham|Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite]]. And because they did not fulfil this, He added: [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]].

paras.t: Cur autem inaniter inde gloriari non debeant, subdit: Dico enim vobis, quia potest Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare, id est procreare seu ad esse deducere, filios Abrahæ. Quod tripliciter intelligi potest et verificari: Primo, per lapides intelligendo ipsa saxa a Joanne ad oculum demonstrata, qui ut communiter fertur, monstravit illos duodecim lapides quos Josue fecit asportari de siccato fundo Jordanis, quum Deus Jordanis alveum desiccasset, et filii Israel per illum transissent, ut in Josue narratur; per filios vero intelligendo homines justos, qui fidem et perfectionem Abrahæ assequendo, spirituales ejus filii essent. Etenim Deus omnipotens, qui cuncta de nihilo fecit, naturas rerum commutare et in se invicem convertere facillime potest. — Secundo, per lapides intelligendo gentiles a Judæis vehementer contemptos, qui instar lapidum spiritualiter duri, impoliti, seu incircumcisi, ac steriles erant, et idola muta lapideaque colendo illis conformati fuerunt, secundum illud Psalmistæ: Similes illis fiant qui faciunt ea, et omnes qui confidunt in eis. — Tertio, per lapides intelligendo saxa præfata seu alia, et per filios Abrahæ intelligendo carnales filios ejus. Sed forte mirum apparet, quomodo fieri id potuerit aut possit, præsertim quum tempore illo Abraham obierit, et carnales filii ex carnali semine propagentur. Nihilo minus Deus cujus potestas est penitus infinita, hoc pluribus modis potest: Primo, quoniam unum exsistens, in aliud subsistens, transsubstantiando potest convertere, sicut quotidie peragit in altari: sicque lapides in Judæos tunc seu nunc exsistentes, convertere quivit et valet. Insuper potuit Abraham resuscitare, et lapides in semen ejus convertere: et hoc, pluribus modis; sed de isto pertranseo, quia ad curiositatem potius quam devotionem pertinere videtur.
paras.en: And why they ought not to glory in it in vain, he adds: [[3:8|For I say unto you that God is able of these stones, to raise up|Dico enim vobis, quia potest Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare]], that is, to beget or bring into being, [[3:8|children to Abraham|filios Abrahæ]]. This can be understood and made true in three ways. First, by the stones understanding the very rocks John pointed out to their eyes: for, as is commonly said, he showed them those twelve stones which Josue had carried out of the dried bed of the Jordan, when God had dried up the channel of the Jordan and the children of Israel had passed through it, as is told in Josue[[Jos 4:8||]]; and by the children understanding just men, who by attaining the faith and perfection of Abraham would be his spiritual sons. For almighty God, who made all things out of nothing, can most easily change the natures of things and turn them into one another[[Esth 13:9||]]. — Secondly, by the stones understanding the gentiles, greatly despised by the Jews, who like stones were spiritually hard, unpolished or uncircumcised, and barren, and by worshipping dumb idols of stone had become like them, according to that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 113:16|Let them that make them become like unto them: and all such as trust in them.|Similes illis fiant qui faciunt ea, et omnes qui confidunt in eis.]] — Thirdly, by the stones understanding the said rocks or others, and by the children of Abraham his sons according to the flesh. But perhaps it seems wonderful how this could have been done, or could be, especially since Abraham had died by that time and children of the flesh are propagated from fleshly seed. Nevertheless God, whose power is wholly infinite, can do it in several ways. First, because He can convert one existing thing into another subsisting thing by transubstantiation, as He does daily on the altar: and so He could and can convert stones into Jews living then or now. Besides, He could raise Abraham up and turn the stones into his seed[[Dan 6:14||]] [the margin gives Dan. vi, 14; the reference is unclear here]: and this in several ways; but I pass over this, since it seems to belong to curiosity rather than devotion.

paras.t: Porro quoad secundum sensum, Deus verba Joannis implevit, quando per Apostolorum prædicationem innumerabiles in toto mundo gentiles convertit, quemadmodum Isaias in libro suo admirans et gratulans ait ad eum: Ecce gentem quam nesciebas, vocabis; et gentes quæ non cognoverunt te, ad te current. Per Zachariam quoque, quum Unigenitus Dei de sua incarnatione dixisset, Lauda et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce ego venio et habitabo in medio tui, adjecit: Et applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illo, et erunt mihi in populum. De quibus ad Galatas Apostolus: Qui (inquit) ex fide sunt, hi sunt filii Abrahæ. De carnalibus vero incredulisque Judæis, in Apocalypsi inducitur: Dicunt se Judæos esse, et non sunt, sed sunt synagoga Satan.
paras.en: Further, as to the second sense, God fulfilled John's words when through the preaching of the Apostles He converted innumerable gentiles in all the world, as Isaias in his book says to Him in wonder and rejoicing: [[Is 55:5|Behold thou shalt call a nation, which thou knewest not: and the nations that knew not thee shall run to thee|Ecce gentem quam nesciebas, vocabis; et gentes quæ non cognoverunt te, ad te current]]. Through Zacharias too, when the Only-begotten of God had said of His incarnation, [[Zach 2:10|Sing praise, and rejoice, O daughter of Sion: for behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee|Lauda et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce ego venio et habitabo in medio tui]], He added: [[Zach 2:11|And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and they shall be my people|Et applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illo, et erunt mihi in populum]]. Of whom the Apostle says to the Galatians: [[Gal 3:7|they who are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham|Qui … ex fide … filii Abrahæ]]. But of the carnal and unbelieving Jews it is said in the Apocalypse: They [[Apoc 2:9|say they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan|Dicunt se Judæos esse, et non sunt, sed sunt synagoga Satan]] [the margin reads Apoc. iii, 9, where the same words end “but do lie”; the synagogue of Satan is at 2:9].

paras.t: Consequenter aliam causam adducit, cur de generis nobilitate se jactare non debeant. Jam enim securis ad radicem arboris posita est. Quidam per securim intelligunt mortem seu mortis sententiam, quæ hominem de præsenti vita præscindit; per radicem autem intelligunt Adam a quo totum genus humanum, vel Abraham a quo plebs Judæorum, velut a radice exorta est; per arborem vero intelligunt genus humanum, vel Israeliticam plebem. Quando autem Joannes hæc dixit, tam Adam quam Abraham, per mortem erant de hac vita sublati. Per hoc patuit posteros eorum similiter esse tollendos citoque morituros, secundum illud: Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora. — Alii per securim intelligunt rigorem divinæ æquitatis; per arborem, personam seu vitam cujuslibet hominis; per radicem, hominis fundamentum seu firmitatem: ut sit sensus, quod rigor seu ultio divinæ justitiæ posita est, seu imminet, homini peccatori, ut funditus eum disperdat ac damnet, nisi pœniteat, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico legitur: Nisi pœnitentiam egerimus, incidemus in manus Dei, et non in manus hominum. Et in Deuteronomio ait Dominus Deus: Ipse est Deus fortis reddens odientibus se statim, ita ut disperdat eos, et ultra non differat, protinus restituens eis quod merentur.
paras.en: Next he brings forward another reason why they ought not to boast of the nobility of their race: [[3:9|For now the axe is laid to the root of the trees|Jam enim securis ad radicem arboris posita est]] [Denis reads *arboris*, “of the tree”, where the Vulgate has *arborum*]. Some by the axe understand death, or the sentence of death, which cuts man off from the present life; by the root, Adam, from whom the whole human race sprang as from a root, or Abraham, from whom the Jewish people sprang; and by the tree, the human race, or the people of Israel. Now when John said this, both Adam and Abraham had been taken from this life by death. By this it was plain that their descendants too were to be taken away and would soon die, according to that saying: [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]. — Others by the axe understand the rigour of the divine equity; by the tree, the person or life of each man; by the root, man's foundation or firmness: so that the sense is that the rigour or vengeance of divine justice is laid to, or hangs over, the sinner, to destroy and damn him utterly unless he repent, as we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 2:22|If we do not penance, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, and not into the hands of men|Nisi pœnitentiam egerimus, incidemus in manus Dei, et non in manus hominum]] [the margin's chapter numeral is unreadable; the words are at Ecclus 2:22]. And in Deuteronomy the Lord God says: He is a strong God[[Deut 7:9||]], [[Deut 7:10|repaying forthwith them that hate him, so as to destroy them, without further delay immediately rendering to them what they deserve|reddens odientibus se statim, ita ut disperdat eos, et ultra non differat, protinus restituens eis quod merentur]].
