paras.t: Iterum, per radicem intelligi potest nativitas hominis; per securim, transitus vitæ præsentis a nativitate incipiens; per arborem, homo. Itaque securis ad radicem arboris est posita, quoniam a nativitatis exordio homo ad mortis occasum tendit continuo. Siquidem nox quasi unus carpentator, unam vitæ præscindit medietatem, diesque aliam, et tandem necesse est hominem velut arborem cadere. Et utique, sicut Salomon ait, Si ceciderit lignum ad austrum, aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit: hoc est, dum homo moriendo defecerit atque transierit ad regnum cœlorum, quod per austrum, in quo calor solaris est fortior, vel ad infernum, qui aquilonis nomine designatur, quia ibidem frigus intentius est, in altero horum locorum æternaliter permanebit. Hinc ait Bernardus: Si vis scire quo casura sit arbor, ramos ascende, et quo ponderosior ramorum est copia, illuc casuram non dubites. Rami arboris sunt desideria hominis: in quo si carnalia desideria præponderent, ad inferos cadet; si spiritualia, ad cœlos volabit.
paras.en: Again, by the root can be understood man's birth; by the axe, the passing of the present life, which begins from birth; by the tree, man. So the axe is laid to the root of the tree, since from the beginning of his birth man tends continually toward the setting of death. For the night, like one woodcutter, cuts away one half of life, and the day the other, and at last man must fall like a tree. And indeed, as Solomon says, [[Eccles 11:3|If the tree fall to the south, or to the north, in what place soever it shall fall, there shall it be|Si ceciderit lignum ad austrum, aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit]]: that is, when man fails in dying and passes over, whether to the kingdom of heaven, signified by the south, where the sun's heat is stronger, or to hell, designated by the name of the north, because the cold there is more intense, in one or other of these places he will remain for ever. Hence Bernard says: If you would know where the tree will fall, climb up its branches, and where the mass of branches is heavier, there doubt not it will fall. The branches of the tree are the desires of man: if in him the carnal desires weigh more, he will fall to hell; if the spiritual, he will fly to heaven.

paras.t: Postremo, secundum Origenem et Cyrillum, sanctus Præcursor prædictis verbis prophetavit populo Judæorum de propinquo imminere interitum, captivitatem, dispersionem, et damnationem, propter eorum infidelitatem atque duritiam.
paras.en: Lastly, according to Origen and Cyril, the holy Forerunner by these words prophesied to the Jewish people that destruction, captivity, dispersion and damnation were close at hand, because of their unbelief and hardness.

paras.t: Ex quibus verbis comminatoriis infert Joannes: Omnis ergo arbor, hoc est quicumque homo viator ratione utens, quæ non fecerit fructum bonum, id est actum virtuosum et meritorium, si adsit facultas, excidetur, hoc est, ab electorum consortio avelletur, atque in hora mortis tolletur, et in ignem æternæ damnationis mittetur: sicut de reprobis ait Psalmista, In ignem dejicies eos, in miseriis non subsistent. Christus quoque in Joanne loquitur: Si quis in me non manserit, mittetur foras sicut palmes, et arescet; et colligent eum, et in ignem mittent, et ardet. Ex his verbis ostenditur, quod sola boni omissio sit peccatum mortale, hominemque condemnet, quando videlicet per eam præceptum affirmativum negligitur. Præcepta autem affirmativa obligant semper, sed non ad semper, sed ad tempus aptum ac debitum; et dum in illo opus jussum omittitur, mortale peccatum est, sive de interiori sive de exteriori operatione accipiatur. Hinc in Matthæo inquit Salvator: Servum inutilem projicite in tenebras exteriores. Unde et Christus in die judicii non perhibet se increpaturum damnaturumque reprobos, nisi propter bonorum omissionem, dicendo: Esurivi, et non dedistis mihi manducare. Denique hoc valde terribile est potissimum acediosis. Nam si sola omissio æterno igne punitur, vitiosa actio quid meretur? Si sterilitas condemnatur, continuata impietas, fœda delectatio, affectuosa peccati prosecutio, quam dire torquebitur?
paras.en: From these threatening words John infers: [[3:9|Every tree therefore|Omnis ergo arbor]], that is, every wayfaring man who has the use of reason, [[3:9|that bringeth not forth good fruit|quæ non fecerit fructum bonum]] [the edition's footnote gives the variant *non faciens*, as in the Vulgate], that is, a virtuous and meritorious act, if he has the means, [[3:9|shall be cut down|excidetur]], that is, shall be torn away from the fellowship of the elect and taken away in the hour of death, [[3:9|and cast into the fire|et in ignem]] of eternal damnation: as the Psalmist says of the reprobate, [[Ps 139:11|thou wilt cast them down into the fire: in miseries they shall not be able to stand|In ignem dejicies eos, in miseriis non subsistent]]. Christ too says in John: [[John 15:6|If any one abide not in me, he shall be cast forth as a branch and shall wither: and they shall gather him up and cast him into the fire: and he burneth.|Si quis in me non manserit, mittetur foras sicut palmes, et arescet; et colligent eum, et in ignem mittent, et ardet]] From these words it is shown that the mere omission of good is a mortal sin and condemns a man, namely when an affirmative precept is neglected by it. Now affirmative precepts bind always, but not for always [that is, the obligation never lapses, but it does not require the act at every moment], but for the fit and due time; and when the commanded work is omitted at that time, it is a mortal sin, whether it is taken of an inward or an outward work. Hence the Saviour says in Matthew: [[Matt 25:30|the unprofitable servant, cast ye out into the exterior darkness|Servum inutilem projicite in tenebras exteriores]]. Hence too Christ does not declare that at the day of judgment He will rebuke and condemn the reprobate for anything but the omission of good, saying: [[Matt 25:42|For I was hungry and you gave me not to eat|Esurivi, et non dedistis mihi manducare]]. Lastly, this is very terrible above all for the slothful [*acediosis*: those given to *acedia*, spiritual sloth; the edition's footnote gives the variant *vitiosis*, “the vicious”]. For if mere omission is punished with eternal fire, what does a sinful act deserve? If barrenness is condemned, how dreadfully will continued impiety, foul delight, and the eager pursuit of sin be tormented?

paras.t: Id quoque pensandum, quod sunt quædam arbores quæ nullum fructum producunt: per quas otiosi et acediosi signantur, quibus Judas apostolus in sua ait Canonica: Hi sunt in epulis suis convivantes sine timore, arbores autumnales, eradicatæ, bis mortuæ. Quibus competit illud Osee: Radix eorum exsiccata est, fructum nequaquam facient; et rursus, Abjiciet eos Dominus Deus meus, quia non audierunt vocem ejus. Aliæ sunt arbores fructum facientes, sed inutilem: per quas designantur hypocritæ, de quibus loquitur Christus, Receperunt mercedem suam. Unde in Job legitur: Laus impiorum brevis est, et gaudium hypocritæ ad instar puncti. Aliæ arbores fructum faciunt malum: per quas notantur hæretici, quibus competit illud Apostoli, Impii proficient in pejus, errantes et in errorem mittentes. Aliæ fructum proferunt bonum: per quas virtuosi signantur. Circa hæc ait Chrysostomus: Eleganter dicitur, Non faciens fructum, et adjicitur, bonum. Officiosum enim hoc animal, scilicet hominem, Deus creavit; et naturalis est ei exercitiorum instantia, otium vero innaturale. Obest enim inertia etiam cunctis corporis membris: nulli autem tantum ut animæ: ipsa namque quum naturaliter sit continuo mobilis, otiari non patitur.
paras.en: This too is to be weighed: that there are some trees which bear no fruit at all: by which the idle and the slothful [*acediosi*: given to *acedia*, the spiritual sloth that finds no relish in the things of God] are signified, to whom the apostle Jude says in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jude 1:12|feasting together without fear|Hi sunt in epulis suis convivantes sine timore]], [[Jude 1:12|trees of the autumn|arbores autumnales]], [[Jude 1:12|twice dead, plucked up by the roots|eradicatæ, bis mortuæ]] [Denis has the last two words in the reverse order]. To them that saying of Osee applies: [[Osee 9:16|their root is dried up, they shall yield no fruit|Radix eorum exsiccata est, fructum nequaquam facient]]; and again: [[Osee 9:17|My God will cast them away, because they hearkened not to him|Abjiciet eos Dominus Deus meus, quia non audierunt vocem ejus]] [Denis has *Dominus Deus meus … vocem ejus* where the Vulgate has *Deus meus … eum*]. There are other trees that bear fruit, but useless fruit: by which hypocrites are meant, of whom Christ says: [[Matt 6:2|they have received their reward|Receperunt mercedem suam]]. Hence we read in Job: [[Job 20:5|the praise of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment|Laus impiorum brevis est, et gaudium hypocritæ ad instar puncti]]. Other trees bear bad fruit: by which heretics are denoted, to whom that saying of the Apostle applies: [[2 Tim 3:13|shall grow worse and worse: erring, and driving into error|proficient in pejus, errantes et in errorem mittentes]] [Denis has *Impii*, “the wicked”, where the Vulgate has *Mali homines et seductores*]. Others bring forth good fruit: by which the virtuous are signified. On this Chrysostom says: It is elegantly said, *not bringing forth fruit*, and then is added, *good*. For God created this creature, man, to be busy; and continual exercise is natural to him, while idleness is against his nature. For sloth harms all the members of the body too, but none so much as the soul: for the soul, being by nature always in motion, cannot bear to be idle.

paras.t: Quam fructuosa autem fuerit prædicatio Præcursoris, mox subditur: Et interrogabant eum turbæ, dicentes: Quid ergo faciemus? id est, quum tam rigorose nos increpasti, et tantum nobis instet periculum, quod das consilium evadendi mala quæ comminaris? Turba hæc, scilicet vulgus, videns immobilem æquitatem, rigorosissimam sanctissimamque vitam Joannis, et quod in omnibus nihil nisi eorum salutem intenderet, verbis ejus credidit, atque ex eis vehementer compuncta ac territa est, idcirco petivit consilium: sicut et in Actibus, Judæi ex verbis Petri compuncti, dixerunt Apostolis: Quid faciemus, viri fratres? Sed Pharisæi et Scribæ nequaquam ita fecerunt, nec petierunt ex corde salutis consilium. Quo patet, quod litterati, et in sua scientia gloriantes, difficilius corriguntur, quam idiotæ ac simplices: imo scioli illi ac sapientes in oculis suis, frequenter irrident idiotas qui convertuntur, quemadmodum apud Joannem doctores Judæorum dixerunt: Numquid aliquis ex principibus credidit in eum (scilicet in Jesum Christum), aut ex Pharisæis? sed turba hæc quæ non novit legem, maledicti sunt.
paras.en: How fruitful the Forerunner's preaching was, is shown at once: [[3:10|And the people asked him, saying: What then shall we do?|Et interrogabant eum turbæ, dicentes: Quid ergo faciemus?]] that is: Since thou hast rebuked us so severely, and so great a danger hangs over us, what counsel dost thou give for escaping the evils thou threatenest? This crowd, the common people, seeing John's unshakeable justice and his most strict and holy life, and that in everything he aimed at nothing but their salvation, believed his words, and was greatly pierced and frightened by them, and so asked for counsel: as in the Acts too the Jews, pierced by Peter's words, said to the Apostles: [[Acts 2:37|What shall we do, men and brethren?|Quid faciemus, viri fratres?]] But the Pharisees and Scribes did nothing of the kind, nor did they ask from the heart for the counsel of salvation. From which it is plain that the learned, who glory in their knowledge, are corrected with more difficulty than the unlettered and simple: nay, those smatterers, wise in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]], often mock the unlettered who are converted, as in John the doctors of the Jews said: [[John 7:48|Hath any one of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees?|Numquid aliquis ex principibus credidit in eum (scilicet in Jesum Christum), aut ex Pharisæis?]] [[John 7:49|But this multitude, that knoweth not the law, are accursed|sed turba hæc quæ non novit legem, maledicti sunt]].

paras.t: Respondens autem, dicebat illis: Qui habet duas tunicas, hoc est quodcumque indumentum superfluum, det non habenti, id est indigenti; et qui habet escas superfluas, id est quodcumque aptum pro alimento, sive sit bladum, sive panis, vel aliquid simile, similiter faciat, hoc est quod sibi et suis necessarium non est, pauperibus largiatur. Non solum caritas, sed et ordo diligendi est in præcepto, ut homo super omnia diligat Deum, deinde se ipsum, deinde proximos, secundum quod majus vel minus sibi conjuncti sunt, aut major est ratio eos amandi. Ideo debet homo primo sibi ipsi necessaria ministrare, deinde quod superest necessitati indigentibus communicare, secundum quod sibi fieri rationabiliter vellet, si in simili esset penuria. Nam et fraterna caritas hoc requirit.
paras.en: [[3:11|And he answering, said to them: He that hath two coats|Respondens autem, dicebat illis: Qui habet duas tunicas]], that is, any superfluous garment, [[3:11|let him give to him that hath none|det non habenti]], that is, to one in need; [[3:11|and he that hath meat|et qui habet escas]] beyond his needs, that is, anything fit for food, whether it be corn or bread or anything like it, [[3:11|let him do in like manner|similiter faciat]]: that is, what is not necessary for himself and his own, let him bestow on the poor. Not only charity, but also the order of charity falls under the commandment: that a man love God above all things[[Deut 6:5||]][[Matt 22:37||]], then himself, then his neighbours, according as they are more or less closely joined to him, or as there is greater reason to love them. Therefore a man ought first to supply what is necessary to himself, and then share what remains over his needs[[Luke 11:41||]] [the margin reads Luc. xi, 44; *quod superest* is at 11:41] with those in want, as he would reasonably wish to be done to himself if he were in like penury. For fraternal charity too requires this.

paras.t: Denique verba ista Joannis attendenda sunt valde, imo et formidanda ac observanda. Si enim quod necessitati superfluit de vestimento, cibo et potu et similibus, pauperibus est misericorditer impertiendum, quid in divino judicio responsuri sunt, qui tot vestimentis pretiosis seu curiosis, non necessariis, abundant? qui tot ferculorum genera sibi quotidie parant, qui tantam sibi pecuniam aggregant, pauperibus vero permodicum, et non nisi siccum panem impendunt? Quod si de patrimonio proprio, seu possessione propria, sic agere tam impium est atque damnabile, quis eloqui queat, quam sacrilegum ac damnosum consistat, de patrimonio Crucifixi, de bonis Ecclesiæ, quæ sunt eleemosynæ pauperum, pretiosa, curiosa, superflua vestimenta habere, delicate ac splendide epulari, pauperibus aut parum aut nihil præstare? præsertim quum teste B. Bernardo in epistola ad quemdam canonicum, Quidquid de talibus bonis ultra simplicem victum et vestitum tenetur, furtum est, sacrilegium ac rapina. Imo S. Hieronymus de omnibus generaliter dicit: Quidquid humano usui necessarium est, pro una tunica habendum est; totum residuum, superfluum, et pauperibus erogandum. Aliena enim rapere convincitur, qui superflua retinere probatur. Ambrosius quoque et Basilius asserunt vestem, pecuniam, calceamentum et alimentum, quæ tibi superfluunt, nec tamen pauperibus tribuuntur, injuste, et velut furto aut vi ablata possideri, nec possidentis esse, sed egenorum.
paras.en: These words of John, then, are to be heeded greatly, nay, to be feared and kept. For if what is over and above our need in clothing, food, drink and the like is to be given mercifully to the poor, what answer will they make at the divine judgment who abound in so many costly or elaborate garments that they do not need? who every day have so many kinds of dishes prepared for themselves, who heap up so much money for themselves, and spend on the poor very little, and that only dry bread? And if to act so with one's own patrimony or one's own property is so wicked and damnable, who could say how sacrilegious and ruinous it is, out of the patrimony of the Crucified, out of the goods of the Church, which are the alms of the poor, to have costly, elaborate, superfluous clothes, to feast delicately and splendidly, and to give the poor little or nothing? especially since, as blessed Bernard testifies in his letter to a certain canon, whatever of such goods is kept beyond simple food and clothing is theft, sacrilege and robbery. Nay, St Jerome says of all men in general: Whatever is necessary for human use is to be had as the one coat; all the rest is superfluous, and to be given out to the poor. For he is convicted of seizing what is another's who is shown to keep back what is superfluous. Ambrose too and Basil assert that the clothing, money, shoes and food that are superfluous to thee, and yet are not given to the poor, are possessed unjustly, as if taken by theft or violence, and belong not to the possessor but to the needy.

paras.t: Præterea, finis corporalium bonorum, est bonum spirituale, præsertim vera felicitas, vel saltem profectus in Dei obsequio atque virtutibus animæ, prout divina lex præcipit. Bonitas autem mediorum ad finem, ex ipso fine attenditur: sicut medicina in tantum est utilis, in quantum confert ad sanitatem: quam si impediret, mala, superflua, et inutilis judicaretur. In tantum ergo bona corporalia, ut vestis, cibus, ac alia, reputanda sunt licita, bona, atque utilia, in quantum proficua sunt ad spiritualem profectum, ad Dei obsequium, ad vitam æternam: a quibus utique spiritualibus bonis abundantia corporalium impedit, potissimum si quis eis plus utatur quam expedit ad hoc quod anima Deo deserviat, et ejus præcepta custodiat. Ideo, quod necessitati superfluit, egentibus dandum est, sicut Apostolus loquitur: Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. In Proverbiis quoque Salomon ait: Tribue tantum victui meo necessaria. Hinc ait Gregorius: Quoniam tunica magis necessaria est quam pallium, ad fructum dignum pœnitentiæ pertinet, ut non solum exteriora quæque, sed etiam valde nobis necessaria, id est utilia, dividere cum proximis debeamus, videlicet tunicam qua vestimur, et escam qua sustentamur. Quia enim in lege scriptum est, Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum, minus proximum amare convincitur, qui non cum eo in necessitate illius, etiam ea quæ sibi necessaria sunt, partitur. Quibus verbis concordans Basilius: Ex his (inquit) docemur, quod ex omni quod affluit supra proprii victus necessitatem, tenemur erogare illi qui non habet, propter Deum, qui quæcumque possidemus, largitus est. Unde Tobias inquit: Quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors. Si multum tibi fuerit, abundanter tribue; si parum tibi fuerit, etiam exiguum libenter impertiri stude.
paras.en: Moreover, the end of bodily goods is spiritual good, above all true happiness, or at least progress in the service of God and in the virtues of the soul, as the divine law commands. Now the goodness of means to an end is measured by the end itself: as medicine is useful just so far as it helps to health, and if it hindered health it would be judged bad, superfluous and useless. So far, then, are bodily goods, such as clothing, food and the rest, to be reckoned lawful, good and useful, as they are profitable for spiritual progress, for the service of God, for eternal life: and from these spiritual goods an abundance of bodily goods holds us back, especially if one uses them more than is expedient for the soul to serve God and keep His commandments. Therefore what is over and above our need is to be given to the needy, as the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. In the Proverbs too Solomon says: [[Prov 30:8|give me only the necessaries of life|Tribue tantum victui meo necessaria]]. Hence Gregory says: Since the coat is more necessary than the cloak, it belongs to the worthy fruit of penance that we should share with our neighbours not only any outward things, but even those very necessary, that is, useful, to us: the coat we are clothed with and the food we live on. For since it is written in the law, [[Lev 19:18|Thou shalt love thy friend as thyself|Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum]][[Matt 22:39||]][[Gal 5:14||]] [Gregory gives the words as they are quoted in the Gospel and by St Paul, *proximum*, “neighbour”], he is convicted of loving his neighbour less who does not share with him in his need even the things that are necessary to himself. In agreement with these words Basil says: From this we are taught that of all that abounds beyond the needs of our own living we are bound to give to him who has not, for the sake of God, who has bestowed on us whatever we possess. Hence Tobias says: [[Tob 4:8|According to thy ability be merciful.|Quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors]] [[Tob 4:9|If thou have much give abundantly: if thou have little, take care even so to bestow willingly a little|Si multum tibi fuerit, abundanter tribue; si parum tibi fuerit, etiam exiguum libenter impertiri stude]].

paras.t: Venerunt autem et publicani ut baptizarentur a Joanne. Publicani, secundum Bedam, dicuntur vectigalium seu rerum publicarum exactores vel conductores; item qui per negotia lucra sæculi hujus sectantur. Sicque publicani vocati sunt, quia de rebus ad rem publicam pertinentibus se intromiserunt: quorum multi ad prædicationem Joannis se emendaverunt. Propter quod apud Matthæum, Christus principibus sacerdotum et Pharisæis locutus est: Publicani et meretrices præcedent vos in regnum Dei, quia crediderunt ei, puta Joanni. Et dixerunt: Magister, quid faciemus? Non dixerunt, Quid sciemus? sed, Quid faciemus? quia non auditores, sed factores legis justi sunt apud Deum, et scientia sine vita virtutum, obest magis quam prodest. Econtrario faciunt multi, maxime clerici. Quærunt enim: Quomodo hoc aut illud intelligemus? quomodo arguemus?
paras.en: [[3:12|And the publicans also came to be baptized|Venerunt autem et publicani ut baptizarentur]] by John. Publicans, according to Bede, is the name for the collectors or farmers of taxes or of public revenues; and also for those who pursue the gains of this world by trade. And they were called publicans because they busied themselves with things belonging to the commonwealth [*res publica*]: many of whom amended their lives at John's preaching. Wherefore in Matthew Christ said to the chief priests and Pharisees: [[Matt 21:31|the publicans and the harlots shall go into the kingdom of God before you|Publicani et meretrices præcedent vos in regnum Dei]], [[Matt 21:32|believed him|crediderunt ei]], namely John. [[3:12|and said to him: Master, what shall we do?|Et dixerunt: Magister, quid faciemus?]] They did not say, What shall we know? but, What shall we do? For [[Rom 2:13|not the hearers of the law are just before God|non auditores, sed factores legis justi sunt apud Deum]], but the doers; and knowledge without a life of virtue harms more than it helps. Many do the contrary, above all clerics. For they ask: How shall we understand this or that? How shall we argue it?

paras.t: At ille dixit ad eos: Nihil amplius quam quod constitutum est vobis, faciatis, hoc est, non plus exigatis, quam præfixum est vobis a jure, seu dominis quorum tributa levatis. Hoc ideo dicit, quoniam tales solent plura exigere quam jussum est eis, ut quod amplius levant, eis clam maneat. Denique, nullus nostrum legem sibi præstitutam, seu metas suæ potestatis vel officii, transgredi debet, ne præsumptionis sit reus maleque audax; sed quod sibi incumbit, observet, nec aliena invadat, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui. In Deuteronomio quoque scriptum est: Non transferes terminos quos fixerunt priores in possessione tua. Quocontra in libro Job de violentis asseritur: Alii terminos transtulerunt.
paras.en: [[3:13|But he said to them: Do nothing more than that which is appointed you|At ille dixit ad eos: Nihil amplius quam quod constitutum est vobis, faciatis]]: that is, exact no more than has been fixed for you by law, or by the lords whose tributes you levy. He says this because such men are wont to exact more than they are ordered, so that what they levy over may stay secretly with them. And indeed none of us ought to overstep the law set for him, or the bounds of his power or office, lest he be guilty of presumption and of wicked boldness; but let him keep to what is his charge, and not invade what belongs to others, according to that saying of the Proverbs: [[Prov 22:28|Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set.|Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui.]] In Deuteronomy too it is written: [[Deut 19:14|remove thy neighbour's landmark, which thy predecessors have set in thy possession|Non transferes terminos quos fixerunt priores in possessione tua]]. Against which it is said of the violent in the book of Job: [[Job 24:2|Some have removed landmarks|Alii terminos transtulerunt]].

paras.t: Interrogabant autem eum et milites, qui sub Romanorum imperio militabant, ac rem publicam et patriam defendebant, dicentes: Quid faciemus et nos? Secundum Origenem, tres fuerunt ordines interrogantium Joannem: unus, turbarum; secundus, publicanorum; tertius, militum. Joannes autem cuilibet ordini proportionatum dedit responsum. Et ait illis: Neminem concutiatis, opprimendo, corporaliter affligendo, injuste terrendo; neque calumniam, id est fraudulenter injuriam, faciatis, innocentes in causam trahendo, seu quempiam mendaciter accusando; et contenti estote stipendiis vestris, hoc est mercede seu retributione vobis ab imperatore vel vicariis ejus præfixa pro exercitiis militiæ, quibus pro defensione rei publicæ laboratis, nec ultra quidquam ab aliquo extorqueatis. Porro, secundum Augustinum contra Faustum Manichæum, sciebat Joannes eos qui militabant non esse homicidas, sed ministros legis, non ultores injuriarum suarum, sed salutis publicæ defensores; alioqui responderet eis: Abjicite militiam, militiam istam deserite, neminem percutite, vulnerate, prosternite. Præterea ponderanda est sapientissimi Præcursoris discretio, quomodo cuilibet ad se accedenti, secundum illius capacitatem dispositionemque loquitur. Siquidem publicanos ac milites, qui majoribus solent vitiis implicari quam vulgus, primo a malis coercet, et facilia eis proponit præcepta, docens eos primo recedere a peccatis illis ad quæ proniores esse noscuntur, ut eos sic paulatim etiam ad bona agenda, suaque aliis misericorditer communicanda induceret. Hinc dicit Chrysostomus: Volebat Joannes publicanos et milites ad majorem perfectionem traducere; sed quoniam nondum erant ad illam idonei, minora proponit, ne si majora proferret, non illis intenderent, et his etiam privarentur. Hanc discretionem sequamur, et juxta Isaiæ oraculum, calamum quassatum non conteramus, nec linum fumigans exstinguamus; sicque implebimus illud Apostoli: Debemus nos firmiores imbecillitates infirmorum portare, et non nobis placere. Hoc est quod alibi legitur: Recupera proximum tuum.
paras.en: [[3:14|And the soldiers also asked him|Interrogabant autem eum et milites]], who served under the Roman empire and defended the commonwealth and their country, [[3:14|saying: And what shall we do?|dicentes: Quid faciemus et nos?]] According to Origen, there were three orders of those who questioned John: one of the crowds, the second of the publicans, the third of the soldiers; and John gave each order an answer suited to it. [[3:14|And he said to them: Do violence to no man|Et ait illis: Neminem concutiatis]], by oppressing, by bodily ill-treatment, by unjust intimidation; [[3:14|neither calumniate any man|neque calumniam faciatis]], that is, do wrong by fraud, by dragging the innocent into lawsuits or by accusing anyone falsely; [[3:14|and be content with your pay|et contenti estote stipendiis vestris]], that is, with the wage or recompense fixed for you by the emperor or his deputies for the exercises of soldiering, in which you labour for the defence of the commonwealth; and extort nothing further from anyone. Further, according to Augustine against Faustus the Manichee, John knew that those who served as soldiers were not murderers but ministers of the law, not avengers of their own wrongs but defenders of the public safety; otherwise he would have answered them: Throw away your arms, desert this service, strike, wound, lay low no man. Moreover we should weigh the discretion of the most wise Forerunner: how he speaks to each who comes to him according to his capacity and disposition. For the publicans and soldiers, who are wont to be entangled in greater vices than the common people, he first restrains from evil, and sets before them easy precepts, teaching them first to withdraw from the sins to which they are known to be more prone, so that he might thus lead them little by little to doing good as well, and to sharing their goods mercifully with others. Hence Chrysostom says: John wished to bring the publicans and soldiers to greater perfection; but since they were not yet fit for it, he sets lesser things before them, lest, if he put forward greater ones, they should not attend to them and be deprived even of these. Let us follow this discretion, and according to Isaias's oracle, [[Is 42:3|The bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench|calamum quassatum non conteramus, nec linum fumigans exstinguamus]] [Denis turns the prophecy of Christ into an exhortation: “let us not break … let us not quench”]; and so we shall fulfil that saying of the Apostle: [[Rom 15:1|we that are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak and not to please ourselves|Debemus nos firmiores imbecillitates infirmorum portare, et non nobis placere]]. This is what we read elsewhere: [[Ecclus 29:26|Recover thy neighbour|Recupera proximum tuum]] [the margin gives Eccli. xxix, 27, the Vulgate's numbering; Denis adds *tuum*].

paras.t: Existimante autem populo, et cogitantibus omnibus ad baptismum Joannis venientibus, imo et aliis multis, de Joanne, ne, pro an, forte ipse esset Christus. Ad quod opinandum inducebantur ex consideratione mirabilium quæ circa ejus conceptionem et nativitatem acciderant: quia de senibus ac sterili matre angelo prænuntiante fuit exortus, et quia tam strictissime atque sanctissime vixit; item propter prædicationis ejus excellentiam, ac baptismatis novitatem, et quoniam de generosa stirpe descendit, scilicet sacerdotali, quæ regiæ tribui communiter fuit admixta; item, quia tunc apud Judæos fuit publica fama de Christi adventu jam facto, propter verba Simeonis et Annæ atque Magorum, et propter Herodis tyrannidem in infantes: quorum omnium memoria jam renovabatur. Imo adhuc multi vixerunt, qui illa audierant sive conspexerant. Hæc in tantum moverunt Judæos, quod etiam principaliores de Jerusalem miserunt sacerdotes et Levitas ad Joannem, ut interrogarent eum, Tu quis es? sicut in Joanne habetur.
paras.en: [[3:15|And as the people were of opinion, and all were thinking|Existimante autem populo, et cogitantibus omnibus]], all who came to John's baptism, and many others besides, [[3:15|of John, that perhaps he might be the Christ|de Joanne, ne, pro an, forte ipse esset Christus]] [*ne* standing for *an*, “whether”]. They were led to think this by considering the wonders that had happened about his conception and birth: that he was born of aged parents and a barren mother, as the angel had foretold[[1:13||]]; and that he lived so very strictly and holily; and also because of the excellence of his preaching and the newness of his baptism; and because he came of a noble stock, the priestly one, which was commonly intermingled with the royal tribe; and again, because there was then a common report among the Jews that Christ had already come, through the words of Simeon and Anna[[2:25||]] and of the Magi, and through Herod's cruelty against the infants[[Matt 2:16||]] [the margin reads Matth. v; the slaughter of the infants is Matt 2:16]: the memory of all which was now being revived. Indeed many were still living who had heard or seen those things. These things so moved the Jews that even the chief men of Jerusalem [[John 1:19|sent from Jerusalem priests and Levites to him, to ask him: Who art thou?|miserunt sacerdotes et Levitas ad Joannem, ut interrogarent eum, Tu quis es?]], as we have it in John.

paras.t: Respondit Joannes, dicens omnibus. Secreta namque cordis illorum Spiritu Sancto revelante cognovit. Vel, quod homines alia de ipso opinarentur, ex præfatorum legatorum interrogatione cognovit, seu aliunde percepit seu perpendit. Ego quidem baptizo vos in aqua, hoc est, corpora vestra materiali elemento intingo, mentes autem vestras directe non purgo, nec donis gratiæ orno; veniet autem fortior me post me, id est, Christus post me per nativitatem ex Virgine Matre mundum istum intravit, jamque in proximo est ut post hanc meam manifestationem ipse vobis omnibus manifestetur, per meam testificationem ac demonstrationem, et per propriam ejus prædicationem atque miracula: qui secundum suam divinitatem, est fortior me infinite, tanquam Deus omnipotens, cujus immensa est potestas; secundum assumptam quoque ipsius humanitatem, data est ei omnis potestas in cælo et in terra, majorque fuit et est virtus, dignitas, et perfectio ejus, quam omnium creaturarum pariter acceptarum, quia non ad mensuram datus est ei Spiritus, et quoniam humanitas ejus, personali seu hypostatica unione unita est Verbo, ita quod in eodem esse in quo Verbum Patris æternaliter est subsistens, ipsa quoque a principio incarnationis subsistat.
paras.en: [[3:16|John answered, saying unto all|Respondit Joannes, dicens omnibus]]. For he knew the secrets of their hearts by the revelation of the Holy Ghost. Or else he knew that men had other opinions of him from the questioning of the envoys just mentioned, or perceived or gathered it in some other way. [[3:16|I indeed baptize you with water|Ego quidem baptizo vos in aqua]], that is, I dip your bodies in a material element, but your minds I do not directly cleanse, nor adorn with the gifts of grace; [[3:16|but there shall come one mightier than I|veniet autem fortior me]] after me: that is, Christ came into this world after me by His birth from the Virgin Mother, and it is now close at hand that, after this manifestation of mine, He Himself should be made manifest to you all, by my testimony and pointing out, and by His own preaching and miracles: who according to His divinity is infinitely mightier than I, as almighty God, whose power is boundless; and according to the humanity He assumed, [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|data est ei omnis potestas in cælo et in terra]] [Denis turns Christ's words into the third person: “is given to Him”], and His power, dignity and perfection was and is greater than that of all creatures taken together, because the Spirit was not given Him by measure[[John 3:34||]], and because His humanity is united to the Word in a personal or hypostatic union, so that from the beginning of the incarnation it subsists in the same being in which the Word of the Father eternally subsists.

paras.t: Cujus non sum dignus solvere corrigiam calceamentorum ejus. Ad litteram loquebatur S. Joannes juxta communem modum loquendi, quo aliquis volens se alteri maxime humiliare, asserit se indignum ferre seu dissoligare calceos ejus. Unde gloriosus humilisque Baptista, quantum se Christo inferiorem senserit plene effari non valens, protulit verba hæc. In quo profundissima ejus patet humilitas: quia quum talis ac tantus ab omnibus reputaretur, non erubuit se tantum publice coram omnibus deprimere, humiliare ac minorare. Unde clarescit, quod reputatione, reverentia ac laudibus hominum nullatenus flectebatur. At vero indignum se perhibet ad solvendum corrigiam calceamentorum Christi, considerando se secundum naturalia tantum, et quoad id quod habuit a se ipso; itemque loquendo de dignitate absoluta, qua aliquis dicitur ad aliquid dignus simpliciter. In quantum vero plenus fuit tot charismatibus Spiritus Sancti, et movebatur in omnibus ab eodem, dignus fuit mereri etiam vitam æternam: præsertim loquendo de dignitate proportionis, utpote secundum modum possibilitatis humanæ. Secundum quem modum, devotus sacerdos dignus est corpus et sanguinem Christi consecrare ac sumere: alioqui communicandum non esset, quum dicat Apostolus, Qui manducat et bibit indigne, judicium sibi manducat et bibit.
paras.en: [[3:16|the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to loose|Cujus non sum dignus solvere corrigiam calceamentorum ejus]]. Literally, St John was speaking according to the common manner of speech by which someone who wishes to humble himself to the utmost before another says that he is unworthy to carry or to untie his shoes. So the glorious and humble Baptist, unable to express fully how far beneath Christ he felt himself to be, uttered these words. Herein his most profound humility is plain: for though he was thought by all to be so great a man, he was not ashamed to abase, humble and lessen himself so much publicly before all. From this it is clear that he was in no way swayed by the esteem, reverence and praises of men. He declares himself unworthy to loose the latchet of Christ's shoes considering himself according to his natural gifts alone, and as to what he had of himself; and also speaking of absolute worthiness, by which someone is said to be simply worthy of something. But inasmuch as he was full of so many gifts of the Holy Ghost, and was moved in all things by Him, he was worthy to merit even eternal life: especially speaking of the worthiness of proportion [that is, worthiness measured by what is possible to a man, not by what the thing itself deserves], according to the measure of human possibility. In this way a devout priest is worthy to consecrate and receive the body and blood of Christ: otherwise one ought not to communicate, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:29|he that eateth and drinketh unworthily eateth and drinketh judgment to himself|Qui manducat et bibit indigne, judicium sibi manducat et bibit]].

paras.t: Rursus, verba Joannis intelligenda non sunt quasi Christus usus sit calceamentis, quum et discipulis quos misit ad prædicandum, prohibuerit ea. Ipse autem cœpit facere et docere. Idcirco, ut dictum est, verbum Joannis secundum morem generalis proverbii est sumendum. In tali namque sermone, sensus litteralis est, non semper ille qui immediate per verba signatur, sed interdum qui per similitudinem insinuatur, aut per res verbis expressas significatur, ut quum in Jeremia et Ezechiele asseritur: Qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus. — Postremo, verba hæc a Gregorio et Beda mystice exponuntur: intelligendo per calceamenta Christi, ejus humanitatem, quæ Verbi persona induta est; per pedem, divinitatem; per corrigiam vero, hypostaticam unionem humanitatis cum Verbo. Sicque Joannes insinuat se inidoneum atque indignum hanc unionem plene exponere, quæ et angelicæ mentis capacitatem transcendit.
paras.en: Again, John's words are not to be understood as though Christ used shoes, since He forbade them even to the disciples whom He sent to preach[[Luke 10:4||]]. And He [[Acts 1:1|began to do and to teach|cœpit facere et docere]] [that is, He did first what He taught]. Therefore, as was said, John's saying is to be taken after the manner of a common proverb. For in such speech the literal sense is not always the one directly signified by the words, but sometimes the one suggested by a likeness, or signified by the things the words express: as when it is said in Jeremias and Ezechiel: [[Jer 31:30|every man that shall eat the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge|Qui comederit uvam acerbam, obstupescent dentes ejus]][[Ezech 18:2||]]. — Lastly, these words are expounded mystically by Gregory and Bede: understanding by Christ's shoes His humanity, which the Person of the Word put on; by the foot, His divinity; and by the latchet, the hypostatic union of the humanity with the Word. And so John suggests that he is unfit and unworthy to explain fully this union, which surpasses even the capacity of the angelic mind.

paras.t: Ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu Sancto et igni. In Joanne habetur, quod Jesus non baptizavit, sed discipuli ejus. Itaque sensus est: Ipse Christus baptizabit vos per suos discipulos, ita quod erit principalis baptizator. Rursus, Christus baptizavit, id est, intus a culpa animam lavit, in Spiritu Sancto, id est virtute et gratia Spiritus Sancti, videlicet gratiam Spiritus Sancti infundendo, per quam culpa aufertur et anima decoratur: imo sic Trinitas tota, seu Christus ut Deus, baptizat. Sed et discipuli Christi, et sacerdotes Ecclesiæ usque in præsens, baptizant in Spiritu Sancto, videlicet virtute et gratia Spiritus, tanquam instrumentales baptizatores mundatoresque baptizatorum, instrumentaliter cooperantes ad Sancti Spiritus infusionem, culpæ deletionem, et animæ justificationem. Non autem datur Baptismus in Spiritu Sancto, quasi in forma Baptismi sufficiat exprimere Spiritum Sanctum; imo sic datur: In nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti.
paras.en: [[3:16|He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire|Ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu Sancto et igni]]. In John we have it that Jesus did not baptize, but His disciples[[John 4:2||]]. So the sense is: Christ Himself will baptize you through His disciples, so that He will be the principal baptizer. Again, Christ baptized, that is, washed the soul inwardly from guilt, *with the Holy Ghost*, that is, by the power and grace of the Holy Ghost, namely by pouring in the grace of the Holy Ghost, by which guilt is taken away and the soul adorned: indeed in this way the whole Trinity, or Christ as God, baptizes. But the disciples of Christ, too, and the priests of the Church down to the present, baptize with the Holy Ghost, that is, by the power and grace of the Spirit, as instrumental baptizers and cleansers of the baptized, cooperating as instruments in the infusion of the Holy Spirit, the blotting out of guilt and the justification of the soul. Baptism, however, is not given *in the Holy Ghost* as though it sufficed, in the form of Baptism, to name the Holy Ghost; rather it is given thus: [[Matt 28:19|in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost|In nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti]].

paras.t: Sed quum apud Joannem dicat Salvator, Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei: cur ait Præcursor, Baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto et igni, et non potius, Spiritu Sancto et aqua, quum aliud non sit renasci, prout ibi accipitur, quam baptizari? Et respondendum, quod Præcursor non exprimit aquam, quoniam intendit assignare differentiam sui baptismi, qui fiebat in aqua, a Baptismate Christi, atque excellentiam Baptismatis Christi: idcirco non nominat elementum in quo fiebat. Unde et ignem non sumit pro solito igne materiali: imo, secundum Hieronymum, per ignem intelligit Spiritum Sanctum, qui ignit seu caritate mentem inflammat: sicque conjunctio, Et, tenetur expositive. Chrysostomus et Beda, per ignem intelligunt tentationis et tribulationis fervorem seu acerbitatem quibus electi in hac vita purgantur, dicente Apostolo: Quia per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum cælorum. Quidam per ignem, caritatis fervorem intelligunt, ad quem ordinatur Christi Baptismus. Caritas enim operit multitudinem peccatorum, et tanquam optimus ignis, consumit vitiorum rubiginem. Sunt qui per ignem intelligunt sensibile atque visibile signum in quo Spiritus Sanctus frequenter dabatur baptizatis in primitiva Ecclesia, ut Apostolis in igneis linguis, prout in Actibus Apostolorum de hoc plura leguntur. Postremo, nonnulli per ignem intelligunt purgatorii pœnam, in qua post hanc vitam purgantur qui cum reatu discedunt, quemadmodum Corinthiis scribit Apostolus: Uniuscujusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit. Et iterum de purgando loquens: Ipse (inquit) salvus erit; sic tamen, quasi per ignem.
paras.en: But since the Saviour says in John: [[John 3:5|unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God|Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, non potest introire in regnum Dei]], why does the Forerunner say, *He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire*, and not rather “with the Holy Ghost and water”, since to be born again, as it is taken there, is nothing else than to be baptized? The answer is that the Forerunner does not mention water because he means to set out the difference between his own baptism, which was done in water, and the Baptism of Christ, and the excellence of Christ's Baptism: so he does not name the element in which it was done. And so he does not take *fire* for ordinary material fire: rather, according to Jerome, by fire he means the Holy Ghost, who sets the mind on fire, or inflames it with charity: and so the conjunction *and* is taken as explaining [that is, “the Holy Ghost, that is, fire”]. Chrysostom and Bede understand by fire the heat or bitterness of temptation and tribulation by which the elect are purified in this life, as the Apostle says: [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God|per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum cælorum]] [Denis has *cælorum*, “of heaven”, where the Vulgate has *Dei*]. Some understand by fire the fervour of charity, to which the Baptism of Christ is ordered. For [[1 Pet 4:8|charity covereth a multitude of sins|Caritas enim operit multitudinem peccatorum]], and like the best of fires it consumes the rust of vices. There are those who understand by fire the sensible and visible sign in which the Holy Ghost was often given to the baptized in the primitive Church, as to the Apostles in tongues of fire[[Acts 2:3||]], as we read more fully of this in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 10:44||]][[Acts 19:6||]]. Lastly, some understand by fire the pain of purgatory, in which those who depart with guilt still owing are purified after this life, as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 3:13|the fire shall try every man's work, of what sort it is|Uniuscujusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit]]. And again, speaking of one to be purified: [[1 Cor 3:15|he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire|Ipse (inquit) salvus erit; sic tamen, quasi per ignem]].

paras.t: Cujus ventilabrum in manu ejus. Per ventilabrum, quod est instrumentum quo blada purgantur paleas abjiciendo, significatur justum Christi judicium, seu judicandi potestas atque sententia: quæ est in manu, id est in actu seu exsecutione suæ justitiæ, vel in potestate ac promptitudine ejus, quemadmodum apud Joannem Christus inquit: Pater omne judicium dedit Filio. Et judicium istud competit Christo secundum quod Deus est, per auctoritatem primam ac principalem; sed secundum formam servi assumptam, convenit ei ut instrumentaliter exsequenti ac judici constituto, quemadmodum in Actibus Apostolorum Petrus testatur: Ipse est qui constitutus est a Deo judex vivorum et mortuorum.
paras.en: [[3:17|Whose fan is in his hand|Cujus ventilabrum in manu ejus]]. By the fan, which is the instrument by which grain is cleaned by throwing off the chaff, is signified the just judgment of Christ, or His power and sentence of judging: which is *in his hand*, that is, in the act or execution of His justice, or in His power and readiness, as Christ says in John: [[John 5:22|hath given all judgment to the Son|Pater omne judicium dedit Filio]]. And this judgment belongs to Christ as He is God, by first and principal authority; but according to the form of a servant that He assumed[[Phil 2:7||]], it belongs to Him as one who carries it out instrumentally and as the appointed judge, as Peter testifies in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 10:42|it is he who was appointed by God to be judge of the living and of the dead|Ipse est qui constitutus est a Deo judex vivorum et mortuorum]].

paras.t: Et permundabit, id est, perfecte purgabit, aream suam, id est militantem Ecclesiam, in qua nunc simul miscentur electi ac reprobi, sicut in area simul ponuntur frumentum et palea. Unde et Synagogæ loquitur Isaias: Tritura mea et filia areæ meæ, quæ audivi a Domino, nuntiavi tibi. Hanc permundationem faciet Christus plene in die novissimo, quando loco et præmio separabuntur boni et mali; quando etiam electi qui tunc aliquid purgandum habebunt, in igne conflagrationis purgandi dicuntur, saltem illi qui tunc vivi reperientur, atque in illo igne morientur, et cum aliis resuscitabuntur. Quotidie demum purgat Deus hanc aream tripliciter: primo, dum per ecclesiasticam censuram, quidam de Ecclesia sacerdotali castigatione ejiciuntur: secundo, dum impii de hac vita tolluntur; tertio, dum electi in vita præsenti per adversa ac aliis modis a suis emundantur peccatis.
paras.en: [[3:17|and he will purge|Et permundabit]], that is, will cleanse perfectly, [[3:17|his floor|aream suam]], that is, the Church militant, in which the elect and the reprobate are now mixed together, as wheat and chaff lie together on the threshing floor. Hence Isaias says to the Synagogue: [[Is 21:10|O my thrashing, and the children of my floor|Tritura mea et filia areæ meæ]], [[Is 21:10|that which I have heard of the Lord|quæ audivi a Domino]], I have declared to thee [Denis has *filia*, “daughter”, and *tibi*, “to thee”, where the Vulgate has *filii* and *vobis*]. This cleansing Christ will make fully on the last day, when the good and the wicked will be separated in place and in reward[[Matt 13:49||]]; when also the elect who then have anything to be purged are said to be purged in the fire of the conflagration, at least those who are found alive then and will die in that fire and rise again with the others. And God purges this floor daily in three ways: first, when by ecclesiastical censure some are cast out of the Church by priestly correction; secondly, when the wicked are taken out of this life; thirdly, when the elect are cleansed of their sins in the present life by adversities and in other ways.

paras.t: Et congregabit triticum, id est electos et virtuosos, solidosque fructus eorum, in horreum suum, id est cæleste susceptaculum Beatorum. Paleas autem, id est reprobos, mente inanes, instabiles, omnique passionum seu concupiscentiarum ac vitiorum impulsu volubiles, comburet, id est, incendet ac puniet, non consumet, igne inexstinguibili, infernali et æternali: de quo in fine dicturus est impiis, Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum. De quo scriptum est in Isaia: Vermis eorum non morietur, et ignis eorum non exstinguetur; et Judith: Dominus omnipotens vindicabit in eis, in die judicii visitabit illos; dabit enim ignem et vermes in carnem eorum, ut urantur et sentiant usque in sempiternum. In Job quoque de transgressore asseritur: Luet (inquiens) quæ fecit omnia, nec tamen consumetur; juxta multitudinem adinventionum suarum, sic et sustinebit.
paras.en: [[3:17|and will gather the wheat|Et congregabit triticum]], that is, the elect and the virtuous, and their solid fruits, [[3:17|into his barn|in horreum suum]], that is, the heavenly dwelling of the Blessed. [[3:17|but the chaff|Paleas autem]], that is, the reprobate, empty in mind, unstable, and whirled about by every impulse of passions, concupiscences and vices, [[3:17|he will burn|comburet]], that is, will set on fire and punish, not consume, [[3:17|with unquenchable fire|igne inexstinguibili]], the everlasting fire of hell: of which at the end He will say to the wicked: Go, [[Matt 25:41|you cursed, into everlasting fire|maledicti, in ignem æternum]]. Of which it is written in Isaias: [[Is 66:24|their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched|Vermis eorum non morietur, et ignis eorum non exstinguetur]]; and in Judith: [[Jdt 16:20|the Lord almighty will take revenge on them, in the day of judgment he will visit them|Dominus omnipotens vindicabit in eis, in die judicii visitabit illos]]; [[Jdt 16:21|For he will give fire, and worms into their flesh, that they may burn, and may feel for ever.|dabit enim ignem et vermes in carnem eorum, ut urantur et sentiant usque in sempiternum]] And in Job it is said of the transgressor: [[Job 20:18|He shall be punished for all that he did, and yet shall not be consumed: according to the multitude of his devices so also shall he suffer.|Luet (inquiens) quæ fecit omnia, nec tamen consumetur; juxta multitudinem adinventionum suarum, sic et sustinebit]]

paras.t: O quam insensati, cæci et crudi mente sunt infelicissimi amatores sæculi hujus, quibus ista non sapiunt, nec terrorem incutiunt, ideo delectant eos carnalia et caduca, atque cum gaudio currunt ad inferos. Denique, teste Alberto super Apocalypsim, damnati non tantum affligentur corpore ab igne inferni, quantum mente, apprehendendo se æternaliter in pœnis mansuros. Sed quum tam variæ sint pœnæ pravorum, ut dicat Psalmista, Pluet super peccatores laqueos; ignis, sulfur, et spiritus procellarum, pars calicis eorum: cur de solo igne inducit mentionem Joannes? Et respondendum, quod ideo, quoniam ignis punitio inter corporalia afflictiva est gravior: sed et nomine ignis, quæcumque magna pœna solet intelligi. Præterea, o miseri filii fallacissimi mundi, propriis vitiis penitus excæcati, cur de carnis nobilitate, de temporalium affluentia, de sæculari potentia, de iniquis factis superbitis, gloriamini, vosque jactatis? cur pauperes et devotos despicitis? quum sacratissimus Christi baptista vos comparet paleis, illosque tritico: imo et Jeremias propheta, vos cum illis computari et esse indignissimos reputans ait, Quid paleis ad triticum?
paras.en: O how senseless, blind and crude of mind are the most unhappy lovers of this world, who have no taste for these things, and are struck with no terror by them; and so carnal and perishing things delight them, and they run with joy to hell! Moreover, as Albert testifies on the Apocalypse, the damned will be afflicted not so much in body by the fire of hell as in mind, perceiving that they will remain in torments for ever. But since the pains of the wicked are so various, as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 10:7|He shall rain snares upon sinners: fire and brimstone, and storms of winds, shall be the portion of their cup.|Pluet super peccatores laqueos; ignis, sulfur, et spiritus procellarum, pars calicis eorum]], why does John make mention of fire alone? The answer is: because the punishment of fire is the heaviest among bodily afflictions; and also by the name of fire any great pain is commonly understood. Furthermore, O wretched sons of a most deceitful world, utterly blinded by your own vices, why do you pride yourselves, glory and boast of nobility of the flesh, of abundance of temporal goods, of worldly power, of wicked deeds? Why do you despise the poor and the devout? when the most holy baptizer of Christ compares you to chaff and them to wheat: indeed Jeremias the prophet too, thinking you most unworthy to be reckoned with them, says: [[Jer 23:28|what hath the chaff to do with the wheat|Quid paleis ad triticum]]?

paras.t: Multa quidem et alia exhortans evangelizabat populo: id est, præter ea quæ dicta sunt, B. Joannes alia quoque quamplurima documenta et hortamenta proposuit populo: quorum unum hoc est, quod in Matthæo fertur dixisse, Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum. Itaque, sicut de Christo scriptum est, quod multa alia fecit quæ scripta non sunt, sic de præcursore ejus hic legitur, quod multa salutaria verba populo prædicavit, quæ non sunt in scriptis redacta.
paras.en: [[3:18|And many other things exhorting did he preach to the people|Multa quidem et alia exhortans evangelizabat populo]]: that is, besides what has been said, blessed John set before the people very many other teachings and exhortations as well: one of which is what he is reported in Matthew to have said: [[Matt 3:2|Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum]] [the margin's numerals are misread; these are John's words at Matt 3:2, repeated by Christ at 4:17]. So, as it is written of Christ that He did many other things which are not written[[John 21:25||]], so it is read here of His forerunner that he preached many saving words to the people which have not been set down in writing.

paras.t: Herodes autem tetrarcha, id est Herodes Antipas, filius Herodis regis sub quo natus est Christus (qui Antipas, cur tetrarcha, non rex vocetur, superius dictum est), quum corriperetur ab illo, videlicet Joanne Baptista, de Herodiade uxore fratris sui, id est de hoc quod Philippi fratris sui uxorem, nomine Herodiadem, filiam Aretæ regis Arabum, duxit in conjugem, fratre ejus vivente, filiamque ex Herodiade ipsa habente: sicque adulterium commisit Herodes atque incestum, quia secundum legem non licuit uxorem fratris accipere, nisi illo defuncto absque prole; et de omnibus malis quæ fecit Herodes: quia non dubium quin et multa alia gravia commiserit scelera, qui præfatum facinus tam enorme committere et continuare non formidavit. Nam et unum peccatum mortale suo pondere trahit ad aliud, et quo enormius fuerit, eo ad graviora inducit. Facit enim hominem a Deo plus deseri: cujus auxilio homo privatus, in profundum labitur vitiorum, fitque insensibilis mente ad ea quæ Dei sunt et veræ salutis, ita quod propria pericula non advertit.
paras.en: [[3:19|But Herod the tetrarch|Herodes autem tetrarcha]], that is, Herod Antipas, son of King Herod under whom Christ was born (why this Antipas is called tetrarch and not king was said above[[3:1||]]), [[3:19|when he was reproved by him|quum corriperetur ab illo]], namely by John the Baptist, [[3:19|for Herodias, his brother's wife|de Herodiade uxore fratris sui]], that is, for having taken to wife the wife of his brother Philip, Herodias by name, daughter of Aretas king of the Arabians, while his brother was living and had a daughter by this same Herodias: and so Herod committed adultery and incest, because according to the law it was not lawful to take a brother's wife[[Lev 18:16||]], except when he had died without offspring[[Deut 25:5||]]; [[3:19|and for all the evils which Herod had done|et de omnibus malis quæ fecit Herodes]]: for there is no doubt that he committed many other grievous crimes too, who did not fear to commit and continue in so enormous a crime as this. For one mortal sin drags a man by its weight to another, and the more enormous it is, the more it leads to graver ones. For it makes a man the more forsaken by God: and deprived of His help, a man slides into the depth of vices, and becomes insensible in mind to the things of God and of true salvation, so that he does not notice his own dangers.

paras.t: Adjecit et hoc malum quod sequitur, super omnia cetera sua peccata: quibus addidit istud, quasi illa non suffecissent; vel, Adjecit et hoc super omnia, id est peccatum istud ceteris gravius; et inclusit Joannem in carcerem. Quare et quomodo fecerit hoc, et qualiter decollavit Joannem, plene describit Matthæus, et Marcus. Unde Lucas sciens hoc satis descriptum, recte dimisit, atque ad Christi gesta ac documenta evolvenda festinat.
paras.en: [[3:20|He added this also|Adjecit et hoc]], the evil that follows, [[3:20|above all|super omnia]] his other sins: he added this to them, as though they had not been enough; or, *He added this also above all*, that is, this sin, graver than the rest; [[3:20|and shut up John in prison|et inclusit Joannem in carcerem]]. Why and how he did this, and how he beheaded John, Matthew[[Matt 14:3||]] and Mark[[Mark 6:17||]] describe fully. So Luke, knowing this had been sufficiently described, rightly left it aside, and hastens on to unfold the deeds and teachings of Christ.

3.title: Prosecutio expositionis capituli hujus tertii: Factum est autem, quum baptizaretur omnis populus
3.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this third chapter: “Now it came to pass, when all the people were baptized”

paras.t: Factum est autem, quum baptizaretur omnis populus. Paulo ante ostendit Evangelista quomodo testificatione Joannis declaratus est Christus hominibus; nunc describit quomodo testimonio Dei Patris et descensu Spiritus Sancti sit manifestatus. Itaque, quum a Joanne baptizaretur omnis populus, id est quidam de quolibet genere Judæorum, præsertim virilis sexus: non enim personæ feminei sexus ab ipso baptizatæ leguntur; et Jesu baptizato a Joanne: quod quomodo factum sit, Matthæus et Marcus plenius recitant, ut ibi patet ac requirendum est; et orante. Quod Jesus suscepto baptismate, statim oravit, alii Evangelistæ non scribunt.
paras.en: [[3:21|Now it came to pass, when all the people were baptized|Factum est autem, quum baptizaretur omnis populus]]. A little before, the Evangelist showed how Christ was made known to men by the testimony of John; now he describes how He was manifested by the testimony of God the Father and the descent of the Holy Spirit. So, [[3:21|when all the people were baptized|baptizaretur omnis populus]] by John, that is, some of every kind among the Jews, chiefly of the male sex (for we do not read that persons of the female sex were baptized by him), [[3:21|that Jesus also being baptized|et Jesu baptizato]] by John (how this was done Matthew[[Matt 3:13||]] and Mark[[Mark 1:9||]] relate more fully, as is plain there and is to be looked for there), [[3:21|and praying|et orante]]. That Jesus prayed immediately after receiving baptism, the other Evangelists do not write.

paras.t: Oravit itaque Christus, non ob sui indigentiam, quia secundum humanitatem jam confirmatus fuit in bono, et quoad superiorem animæ partem beatifice fruens Deo; sed ad nostram instructionem, et ad nostram subventionem, imo pro nostra salute: quanquam Christus aliquando orasse dicatur pro corporis sui glorificatione, accidentalique præmio. Itaque, sumpto baptismo oravit Salvator: Primo, ad innuendum quod preces nostræ non sunt Deo acceptæ et meritoriæ, nisi a peccatis mortalibus simus immunes et caritate ac gratia decorati. Caritas namque vita est animæ, sine qua nec anima, nec actio ejus, spiritualiter viva est Deoque placita. Ideo dicit Apostolus: Si caritatem non habeam, nihil sum. Ideo oportet primo a sordibus vitiorum lavari. Unde quum Dominus per Isaiam dixisset, Quum multiplicaveritis orationes, non exaudiam; adjecit, Lavamini, mundi estote. Secundo, ad innuendum quod gratia in Baptismo aliisque sacramentis adepta, per orationes continuas indiget custodiri, ne per culpam tollatur. Tertio, ad innuendum quod in sacramentorum susceptione, et statim post hoc, elevanda est mens ad Deum oratione seu gratiarum actione. Oravit itaque Christus, ut merito suæ baptizationis spiritualiter mundaremur.
paras.en: So Christ prayed, not out of any need of His own, since according to His humanity He was already confirmed in good, and as to the higher part of His soul was enjoying God in beatitude; but for our instruction and for our help, indeed for our salvation: although Christ is said at times to have prayed for the glorification of His body and for His accidental reward [that is, the glory added to the essential bliss of the vision of God, such as the glory of the risen body]. So the Saviour prayed when He had received baptism: First, to give us to understand that our prayers are not acceptable to God and meritorious unless we are free of mortal sins and adorned with charity and grace. For charity is the life of the soul, without which neither the soul nor its action is spiritually alive and pleasing to God. Therefore the Apostle says: If I [[1 Cor 13:2|have not charity, I am nothing|caritatem non habeam, nihil sum]]. Therefore we must first be washed from the filth of vices. Hence when the Lord had said through Isaias, [[Is 1:15|when you multiply prayer, I will not hear|Quum multiplicaveritis orationes, non exaudiam]], He added, [[Is 1:16|Wash yourselves, be clean|Lavamini, mundi estote]]. Secondly, to give us to understand that the grace obtained in Baptism and the other sacraments needs to be guarded by continual prayers, lest it be taken away through sin. Thirdly, to give us to understand that in receiving the sacraments, and immediately afterwards, the mind is to be raised to God in prayer or thanksgiving. So Christ prayed, that by the merit of His baptism we might be spiritually cleansed.

paras.t: Christus autem in mundo conversans et comprehensor quodammodo fuit secundum quod homo, et viator: comprehensor quidem, quantum ad superiores et intellectuales animæ suæ vires, per comparationem earum ad increatum objectum, videlicet æternam veritatem, summamque bonitatem; viator autem, quantum ad inferiores animæ vires, vel etiam quantum ad superiores vires per comparationem earum ad essentiam animæ, in qua radicatæ fuerunt, itemque per comparationem earum ad objectum creatum: sic namque passibilis fuit Christus, etiam quoad vires superiores aliquo modo, videlicet ratione subjecti earum. Christo ergo homini, in quantum fuit comprehensor, competebat orare pro aliis; sed ut viator, oravit utique et pro se.
paras.en: Now Christ, while living in the world, was in a certain manner, as man, both a comprehensor and a wayfarer [*comprehensor*: one who already possesses the vision of God, as the blessed in heaven; *viator*, 'wayfarer': one still on the way to it]: a comprehensor as to the higher and intellectual powers of His soul, in their relation to their uncreated object, namely the eternal Truth and the supreme Goodness; but a wayfarer as to the lower powers of the soul, or even as to the higher powers in their relation to the essence of the soul in which they were rooted, and likewise in their relation to a created object: for in this way Christ was passible [that is, capable of suffering] in some manner even as to the higher powers, namely by reason of their subject. So to Christ as man, inasmuch as He was a comprehensor, it belonged to pray for others; but as a wayfarer He certainly prayed for Himself as well.

paras.t: Cur autem voluerit Christus baptizari, et quæ fuit forma baptismi Joannis, item an baptizati baptismo Joannis erant rebaptizandi, de octo quoque generibus baptismatis secundum Damascenum, et de quinque generibus baptismatis secundum Gregorium Nazianzenum, hoc loco prætereo, quoniam super Matthæum inde locutus sum. — Præterea quæri hic potest, quod ibi non tetigi, an scilicet Joannes sub eadem forma verborum baptizavit Christum, qua alios. De hoc nihil inveni conscriptum; et arbitror quod sicut omnino alia fuit ratio baptizationis Christi quam aliorum, sic in baptizatione Christi Joannes usus non sit communi forma baptismatis, quæ fuit, secundum doctores: Ego te baptizo in nomine venturi. Unde in Actibus Paulus testatur: Joannes baptizabat populum, dicens in eum qui venturus esset post ipsum, ut crederent, hoc est in Jesum. Hinc acceptio baptismi Joannis, dicitur fuisse protestatio credendi in Christum. Unde patet, quod talis forma ad Christum non congruebat, saltem univoce. Insuper, sub qua forma verborum baptizaverit Christum, vel, an sine forma verborum baptizaverit, puto incertum.
paras.en: Why Christ willed to be baptized, what the form of John's baptism was, and whether those baptized with John's baptism had to be baptized again; also of the eight kinds of baptism according to Damascene, and of the five kinds of baptism according to Gregory Nazianzen: all this I pass over here, since I have spoken of it on Matthew [the margin refers to Art. VI of the commentary on Matthew]. — Besides, a question may be asked here which I did not touch on there: namely, whether John baptized Christ under the same form of words as the others. On this I have found nothing written; and I judge that, as the reason for Christ's baptism was altogether other than for that of the rest, so in baptizing Christ John did not use the common form of his baptism, which, according to the doctors, was: *I baptize thee in the name of Him who is to come.* Hence in the Acts Paul testifies: [[Acts 19:4|John baptized the people|Joannes baptizabat populum]], [[Acts 19:4|saying: That they should believe in him, who was to come after him, that is to say, in Jesus|dicens in eum qui venturus esset post ipsum, ut crederent, hoc est in Jesum]]. Hence the receiving of John's baptism is said to have been a profession of believing in Christ. So it is plain that such a form did not befit Christ, at least not univocally [that is, not in the same sense as for the others]. Moreover, under what form of words he baptized Christ, or whether he baptized Him without a form of words, I think uncertain.

paras.t: Apertum est cælum: non reali apertione, scissione seu divisione cælestium corporum, quæ incorruptibilia affirmantur; sed per apparentiam quamdam, quoniam tantus desuper splendor super Christum apparuit et descendit, ut cælum videretur apertum seu reseratum, sicut et tempore fulguris magni apparet. Rursus, quum Deus in cælis habitare et esse dicatur, tunc cælum aperiri narratur, dum Deus per subjectam creaturam descendit et apparet hominibus, novo modo operans circa eos, quemadmodum in Christi baptismo accidisse mox subditur.
paras.en: [[3:21|heaven was opened|Apertum est cælum]]: not by a real opening, cleaving or dividing of the heavenly bodies, which are held to be incorruptible; but by a kind of appearance, since so great a splendour appeared from above and came down upon Christ that heaven seemed to be opened or unlocked, as also seems to happen at the time of a great flash of lightning. Again, since God is said to dwell and to be in the heavens[[Ps 10:5||]][[Ps 113:24||]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 5 and a second psalm reference, partly unreadable, marked *sec. Hebr.*: probably “The heaven of heaven is the Lord's,” Ps 115:16 in the Hebrew numbering, Ps 113:24 in the Vulgate], heaven is said to be opened when God, by means of a creature subject to Him, comes down and appears to men, working upon them in a new way: as is presently added to have happened at Christ's baptism.

paras.t: Et descendit Spiritus Sanctus corporali specie sicut columba in ipsum. Itaque Spiritus Sanctus, verus, incommutabilis et incircumscriptibilis Deus, secundum se seu in propria natura nunquam movetur, neque descendit; sed dicitur descendisse, quia columba ipsum repræsentans, descendit, et super Christum mansit, quia super caput ipsius sedit: sicut in die Pentecostes sedit super Apostolos in igneis linguis, id est per hoc quod igneæ linguæ ipsum repræsentantes, ejusque gratiam figurantes, super Apostolos descenderunt. Cur autem in specie columbæ Spiritus Sanctus descenderit? Respondendum, quia proprietates columbæ, tam Spiritui Sancto apparenti, quam Christo super quem apparuit, potissimum competunt. Ait enim Cyprianus in libro de Unitate Ecclesiæ: Est autem columba simplex et lætum animal, non felle amarum, non morsibus sævum, non unguium laceratione violentum. Hospitia humana diligere, unius domus consortium nosse solent columbæ; quum generant filios simul sedent, volando quoque sibi cohærent, communi conversatione vitam degunt, osculo oris concordiam pacis ostendunt. Itaque per columbam, bona simplicitas, spiritualeque gaudium, suavitas, innocentia, concordia, dilectio, unio designantur: quæ omnia Spiritui Sancto conveniunt; et aliqua horum ei appropriantur, videlicet suavitas, dilectio, pax, gaudium.
paras.en: [[3:22|And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape, as a dove, upon him|Et descendit Spiritus Sanctus corporali specie sicut columba in ipsum]]. Now the Holy Spirit, true, unchangeable and uncircumscribable God, in Himself, that is, in His own nature, is never moved and does not descend; but He is said to have descended because the dove which represented Him descended and remained upon Christ, for it settled upon His head: just as on the day of Pentecost He sat upon the Apostles in tongues of fire[[Acts 2:3||]], that is, inasmuch as tongues of fire, representing Him and figuring His grace, came down upon the Apostles. But why did the Holy Spirit descend in the form of a dove? The answer is: because the properties of the dove belong above all both to the Holy Spirit who appeared and to Christ upon whom He appeared. For Cyprian says in the book *On the Unity of the Church*: “The dove is a simple and joyful creature, not bitter with gall, not cruel in its bite, not violent with tearing claws. Doves love human dwellings and keep to the fellowship of one house; when they bring forth young they sit together, in flying too they keep close to one another, they spend their life in common converse, and with the kiss of the beak they show the concord of peace.” So the dove signifies good simplicity, spiritual joy, sweetness, innocence, concord, love and union: all of which befit the Holy Spirit; and some of them are appropriated to Him [that is, though common to the whole Trinity, they are ascribed in a special way to this Person], namely sweetness, love, peace and joy.

paras.t: Denique Spiritus Sanctus super Christum baptizatum descendit, non quod tunc cœpit esse in eo, vel quod tunc gratia aucta est; sed ad manifestandum excellentiam, dignitatem, et gloriam Christi, et ut Joannes illas populo propalaret, protestando quid vidisset. Quod et fecisse narratur in Joanne, quo legitur: Testimonium perhibuit Joannes, dicens, Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem, et mansit super eum; itemque, Ego vidi, et testimonium perhibui, quia hic est Filius Dei. Secundo, ut Joannes Baptista de Christo et efficacia Baptismatis ejus plenius instrueretur. Paulatim namque proficere habuit in divinorum notitia. Propter quod ait in Joanne: Ego nesciebam eum; sed qui me misit baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem, hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto. Tertio, quoniam tunc potissimum decuit Christi innocentiam, puritatem et simplicitatem declarari, quando ipse se peccatoribus magis forinsecus in licitis conformavit. Quoniam ergo tempore suæ baptizationis, inter peccatores Joannem accessit, vestimenta deposuit, nudus manibus se servi supposuit, baptismum ab eo suscepit, in quibus omnibus se peccatoribus conformavit, non tamen ut talibus; idcirco tunc maxime decuit ejus innocentiam, sanctitatem et sinceritatem ostendi, quod per columbæ descensum Joannisque prædicationem perfectum est, ne Christus peccator ut alii putaretur. Et quia tunc tantum se humiliavit, decuit eum tunc tam præclarissime sublimari, sicut et tempore passionis quando se summe exinanivit, per maxima miracula tunc facta, est clarificatus. Quarto, ad insinuandum quod per Christi baptizationem data est aquis vis purgativa peccati, et quod Baptismate Christi baptizatis Spiritus Sanctus infunditur, cælesteque regnum aperitur. Christus etenim sua baptizatione, nostram baptizationem secundum modum ab ipso institutum, præfiguravit.
paras.en: Further, the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ when He had been baptized, not because He then began to be in Him, or because His grace was then increased; but, first, to make manifest the excellence, dignity and glory of Christ, and so that John might make these known to the people by testifying to what he had seen. And this he is related to have done in John, where we read: [[John 1:32|John gave testimony, saying: I saw the Spirit coming down|Testimonium perhibuit Joannes, dicens, Quia vidi Spiritum descendentem]] … [[John 1:32|and he remained upon him|et mansit super eum]]; and again: [[John 1:34|I saw: and I gave testimony that this is the Son of God|Ego vidi, et testimonium perhibui, quia hic est Filius Dei]]. Secondly, so that John the Baptist might be more fully instructed about Christ and the power of His Baptism. For he was to advance little by little in the knowledge of divine things. That is why he says in John: [[John 1:33|I knew him not: but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending|nesciebam eum; sed qui me misit baptizare in aqua, ille mihi dixit: Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem]], [[John 1:33|he it is that baptizeth with the Holy Ghost|hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto]]. Thirdly, because it was most fitting that Christ's innocence, purity and simplicity should be declared then, when outwardly, in lawful things, He made Himself more like sinners. Since, then, at the time of His baptism He came to John among sinners, laid aside His garments, put Himself naked under the hands of a servant, and received baptism from him, in all of which He made Himself like sinners, though not as being one of them; therefore it was most fitting that His innocence, holiness and sincerity should then be shown, which was done by the descent of the dove and by John's preaching, lest Christ be thought a sinner like the rest. And because He then humbled Himself so much, it was fitting that He should then be exalted so very gloriously; as also at the time of the passion, when He emptied Himself to the utmost[[Phil 2:7||]], He was glorified by the very great miracles then done[[Matt 27:51||]][[Luke 23:45||]]. Fourthly, to intimate that through Christ's baptism a power of cleansing from sin was given to the waters, and that the Holy Spirit is poured into those baptized with Christ's Baptism and the heavenly kingdom is opened to them. For by His own baptism Christ prefigured our baptism, according to the manner instituted by Himself.

paras.t: Et vox de cælo facta est: Tu es Filius meus dilectus. Vox ista de cælo facta asseritur, quia cælesti virtute in aere est prolata. Siquidem ab angelo est formata in persona Dei Patris, quemadmodum in Joanne Christus dixit: Pater, clarifica Filium tuum. Ubi mox subditur: Venit ergo vox de cælo, dicens: Et clarificavi, et iterum clarificabo. Quo audito, turba asseruit tonitruum factum esse; alii dicebant, Angelus ei locutus est. Et secundum expositores, illi alii veritatem locuti sunt, quia videlicet in persona Patris angelus dixit hoc. Hinc in Christi baptismo dicitur Pater apparuisse in voce, non quia in ea sit visus, sed quia auditus. Et convenienter in voce apparuit, ad pandendum quod dicendo genuit unigenitum Filium suum, qui est Verbum æternum, ore Patris æternaliter intellectualiterque prolatum.
paras.en: [[3:22|And a voice came from heaven: Thou art my beloved Son|Et vox de cælo facta est: Tu es Filius meus dilectus]]. This voice is said to have come from heaven because it was uttered in the air by a heavenly power. For it was formed by an angel in the person of God the Father, as in John Christ said: Father, [[John 17:1|Glorify thy Son|clarifica Filium tuum]] [the margin gives John 12:28, where the words are “Father, glorify thy name”; Denis's “glorify thy Son” are those of John 17:1]. Where it is presently added: [[John 12:28|A voice therefore came from heaven|Venit ergo vox de cælo]], saying: [[John 12:28|I have both glorified it and will glorify it again|Et clarificavi, et iterum clarificabo]]. When they heard this, the multitude [[John 12:29|said that it thundered|tonitruum factum esse]]; [[John 12:29|Others said: An angel spoke to him|alii dicebant, Angelus ei locutus est]]. And according to the expositors, those others spoke the truth, since an angel said this in the person of the Father. Hence at Christ's baptism the Father is said to have appeared in the voice, not because He was seen in it, but because He was heard.
