And fittingly He appeared in a voice, to make known that by speaking He begot His only-begotten Son, who is the eternal Word, uttered eternally and intellectually by the mouth of the Father.

paras.t: Itaque dixit: Tu es Filius meus dilectus: Filius utique consubstantialis, coæternus et coæqualis, non minor, aut pura creatura, ut mentitus est Arius sceleratus. Denique, Pater Christum secundum divinitatem non minus diligit quam se ipsum, imo superardentissimo, supersuavissimo, penitusque infinito diligit eum amore, quum infinitæ sit bonitatis ac pulchritudinis, et quia totum quod habet communicat Filio. Filius quoque infinite diligit Patrem; sed et Pater ac Filius non minus diligunt Spiritum Sanctum, et ille infinite diligit Patrem ac Filium. Pater quoque seu tota Trinitas diligit Christum secundum naturam assumptam, ut Verbo unitam, magis quam omnia simul creata, quoniam majus bonum præstitit ei, utpote hypostaticam unionem cum Verbo, et gratiam quodammodo sine mensura.
paras.en: So He said: [[3:22|Thou art my beloved Son|Tu es Filius meus dilectus]]: a Son, that is, consubstantial, coeternal and coequal, not lesser, nor a mere creature, as the wicked Arius lyingly said. Further, the Father loves Christ according to His divinity no less than Himself; indeed He loves Him with a love more than most ardent, more than most sweet, and wholly infinite, since He is of infinite goodness and beauty, and because He communicates to the Son all that He has. The Son too loves the Father infinitely; and the Father and the Son love the Holy Spirit no less, and He infinitely loves the Father and the Son. The Father also, or the whole Trinity, loves Christ according to the nature He assumed, as united to the Word, more than all created things together, since He bestowed on it a greater good, namely the hypostatic union with the Word, and grace in a certain manner without measure[[John 3:34||]].

paras.t: In te complacui mihi. Quemadmodum Pater diligit Filium secundum divinitatem tantum sicut se ipsum, sic tantam habet complacentiam in illo sicut in semetipso: nempe superbeatissimæ Trinitatis mutua complacentia, est prorsus immensa, quum nil dissimilitudinis, nil contrarietatis, nil defectibilitatis aut imperfectionis consistat in eis, sed unaquæque infinitæ sit bonitatis, sapientiæ, pulchritudinis, sanctitatis, omnisque ratio perfectæ mutuæ dilectionis ac complacentiæ inveniatur in eis, videlicet clarissima intuitio, plena communio, summa similitudo, illimitata bonitas, simpliciterque infinita perfectio, voluntatis vero non conformitas solum, sed et unitas sempiterna. Postremo, in Christo secundum humanam ejus naturam, habet Deus Pater seu Trinitas complacentiam præcipuam, imo majorem quam in omnibus simul creatis, sicut in obedientissimo Filio in quo nulla unquam exstitit culpa, sed qui a principio creationis animæ suæ Deo perfectissime affectuosissimeque adhæsit, omni quoque gratiarum charismate pulcherrime fuit ornatus. Insuper, Patri in Christo secundum humanitatem ejus complacuit, quia videlicet placuit Patri tanta pietate et gratia prævenire animam ejus, atque per Christum hominem seu ejus humanitatem salvare omne genus humanum. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Quia in Christo complacuit omnem plenitudinem inhabitare, et omnia reconciliare per ipsum. His verbis consonat quod per Isaiam Pater ait de Christo: Ecce puer meus, suscipiam eum; electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea: dedi spiritum meum super eum.
paras.en: [[3:22|In thee I am well pleased|In te complacui mihi]]. As the Father loves the Son according to His divinity as much as Himself, so He has as great a pleasure in Him as in Himself: for the mutual good pleasure of the more than most blessed Trinity is altogether immeasurable, since there is in Them nothing of unlikeness, nothing of contrariety, nothing of defectibility or imperfection, but each is of infinite goodness, wisdom, beauty and holiness, and every ground of perfect mutual love and good pleasure is found in Them: namely the clearest vision, full communion, the highest likeness, unlimited goodness, and simply infinite perfection; and of will, not conformity only, but an everlasting unity. Lastly, in Christ according to His human nature God the Father, or the Trinity, has a special good pleasure, indeed a greater one than in all created things together, as in a most obedient Son in whom there was never any fault, but who from the beginning of the creation of His soul cleaved to God most perfectly and most lovingly, and was most beautifully adorned with every gift of graces. Moreover, the Father was well pleased in Christ according to His humanity, because it pleased the Father to go before His soul with such great kindness and grace, and through Christ as man, or through His humanity, to save the whole human race. That is why the Apostle says: [[Col 1:19|Because in him, it hath well pleased the Father that all fulness should dwell|Quia in Christo complacuit omnem plenitudinem inhabitare]], [[Col 1:20|And through him to reconcile all things|et omnia reconciliare per ipsum]]. With these words agrees what the Father says of Christ through Isaias: [[Is 42:1|Behold my servant, I will uphold him: my elect, my soul delighteth in him: I have given my spirit upon him|Ecce puer meus, suscipiam eum; electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea: dedi spiritum meum super eum]] [Denis's text has *puer*, 'child' or 'servant', where the Vulgate has *servus*].

paras.t: Postremo, Augustinus in libro de Consensu Evangelistarum disseruit: Quod Matthæus ait dictum a Patre, Hic est Filius meus dilectus, Lucas autem, Tu es Filius meus dilectus, ad eamdem sententiam explicandam valet. Vox enim cælestis unum horum dixit; sed Matthæus ostendere voluit ad id valere verba illa quæ dicta sunt, ut illis potius qui audiebant, indicaretur quod ipse esset Filius Dei. Non enim Christo indicabatur quod sciebat; sed audiebant qui aderant, propter quos etiam ipsa vox facta est. Itaque secundum B. Augustinum, alii quam Joannes audierant vocem illam: et forte secundum Augustinum simili modo etiam dicendum, quod columbam quoque viderunt. — Porro, ego antequam verba hæc legi, ita de ista materia scripsi super Matthæum: Quæritur, an solus Joannes viderit columbam super Christum descendere seu sedentem, an etiam ipse solus vocem Patris audierit, præsupposito quod Christus vidit columbam, audivitque vocem præfatam. Ad quod respondi ibidem: De hoc nil legi; sed apparet quod sic: aliter non indiguisset Joannes testari populo, quemadmodum viderit Spiritum Sanctum descendentem in Christum. Hoc ergo ibi opinative locutus sum: quod adhuc probabiliter dici posse opinor, quamvis S. Augustino contradicere non intendam. Nec sequitur, quod vox illa formata sit ut præsentes eam audirent, quoniam facta non est ut Christo aliquid indicaretur. Nam facta est propter Joannem, ut dictum est, atque ut ipse populo ea quæ vidit et audivit insinuaret.
paras.en: Lastly, Augustine, in the book *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, explains: “That Matthew says the Father said, [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]], while Luke says, [[3:22|Thou art my beloved Son|Tu es Filius meus dilectus]], serves to set out the same meaning. For the heavenly voice said one of these; but Matthew wished to show that the words spoken had this purpose, that it might rather be made known to those who heard that He was the Son of God. For Christ was not being told what He knew; but those present heard, for whose sake the voice itself was made.” So, according to blessed Augustine, others besides John heard that voice; and perhaps, according to Augustine, it must likewise be said that they also saw the dove. — Now, before I had read these words, I wrote on this matter on Matthew as follows [the margin refers to the end of Art. VI on Matthew]: “It is asked whether John alone saw the dove coming down upon Christ or resting on Him, and whether he alone also heard the voice of the Father, it being presupposed that Christ saw the dove and heard that voice.” To which I replied there: “I have read nothing on this; but it appears so: otherwise John would not have needed to testify to the people how he had seen the Holy Spirit descending upon Christ.” This, then, I said there by way of opinion: and I still think it can probably be said, though I do not mean to contradict St Augustine. Nor does it follow that the voice was formed in order that those present should hear it, since it was not made to tell Christ anything. For it was made for John's sake, as has been said, and so that he might make known to the people what he saw and heard.

paras.t: Subinde ponitur ætas in qua Christus suscepit baptismum. Et ipse Jesus erat incipiens, id est, fieri incipiebat, quasi annorum triginta. Jam enim et vicesimum nonum annum complevit, tricesimumque incepit, habens de illo tredecim dies, secundum expositores communiter: qui etiam asserunt eum illo die baptizatum, quo et tribus Magis ostensus est, scilicet tertiodecimo die a sua nativitate. Hinc Evangelista ait, Quasi annorum triginta, quia de tricesimo anno modicum habuit; vel, Quasi, dicit hic veritatem, quia annum tricesimum vere incepit. Et taliter exponentes asserunt Christum prædicasse tribus annis cum medio, quamvis in computatione medii anni accipiant partem pro toto. Verumtamen Augustinus atque Chrysostomus aliter exponunt, hoc modo: Ipse Jesus erat triginta annorum incipiens, quasi scilicet tricesimum primum ætatis suæ. Dicunt namque, quod Christus tunc fuit plene triginta annorum, et de tricesimo primo anno habuerit tredecim dies; item, quod prædicavit duobus annis cum medio. Prima tamen expositio est consonantior textui, communiusque tenetur.
paras.en: Next is given the age at which Christ received baptism. [[3:23|And Jesus himself was beginning|Et ipse Jesus erat incipiens]], that is, was beginning to be, [[3:23|about the age of thirty years|quasi annorum triginta]]. For He had already completed His twenty-ninth year and begun His thirtieth, having thirteen days of it, according to the expositors generally: who also assert that He was baptized on the same day on which He was shown to the three Magi, namely the thirteenth day from His birth. Hence the Evangelist says, *about thirty years*, because He had little of the thirtieth year; or *about* here expresses the truth, because He truly had begun His thirtieth year [*quasi* can mean either 'about' or 'as being in truth']. And those who expound it in this way assert that Christ preached for three years and a half, though in reckoning the half-year they take the part for the whole. Augustine and Chrysostom, however, expound it otherwise, thus: *Jesus himself was beginning*, at thirty years, that is, His thirty-first year of age. For they say that Christ was then fully thirty years old and had thirteen days of His thirty-first year; and also that He preached for two years and a half. The first exposition, however, agrees better with the text, and is more commonly held.

paras.t: Quæritur, cur Christus tam diu distulit manifestari, baptizari, prædicare et miracula perpetrare. Et respondendum, quod ideo, quoniam ætas illa perfecta et virilis vocatur: in qua sensus et intellectus vigent in homine, roburque corporis, idcirco doctoribus et prædicatoribus competit, nec oportet differre diutius, ne tempus ad fructificandum aliis congruum minus utiliter expendatur. Unde Ezechiel tricesimo ætatis suæ anno orsus est vaticinari et loqui ad populum: quo etiam anno David cœpit regnare, et Joseph Ægypti constitutus est princeps. Nec obest, quod Jeremias et Daniel in recentiori ætate prophetare cœperunt: quoniam gratia Dei communi lege non coarctatur, nec operatio miraculosa ad communem imitationem trahenda est. Id quoque quod raro contingit, non est lex Ecclesiæ, secundum Gregorium Nazianzenum, quia nec una hirundo ver statuit. Christus autem docuit quod communitatem assequi decet. Unde et ideo tam diu distulit ista, ut nos suo exemplo instrueret, omnem vanitatem, pompam, præcipitationem, jactantiamque vitare, ne ante debitum aut congruum tempus procedamus ad publicum, vel docere alios præsumamus.
paras.en: It is asked why Christ put off so long being made manifest, being baptized, preaching and working miracles. The answer is: because that age is called the perfect and manly age, in which a man's senses and understanding are vigorous, and the strength of his body; therefore it befits teachers and preachers, and they ought not to put it off longer, lest the time fit for bearing fruit for others be spent less profitably. Hence Ezechiel began to prophesy and to speak to the people in the thirtieth year of his age[[Ezech 1:1||]]: in which year also David began to reign[[2 Kings 5:4||]], and Joseph was made ruler of Egypt[[Gen 41:46||]]. Nor does it stand in the way that Jeremias[[Jer 1:6||]] and Daniel began to prophesy at a younger age: for the grace of God is not confined by the common law, nor is miraculous working to be drawn into common imitation. Also, what happens rarely is not the law of the Church, according to Gregory Nazianzen, for one swallow does not make the spring. And Christ taught what it befits the community to follow. So He put these things off so long for this reason too: to teach us by His example to avoid all vanity, pomp, haste and boasting, lest we go out in public, or presume to teach others, before the due or fitting time.

paras.t: Tot ergo annorum exstitit Jesus tempore baptizationis, ut putabatur filius Joseph, id est quod, seu quando, adhuc æstimabatur naturalis filius ipsius Joseph, quem putabant cognovisse Mariam et ex ea Jesum genuisse. Sed ex isto tempore, per testimonium desuper factum, et per prædicationem Joannis, deinde per verba et opera Jesu, cœpit patere et comprobari quampluribus, quod Jesus est Christus in lege promissus, et per consequens ex virgine natus, juxta quod Isaias prædixit: Ecce virgo concipiet. Qui fuit Heli, id est, qui Joseph fuit filius Heli. Sed videtur contrarium, quia apud Matthæum dicitur filius Jacob. Ad quod respondetur, quod fuit filius Jacob vere, secundum carnalem propagationem, sed filius Heli, secundum legis institutionem. Heli namque accepta conjuge, mortuus est absque prole: ideo frater ejus Jacob juxta legis præceptum sumpsit conjugem illius in uxorem, ut fratri suo defuncto semen seu prolem procrearet, genuitque ex ea Joseph: qui secundum legem vocatus est filius Heli, quoniam lex præcepit, ut fratre uxorato sine liberis defuncto, frater ejus seu propinquus uxorem ejus acciperet, filiumque ex ea natum defuncto adscriberet, ne nomen ejus deleretur ex Israel. De hoc et aliis multis quæ hoc loco et in variis hujus voluminis locis possent induci, prætermitto, quia super Matthæum plura inde conscripsi.
paras.en: So many years old, then, was Jesus at the time of His baptism, [[3:23|being (as it was supposed) the son of Joseph|ut putabatur, filius Joseph]], that is, while, or when, He was still thought to be the natural son of Joseph, who they supposed had known Mary and begotten Jesus of her. But from that time on, through the testimony given from above and the preaching of John, and then through the words and works of Jesus, it began to be plain and proved to very many that Jesus is the Christ promised in the law, and consequently born of a virgin, as Isaias foretold: [[Is 7:14|Behold a virgin shall conceive|Ecce virgo concipiet]]. [[3:23|who was of Heli|Qui fuit Heli]], that is, which Joseph was the son of Heli. But the contrary seems to be the case, since in Matthew he is called the son of Jacob[[Matt 1:16||]]. To this the answer is that he was truly the son of Jacob by carnal descent, but the son of Heli by the ordinance of the law. For Heli took a wife and died without offspring: so his brother Jacob, according to the precept of the law, took his wife to wife, to raise up seed or offspring for his dead brother, and of her begot Joseph: who according to the law was called the son of Heli, since the law commanded that when a married brother died without children, his brother or kinsman should take his wife, and ascribe the son born of her to the dead man, so that his name might not be blotted out of Israel[[Deut 25:5||]][[Deut 25:6||]]. Of this, and of many other things which might be brought in at this place and in various places of this volume, I say nothing, because I wrote more on them on Matthew [the margin refers to Art. II on Matthew].

paras.t: Qui fuit Neri, id est, qui Salathiel fuit filius Neri. Circa quod quæritur, quomodo verum sit hoc, quum in Matthæo Salathiel dicatur filius Jechoniæ. Dicendum, quod Jechonias fuit naturalis pater istius Salathiel: Neri autem fuit pater ejus legalis, seu per adoptionem activam. — Qui fuit Nathan, qui fuit David, id est, Nathan fuit filius David. Qualiter hoc intelligendum sit, et de quo Nathan istud dicatur, diffuse ac diligenter prosecutus sum super Matthæum. — Porro a Salathiel usque ad David fuerunt reges, quos Lucas non ponit, sed Matthæus; Lucas vero personas privatas commemorat. Matthæus enim versatur principaliter circa Christi regnum seu regiam dignitatem, Lucas vero circa sacerdotium ejus. Insuper a David usque ad Abraham Lucas ascendendo, et Matthæus ab Abraham usque ad David descendendo, easdem personas et sub eisdem nominibus exprimunt: unde de expositione hujus particulæ textus satis super Matthæum dictum existimo.
paras.en: [[3:27|who was of Neri|Qui fuit Neri]], that is, which Salathiel was the son of Neri. On this it is asked how this can be true, since in Matthew Salathiel is called the son of Jechonias[[Matt 1:12||]]. It must be said that Jechonias was the natural father of this Salathiel, while Neri was his legal father, that is, by active adoption [that is, Neri adopted him]. — [[3:31|who was of Nathan, who was of David|Qui fuit Nathan, qui fuit David]], that is, Nathan was the son of David. How this is to be understood, and of which Nathan it is said, I have treated at length and carefully on Matthew [the margin refers to an article on Matthew 1]. — Further, from Salathiel back to David there were kings, whom Luke does not give, but Matthew does; Luke names private persons. For Matthew is concerned chiefly with the kingdom of Christ, that is, His royal dignity, Luke with His priesthood. Moreover, from David to Abraham, Luke going up and Matthew coming down from Abraham to David name the same persons, and under the same names: so I think enough has been said on Matthew about the exposition of this part of the text.

paras.t: Qui, scilicet Sarug, fuit filius Ragau. Iste Ragau in translatione Hieronymi dicitur Reu, ut in Genesi patet. — Qui, scilicet Sale, fuit filius Cainan, qui fuit Arphaxad, id est, qui Cainan fuit filius ipsius Arphaxad. Contra istud videtur quod in Genesi legitur, Arphaxad genuisse ipsum Sale; nec Cainan exprimitur ibi, nec interponitur. Idem quoque habetur in libro Paralipomenon. Cur autem Lucas ponit Cainan inter Arphaxad et Sale? Ad quod ab aliquibus respondetur, quod Arphaxad adhuc vivens adoptavit nepotem suum Sale, ideoque ejus filius appellatur: sicque Cainan fuit pater naturalis præfati Sale. Alii putant quod Sale fuit filius adoptivus ipsius Cainan et naturalis filius ipsius Arphaxad. Itaque in hoc omnes concordant, quod unus istorum duorum fuit pater naturalis istius Sale, alter autem pater ejusdem legalis seu active adoptivus. Septuaginta vero interpretes ponunt hunc Cainan inter Arphaxad et Sale: quorum translationem sequitur Lucas, quia suis temporibus tota Ecclesia ea utebatur.
paras.en: Who (namely Sarug) [[3:35|was of Ragau|fuit filius Ragau]]. This Ragau in Jerome's translation is called Reu, as is plain in Genesis[[Gen 11:18||]]. — Who (namely Sale) [[3:36|was of Cainan, who was of Arphaxad|fuit filius Cainan, qui fuit Arphaxad]], that is, which Cainan was the son of Arphaxad. Against this seems to stand what we read in Genesis, that Arphaxad begot Sale[[Gen 11:12||]]; and Cainan is neither named there nor put in between. The same is found also in the book of Paralipomenon[[1 Par 1:18||]]. Why then does Luke put Cainan between Arphaxad and Sale? To this some answer that Arphaxad, while still living, adopted his grandson Sale, and so Sale is called his son: and thus Cainan was the natural father of this Sale. Others think that Sale was the adopted son of Cainan and the natural son of Arphaxad. So all agree in this, that one of these two was the natural father of this Sale, and the other his legal father, that is, his father by active adoption. The Seventy translators, for their part, put this Cainan between Arphaxad and Sale: and Luke follows their translation, because in his time the whole Church used it.

paras.t: Qui, scilicet Sem, fuit filius Noe. Quem Sem Hebræi putant fuisse Melchisedech, et quod vixit usque ad tempora Isaac. Nam in Genesi scribitur Sem vixisse annis sexcentis. Propter quod, ut dicunt, Melchisedech dicitur fuisse absque patre et matre, non quia non habuit, sed ob nimiam ejus senectutem, et quia Scriptura parentes ejus sub nomine Melchisedech non describit. Qui fuit filius Noe, qui fuit filius Lamech. Iste est Lamech descendens de stirpe Seth, ut patet in Genesi. Fuit autem et alter Lamech de genere Cain, qui et interfecit ipsum Cain, et bigamiam incepit, quemadmodum fertur in Genesi. Qui Lamech fuit filius Mathusale. Iste Mathusale omnibus senior fuit, quoniam vixit annis nongentis sexaginta novem; obiitque ante diluvium, anno eodem quo inundavit, secundum Hieronymum.
paras.en: Who (namely Sem) [[3:36|was Of Noe|fuit filius Noe]]. This Sem the Hebrews think was Melchisedech, and that he lived until the times of Isaac. For it is written in Genesis that Sem lived six hundred years[[Gen 11:10||]][[Gen 11:11||]]. That is why, as they say, Melchisedech is said to have been without father and mother[[Heb 7:3||]]: not because he had none, but because of his great age, and because Scripture does not record his parents under the name of Melchisedech. Who was the son of Noe, [[3:36|who was of Lamech|qui fuit filius Lamech]]. This is the Lamech descended from the stock of Seth, as is plain in Genesis[[Gen 5:25||]]. But there was also another Lamech, of the race of Cain[[Gen 4:18||]], who also killed Cain himself[[Gen 4:23||]] and began bigamy[[Gen 4:19||]] [that is, having two wives at once], as is related in Genesis. Which Lamech [[3:37|Who was of Mathusale|fuit filius Mathusale]]. This Mathusale was older than all, since he lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years[[Gen 5:27||]]; and he died before the flood, in the same year in which it flooded, according to Jerome.

paras.t: Qui Mathusale fuit filius Enoch: de quo Judas scribit in sua Canonica, Prophetavit autem de his septimus ab Adam Enoch. Unde patet, quod septimus fuit post Adam per descensum a Seth. Quocirca quæri potest, quia si Enoch septimus fuit ab Adam, videtur Noe decimus exstitisse: siquidem inter Enoch et Noe fuerunt Mathusale et Lamech. Sed Petrus apostolus in sua Canonica dicit, Noe fuisse octavum: sic enim legitur: Deus octavum Noe præconem justitiæ custodivit. Et respondendum, quod Enoch dicitur septimus ab Adam, per inclusionem utriusque extremi, videlicet tam ipsum Adam, quam Enoch connumerando; Noe vero octavus, per exclusionem utriusque extremi. Iste est Enoch, de quo scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Enoch translatus est in paradisum, ut det gentibus sapientiam; itemque, Nemo natus est in terra qualis Enoch; et in Genesi, Ambulavit Enoch cum Deo et non apparuit, quia transtulit illum Dominus. Denique ipse est qui cum Elia venturus est et prædicaturus contra Antichristi fallacias, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi prædicit Joannes. Cujus beatissimi Enoch præconia in libro Sapientiæ, et ad Hebræos plenius continentur.
paras.en: Which Mathusale [[3:37|was of Henoch|fuit filius Enoch]]: of whom Jude writes in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jude 1:14|Now of these Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied|Prophetavit autem de his septimus ab Adam Enoch]]. Hence it is plain that he was the seventh after Adam in descent from Seth. On this it may be asked: if Enoch was the seventh from Adam, Noe seems to have been the tenth, since between Enoch and Noe came Mathusale and Lamech. But the apostle Peter in his Canonical Epistle says that Noe was the eighth: for so we read: God [[2 Pet 2:5|preserved Noe, the eighth person, the preacher of justice|octavum Noe præconem justitiæ custodivit]]. The answer is that Enoch is called the seventh from Adam by including both ends, that is, counting both Adam himself and Enoch; but Noe the eighth by excluding both ends. This is the Enoch of whom it is written in Ecclesiasticus: Enoch [[Ecclus 44:16|was translated into paradise|translatus est in paradisum]], that he may give wisdom to the nations [Denis's text has *sapientiam*, 'wisdom', where the Vulgate has *pœnitentiam*, 'repentance']; and again, [[Ecclus 49:16|No man was born upon earth like Henoch|Nemo natus est in terra qualis Enoch]]; and in Genesis, [[Gen 5:22|Henoch walked with God|Ambulavit Enoch cum Deo]] [[Gen 5:24|and was seen no more|et non apparuit]], because the Lord translated him. Lastly, he it is who is to come with Elias and preach against the deceits of Antichrist, as John foretells in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 11:3||]]. The praises of this most blessed Enoch are set out more fully in the book of Wisdom[[Wis 4:10||]] and in Hebrews[[Heb 11:5||]].

paras.t: Qui Cainan fuit filius Enos. Iste est alius a Cainan supra dicto. Qui Enos fuit filius Seth. Iste Enos fuit homo magnæ devotionis. Unde in Genesi habetur, Iste cœpit invocare nomen Domini: quod non est intelligendum quasi pater ejus Seth et Adam non invocaverint Deum, sed quia Enos cum præcipua devotione coluit Deum. Qui, scilicet Seth, fuit filius Adam. Unde nato Seth, dixit Eva: Posuit mihi Deus aliud semen pro Abel, quem occidit Cain: ut patet in Genesi. Qui, scilicet Adam, fuit filius Dei, non ita sicut ipse fuit pater Seth: qui non fuit Dei filius naturalis, quum hoc Unigenito Dei sit proprium; sed fuit filius Dei ratione creationis, et quoniam manibus Dei de limo terræ plasmatus est, quantum ad corpus, quantum vero ad animam factus est ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei. Unde et filius ejus per similitudinem imitativam vocatur, quoniam intellectualis rationalisque creatura, quo Creatori exstat similior, eo plus competit ei nomen et ratio filii, quantum ad Deum. Iterum, fuit filius Dei per gratiam adoptionis, tanquam prædestinatus. Quamvis enim transgressus sit, tamen pœnituisse atque deinceps virtuose vixisse non dubitatur. Unde et in Josue maximus dicitur. Ait namque ibi Scriptura: Adam maximus ibi situs est, hoc est sepultus in spelunca, videlicet duplici, in qua Abraham quoque, Isaac et Jacob sepulti sunt.
paras.en: Which Cainan [[3:38|was of Henos|fuit filius Enos]]. He is another than the Cainan mentioned above. Which Henos [[3:38|was of Seth|fuit filius Seth]]. This Henos was a man of great devotion. Hence it is said in Genesis: [[Gen 4:26|this man began to call upon the name of the Lord|Iste cœpit invocare nomen Domini]]: which is not to be understood as though his father Seth and Adam had not called upon God, but because Henos worshipped God with special devotion. Who (namely Seth) [[3:38|was of Adam|fuit filius Adam]]. Hence when Seth was born, Eve said: [[Gen 4:25|God hath given me another seed for Abel, whom Cain slew|Posuit mihi Deus aliud semen pro Abel, quem occidit Cain]], as is plain in Genesis. Who (namely Adam) [[3:38|was of God|fuit filius Dei]]: not in the way that he himself was the father of Seth: for he was not the natural son of God, since this is proper to the Only-begotten of God; but he was the son of God by reason of creation, and because he was formed by the hands of God [[Gen 2:7|of the slime of the earth|de limo terræ]] as to his body, while as to his soul he was made to the image and likeness of God[[Gen 1:27||]]. Hence he is also called His son by an imitative likeness, since the more an intellectual and rational creature is like its Creator, the more the name and the nature of son belong to it in relation to God. Again, he was the son of God by the grace of adoption, as one predestined. For though he transgressed, there is no doubt that he repented and afterwards lived virtuously. Hence in Josue too he is called the greatest. For Scripture says there: [[Jos 14:15|Adam the greatest|Adam maximus ibi]] … [[Jos 14:15|was laid there|situs est]] [Denis takes *Adam* here as the first man; the Hebrew means 'the greatest man among the Enacim'], that is, buried in the cave, namely the double cave, in which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were also buried.

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur, cur Lucas generationem Christi describit a posterioribus ascendendo, Matthæus vero a prioribus descendendo. Et respondendum, quod Lucas tractat de Christi generatione quodammodo spirituali, et prout per eam ad Deum reducimur. Propter quod incipit statim post Christi baptizationem, quia in Baptismo spiritualiter regeneramur, atque ad Deum reducimur. Talis autem reductio seu regeneratio fit per gratiam ascendendo. Matthæus vero tractat de Christi generatione et genealogia, secundum quod per carnis assumptionem descendit ad nos: quod factum est per carnalis propagationis descensum. Hinc quoque Lucas plures personas ponit inter Joseph et Abraham, quam Matthæus, quia triplices patres inducit, videlicet naturales ac legales et adoptivos. Etenim filiatio adoptiva spiritualis censetur. Matthæus vero non nisi carnales seu naturales patres commemorat. Insuper Lucas non sistit in Abraham sicut Matthæus, sed ascendit usque ad Adam: quia per Christum ad Deum reducti sunt, quicumque a principio mundi salvati sunt, quia oportuit eos aliquo modo habere fidem de Christo, videlicet explicite sive implicite.
paras.en: On what has gone before it is asked why Luke describes the generation of Christ going up from the later to the earlier, while Matthew goes down from the earlier. The answer is that Luke treats of a generation of Christ that is in a certain manner spiritual, and as through it we are brought back to God. That is why he begins straight after Christ's baptism, because in Baptism we are spiritually reborn and brought back to God. And such a bringing back, or rebirth, takes place by grace, going upward. Matthew, on the other hand, treats of Christ's generation and genealogy according as He came down to us by taking flesh: which was done by descent through carnal propagation. Hence too Luke puts more persons between Joseph and Abraham than Matthew does, because he brings in three kinds of fathers, namely natural, legal and adoptive. For adoptive sonship is reckoned spiritual. But Matthew names none but carnal, that is, natural, fathers. Moreover, Luke does not stop at Abraham as Matthew does, but goes up to Adam: because all who have been saved from the beginning of the world have been brought back to God through Christ, since they had to have faith in Christ in some way, namely explicitly or implicitly.

paras.t: Ex his demum redditur ratio, cur Lucas in generatione quam texit, nullam interserit feminam, quum tamen Matthæus quasdam admisceat, scilicet Thamar, Ruth, et Bethsabee. Matthæus quippe carnalem Christi ad nos descensum determinat: in quo mulieres concurrunt. Lucas autem de generatione ista pertractat, secundum quod per eam ad Deum ascendimus: quem ascensum mulieres impediunt magis quam juvant. Hinc rursus Matthæus describendo Christi generationem, in omnibus utitur verbo hoc, Genuit, Lucas autem verbo hoc, Fuit: quia Matthæus non ponit patres et filios, nisi secundum veram ac realem generationem, demptis Jesu et Joseph quoad se invicem comparatis. Lucas vero ponit non solum patres per carnalem generationem, sed etiam patres legales et adoptivos. Denique, quoniam teste Apostolo, non prius quod spirituale, sed quod animale, deinde quod spirituale, Matthæus qui descensum Christi ad nos per carnalem descensum describit, convenienter evangelium suum a Christi generatione exorsus est. Lucas autem, qui spiritualem ascensum prætendit, Christi genealogiam scribere cœpit post descriptionem baptismatis ejus, volens ostendere quomodo per Christum efficimur filii Dei: quod agitur per Baptismum.
paras.en: From this, finally, is given the reason why Luke, in the generation he weaves, puts in no woman, whereas Matthew mixes in some, namely Thamar, Ruth and Bethsabee[[Matt 1:3||]][[Matt 1:5||]][[Matt 1:6||]]. For Matthew sets out Christ's carnal descent to us, in which women have their part. But Luke treats of this generation as it is the way by which we go up to God: an ascent which women hinder more than help. Hence again Matthew, in describing the generation of Christ, uses throughout the word *begot*, but Luke the word *was*: because Matthew gives fathers and sons only according to true and real generation, Jesus and Joseph excepted when compared with each other. But Luke gives not only fathers by carnal generation, but also legal and adoptive fathers. Lastly, since, as the Apostle testifies, [[1 Cor 15:46|that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural: afterwards that which is spiritual|non prius quod spirituale, sed quod animale, deinde quod spirituale]], Matthew, who describes Christ's descent to us through carnal descent, fittingly began his Gospel with the generation of Christ. Luke, on the other hand, whose aim is the spiritual ascent, began to write Christ's genealogy after describing His baptism, wishing to show how through Christ we are made sons of God: which is done through Baptism.

4.title: Elucidatio capituli quarti: Jesus autem plenus Spiritu Sancto, regressus est a Jordane
4.title_en: Explanation of the fourth chapter: “And Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost, returned from the Jordan”
4.note: Some words at the line ends on PDF 483–484 (pp. 463–464) are lost in the scan's OCR; words supplied from the sense are in square brackets in the Latin, and two short gaps are marked […].

paras.t: Subinde prosequitur Evangelista opera Christi, et primo quomodo majestatem suam declaravit, superando diabolum. Jesus autem plenus Spiritu Sancto, regressus est a Jordane. Multi sunt gradus plenitudinis Spiritus Sancti, seu gratiæ ejus. Nam et Joannes Baptista dicitur Spiritu Sancto repletus in utero matris; et de Apostolis legitur, Repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto; et postea de Stephano scriptum est, Quum esset Stephanus plenus Spiritu Sancto. Itaque una est plenitudo Spiritus Sancti, seu gratiæ, quæ dicitur plenitudo proportionis seu comparationis: secundum quam dicitur aliquis plenus gratia vel Spiritu Sancto, quantum ad suam pertinet mensuram sive ætatem, vel comparatione aliorum. Alia dicitur plenitudo sufficientiæ: qua aliqui dicunt Apostolos et Stephanum atque consimiles fuisse repletos Spiritu Sancto. Verumtamen, quoniam tales fuerunt viri heroici atque perfecti, etiam quantum ad opera supererogationis, per observantiam consiliorum præcipuam, videtur illorum plenitudo dicenda plenitudo abundantiæ. Alia est autem plenitudo prærogativæ: quæ fuit in Virgine benedicta, cui dictum est: Ave, gratia plena. Hæ plenitudines accipiunt augmentum durante hac vita, quia et Virgo gloriosa profecit quotidie in caritate et gratia, ceterisque virtutibus. Quarta vero ponitur plenitudo superabundantiæ: qua Christus ut homo fuit plenus Spiritu Sancto, omnique gratia, dono et virtute ipsius. Denique in tantum fuit plenus Spiritu Sancto et donis ipsius, quod tota animæ suæ capacitas fuit repleta, ita quod in habitu gratiæ ac virtutum nunquam profecit, ut declaratum est clarius articulo septimo. Hæc autem plenitudo propria est Christo homini, cui datus est Spiritus non ad mensuram, videlicet qua datus est aliis, ut in Joanne fertur.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist goes on to the works of Christ, and first how He declared His majesty by overcoming the devil. [[4:1|And Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost, returned from the Jordan|Jesus autem plenus Spiritu Sancto, regressus est a Jordane]]. There are many degrees of the fulness of the Holy Ghost, or of His grace. For John the Baptist too is said to have been filled with the Holy Ghost in his mother's womb[[Luke 1:15||]]; and of the Apostles we read: [[Acts 2:4|they were all filled with the Holy Ghost|Repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto]]; and afterwards it is written of Stephen: [[Acts 7:55|being full of the Holy Ghost|plenus Spiritu Sancto]]. So there is one fulness of the Holy Ghost, or of grace, which is called the fulness of proportion or comparison: according to which someone is said to be full of grace or of the Holy Ghost as far as his own measure or age is concerned, or in comparison with others. Another is called the fulness of sufficiency: with which some say the Apostles and Stephen and the like were filled with the Holy Ghost. Yet since such men were heroic and perfect, even as regards works of supererogation [that is, works beyond what is commanded], through a special observance of the counsels, it seems their fulness should be called the fulness of abundance. Another again is the fulness of prerogative, which was in the blessed Virgin, to whom it was said: [[Luke 1:28|Hail, full of grace|Ave, gratia plena]]. These fulnesses receive increase while this life lasts, for the glorious Virgin too advanced daily in charity and grace and the other virtues. A fourth is set down, the fulness of superabundance: with which Christ as man was full of the Holy Ghost and of all His grace, gift and virtue. Indeed He was so full of the Holy Ghost and His gifts that the whole capacity of His soul was filled, so that He never advanced in the habit of grace and of the virtues, as was shown more clearly in the seventh article [Art. VII, on 2:52]. This fulness is proper to Christ as man, to whom the Spirit was given not by measure, that is, as He was given to others, as we read in John[[John 3:34||]] [the margin reads Joann. ii; the words are at John 3:34].

paras.t: Quæritur, an Christus secundum divinitatem, seu ut Verbum æternum, fuit plenus Spiritu Sancto. Et respondendum, quod secundum Damascenum ceterosque theologos, quælibet divina et increata Persona est in alia per circumincessionem, ita quod Pater totus est in Filio et econtra, similiter Spiritus Sanctus est totus in Patre et Filio, Pater quoque et Filius in Spiritu Sancto. Nam et quælibet divina Persona est incircumscriptibilis et immensa. Itaque, juxta hunc sensum dici posset Jesus, ut Deus, plenus Spiritu Sancto, ita quod Spiritus Sanctus totus et plene omnino in ipso est. In rationalibus vero creaturis dicitur Spiritus Sanctus esse per dona sua. Unde sicut illis dari asseritur, quibus gratiæ suæ munera infunduntur, sic illi feruntur pleni Spiritu Sancto, qui ejus gratia et virtute infusa replentur.
paras.en: It is asked whether Christ according to His divinity, or as the eternal Word, was full of the Holy Ghost. The answer is that, according to Damascene and the other theologians, each divine and uncreated Person is in the other by circumincession [that is, the mutual indwelling of the three Persons], so that the Father is wholly in the Son and the converse, and likewise the Holy Ghost is wholly in the Father and the Son, and the Father and the Son in the Holy Ghost. For each divine Person is uncircumscribable and immense. So in this sense Jesus, as God, could be called full of the Holy Ghost, in that the Holy Ghost is wholly and altogether fully in Him. But in rational creatures the Holy Ghost is said to be by His gifts. Hence, as He is said to be given to those into whom the gifts of His grace are poured, so those are said to be full of the Holy Ghost who are filled with His grace and infused virtue.

paras.t: Itaque, Jesus baptizatus a Joanne discessit, regrediens a Jordane in quo fuit jam baptizatus, et agebatur a Spiritu, hoc est, a Spiritu Sancto inducebatur seu movebatur, in desertum, hoc est in solitudinem, quæ est aptissimus locus ad illa exercitia propter quæ Christus desertum ingressus est. Itaque, Agi, sumitur hic eo modo quo ad Romanos ait Apostolus: Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, id est, moventur, reguntur, seu diriguntur, hi filii Dei sunt. Præterea, Christi humanitas fuit instrumentum seu organum Spiritus Sancti, imo totius superbeatissimæ Trinitatis, in opere indivisæ, operantis per illam: præsertim tamen dicitur fuisse instrumentum Verbi a quo fuit assumpta. Unde sicut corpus nostrum est instrumentum immediatum animatum, conjunctum et proprium animæ nostræ, sic Christi humanitas fuit Verbi animatum, unitum, immediatum ac proprium instrumentum. Idcirco Christus ut homo, in omnibus agebatur seu movebatur a Verbo æterno, seu a se ipso secundum quod Deus est.
paras.en: So Jesus, baptized by John, departed, returning from the Jordan in which He had now been baptized, [[4:1|and was led|et agebatur a Spiritu]] by the Spirit, that is, was brought or moved by the Holy Ghost, [[4:1|into the desert|in desertum]], that is, into solitude, which is the fittest place for those exercises for which Christ entered the desert. *Was led* [*agi*] is taken here in the way in which the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 8:14|whosoever are led by the Spirit of God|Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur]], that is, are moved, ruled or directed, [[Rom 8:14|they are the sons of God|hi filii Dei sunt]]. Moreover, the humanity of Christ was the instrument or organ of the Holy Ghost, nay of the whole most blessed Trinity, undivided in its working, working through it: yet it is said above all to have been the instrument of the Word, by whom it was assumed. Hence, as our body is the immediate, living, conjoined and proper instrument of our soul, so the humanity of Christ was the living, united, immediate and proper instrument of the Word. Therefore Christ as man was in all things led or moved by the eternal Word, that is, by Himself as He is God.

paras.t: Itaque, Agebatur a Spiritu in desertum quod fuit inter Jericho et Jerusalem, quadraginta diebus, id est, tot diebus ibidem Spiritu agente permansit. Loquitur autem Lucas de die naturali, quæ noctem includit: est enim spatium viginti quatuor horarum. Matthæus vero loquens de die artificiali, ait quod Christus fuit seu jejunavit in deserto quadraginta diebus et totidem noctibus. De quo etiam die ait Salvator: Nonne duodecim sunt horæ diei?
paras.en: So *He was led by the spirit into the desert*, which lay between Jericho and Jerusalem, [[4:2|For the space of forty days|quadraginta diebus]], that is, He remained there so many days, the Spirit leading Him. Luke speaks of the natural day, which includes the night: for it is the space of twenty-four hours. But Matthew, speaking of the artificial day [that is, the daylight hours], says that Christ was, or fasted, in the desert forty days and as many nights[[Matt 4:2||]]. Of this day too the Saviour says: [[John 11:9|Are there not twelve hours of the day?|Nonne duodecim sunt horæ diei?]]

paras.t: Circa hæc multa sunt intuenda. Primo, cur Christus, qui peccare non potuit, nec populo impediri a bonis, nec solitudine adjuvari, ingressus est eremum? Et respondendum, quod Christus non solum voluit omnem perfectionem implere, sed insuper diversas species, gradus et modos perfectionis seu perfectæ conversationis ostendere et docere. Hinc in pueritia cum Matre et ejus ministro moratus est, fuitque subditus eis, ut conversationem sub obedientia spiritualis patris seu matris, exemplariter demonstraret et efficaciter approbaret. Deinde ingressus est solitudinem, ut eremiticæ ac anachoreticæ vitæ præberet exemplum, et solitariam vitam opere commendaret. Secundo, ut instrueret nos, quod ad pœnitentiam peragendam contemplationisque apicem adipiscendum, solitarius præcipue conferat locus, præsertim desertum, in quo sensualium delectationum desunt objecta, ut supra plenius dictum est, ubi ostendebatur cur Joannes Baptista ad desertum confugit. Tertiam causam tangit evangelista Matthæus, dicendo: Ductus est Jesus in desertum, ut tentaretur a diabolo.
paras.en: Many things are to be considered here. First, why did Christ, who could not sin, nor be hindered from good by the crowd, nor be helped by solitude, enter the wilderness? The answer is that Christ willed not only to fulfil all perfection[[Matt 3:15||]], but also to show and teach the different kinds, degrees and ways of perfection, or of the perfect life. Hence in His boyhood He lived with His Mother and her minister [Joseph], and was subject to them[[Luke 2:51||]], so as to show by example and approve with effect the life lived under obedience to a spiritual father or mother. Then He entered solitude, to give an example of the eremitical and anchoritic life and to commend the solitary life by deed. Secondly, to teach us that for doing penance and reaching the summit of contemplation a solitary place helps above all, especially the desert, where the objects of sensual delights are lacking, as was said more fully above, where it was shown why John the Baptist fled to the desert[[1:80||]]. The third cause the evangelist Matthew touches on, saying: [[Matt 4:1|Jesus was led by the spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil|Ductus est Jesus in desertum, ut tentaretur a diabolo]].

paras.t: Sed nonne et extra desertum quivit tentari? Cur ergo hoc ait Matthæus? nisi ut innuat quod Jesus propter certas causas voluit singulariter, hoc est acerrime atque fortissime, tentari a dæmone, et quasi manu ad manum contra eum confligere.
paras.en: But could He not have been tempted outside the desert too? Why then does Matthew say this? Only to hint that Jesus, for certain reasons, willed to be tempted by the demon in a singular way, that is, most sharply and most strongly, and to fight against him as it were hand to hand.

paras.t: Quarto, ingressus est desertum protinus post baptismum testimoniumque Joannis, imo post tam sublime testimonium Dei Patris ac Spiritus Sancti de ipso, ut formam præstaret vitandi laudem humanam et omnem gloriam vanam, quatenus et nos laudati, aut honorati, quæramus latere, et optemus nesciri. Quinto, post baptismum statim introiit eremum, volens docere quod tunc potissimum debemus custodiæ cordis insistere, profectuique spirituali vacare, quum aliquam specialem a Deo purificationem et gratiam sortiti fuerimus, ne Deo ingrati reddamur, et tanto gravius offendamus, quo ampliorem paulo ante misericordiam consecuti eramus, pensantes illud Apostoli: Impossibile est eos qui semel sunt illuminati, et gustaverunt donum cæleste, et prolapsi sunt, rursus renovari ad pœnitentiam. In qua auctoritate, Impossibile, pro difficili, secundum unam expositionem, accipitur. Joannes quoque in Apocalypsi: Tene, inquit, quod habes, ne alter accipiat coronam tuam. Sexto, ut in solitudine pro nostris peccatis corpus suum abstinendo affligeret, atque in aliis se actibus satisfactoriis exerceret. Puto equidem, quod ibidem mundi peccata copiose defleverit, et pro nostra salute jugiter preces fuderit.
paras.en: Fourthly, He entered the desert straight after His baptism and John's testimony, nay after so sublime a testimony of God the Father and the Holy Ghost concerning Him, to give a pattern of avoiding human praise and all vainglory, so that we too, when praised or honoured, may seek to lie hidden and wish to be unknown. Fifthly, He went into the wilderness immediately after His baptism, wishing to teach that we ought above all to keep watch over the heart and give ourselves to spiritual progress when we have received some special purification and grace from God, lest we become ungrateful to God and offend the more gravely, the greater the mercy we had obtained a little before; weighing that saying of the Apostle: [[Heb 6:4|it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have tasted also the heavenly gift|Impossibile est eos qui semel sunt illuminati, et gustaverunt donum cæleste]], [[Heb 6:6|And are fallen away: to be renewed again to penance|et prolapsi sunt, rursus renovari ad pœnitentiam]]. In this text *impossible* is taken, according to one exposition, for *difficult*. John too says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:11|hold fast that which thou hast, that no man take thy crown|Tene, inquit, quod habes, ne alter accipiat coronam tuam]]. Sixthly, that in solitude He might afflict His body by abstinence for our sins, and exercise Himself in other works of satisfaction. Indeed I think that there He wept abundantly for the sins of the world and poured out prayers unceasingly for our salvation.

paras.t: Præterea, desertum aptissimus locus est pœnitendi, orandi et contemplandi, et hoc, ordine quodam: quoniam abstinendo perducitur homo ad gratiam orationis devotæ; per orationem vero, ad gratiam contemplationis sinceræ: atque per tria hæc, ad aliorum instructionem, prædicationem, gubernationem, aptissimus redditur, ut sic gratiam, sapientiam et fervorem, quæ in abscondito desuper sumpsit, aliis per ignea atque idonea verba communicet et proponat. Unde Christus mox aliis prædicaturus, ad nos exemplariter instruendos, primo in solitudine, jejunio, orationi et contemplationi vacavit, instruens aliorum rectores, prædicatores, prælatos, ut in primis se ipsos in prædictis exerceant, sicque sancte conversando mereantur a Deo gratiam efficaciter prædicandi ac fructuose regendi, ut scilicet verba quæ proferunt, non ex arido corde, sed ex gustu interno, ex caritatis ardore, ex spirituali experientia profluant, juxta illud Psalmi: Memoriam abundantiæ suavitatis tuæ eructabunt.
paras.en: Besides, the desert is the fittest place for doing penance, for praying and for contemplating, and that in a certain order: for by abstinence a man is brought to the grace of devout prayer; by prayer, to the grace of pure contemplation; and by these three he is made most fit for the instruction, preaching and government of others, so that he may impart and set before others, in fiery and fitting words, the grace, wisdom and fervour that he has received from above in secret. Hence Christ, being about to preach to others, in order to instruct us by example first gave Himself to solitude, fasting, prayer and contemplation, teaching the rulers, preachers and prelates of others first to exercise themselves in these things, and so, by living holily, to merit from God the grace of preaching with effect and governing with fruit; so that the words they utter may flow not from a dry heart but from inward relish, from the ardour of charity, from spiritual experience; according to the Psalm: [[Ps 144:7|They shall publish the memory of the abundance of thy sweetness|Memoriam abundantiæ suavitatis tuæ eructabunt]].

paras.t: Et tentabatur a diabolo. Secundum Origenem, toto tempore quadraginta dierum illorum tentabatur, et quæ fuerint tentamenta, nescimus: quæ ideo forsitan prætermissa sunt, quia majora erant quam ut litteris traderentur. Verumtamen verbum hoc Origenis pie accipi debet, præsertim quum beatissimi evangelistæ Matthæus et Lucas tres tentationes quas ibi passus est Christus commemorent. Basilius quoque sentire videtur, quod completis quadraginta diebus jejunii, sit tentatus. Ait namque: Christus per quadragenam intentatus mansit: noverat enim diabolus quod jejunabat nec famescebat, ideoque non audebat accedere. Et istud evangelicæ veritati magis consonum reor, quia in Matthæo habetur: Quum jejunasset quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, postea esuriit; et accedens tentator, dixit. Unde apparet, quod consummato jejunio, et visa fame ipsius, tentator aggressus sit eum. Hinc aliqui expositores affirmant, quod esuries Christi, fuit diabolo tentandi occasio.
paras.en: [[4:2|and was tempted by the devil|Et tentabatur a diabolo]]. According to Origen, He was tempted during the whole time of those forty days, and what the temptations were we do not know: perhaps they were passed over because they were greater than could be committed to writing. Yet this saying of Origen must be taken piously, especially since the most blessed evangelists Matthew and Luke record three temptations which Christ underwent there. Basil too seems to hold that He was tempted when the forty days of fasting were completed. For he says: Christ remained untempted through the forty days: for the devil knew that He was fasting and was not hungry, and so did not dare to approach. And this I think more in accord with the gospel truth, since in Matthew we have: [[Matt 4:2|when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry|Quum jejunasset quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, postea esuriit]]; and the tempter coming said[[Matt 4:3||]]. From which it appears that, when the fast was ended and His hunger seen, the tempter set upon Him. Hence some expositors affirm that Christ's hunger was the devil's occasion for tempting.

paras.t: Denique, sicut pro nostra salute Unigenitus Dei dignatus est incarnari, circumcidi, baptizari, et crucifigi, ita etiam et tentari: Primo, ut nobis virtutem et gratiam triumphandi in omni tentatione promereretur. In omnibus namque quæ egit et pertulit, nobis promeruit. Secundo, ut nos ad sustinenda omnia tentamenta animaret et provocaret. Membra quippe et famuli domino suo capiti debent libenter et proportionabiliter conformari. Tertio, ne quis fidelium in tentationibus quantumlibet gravibus constitutus, pusillanimitate dejiciatur, aut a Deo se suspicetur relictum, dum et Unigenitus Dei graviter est tentatus. Quarto, ut formam resistendi atque vincendi nobis monstraret. Unde in qualibet tentatione, Scripturam objecit diabolo. Quinto, ut potestatem tentatoris debilitaret, nosque ab omni tentatione erueret. Insuper, in hoc potissimum incomprehensibilem suam dignationem et humilitatem ostendit, quod a dæmone ita tentari dignatus est, ut duceretur seu assumeretur a diabolo de loco ad locum. Itaque in omni tentatione Christum fiducialiter invocemus, ut virtute et merito suæ tentationis nos roboret superareque faciat, quia ut Apostolus loquitur ad Hebræos: Debuit Christus per omnia fratribus assimilari, ut misericors fieret, et fidelis pontifex ad Deum: in quo enim passus est ipse et tentatus, potens est et eis qui tentantur auxiliari. Christi ergo dignationem et humilitatem sectemur, omni indignatione superbiæ refutata.
paras.en: Lastly, as for our salvation the Only-begotten of God deigned to be made flesh, circumcised, baptized and crucified, so too He deigned to be tempted. First, to merit for us the strength and grace to triumph in every temptation: for in all that He did and suffered He merited for us. Secondly, to encourage and rouse us to bear all temptations: for the members and servants ought willingly and in due proportion to be conformed to their lord and head. Thirdly, lest any of the faithful, placed in temptations however grievous, should be cast down by faintheartedness, or suspect himself forsaken by God, since the Only-begotten of God was also grievously tempted. Fourthly, to show us a pattern of resisting and conquering: hence in each temptation He set Scripture against the devil. Fifthly, to weaken the tempter's power and to rescue us from every temptation. Moreover, in this above all He showed His incomprehensible condescension and humility, that He deigned to be tempted by the demon so far as to be led or taken up by the devil from place to place. So in every temptation let us call on Christ with confidence, that by the power and merit of His temptation He may strengthen us and make us overcome; for, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:17|it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God|Debuit Christus per omnia fratribus assimilari, ut misericors fieret, et fidelis pontifex ad Deum]]; [[Heb 2:18|For in that wherein he himself hath suffered and been tempted he is able to succour them also that are tempted|in quo enim passus est ipse et tentatus, potens est et eis qui tentantur auxiliari]]. Let us then follow the condescension and humility of Christ, rejecting all the disdain of pride.

paras.t: Et nihil manducavit in illis diebus, hoc est, intra quadraginta hos dies nullum sumpsit corporeum alimentum. Non ergo jejunavit ut nos, qui quotidie semel reficimur. Quod autem contra diabolum dimicaturus voluit primo abstinere, patefecit quod volentibus dæmonum tentamenta prosternere, opus sit carnem suam a voluptatibus gustus et tactus abstrahere, quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Castigo corpus meum, et in servitutem redigo; et rursus, Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis. Et consummatis illis esuriit, hoc est, post quadraginta dierum finem Christus statim famem perpessus est: et forsitan magnam, ad profectum et commodum nostrum. Nam ea quæ propter nos passus est, in abundantia passus est, ex magnitudine caritatis ad nos, et ob multiplicem fructum nobis inde manantem. Hinc Christus ait in Psalmo: Genua mea infirmata sunt a jejunio, et caro mea immutata est propter oleum, hoc est olei defectum; et denuo, Humiliabam in jejunio animam meam.
paras.en: [[4:2|And he ate nothing in those days|Et nihil manducavit in illis diebus]], that is, within these forty days He took no bodily food at all. He did not, then, fast as we do, who take a meal once a day. And that, being about to fight against the devil, He willed first to abstain, made it plain that those who wish to overthrow the temptations of the demons must withdraw their flesh from the pleasures of taste and touch, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 9:27|I chastise my body and bring it into subjection|Castigo corpus meum, et in servitutem redigo]]; and again: [[Gal 5:24|they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences|Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis]]. [[4:2|And when they were ended, he was hungry|Et consummatis illis esuriit]]: that is, after the end of the forty days Christ at once suffered hunger, and perhaps great hunger, for our progress and profit. For what He suffered for our sake He suffered in abundance, out of the greatness of His charity towards us and for the manifold fruit that flows to us from it. Hence Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 108:24|My knees are weakened through fasting: and my flesh is changed for oil|Genua mea infirmata sunt a jejunio, et caro mea immutata est propter oleum]], that is, for want of oil; and again: [[Ps 34:13|I humbled my soul with fasting|Humiliabam in jejunio animam meam]].

paras.t: Denique Moyses et Elias tanto tempore jejunarunt ut Christus, nihil edentes neque bibentes; nec tamen esuriisse leguntur, quamvis postea esuriisse credantur. Noluit autem Christus diutius jejunare quam præfati ejus ministri, ne diabolus de ejus divinitate majorem æstimationem acciperet; itemque propter mysticam rationem, quoniam quadragenarius numerus pœnitentiæ congruit: constat etenim ex denario quater accepto, sicque designat hominis ex quatuor elementis compositi castigationem, cum observatione Decalogi secundum quatuor Evangeliorum doctrinam; et rursus, quoniam tot diebus jejunando, offerimus Deo decimas dierum anni (secundum Gregorium), cui et aliarum rerum decimas offerre præcipimur; insuper, ut singularitatem et ostentationem doceret vitandam.
paras.en: Moses and Elias, moreover, fasted for as long a time as Christ[[Ex 34:28||]][[3 Kings 19:8||]], eating and drinking nothing; yet we do not read that they were hungry, though they are believed to have been hungry afterwards. But Christ would not fast longer than these His ministers, lest the devil should form a higher estimate of His divinity; and also for a mystical reason, since the number forty befits penance: for it is made up of ten taken four times, and so signifies the chastisement of man, who is composed of four elements, together with the keeping of the Decalogue according to the teaching of the four Gospels. And again, because by fasting so many days we offer God the tithe of the days of the year (according to Gregory), to whom we are commanded to offer the tithes of other things as well [forty days are roughly a tenth of the year, reckoned as in Lent without the Sundays]. And besides, so as to teach that singularity and ostentation are to be avoided.

paras.t: Esuriit autem non ex infirmitate aut necessitate naturæ, sed divina dispensatione ac propria voluntate. Licet enim in communi loquendo, mirum et supernaturale sit hominem tanto tempore sine omni edulio et potu subsistere, nihilo minus in Christo mirabilius fuit quod postea esuriit, quam quod interim nil comedit. Ad quod intelligendum scire oportet, quod post resurrectionem futuram corpora Beatorum erunt animabus glorificatis perfectissime ad imperiumque subjecta, ita quod ex redundantia beatitudinis animarum in corpora, erunt corpora illa quatuor dotibus decorata, videlicet claritate, agilitate, subtilitate, et impassibilitate. Quum ergo anima Christi fuerit a principio suæ creationis præ cunctis creaturis intellectualibus præexcellenter Deo fruens, atque beata quoad præmium essentiale: constat quod ex redundantia beatitudinis suæ in corpus poterat præservari, et præservata fuisset ab omni passione corporisque incommodo, nisi Deo sic ordinante, dilata atque suspensa fuisset redundantia illa usque ad tempus, videlicet usque ad resurrectionem. Non ergo indiguit alimento, nisi ea voluntate qua redundantiam illam suspendit. Iterum, famem assumpsit, ut veram in se humanitatem ostenderet; item per famis suæ pœnalitatem magnam, nobis gratiam saturitatemque animæ mereretur. Omnis quippe afflictio ejus nobis meritoria exstitit. Rursus, ut diabolo occasionem tentandi se exhiberet, quemadmodum fortissimus pugil adversarium provocat ad congressum. Hinc asserit Glossa: Fames Christi pia fraus est, ne diabolus eum tentare caveret. Fraus itaque fuit fames illa, non quasi non fuerit vera fames, sed quoniam divinitatem celavit, dæmonemque fefellit.
paras.en: He was hungry, however, not from weakness or the necessity of nature, but by divine dispensation and His own will. For though, speaking generally, it is wonderful and above nature that a man should live so long without any food or drink, yet in Christ it was more wonderful that afterwards He was hungry than that meanwhile He ate nothing. To understand this we must know that after the future resurrection the bodies of the Blessed will be most perfectly subject to their glorified souls and to their command, so that from the overflow of the souls' beatitude into the bodies, those bodies will be adorned with four endowments, namely clarity, agility, subtlety and impassibility [the four “dowries” of the glorified body]. Since, then, the soul of Christ from the beginning of its creation enjoyed God pre-eminently above all intellectual creatures, and was blessed as to the essential reward, it is clear that by the overflow of its beatitude into the body it could have been kept, and would have been kept, from every suffering and bodily hardship, had not that overflow, by God's ordinance, been delayed and held back until a set time, namely until the resurrection. He did not, then, need food, except by that will by which He held back that overflow. Again, He took on hunger to show that His humanity was real; and also that by the great pain of His hunger He might merit for us grace and the soul's fulness. For every affliction of His was meritorious for us. Again, to offer the devil an occasion of tempting Him, as a very strong champion challenges his adversary to the fight. Hence the Gloss says: The hunger of Christ is a holy deceit, lest the devil should beware of tempting Him. That hunger, then, was a deceit, not as though it were not true hunger, but because it hid His divinity and deceived the demon. [The OCR of this passage, PDF 483 (p. 463), top of the right column, has lost letters at the line-ends; the wording is restored from the sense.]

paras.t: At vero, ex hoc quod diabolus Christum post baptismum atque jejunium tentare aggressus est, innotescit quod [diabolus] potissimum nititur hominem impe[tere ac] vincere, quum viderit eum in [bono] profectum, et aliquo ferventiori [proficiendi] desiderio inflammatum. Ideo in Ecclesiastico docetur: Fili, accedens ad servitutem Dei, sta in justitia et timore, et præpara animam tuam ad tentationem. Per hoc autem quod non legitur Christum [diabolus] tentasse nisi quum desertum ingressus est, designatur quod illos præcipue [nititur] dejicere, qui student perfectioni [soli]que Deo, omni hominum relicta frequentia, vacare nituntur. Hinc secundum doctores, solitaria vita, scilicet quæ est penitus solitaria, et extra cœnobium seu congregationem aut societatem, periculosa est, potissimum imperfectis. Postremo, per illud quod completo mirabili ac longo jejunio Christum aggressus est dæmon, ostenditur quod virtuosos ac religiosos etiam tunc de spiritualibus vitiis tentare molitur, quum eos carnalia viderit vitia superasse. Nunquam ergo securi ac improvidi simus, sed timorati semper et circumspecti, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Nisi in timore Dei tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua.
paras.en: Further, from the fact that the devil set about tempting Christ after His baptism and fast, it becomes known that the devil strives above all to attack and overcome a man when he sees him advanced in good and inflamed with some more fervent desire of progress [several words at the line-ends here, PDF 483, right column, are lost in the OCR and supplied from the sense]. So in Ecclesiasticus we are taught: [[Ecclus 2:1|Son, when thou comest to the service of God, stand in justice and in fear, and prepare thy soul for temptation|Fili, accedens ad servitutem Dei, sta in justitia et timore, et præpara animam tuam ad tentationem]]. And by the fact that we do not read that the devil tempted Christ except when He had gone into the desert, it is signified that he strives above all to cast down those who study perfection and endeavour, leaving all the company of men, to give themselves to God alone. Hence, according to the doctors, the solitary life, that is, one wholly solitary and outside a monastery, congregation or company, is dangerous, above all for the imperfect. Lastly, by the fact that the demon attacked Christ when His wonderful and long fast was completed, it is shown that he endeavours to tempt the virtuous and religious with spiritual vices even then, when he sees that they have overcome the carnal ones. Let us never, then, be secure and improvident, but always fearful and circumspect, as is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 27:4|Unless thou hold thyself diligently in the fear of the Lord, thy house shall quickly be overthrown|Nisi in timore Dei tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua]].

paras.t: Consequenter describitur tentationis processus. Dixit autem illi diabolus. Diabolus iste a multis fertur fuisse primus ille apostata angelus, qui Lucifer dicitur. Si Filius Dei es. Novit diabolus quod in Scripturis, tam homines virtuosi quam angeli sancti, appellentur filii Dei. Quum ergo loquitur Christo, Si Filius Dei es, intendit de unigenito [Filio] Patris æterni, an scilicet Christus [sit] unicus ille naturalisque Filius Dei, de cujus incarnatione, adventu et passione [noverat] diabolus Prophetas esse locutos. Diabolus quoque non dubitavit de Jesu sanctitate, sed de ejus vera divinitate. Dic lapidi huic, hoc est, propria auctoritate [impera], præcipiendoque age, ut lapis [iste] jacens panis fiat, hoc est, convertatur in panem.
paras.en: Next the course of the temptation is described. [[4:3|And the devil said to him|Dixit autem illi diabolus]]. This devil is said by many to have been that first apostate angel who is called Lucifer. [[4:3|If thou be the Son of God|Si Filius Dei es]]. The devil knew that in the Scriptures both virtuous men and holy angels are called sons of God. When, then, he says to Christ, *If thou be the Son of God*, he means the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father: whether, namely, Christ is that unique and natural Son of God of whose incarnation, coming and passion the devil knew the Prophets had spoken. The devil, moreover, did not doubt of Jesus' holiness, but of His true divinity. [[4:3|say to this stone|Dic lapidi huic]], that is, command by Thine own authority, and by commanding bring it about that this stone lying here [[4:3|be made bread|panis fiat]], that is, be turned into bread. [The OCR of this page, PDF 484 (p. 464), left column, has lost letters at the line-ends; the bracketed words in the Latin are supplied from the sense.]

paras.t: Primo [ergo tentat] diabolus Christum de vitio gulæ, [suadendo mut]ationem lapidis in panem, quia vidit Christum esuriisse, sicque magis [inclinatum] esse ad panis affectum […]. Denique non tentavit Christum primo de aliquo manifeste [enormi] seu vitioso, quia sanctitatem [ejus] scivit, ideo non confidebat quod ad tale aliquid posset eum statim inducere. [Cautus] est etiam dæmon […]: non enim dixit, Roga Deum ut lapidem convertat in panem, vel, Peto a te ut hoc facias; sed ait, Dic, hoc est solo imperio seu puro verbo hoc fac. Cognovit namque tentator, quod taliter rerum naturas mutare, Deo sit proprium: de quo ait Psalmista, Ipse dixit et facta sunt; cui et in libro Sapientiæ dicitur, Subest tibi, quum volueris, posse. Itaque cogitavit tentator: Si sic poterit lapidem in panem convertere, sciam quod Unigenitus Dei sit verusque Deus; quod si non poterit, patebit mihi quod purus sit homo. — Porro, in Matthæo legitur Christo dixisse: Dic ut lapides isti panes fiant. Aut ergo Lucas ponit singulare pro plurali, aut Matthæus plurale pro singulari: quorum utrumque sæpe fit in Scripturis.
paras.en: First, then, the devil tempts Christ with the vice of gluttony, urging Him to change the stone into bread, because he saw that Christ was hungry and so more inclined to the desire of bread […]. Again, he did not tempt Christ first with anything manifestly enormous or vicious, because he knew His holiness, and so did not trust that he could at once lead Him to anything of the kind. The demon is also very cunning […] [some words lost in the OCR, PDF 484, left column]: for he did not say, Ask God to turn the stone into bread, or, I ask Thee to do this; but he says, *Say*: that is, do it by command alone, by a bare word. For the tempter knew that to change the natures of things in this way belongs to God, of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made|Ipse dixit et facta sunt]]; and to whom it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 12:18|thy power is at hand when thou wilt|Subest tibi, quum volueris, posse]]. So the tempter thought: If He can turn the stone into bread in this way, I shall know that He is the Only-begotten of God and true God; but if He cannot, it will be plain to me that He is mere man. — Now in Matthew we read that he said to Christ: [[Matt 4:3|command that these stones be made bread|Dic ut lapides isti panes fiant]]. Either, then, Luke puts the singular for the plural, or Matthew the plural for the singular: both of which often happen in the Scriptures.

paras.t: Præterea secundum Ambrosium, ex eo quod diabolus explorando et tentando loquitur Christo, Si Filius Dei es, constat quod noverat Filium Dei venturum, sed hunc esse Jesum non æstimavit, propter infirmitatem corporis quam in ipso perpendit. Chrysostomus vero affirmat, quod diabolus audivit angelos Deo gloriam in Christi nativitate cantantes, angelum quoque pastoribus annuntiantem, Quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus; itemque quod vidit tres Magos puerum adorantes, Simeonem quoque et Annam ac Joannem Baptistam Jesu Christo testimonia perhibentes; ex prophetia etiam Danielis de numero hebdomadarum, agnovit tempus adventus Christi impletum; ex aliorum quoque oraculis Prophetarum, cognovit quod Christus sit Deus: ex quibus omnibus vehementer putavit quod Jesus esset Christus Unigenitus Dei. Porro, ex alia parte, videns eum inter populares et peccatores baptizatum, et fame confectum, dubitavit et fluctuavit quomodo talis posset esse Deus: ideo veritatem explorans, dicebat, Si Filius Dei es. Hinc et alii quidam dicunt, quod diabolus humilia in Deo non potuit credere.
paras.en: Besides, according to Ambrose, from the fact that the devil, probing and tempting, says to Christ, *If thou be the Son of God*, it is clear that he knew the Son of God was to come, but did not judge this Jesus to be He, because of the weakness of body that he perceived in Him. Chrysostom, however, affirms that the devil heard the angels singing glory to God at Christ's birth[[2:13||]], and the angel announcing to the shepherds: [[2:11|For, this day is born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord|Quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus]]; and that he saw the three Magi adoring the Child, and Simeon also and Anna and John the Baptist bearing witness to Jesus Christ; and from the prophecy of Daniel about the number of the weeks[[Dan 9:24||]] he recognised that the time of Christ's coming was fulfilled [the margin reads Dan. x, 24–27; the seventy weeks are Dan 9:24–27]; and from the oracles of the other Prophets he knew that Christ is God: from all of which he strongly thought that Jesus was the Christ, the Only-begotten of God. But on the other hand, seeing Him baptized among the common people and sinners, and worn with hunger, he doubted and wavered how such a one could be God: and so, probing the truth, he said, *If thou be the Son of God*. Hence certain others too say that the devil could not believe lowly things of God.

paras.t: Sed circa hæc verba dubitationes non parvæ occurrunt. Quum enim diabolus tantæ sit subtilitatis atque scientiæ, certissime noscit angelos sanctos nunquam mentiri, imo mentiri non posse. Si ergo audivit præfata angelorum testimonia de Christi nativitate peracta, viditque quod puerum illum Magi adoraverunt quem angelus asseruit esse Christum, nequaquam dubitavit quin Jesus fuerit Christus. Rursus, sicut ex dictis Prophetarum cognovit Dei Filium incarnandum, sic quoque ex eisdem scivit eum pro mundi salute passurum, imo ignominiosissima morte necandum. Hoc enim in Isaia, et in psalmo qui incipit, Deus, Deus meus, respice in me, quare me dereliquisti? apertissime fuit prædictum. Itaque apparet, quod non ideo æstimasset Jesum non esse Christum, quia abjecta sustinuit: præsertim, quoniam scivit Christum inter homines conversaturum, atque in magna paupertate victurum, prout in Zacharia et Baruch dictum erat; imo tempore passionis Christi, videns ineffabilem patientiam Christi, suggessit uxori Pilati ut persuaderet Pilato: Nihil tibi et justo illi.
paras.en: But about these words no small difficulties arise. For since the devil is of such subtlety and knowledge, he knows most certainly that the holy angels never lie, nay, cannot lie. If, then, he heard the aforesaid testimonies of the angels given at Christ's birth, and saw that the Magi adored that Child whom the angel declared to be the Christ, he in no way doubted that Jesus was the Christ. Again, just as from the sayings of the Prophets he knew that the Son of God was to be incarnate, so also from the same he knew that He was to suffer for the salvation of the world, nay, be put to a most shameful death. For this was most plainly foretold in Isaias[[Is 53:1||]], and in the psalm that begins: [[Ps 21:2|O God my God, look upon me: why hast thou forsaken me?|Deus, Deus meus, respice in me, quare me dereliquisti?]] It appears, then, that he would not have judged Jesus not to be the Christ because He bore lowly things: especially since he knew that Christ was to converse among men and live in great poverty, as had been said in Zacharias[[Zach 9:9||]] and Baruch[[Bar 3:38||]] [the margin gives Zach. ix, 9 and Baruch iii, chapter only]. Nay, at the time of Christ's passion, seeing Christ's ineffable patience, he prompted Pilate's wife to urge Pilate: [[Matt 27:19|Have thou nothing to do with that just man|Nihil tibi et justo illi]].

paras.t: Propter hæc et multa similia quæ possem inducere, non video quid ad hanc difficultatem solvendam aptius valeat responderi, nisi quod nono de Civitate Dei, capitulo 21, asserit Augustinus: Dæmonibus, inquit, Jesus Christus tantum innotuit quantum voluit; tantum autem voluit quantum oportuit, id est, expediens fuit, hoc est, quantum tumidis innotescendum fuit. Innotuit quoque eis, non per id quod est vita æterna et lumen incommutabile, sed per quædam temporalia suæ virtutis effecta seu opera, et occultissimæ signa præsentiæ, quæ angelicis mentibus etiam malignorum spirituum, potius quam infirmitati humanæ, possunt esse conspicua. Denique, quando ea Christus paululum supprimenda judicavit, et aliquanto altius latuit, tunc dubitavit de illo dæmonum princeps, eumque tentavit, an Christus esset explorans, quantum se ipse tentari permisit, ut hominem quem gerebat, ad nostræ imitationis temperaret exemplum.
paras.en: Because of these and many like things that I could bring forward, I do not see what can more fittingly be answered to solve this difficulty than what Augustine asserts in the ninth book of *The City of God*, chapter 21: Jesus Christ, he says, was made known to the demons as much as He willed; and He willed as much as was fitting, that is, as was expedient, namely as much as He had to be made known to the proud. And He was made known to them not by that which is eternal life and unchangeable light, but by certain temporal effects or works of His power and signs of His most hidden presence, which can be perceptible to angelic minds, even those of the evil spirits, rather than to human weakness. Then, when Christ judged that these should be a little suppressed, and He lay somewhat more deeply hidden, the prince of the demons doubted of Him and tempted Him, probing whether He was the Christ, as far as He Himself allowed Himself to be tempted, so as to temper the manhood He bore into an example for our imitation.

paras.t: Ex his B. Augustini eloquiis elucescit, quod dæmon tantam de Christo notitiam habuit, quantam Christus permisit. Unde et arbitror quod diabolus, ex præinductis et aliis variis verbis, factis, signisque Christi, certitudinaliter atque stabiliter cognovisset Jesum esse Christum, si Christus hoc permisisset, potissimum quando Christus postea aperte docuit se esse Dei Unigenitum, verumque Deum, atque hoc ipsum per miracula soli Deo possibilia confirmavit. Talia quippe diabolum non latuissent, si Christus permisisset. Nihilo minus Christus dicitur aliqua fecisse, ne diabolus cognosceret eum jam natum: et tamen quædam illorum non fuerant talia, quin si Christus permisisset, diabolus illis non obstantibus cognovisset Christum jam natum, et Jesum esse Christum. Communiter etenim dicitur, quod voluit Matrem suam quamvis virginem, esse desponsatam viro, ne Matris virginitas pateret diabolo, sicque Virginis filium agnosceret Christum: et tamen desponsatione illa non obstante, diabolus sua naturali industria bene explorasset, atque novisset, an Mater Jesu exsisteret virgo, ut doctores evidenter ostendunt. Unde quod hoc latuit dæmonem, fuit ex hoc quod divinitus fuit prohibitus, nec explorare permissus. Sic ad propositum dico, quod testimonia angelorum hominumque sanctorum præfata de Christo, tantum innotuerunt diabolo quantum Deus voluit et permisit: cujus moderamine factum est, ut diabolus sæpe sic fluctuaret ex consideratione diversorum circa Christum ejusque actus. — Hæc tam prolixe inserui, quia inferius sæpe locum habebunt, dum inquiretur qualiter dæmones et Judæi noverant Jesum esse Christum.
paras.en: From these words of blessed Augustine it shines out that the demon had as much knowledge of Christ as Christ allowed. Hence I also think that the devil, from the things brought forward above and from various other words, deeds and signs of Christ, would have known with certainty and firmly that Jesus was the Christ, had Christ allowed it; above all when Christ afterwards openly taught that He was the Only-begotten of God and true God, and confirmed this by miracles possible to God alone.
