For such things would not have been hidden from the devil, had Christ allowed it. Nevertheless Christ is said to have done some things so that the devil should not know that He was already born: and yet some of them were not such that, had Christ allowed it, the devil would not have known, in spite of them, that Christ was already born and that Jesus was the Christ. For it is commonly said that He willed His Mother, though a virgin, to be espoused to a husband, lest His Mother's virginity should be plain to the devil, and so he should recognise the Virgin's Son as the Christ: and yet, that espousal notwithstanding, the devil by his natural skill could well have searched out and known whether the Mother of Jesus was a virgin, as the doctors clearly show. So that this was hidden from the demon came from his being forbidden by God and not permitted to search it out. So, to the point, I say that the aforesaid testimonies of the angels and of holy men about Christ were made known to the devil as far as God willed and allowed: by whose governance it came about that the devil often wavered in this way, from considering the different things about Christ and His acts. — I have put this in at such length because it will often find a place further on, when it is asked how the demons and the Jews knew that Jesus was the Christ.

paras.t: Postremo et illud notandum, quod Augustinus adstruit Christum a principe dæmonum esse tentatum. Unde communiter fertur a Lucifero tentatus, quodque victus ille a Christo sit in infernum detrusus, nec exiturus nisi in Antichristi adventu: cujus ille possessor erit in omnibus et director.
paras.en: Lastly, this too is to be noted: Augustine maintains that Christ was tempted by the prince of the demons. Hence it is commonly said that He was tempted by Lucifer, and that he, overcome by Christ, was thrust down into hell, not to come out except at the coming of Antichrist, whose possessor and director he will be in all things.

paras.t: Et respondit ad illum Jesus: Scriptum est in Deuteronomio: Non in solo pane vivit homo, hoc est, non solo corporeo alimento homo indiget, subsistit, et sustentatur, sed in omni verbo Dei, id est per divina verba seu sacræ Scripturæ eloquia, vel per internas Dei inspirationes, seu allocutiones secretas. Itaque, sicut homo quantum ad corpus et conservationem in vita naturæ, indiget nutrimento corporeo, sic quantum ad animam et quoad adeptionem seu conservationem in vita gratiæ, indiget verbo Dei, quod rite asseritur animæ cibus. Hoc namque spiritualiter verbum Dei facit in anima, quod panis aut alius cibus materialis corporaliter agit in carne. Materialis etenim cibus restaurat deperditum, confortat naturam, ad debitam quantitatem perducit, in vita conservat: sic verba divina mentem ad pœnitentiam ducunt, qua deperdita tempora et omissa bona recuperantur; interiores animæ vires confortant, secundum illud Machabæorum: Judas singulos armavit, non hasta et clypeo, sed optimis sermonibus et exhortationibus. Insuper, verbum Dei ad debitam spiritualis profectus mensuram seu quantitatem perducit, nunc hortando, nunc comminando, nunc blandiendo, nunc jubendo, nunc consulendo, quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad erudiendum in justitia, ut perfectus sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum. Postremo, conservat animam in vita gratiæ actibusque virtutum. Et breviter, verbum Dei mortem peccati, videlicet errores, passiones, et vitia, omneque malum exstirpat, et ad omnem disponit, confert, inducit virtutem, consolatur, illuminat, dirigit, dicente Psalmista: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis; et rursus, In via testimoniorum tuorum delectatus sum, sicut in omnibus divitiis. Hinc in libro Sapientiæ legitur: Non nativitatis fructus pascunt homines, sed sermo tuus, Domine, eos qui in te credunt conservat.
paras.en: [[4:4|And Jesus answered him|Et respondit ad illum Jesus]]: It is written in Deuteronomy[[Deut 8:3||]]: [[4:4|Man liveth not by bread alone|Non in solo pane vivit homo]], that is, man does not need only bodily food, nor subsist and be sustained by it alone, [[4:4|but by every word of God|sed in omni verbo Dei]], that is, by the divine words or utterances of Holy Scripture, or by God's inward inspirations or secret speakings. So, as man, with regard to the body and its preservation in the life of nature, needs bodily nourishment, so, with regard to the soul and the gaining or keeping of the life of grace, he needs the word of God, which is rightly called the food of the soul. For the word of God does spiritually in the soul what bread or other material food does bodily in the flesh. Material food restores what was lost, strengthens nature, brings it to its due size, and keeps it in life: so the divine words lead the mind to penance, by which lost time and good things left undone are recovered; they strengthen the inward powers of the soul, according to that saying of the Machabees: Judas [[2 Mach 15:11|armed every one of them, not with defence of shield and spear, but with very good speeches, and exhortations|singulos armavit, non hasta et clypeo, sed optimis sermonibus et exhortationibus]]. Further, the word of God brings us to the due measure or stature of spiritual progress, now exhorting, now threatening, now coaxing, now commanding, now counselling, as the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 3:16|All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice|Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad erudiendum in justitia]], [[2 Tim 3:17|That the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work|ut perfectus sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum]] [the margin reads I Tim. iii, 16, 17; the words are those of the Second Epistle]. Lastly, it keeps the soul in the life of grace and in acts of virtue. In short, the word of God roots out the death of sin, namely errors, passions and vices, and every evil; and it disposes to, confers and brings in every virtue; it consoles, enlightens, directs, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:105|Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths.|Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis.]]; and again: [[Ps 118:14|I have been delighted in the way of thy testimonies, as in all riches.|In via testimoniorum tuorum delectatus sum, sicut in omnibus divitiis.]]. Hence we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 16:26|it is not the growing of fruits that nourisheth men, but thy word preserveth them that believe in thee|Non nativitatis fructus pascunt homines, sed sermo tuus, Domine, eos qui in te credunt conservat]].

paras.t: Victus diabolus in prima tentatione aggreditur aliam, tentans Christum de ambitione et avaritia, sciens quod multi qui vitia gustus et tactus, seu gulæ atque luxuriæ, fugiunt, ambitione et avaritia superantur ac pereunt. Et ducit illum diabolus in montem excelsum. Matthæus asserit quod assumpsit eum. Unde aliqui putant quod volando per aerem eum portavit: quod non videtur, præsertim quia communiter dicitur, et verisimile est, quod diabolus in forma humana, imo in specie hominis religiosi seu eremitæ, Christum in prima tentatione accessit, ut eum per simulatam sanctitatem citius falleret; et hanc speciem in secunda tentatione servasse videtur, in qua adhuc sub specie boni Christum tentavit: et hoc dico de secunda tentatione secundum ordinem quo Matthæus tres tentationes has recitat. Matthæus enim hanc quam Lucas secundo loco commemorat, tertiam ponit: in qua diabolus ostendit se esse malignum, ut verba ejus declarant.
paras.en: Beaten in the first temptation, the devil attacks with another, tempting Christ to ambition and avarice, knowing that many who flee the vices of taste and touch, that is, gluttony and lust, are overcome by ambition and avarice and perish. [[4:5|And the devil led him into a high mountain|Et ducit illum diabolus in montem excelsum]]. Matthew says that he *took him up*[[Matt 4:8||]]. Hence some think that he carried Him flying through the air: which does not seem so, above all because it is commonly said, and is likely, that the devil approached Christ in the first temptation in human form, indeed in the guise of a religious man or hermit, so as to deceive Him the more quickly by feigned holiness; and he seems to have kept this guise in the second temptation, in which he still tempted Christ under the appearance of good: and I say this of the second temptation according to the order in which Matthew relates these three temptations. For Matthew puts third the one that Luke mentions in the second place: in which the devil shows himself to be wicked, as his words make plain.

paras.t: Et ostendit illi omnia regna orbis terræ, id est quædam regna de omnibus mundi regnis; vel, omnia regna ostendit ei, non ad oculum corporalem, sed intellectualem, species et dispositiones regnorum ei proponendo, seu concupiscibilia illorum commemorando. Porro secundum Theophilum, ostendit ei omnia regna in phantasia: et forte per phantasiam intelligit Theophilus imaginariam visionem. Chrysostomus vero imaginatur, quod regna viciniora ostendit illi ad visum quantum fieri potuit, cetera quodam indicio, velut si quis cum aliquo stans, digitum versus diversas mundi plagas extendat, dicendo: Ecce ibi est Francia, ibi Italia. Huic modo videtur littera amplius consonare: ideo enim duxit Christum in altum montem, ut tentationi congrueret locus. Ceteras autem ostensiones potuisset fecisse in valle sicut in monte. Hæc ergo Christo ostendit, in momento temporis, id est valde celeriter seu brevissimo tempore, non in instanti, saltem quantum ad omnia quæ ostensionem illam circumstabant. Ideo autem tam multa objecta pariter sibi ostendit, ut fortius appetitum ejus moverent atque allicerent.
paras.en: [[4:5|and shewed him all the kingdoms of the world|Et ostendit illi omnia regna orbis terræ]], that is, some kingdoms out of all the kingdoms of the world; or else he showed Him all the kingdoms, not to the bodily eye but to the understanding, setting before Him the appearance and ordering of the kingdoms, or recounting what is desirable in them. Further, according to Theophilus [Theophylact], he showed Him all the kingdoms in fantasy [*in phantasia*]: and perhaps by fantasy Theophilus means an imaginary vision [that is, a vision in the imagination]. Chrysostom, however, pictures it thus: that he showed Him the nearer kingdoms to the sight, as far as could be done, and the rest by a kind of pointing, as if someone standing with another were to stretch out his finger towards the different regions of the world, saying: Look, there is France, there is Italy. The letter seems to agree more with this way: for this is why he led Christ up a high mountain, that the place might suit the temptation. The other showings he could have made in a valley as well as on a mountain. These things, then, he showed Christ [[4:5|in a moment of time|in momento temporis]], that is, very quickly, or in a very short time, not in an instant, at least as to all the circumstances of that showing. And he showed Him so many objects together so that they might move and allure His appetite the more strongly.

paras.t: Et ait illi: Tibi dabo potestatem hanc universam, hoc est, omnium regnorum istorum potentiam, fortalitia, populosque tibi subjiciam, et mundi monarcham te procreabo, seu omnium horum regem constituam, et gloriam, delicias, famam, honorem illorum, ita quod omnes te reverebuntur, et delectaberis de tua possessione, omnibus tibi subjectis; quia mihi tradita sunt. Hoc mentitur diabolus, quamvis aliquo modo verbum hoc possit verificari, præsertim quia et Christus in Joanne vocat diabolum hujus mundi principem, et de eodem scribit Apostolus: Deus, inquiens, hujus sæculi excæcavit mentes infidelium. Si ergo per regna intelligantur habitatores regnorum, præsertim iniqui, illi traditi sunt diabolo, hoc est, justo Dei judicio permissi sunt diabolo subjici, et tentari, vinci, possideri, seu captivi teneri ab eo, secundum illud Apostoli: Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. Unde et rex impiorum vocatur, juxta quod in Job habetur: Ipse est rex super universos filios superbiæ. Imo isti verius dicuntur se ipsos diabolo tradere, per hoc quod sponte ei consentiunt. Si autem per regna intelligantur regiones, urbes, opes, similesque possessiones habitantium super terram; talia, sicut et ipsi homines, generaliter tradita sunt diabolo, non ad jus dominandi ac possidendi, sed ad usum tentandi, sicut et sanctus Job dæmoni traditus fuit, dicente Domino ad Satan: Ecce in manibus tuis est. Et cui volo do illa. Hoc rursus mendaciter protulit; nec mirum, quum de ipso dicat Salvator: In veritate non stetit, quia veritas non est in eo; quum loquitur mendacium, ex propriis loquitur, quia mendax est, et pater ejus. Verumtamen permissione divina diabolus frequenter cooperatur hominibus ad obtinenda terrena ac mundi dominia. Propter quod dicit Ambrosius: Ambitio diabolicæ subjacet potestati.
paras.en: [[4:6|And he said to him: To thee will I give all this power|Et ait illi: Tibi dabo potestatem hanc universam]], that is, the might of all these kingdoms, their strongholds, and I will subject the peoples to thee, and make thee monarch of the world, or set thee up as king of all these things, [[4:6|and the glory|et gloriam]], the delights, fame and honour [[4:6|of them|illorum]], so that all will revere thee, and thou shalt delight in thy possession, with all things subject to thee; [[4:6|For to me they are delivered|quia mihi tradita sunt]]. In this the devil lies, although in some way this word can be made true, above all because Christ too in John calls the devil [[John 14:30|the prince of this world|hujus mundi principem]], and of him the Apostle writes: [[2 Cor 4:4|the god of this world hath blinded the minds of unbelievers|Deus, inquiens, hujus sæculi excæcavit mentes infidelium]]. If, then, by kingdoms are understood the inhabitants of kingdoms, especially the wicked, these have been delivered to the devil: that is, by the just judgment of God they have been allowed to be subject to the devil, and to be tempted, overcome, possessed or held captive by him, according to that saying of the Apostle: [[2 Tim 2:26|they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil by whom they are held captive at his will|Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]]. Hence he is also called the king of the wicked, as we have in Job: [[Job 41:25|he is king over all the children of pride|Ipse est rex super universos filios superbiæ]]. Nay, these are more truly said to deliver themselves to the devil, by consenting to him of their own accord. But if by kingdoms are understood the lands, cities, wealth and like possessions of those who dwell upon the earth, such things, like men themselves, have in general been delivered to the devil, not with the right of ruling and possessing them, but for the purpose of tempting, as holy Job too was delivered to the demon, when the Lord said to Satan: [[Job 2:6|Behold, he is in thy hand|Ecce in manibus tuis est]]. [[4:6|and to whom I will, I give them|Et cui volo do illa]]. This again he uttered falsely; and no wonder, since the Saviour says of him: [[John 8:44|he stood not in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father thereof|In veritate non stetit, quia veritas non est in eo; quum loquitur mendacium, ex propriis loquitur, quia mendax est, et pater ejus]]. Yet by God's permission the devil often works with men to gain earthly things and lordships of the world. Wherefore Ambrose says: Ambition lies under the power of the devil.

paras.t: Tu ergo si adoraveris coram me, hoc est, si me ipsum suppliciter adoraveris me præsente, erunt tua omnia regna mundi. Ecce quanta et quam inveterata ac indurata diaboli pompa. Olim propter superbiam suam pulsus est cœlo, quoniam dixit, Similis ero Altissimo: et nunc rursus vult ei assimilari, requirendo sibi impendi cultum soli Altissimo congruentem ac debitum; imo hoc quærit ab eo qui vere Altissimus est. Quod quamvis diabolus certitudinaliter non sciret, quod scilicet ille cui hæc dixit, esset Altissimus, tamen suspicabatur hoc ipsum, saltem in prima tentatione, sicque posuit se in periculo postulandi adorationem ab Altissimo et præferendi se illi: tanta est impudentia diaboli, aviditasque ipsius ad divinos honores, ex intolerabili ejus superbia nascens. Cujus impietatem ac cæcitatem multi superbi et ambitiosi sequuntur, prout Sapiens asserit: Imitantur illum qui sunt ex parte illius.
paras.en: [[4:7|If thou therefore wilt adore before me|Tu ergo si adoraveris coram me]], that is, if thou wilt humbly adore me myself in my presence, [[4:7|all shall be thine|erunt tua omnia]], all the kingdoms of the world. See how great, how inveterate and how hardened is the pride of the devil. Of old he was driven out of heaven for his pride, because he said: [[Is 14:14|I will be like the most High|Similis ero Altissimo]]; and now again he wishes to be like Him, demanding that the worship fitting and due to the Most High alone be paid to himself; nay, he asks this of Him who is truly the Most High. And although the devil did not know for certain that He to whom he said these things was the Most High, yet he suspected this very thing, at least in the first temptation; and so he put himself in danger of demanding adoration from the Most High and of setting himself above Him: so great is the shamelessness of the devil, and his greed for divine honours, springing from his intolerable pride. His impiety and blindness many proud and ambitious men follow, as the Wise man says: [[Wis 2:25|they follow him that are of his side|Imitantur illum qui sunt ex parte illius]].

paras.t: Et respondens Jesus, dixit illi: Scriptum est in Deuteronomio: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, cui tanquam altissimo principio, ac maximo benefactori, propriaque virtute salvare potenti, debetur summus singularisque honor, videlicet latriæ cultus, interior atque exterior. Quum ergo, diabole, sis creatura, non Deus, cur adorari exquiris? Interdum tamen adoratio sumitur pro honore seu reverentia duliæ: sicque creaturis impenditur. Unde frequenter in Scripturis leguntur quidam, homines vel angelos adorasse, ut Josue angelum, et Nathan propheta David regem. Et illi soli servies. Si hoc de servitute latriæ accipiatur, sicut expositores communiter sumunt, palam est quod soli Deo serviendum sit servitute latriæ. Porro, latria virtus est quæ Deo cultum cærimoniamque impendit; dulia vero est virtus qua personis creatis debitum seu decentem impendit honorem. Si autem verbum præfatum de quacumque servitute intelligatur, sensus est, quod soli Deo serviendum sit propter se atque finaliter: ita ut quidquid servitutis exhibeatur creaturis, totum ad Dei referatur honorem, et propter ejus ordinationem ac voluntatem agatur, ut quum homini ministramus, non tam homini, quam Deo in homine obsequamur. Hinc Samuel ait: Præparate corda vestra Domino, et servite illi soli.
paras.en: [[4:8|And Jesus answering said to him. It is written|Et respondens Jesus, dixit illi: Scriptum est]] in Deuteronomy[[Deut 6:13||]][[Deut 10:20||]] [where the words are “Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve him only”]: [[4:8|Thou shalt adore the Lord thy God|Dominum Deum tuum adorabis]], to whom, as the highest principle and the greatest benefactor, able to save by His own power, is due the supreme and singular honour, namely the worship of *latria* [the adoration due to God alone], both inward and outward. Since, then, devil, thou art a creature, not God, why dost thou seek to be adored? Sometimes, however, adoration is taken for the honour or reverence of *dulia* [the honour paid to creatures for their excellence]: and in this way it is paid to creatures. Hence we often read in the Scriptures that some adored men or angels, as Josue adored the angel[[Jos 5:15||]], and Nathan the prophet king David[[3 Kings 1:23||]]. [[4:8|and him only shalt thou serve|Et illi soli servies]]. If this is taken of the service of *latria*, as the expositors commonly take it, it is plain that God alone is to be served with the service of *latria*. Now *latria* is the virtue that pays worship and ceremony to God; *dulia* is the virtue by which due or fitting honour is paid to created persons. But if the said word is understood of any service whatever, the sense is that God alone is to be served for His own sake and as our final end: so that whatever service is shown to creatures is all referred to the honour of God and done because of His ordinance and will; so that when we minister to a man, we serve not so much the man as God in the man. Hence Samuel says: [[1 Kings 7:3|prepare your hearts unto the Lord, and serve him only|Præparate corda vestra Domino, et servite illi soli]].

paras.t: Consequenter, secundum ordinem hujus narrationis, ponitur tentatio tertia, quæ fuit de superbia, jactantia seu gloria vana. Et ducit illum in Jerusalem. Quia etenim voluit Christum tentare de arrogantiæ vanitate, duxit eum ad civitatem totius Judææ metropolim seu principalem, ubi major fuit occasio seu fortius incitamentum appetendi laudem humanam. Et statuit eum supra pinnaculum templi, hoc est supra planum quoddam deambulatorium, quod fuit supra templum vel portam ipsius, in quo sacerdotes sedebant quum populo prædicarent. Ibi enim solitus fuit magistros Judæorum ad multiplicem inducere vanitatem. Porro, de modo quo duxit Christum, an scilicet volavit secum per aerem, an duxit eum manu ad manum, an tulit eum in brachiis vel super humeros, scripsi super Matthæum. Origenes vero hic ait: Sequebatur plane Christus, quasi athleta ad tentationem sponte proficiscens, et quodammodo loquens: Duc me quo vis, invenies me in omnibus fortiorem.
paras.en: Next, following the order of this narrative, the third temptation is set down, which was of pride, boasting or vainglory. [[4:9|And he brought him to Jerusalem|Et ducit illum in Jerusalem]]. For since he wished to tempt Christ with the vanity of arrogance, he brought Him to the metropolis or chief city of all Judea, where there was greater occasion, or a stronger incitement, to desire human praise. [[4:9|and set him on a pinnacle of the temple|Et statuit eum supra pinnaculum templi]], that is, on a kind of level walk that was above the temple, or above its gate, on which the priests sat when they preached to the people. For there he was wont to lead the masters of the Jews into manifold vanity. As to the manner in which he brought Christ, whether he flew with Him through the air, or led Him hand in hand, or carried Him in his arms or on his shoulders, I have written on Matthew. Origen, however, says here: Christ plainly followed, as an athlete going of his own will to the contest, and as it were saying: Lead me where thou wilt; thou shalt find me stronger in all things.

paras.t: Et dixit illi: Si Filius Dei es, scilicet secundum sensum expositum, mitte te hinc deorsum, id est, de loco hoc alto te ipsum præcipita in conspectu adstantium, ut videntes te sine læsione cadere, aut sine casu volare, admirentur teque collaudent, et magnus de cetero habearis ab omnibus, qui tam diu quodammodo latuisti.
paras.en: [[4:9|and said to him: If thou be the Son of God|Et dixit illi: Si Filius Dei es]], namely in the sense explained, [[4:9|cast thyself from hence|mitte te hinc deorsum]], that is, throw thyself down from this high place in the sight of those standing by, so that, seeing thee fall without hurt, or fly without falling, they may marvel and praise thee together, and thou who hast so long been in a manner hidden may henceforth be held great by all.

paras.t: Nec timendum est tibi, scriptum est enim, quia angelis suis mandavit de te, id est, angelis sanctis Deus Pater commisit et jussit, ut tibi impendant quod subditur: ut conservent te, scilicet, ab omni læsione seu nocumento præservent. Hoc quod fuit contra diabolum, ipse dolose subticuit. Sic enim ait Psalmista: Ut custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis. Ideo diabolus vanum præcipitium suggerens, de viis obmutuit, ne sua fraudulentia panderetur. Et quia in manibus tollent te, id est, suis potestatibus et actibus te fulcient et defendent, seu corporaliter ferent, si fuerit opportunum, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum, id est, ne aliquod tibi impedimentum aut nocumentum obviet aut resistat. Hanc scripturam, apparenter, tamen impertinenter atque ad falsum intellectum allegat diabolus: Primo, quoniam psalmus ille, et scriptura hæc allegata, non loquitur ad litteram de Christo, sed de membris ejus electis fidelibus, secundum Hieronymum. Christus autem angelorum custodia seu auxilio non egebat, præsertim quia et comprehensor fuit secundum superiores animæ vires, et cunctis angelis altior atque potentior, non solum ut Deus imo etiam secundum naturam humanam propter suppositalem unionem ejus cum Verbo. Insuper scriptura ista intelligenda non est, quasi electi in vita hac per angelicam custodiam a malis pœnæ seu adversitatibus et tormentis præserventur, vel eripiantur, quamvis quandoque hoc accidat: Multæ enim tribulationes justorum; sed a malis culpæ præsertim, et etiam ab aliquibus corporalibus nocumentis, per angelos custodiuntur.
paras.en: Nor needest thou fear, [[4:10|For it is written that He hath given his angels charge over thee|scriptum est enim, quia angelis suis mandavit de te]], that is, God the Father has entrusted and commanded the holy angels to render thee what follows: [[4:10|that they keep thee|ut conservent te]], namely, preserve thee from all hurt or harm. What told against the devil he craftily left out. For the Psalmist says: [[Ps 90:11|to keep thee in all thy ways|Ut custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis]]. So the devil, suggesting a vain leap, kept silent about *ways*, lest his deceit be laid bare. [[4:11|And that in their hands they shall bear thee up|Et quia in manibus tollent te]], that is, by their powers and acts they will uphold and defend thee, or carry thee bodily if need be, [[4:11|lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone|ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum]], that is, lest any hindrance or harm meet or withstand thee. This scripture the devil cites plausibly, yet beside the point and in a false sense. First, because that psalm and this scripture cited do not speak literally of Christ, but of His members, the elect faithful, according to Jerome. But Christ had no need of the angels' guard or help, above all because He was a *comprehensor* [one already enjoying the vision of God] in the higher powers of His soul, and higher and mightier than all the angels, not only as God but even in His human nature, because of its union with the Word in one Person. Moreover, this scripture is not to be understood as if the elect in this life were preserved or rescued by the guard of angels from the evils of punishment, from adversities and torments, though this sometimes happens; for [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|Multæ enim tribulationes justorum]]: but they are guarded by the angels from the evils of guilt above all, and also from some bodily harms.

paras.t: Circa hunc locum loquitur Origenes: Unde tibi, diabole, scire quod ista scripta sunt? Numquid legisti Prophetas, aut divina eloquia? Legisti quidem, non ut ipse ex lectione eorum melior fieres, sed ut de simplici littera eos qui amici sunt litteræ, interficias. Scis quia si de aliis voluminibus loqui eis volueris, non decipies. Vide autem, quomodo diabolus et in ipsis testimoniis versipellis est. Vult enim minuere gloriam Salvatoris, quasi indigeat auxilio angelorum, offensurus pedem, nisi illorum manibus sublevetur. Hoc enim testimonium, non de Christo, sed de Sanctis generaliter scriptum est: non enim indiget angelorum auxilio, qui major est angelis. Quin potius disce, diabole, quod nisi Jesus adjuvaret angelos, offenderent pedem suum. Quare autem siles quod sequitur, Super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis? nisi quia tu es basiliscus, tu draco, tu leo. Hæc Origenes.
paras.en: On this place Origen says: Whence knowest thou, devil, that these things are written? Hast thou read the Prophets, or the divine oracles? Thou hast read them indeed, not to become better thyself by reading them, but to slay with the bare letter those who are friends of the letter. Thou knowest that if thou wouldst speak to them out of other books, thou wouldst not deceive them. But see how the devil is shifty even in the very testimonies. For he wishes to lessen the Saviour's glory, as though He needed the help of angels and would strike His foot unless He were lifted up by their hands. For this testimony is written not of Christ but of the Saints in general: He who is greater than the angels does not need the angels' help. Learn rather, devil, that unless Jesus helped the angels, they would strike their foot. But why art thou silent about what follows, [[Ps 90:13|Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk|Super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis]]? unless because thou art the basilisk, thou the dragon, thou the lion. Thus Origen.

paras.t: Et respondens Jesus, ait illi: Dictum est, Deo loquente per Moysen in Deuteronomio: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum. Hoc protulit Christus, non appellando se Deum diaboli, quamvis esset ejus creator, Deus, ac Dominus, nec increpando directe diabolum de hoc quod Christum creatorem suum tentare aggressus sit: non enim voluit insinuare diabolo Deum se esse. Sed iste est sensus: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum, hoc est, o homo quicumque, non præsumas Deum tentare.
paras.en: [[4:12|And Jesus answering, said to him: It is said|Et respondens Jesus, ait illi: Dictum est]], God speaking through Moses in Deuteronomy[[Deut 6:16||]]: [[4:12|Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God|Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum]]. Christ said this not calling Himself the devil's God, though He was his Creator, God and Lord, nor rebuking the devil directly for having set about tempting Christ his Creator: for He did not wish to let the devil know that He was God. But this is the sense: *Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God*, that is, O man, whoever thou art, presume not to tempt God.

paras.t: Porro, Deum tentare, est absque necessitate de ejus sapientia, providentia, vel potestate experimentum accipere, utpote omittendo quod aliunde habet vel potest. Multipliciter quoque homo sic tentat Deum: Primo, inquirendo, seu experimentum sumendo de sapientia ejus, an scilicet omnia sciat; vel de providentia ejus, an humana gubernet, vel servientibus sibi adsit, quemadmodum in Exodo de filiis Israel scriptum est: Tentaverunt Deum, dicentes, Estne Dominus in nobis, an non? Vel de omnipotentia Dei, secundum illud Psalmistæ: Tentaverunt Deum in cordibus suis; et male locuti sunt de Deo; dixerunt, Numquid poterit Deus parare mensam in deserto? Insuper istud fit, indebite experiendo voluntatem Dei, ut illi qui volunt experiri an Deus infra determinatum tempus eos velit liberare, ita quod postea ejus auxilium non exspectent, nisi interim eis subvenerit, juxta illud Judith: Qui estis vos, qui tentatis Dominum? Posuistis vos tempus miserationis Domini, et in arbitrio vestro diem constituistis ei. Rursus hoc agitur, indebite experiendo quid homo possit apud Deum: et hoc diabolus Christo suasit. Hæc ergo vitanda sunt, quamdiu habet quis aliud quod faciat, et quo sibi provideat seu veritatem cognoscat. Quod si non habuerit, seu aliunde adipisci nequiverit, tunc fiducialiter se convertat ad Deum, quemadmodum scriptum est: Quum ignoremus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te. Quoniam itaque a pinnaculo templi usque ad terram fuit descensus per gradus, præcipitare se de pinnaculo pertinuisset ad Dei tentationem.
paras.en: Now to tempt God is, without necessity, to put His wisdom, providence or power to the proof, namely by neglecting what one has or can do by other means. And man tempts God in this way in many manners. First, by inquiring into, or making trial of, His wisdom, whether He knows all things; or of His providence, whether He governs human affairs or stands by those who serve Him, as is written in Exodus of the children of Israel: They tempted God, saying, [[Ex 17:7|Is the Lord amongst us or not?|Estne Dominus in nobis, an non?]] [the Vulgate has *Dominum*, “the Lord”, where Denis has *Deum*]. Or of the omnipotence of God, according to that saying of the Psalmist: [[Ps 77:18|And they tempted God in their hearts|Tentaverunt Deum in cordibus suis]]; [[Ps 77:19|And they spoke ill of God: they said: Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?|et male locuti sunt de Deo; dixerunt, Numquid poterit Deus parare mensam in deserto?]]? Further, this is done by unduly making trial of God's will, as those do who wish to find out whether God will deliver them within a fixed time, so that afterwards they will not wait for His help unless He has come to their aid meanwhile; according to that of Judith: [[Jdt 8:11|who are you that tempt the Lord|Qui estis vos, qui tentatis Dominum]]? [[Jdt 8:13|You have set a time for the mercy of the Lord, and you have appointed him a day, according to your pleasure.|Posuistis vos tempus miserationis Domini, et in arbitrio vestro diem constituistis ei]] [the margin reads Judith viii, 11, 13]. Again, this is done by unduly making trial of what a man can do with God: and this is what the devil urged on Christ. These things, then, are to be avoided so long as one has something else to do, by which to provide for oneself or to know the truth. But if one has not, or cannot obtain it otherwise, then let him turn to God with confidence, as it is written: [[2 Par 20:12|as we know not what to do, we can only turn our eyes to thee|Quum ignoremus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te]]. Since, then, there was a way down by steps from the pinnacle of the temple to the ground, to throw Himself down from the pinnacle would have been tempting God.

paras.t: Et consummata omni tentatione jam dicta: nam et ceteræ tentationes reducuntur ad istas. Estque in tribus his tentamentis omnium materia delictorum, secundum Ambrosium, atque origo vitiorum cunctorum, secundum Glossam, juxta illud Joannis: Omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis est, et concupiscentia oculorum, et superbia vitæ. Diabolus recessit ab illo, tanquam victus et fine optato frustratus, quia incertus permansit de Christi divinitate, et an esset Messias in lege promissus. Recessit autem usque ad tempus: quia et postea rursus eum tentavit, dum Judæos ad ejus persecutiones induxit; maxime autem tempore passionis per vasa sua, scilicet per homines pravos, eum impugnavit; imo et tunc Christum accedere ausus est, quemadmodum in Joanne protestatur: Venit ad me princeps mundi hujus, et in me non habet quidquam. Denique hostis antiquus etiam nos sæpe ad tempus intentatos relinquit, ut interim vana securitate, torpore seu otio resolvamur et tepescamus, sicque improvise ac subito rediens facilius nos prosternat. Itaque indesinenter custoditi simus, ac circumspecti; et ab omni tentatione erepti, mox aliam præstolemur; et contra aciem vitiorum semper stemus parati virtutibusque armati, quemadmodum Augustinus hortatur: Persevera usque ad finem, quia tentatio perseverat usque in finem. Insuper aliqui dicunt, quod dæmon ab homine semel victus nunquam amplius tentat eumdem, vel saltem nunquam de cetero tentat eum de eodem peccato. Quibus obviare videtur, quod Evangelista hic ait, videlicet, quod diabolus recessit a Christo usque ad tempus: quo innuit quod postmodum rursus tentaverit eum per se aut per suos ministros.
paras.en: [[4:13|And all the temptation being ended|Et consummata omni tentatione]], that is, the temptation already spoken of: for the other temptations too are reduced to these. And in these three temptations is the matter of all sins, according to Ambrose, and the origin of all vices, according to the Gloss, according to that saying of John: [[1 John 2:16|all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes and the pride of life|Omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis est, et concupiscentia oculorum, et superbia vitæ]]. [[4:13|the devil departed from him|Diabolus recessit ab illo]], as one beaten and cheated of the end he desired, because he remained uncertain of Christ's divinity, and whether He was the Messias promised in the law. But he departed [[4:13|for a time|usque ad tempus]]: for afterwards he tempted Him again, when he stirred up the Jews to persecute Him; and above all at the time of the passion he assailed Him through his vessels, that is, through wicked men; nay, he even dared then to come near Christ, as He declares in John: [[John 14:30|the prince of this world: cometh: and in me he hath not any thing|Venit ad me princeps mundi hujus, et in me non habet quidquam]] [Denis has *Venit ad me*, “cometh to me”]. Further, the old enemy often leaves us too untempted for a time, so that meanwhile we may grow slack and lukewarm in vain security, torpor or idleness, and so, coming back unforeseen and suddenly, he may overthrow us the more easily. Let us therefore be ceaselessly on our guard and watchful; and when rescued from one temptation, let us at once expect another; and let us always stand ready against the battle-line of the vices, armed with the virtues, as Augustine exhorts: Persevere to the end, because temptation perseveres to the end. Moreover, some say that a demon once overcome by a man never tempts him again, or at least never again tempts him to the same sin. Against this seems to be what the Evangelist says here, namely that the devil departed from Christ *for a time*: by which he hints that afterwards he tempted Him again, by himself or through his ministers.

paras.t: Postremo, de hac triplici Christi tentatione et ordine earumdem plura dici hic possent, quæ quia super Matthæum conscripsi, nunc prætereo.
paras.en: Lastly, more might be said here of this threefold temptation of Christ and of their order; but since I have written of these things on Matthew, I pass them over now.

4.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli quarti, a loco quo dicitur: Et regressus est Jesus in virtute Spiritus in Galilæam
4.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this fourth chapter, from the place where it is said: “And Jesus returned in the power of the spirit, into Galilee”

paras.t: Christi actio nostra perhibetur instructio. Igitur qualis debeat esse doctor et prædicator verbi cælestis, ex hoc processu vitæ Christi ostenditur. Non enim orsus est prædicare, nisi circa tricesimum ætatis suæ annum, et post baptismum, item post eremiticam conversationem, et abstinentiam, dæmonisque superationem, ad innuendum quod prædicator et doctor debet esse maturæ ætatis, et a vitiis emundatus. Peccatori enim dixit Deus: Quare tu enarras justitias meas? Erit quoque virtutibus exercitatus, ut primo faciat quod alios docet, sicut de Christo dicitur in Actibus: Cœpit Jesus facere et docere. Tentamenta etiam diaboli et carnis petulantiam debet vicisse, sicut Apostolus loquitur: Castigo corpus meum, et in servitutem redigo, ne aliis prædicans, ipse reprobus efficiar. Unde de Christo jam dicitur: Et regressus est Jesus, hoc est, post tentamenta atque jejunia ejus in deserto rediit ad homines, ut quod ipse fecit, eos doceret, in virtute Spiritus, id est in magna potestate Spiritus Sancti, per quam cœpit operari miracula; in virtute quoque Spiritus, id est plenus omni virtute et dono Spiritus Sancti. Et quamvis hac potestate atque virtutibus plenus exstiterit in anima ab incarnationis exordio, tamen nunc scribitur in virtute Spiritus esse regressus, quia post reditum a deserto cœpit sanctitatem atque potentiam suam abundantissime manifestare. Itaque virtus Spiritus, nominatur spiritualis virtus operativa signorum quæ datur a Spiritu Sancto. Unde in libris Regum legitur spiritus Eliæ requievisse super Eliseum.
paras.en: Christ's action is held to be our instruction. So what kind of man the teacher and preacher of the heavenly word ought to be is shown from this course of Christ's life. For He did not begin to preach until about the thirtieth year of His age, and after His baptism, and also after His life in the desert, His fasting, and His overcoming of the devil: to give us to understand that the preacher and teacher must be of mature age and cleansed of vices. For to the sinner God hath said: [[Ps 49:16|Why dost thou declare my justices|Quare tu enarras justitias meas?]]? He will also be practised in the virtues, so as first to do what he teaches others, as is said of Christ in the Acts: [[Acts 1:1|Jesus began to do and to teach|Cœpit Jesus facere et docere]]. He must also have overcome the temptations of the devil and the wantonness of the flesh, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 9:27|I chastise my body and bring it into subjection: lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway|Castigo corpus meum, et in servitutem redigo, ne aliis prædicans, ipse reprobus efficiar]]. Hence it is now said of Christ: [[4:14|And Jesus returned|Et regressus est Jesus]], that is, after His temptations and fasts in the desert He came back to men, to teach them what He Himself had done, [[4:14|in the power of the spirit|in virtute Spiritus]], that is, in the great power of the Holy Spirit, by which He began to work miracles; and *in the power of the Spirit* also means: full of every virtue and gift of the Holy Spirit. And although He was full of this power and of the virtues in His soul from the first moment of the incarnation, yet it is now written that He returned in the power of the Spirit, because after coming back from the desert He began to show His holiness and power most abundantly. So the power of the Spirit is the name given to the spiritual power of working signs which is given by the Holy Spirit. Hence we read in the books of Kings that [[4 Kings 2:15|The spirit of Elias hath rested upon Eliseus|spiritus Eliæ requievisse super Eliseum]].

paras.t: Porro Christi, secundum quod Deus est, et Spiritus Sancti una est virtus, una omnipotentia, et quoad hoc Christus increata ac propria virtute fecit miracula: quæ virtus toti superbenedictæ Trinitati communis est, cui competit operari miracula auctoritative, imperialiter ac principaliter, juxta illud: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus. Præter hanc increatam virtutem, fuit in Christo secundum naturam assumptam, virtus seu potestas super omnem creaturam: de qua alibi ait, Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra; quæ fuit potestas creata et data a Spiritu Sancto, imo a tota supergloriosissima Trinitate: de qua videtur nunc potissimum loqui Evangelista. Præterea Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei movet quæstionem, an Sancti fecerunt miracula per aliquam virtutem exsistentem in eis, concessamque eis divinitus, ita quod effective cooperati sint in miraculosis effectibus. Sicque posset de Christo inquiri, an præter potestatem increatam divinam fuit in eo virtus creata miraculorum productiva: potestque dici, quod ad agenda miracula sufficiat in eo ponere duplicem virtutem seu potestatem præfatam. De potentia vero animæ Christi, an habuit omnipotentiam, et qualem potentiam habuit respectu immutationis creaturarum, et quantum ad proprium corpus, itemque quoad exsecutionem propriæ voluntatis, loquitur S. Thomas in tertia parte, quæstione 13, et infra forte tangetur.
paras.en: Now Christ, as He is God, and the Holy Spirit have one power, one omnipotence; and in this respect Christ worked miracles by an uncreated power that was His own: a power common to the whole more than blessed Trinity, to which it belongs to work miracles with authority, as sovereign and as principal cause, according to that saying: [[Ps 71:18|Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone doth wonderful things|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus]]. Besides this uncreated power, there was in Christ, according to the nature He assumed, a power or authority over every creature: of which He says elsewhere, [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo et in terra]]; and this was a created power, given by the Holy Spirit, indeed by the whole more than most glorious Trinity: and it is of this that the Evangelist seems chiefly to speak here. Augustine, moreover, in the book *On the City of God*, raises the question whether the Saints worked miracles by some power existing in them and granted them by God, so that they cooperated as efficient causes in the miraculous effects. And so it might be asked of Christ whether, besides the uncreated divine power, there was in Him a created power productive of miracles: and it may be said that for working miracles it is enough to place in Him the twofold power or authority just mentioned. As for the power of Christ's soul, whether it had omnipotence, and what power it had with respect to changing creatures, and over its own body, and in carrying out its own will, St Thomas speaks of this in the third part, question 13; and it will perhaps be touched on below.

paras.t: Itaque, Regressus est in Galilæam, ex qua fuerat oriundus, et de qua ierat ad Joannis baptismum, et fama exiit per universam regionem Galilææ de illo, propter sapientiam, eloquentiam, sanctitatem, et miracula ejus quæ cœpit tunc agere. Arbitror quoque, quod testimonium Præcursoris tam præclarum atque credibile, fecit eum non parum famosum: quod multi Galilæorum audierant. Unde, quia post illud testimonium Christus mox desertum ingressus est, quum redeuntem viderunt, memorati sunt verborum Joannis. Et ipse docebat in synagogis eorum. Synagoga enim vocabatur, vel ipsa Judæorum collectio, vel domus in qua ad orandum vel audiendum lectionem legis et Prophetarum conveniebant. Ibi ergo prædicavit tanquam magister magnæ auctoritatis, et quoniam ibi major audientia fuit. Et magnificabatur, id est, magnæ sapientiæ ac virtutis reputabatur, ab omnibus audientibus eum.
paras.en: So He returned [[4:14|into Galilee|in Galilæam]], where He came from, and from which He had gone to John's baptism, [[4:14|and the fame of him went out through the whole country|et fama exiit per universam regionem Galilææ de illo]] of Galilee, because of His wisdom, eloquence and holiness, and the miracles which He then began to do. I think too that the Forerunner's testimony, so glorious and so credible, made Him not a little famous: for many Galileans had heard it. Hence, since straight after that testimony Christ went into the desert, when they saw Him come back they remembered John's words. [[4:15|And he taught in their synagogues|Et ipse docebat in synagogis eorum]]. For a synagogue was the name either of the assembly of the Jews itself, or of the house where they gathered to pray or to hear the reading of the law and the Prophets. There, then, He preached as a master of great authority, and because the audience was larger there. [[4:15|and was magnified|Et magnificabatur]], that is, was held to be of great wisdom and virtue, [[4:15|by all|ab omnibus]] who heard Him.

paras.t: Et venit Nazareth ubi erat nutritus. Ibi enim conceptus fuit, et in pueritia habitavit usque ad tempus quo ad baptismum Joannis accessit, prout supra dictum est. Et intravit secundum consuetudinem suam die sabbati in synagogam: quoniam illo die celebri magis convenerunt Judæi ad audiendum verbum Dei et ad deprecandum faciem Domini, sicut nunc faciunt Christiani in die dominico. Etenim festivis temporibus idcirco ab exteriori occupatione cessatur, ut homines divinis exercitiis quietius devotiusque intendant, et quod ferialibus diebus per omissionem vel commissionem peccaverunt, corrigant et emendent, ac perditum tempus recuperent. Ideo Christi consuetudo fuit tunc ingredi synagogam, quia tunc plures auditores invenit, et quoniam bonas aliorum consuetudines voluit approbare, seque conformare eisdem, præsertim quoniam laudabilis consuetudo vim legis sortitur, secundum Augustinum.
paras.en: [[4:16|And he came to Nazareth, where he was brought up|Et venit Nazareth ubi erat nutritus]]. For there He was conceived, and there He lived in His boyhood until the time when He went to John's baptism, as was said above. [[4:16|and he went into the synagogue, according to his custom, on the sabbath day|Et intravit secundum consuetudinem suam die sabbati in synagogam]]: because on that solemn day the Jews gathered in greater numbers to hear the word of God and to entreat the face of the Lord, as Christians now do on the Lord's day. For on feast days outward work stops for this reason: that men may give themselves more quietly and devoutly to divine exercises, and correct and amend what they have done wrong on working days by omission or commission, and recover lost time. So it was Christ's custom to go into the synagogue then, because He found more hearers then, and because He wished to approve the good customs of others and to conform Himself to them, especially since a praiseworthy custom acquires the force of law, according to Augustine.

paras.t: Et surrexit legere, id est, surgendo disposuit se ad legendum, et monstravit velle se legere: ut ex ipsa Scriptura quasi thema acciperet sui sermonis; item, ut insinuaret quod prædicator et doctor sermocinationem suam in sacra debet fundare Scriptura; et iterum, ut testimonio Scripturarum, se audiendum probaret, et Christum esse adstrueret; postremo, ut unum de minoribus Ordinibus, scilicet Ordinem officiumque lectoris impleret et approbaret: quemadmodum etiam officium exorcistæ explevit dæmones expellendo; acolythi seu ceroferarii, protestando, Ego sum lux mundi; ostiarii quoque, ementes et vendentes de templo ejiciendo. Sicque patet Christum per quatuor suos actus, approbasse quatuor Ordinum inferiorum officia: ideo nullus, quantumlibet vita aut scientia magnus, contemnere debet accipere Ordines istos, eorumve officia exsequi, quoniam non est servus major domino suo.
paras.en: [[4:16|and he rose up to read|Et surrexit legere]], that is, by rising He made ready to read and showed that He wished to read: so as to take from Scripture itself, as it were, the theme of His sermon; also, to intimate that the preacher and teacher must ground his preaching on sacred Scripture; again, to prove by the testimony of the Scriptures that He ought to be heard, and to establish that He was the Christ; lastly, to fulfil and approve one of the minor Orders, namely the Order and office of lector: as He also fulfilled the office of exorcist by casting out devils; of acolyte or taper-bearer, by declaring, [[John 8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego sum lux mundi]]; and of porter, by casting the buyers and sellers out of the temple. So it is plain that by these four acts of His Christ approved the offices of the four lower Orders: therefore no one, however great in life or learning, should disdain to receive these Orders or to carry out their offices, since [[John 13:16|The servant is not greater than his lord|non est servus major domino suo]] [the margin's numerals are hard to read: John 13:16 or 15:20, where the same words occur].

paras.t: Et traditus est illi liber Isaiæ prophetæ a ministris synagogæ, quorum officium fuerat legere: et forte mirabantur quod legere vellet, scientes quod non didicerat litteras. Et ut revolvit librum, invenit locum ubi scriptum erat. Christus non solum per divinam et increatam scientiam, sed etiam per scientiam suæ animæ a principio creationis ejus ei inditam, distinctissime novit cuncta creata, quantumlibet parva et magna: ideo constat quod scivit quot folia, quot rigæ, quot verba continebantur in libro, et ubi quilibet passus staret. Unde primo ictu reperit passum quem voluit, non utique fortuito, sed deliberate.
paras.en: [[4:17|And the book of Isaias the prophet was delivered unto him|Et traditus est illi liber Isaiæ prophetæ]] by the ministers of the synagogue, whose office it had been to read: and perhaps they wondered that He wished to read, knowing that He had not learned letters. [[4:17|And as he unfolded the book, he found the place where it was written|Et ut revolvit librum, invenit locum ubi scriptum erat]]. Christ knew all created things most distinctly, however small and great, not only by His divine and uncreated knowledge but also by the knowledge put into His soul from the beginning of its creation: so it is certain that He knew how many leaves, how many lines, how many words the book contained, and where each passage stood. Hence at the first stroke He found the passage He wanted, not by chance but deliberately.

paras.t: Spiritus Domini, id est Spiritus Sanctus, qui est Spiritus Patris, imo Patris et Filii tanquam unius principii uniusque fontis ac spiratoris Spiritus Sancti: de quo scriptum est, Spiritus Domini replevit orbem terrarum; et de quo ait Apostolus, Ubi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas; super me, id est, desuper venit in me, et est habitans in me secundum quod homo sum. Anima enim Christi plena fuit Spiritu Sancto ab incarnationis exordio: unde Spiritus Sanctus per inexsistentiam donorum suorum dicitur super Christum hominem requievisse, secundum illud Isaiæ: Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus. Insuper fuit et requievit super Christum tanquam motor, ductor et præceptor seu inclinator Christi in omnibus secundum naturam assumptam, quæ fuit Spiritus Sancti, imo totius Trinitatis, electissimum ac obedientissimum instrumentum seu organum, divinum in omnibus sequens instinctum, sicut in Joanne testatur: Quia quæ placita sunt Patri, facio semper.
paras.en: [[4:18|The spirit of the Lord|Spiritus Domini]], that is, the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Father, indeed of the Father and the Son as of one principle and one source and spirator of the Holy Spirit [that is, the one from whom the Spirit proceeds by "spiration"]: of whom it is written, [[Wis 1:7|the Spirit of the Lord hath filled the whole world|Spiritus Domini replevit orbem terrarum]]; and of whom the Apostle says, [[2 Cor 3:17|where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty|Ubi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas]]; [[4:18|is upon me|super me]], that is, He came into me from above, and dwells in me according as I am man. For Christ's soul was full of the Holy Spirit from the first moment of the incarnation: hence the Holy Spirit, by the indwelling of His gifts, is said to have rested upon Christ as man, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 11:2|the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding|Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus]]. Moreover He was upon Christ and rested upon Him as the mover, guide and instructor or inclining force of Christ in all things according to the nature He assumed, which was the most chosen and most obedient instrument or organ of the Holy Spirit, indeed of the whole Trinity, following the divine prompting in all things, as He testifies in John: [[John 8:29|I do always the things that please him|Quia quæ placita sunt Patri, facio semper]].

paras.t: Propter quod unxit me: id est, quia sic placuit Spiritui Sancto venire et quiescere super me, ideo plenitudine gratiæ et virtutum me hominem spiritualiter irrigavit, perfudit, implevit: quemadmodum scriptum est, Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ; et in Actibus, Unxit eum Deus Spiritu Sancto et virtute. Sicque quod ait, Propter quod, dicit causam a priori. Potest quoque notare causam a posteriori, ut sit sensus: Propter quod unxit me, id est, ex hoc quod Spiritus Domini sic fuit et est super me, patet atque probatur ac sequitur quod unxit me, quemadmodum causa ostenditur per effectum. Denique Christus non solum plenus fuit donis gratiæ gratum facientis, sed et donis gratiæ gratis datæ: unde et unctus dicitur fuisse in regem, in pontificem seu sacerdotem, atque Prophetam. Et totum hoc factum est in incarnationis exordio. Quod si postea factum legatur, intelligendum est quantum ad manifestationem: imo sicut in die Parasceves obtulit se tanquam sacerdos oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis per effectum, ita affectualiter cœpit hoc facere a principio creationis animæ suæ, atque ex tunc cœpit esse mediator ac reconciliator, orator et pontifex inter Deum et homines. Insuper unctus est in templum seu tabernaculum Divinitatis, quia ut ait Apostolus, in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter. Christus quoque in Joanne ait Judæis: Solvite templum hoc, et in tribus diebus excitabo illud. Hoc autem dixit de templo corporis sui, ut Evangelista exponit. In figura hujus, de unctione tabernaculi scriptum est in Levitico; de unctione vero pontificali, in eodem libro habetur; de aliis, in libris Regum.
paras.en: [[4:18|Wherefore he hath anointed me|Propter quod unxit me]]: that is, because it so pleased the Holy Spirit to come and rest upon me, therefore He has spiritually watered, steeped and filled me, as man, with the fulness of grace and the virtues: as it is written, [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ]]; and in the Acts, [[Acts 10:38|God anointed him with the Holy Ghost and with power|Unxit eum Deus Spiritu Sancto et virtute]]. And so when He says, *Wherefore*, He gives the cause *a priori* [that is, from the cause to the effect]. It can also mark the cause *a posteriori*, so that the sense is: *Wherefore he hath anointed me*, that is, from the fact that the Spirit of the Lord was and is so upon me, it is plain, proved and follows that He has anointed me, as a cause is shown by its effect. Further, Christ was full not only of the gifts of sanctifying grace but also of the gifts of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: gifts such as prophecy or miracles, given for the good of others]: hence He is also said to have been anointed king, high priest or priest, and Prophet. And all this was done at the first moment of the incarnation. If we read that it was done later, it is to be understood as to its being made manifest: indeed, as on the day of the Parasceve [Good Friday] He offered Himself as a priest, [[Eph 5:2|an oblation and a sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness|oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis]], in deed, so in desire He began to do this from the beginning of the creation of His soul, and from then on He began to be mediator and reconciler, intercessor and high priest between God and men. Moreover He was anointed as the temple or tabernacle of the Godhead, since, as the Apostle says, [[Col 2:9|in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally|in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter]]. Christ too says to the Jews in John: [[John 2:19|Destroy this temple; and in three days I will raise it up|Solvite templum hoc, et in tribus diebus excitabo illud]]. [[John 2:21|But he spoke of the temple of his body|Hoc autem dixit de templo corporis sui]], as the Evangelist explains. As a figure of this, the anointing of the tabernacle is written of in Leviticus[[Lev 8:10||]]; the anointing of the high priest is found in the same book[[Lev 8:12||]]; and the other anointings in the books of Kings[[1 Kings 10:1||]][[1 Kings 16:13||]][[3 Kings 1:39||]][[3 Kings 19:16||]].

paras.t: Evangelizare pauperibus misit me, id est regnum cæleste prædicare humilibus: quod egit, dicendo, Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cælorum. Secundum Origenem, per pauperes intelliguntur gentiles seu nationes, nihil omnino spiritualiter possidentes, non Deum, non legem, non Prophetas, non justitiam reliquasque virtutes. Istis evangelizavit Christus per Apostolos, aliquibus etiam, quamvis paucis, per se ipsum, ut Evangelistæ testantur. Unde et Paulus de Christo loquens: Veniens evangelizavit his qui longe et his qui prope. Præterea advertendum, quod Lucas allegat hunc locum secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum. Hieronymus autem partim aliter transtulit, et pro inducto verbo sic dixit: Ad annuntiandum mansuetis misit me.
paras.en: [[4:18|to preach the gospel to the poor, he hath sent me|Evangelizare pauperibus misit me]], that is, to preach the heavenly kingdom to the humble: which He did, saying, [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.|Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cælorum]]. According to Origen, by the poor are understood the Gentiles or nations, who possessed nothing at all spiritually: not God, not the law, not the Prophets, not justice and the other virtues. To these Christ preached the gospel through the Apostles, and to some, though few, by Himself, as the Evangelists testify. Hence Paul too, speaking of Christ: [[Eph 2:17|coming, he preached|Veniens evangelizavit]] to them that were afar off and [[Eph 2:17|to them that were nigh|his qui prope]]. Note besides that Luke cites this place according to the translation of the Seventy. Jerome, however, translated it partly otherwise, and for the words given here said: [[Is 61:1|he hath sent me to preach to the meek|Ad annuntiandum mansuetis misit me]].

paras.t: Sanare contritos corde. Per contritos corde Cyrillus intelligit debiles fragilem mentem habentes, et insultibus passionum resistere non valentes. Basilius vero per contritos corde intelligit eos qui peccando a Satana pressi sunt, spiritualiterque destructi. His ergo venit Salvator impendere salutare remedium, quo curentur peccata et felicitas obtineatur, secundum quod ait: Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat. Sacramentum namque Baptismi tanquam primam post naufragium tabulam, sacramentum vero Pœnitentiæ tanquam tabulam post naufragium secundam instituit. Rursus, contriti corde intelligi possunt veraciter pœnitentes, juxta illud, Cor contritum et humiliatum, Deus, non despicies: quos venit Christus sanare per gratiam. Quamvis enim in quantum contriti jam ab ipsa læsione peccati seu culpa sanati sint, nihilominus ab effectu reliquiisque peccati, quæ sunt pronitas ad malum, debilitatio ad recidivum, egent curari: quod potissimum fit per septem dona Spiritus Sancti, quæ a capite Christo in ejus membra descendunt. Nempe ut Deus, dat ea efficienter, creative et auctoritative, sed ut homo mediator, dat ea ut causa instrumentalis superabundanter meritoria.
paras.en: [[4:18|to heal the contrite of heart|Sanare contritos corde]]. By the contrite of heart Cyril understands the weak, who have a frail mind and cannot resist the assaults of the passions. Basil, however, understands by the contrite of heart those who by sinning have been crushed by Satan and spiritually destroyed. To these, then, the Saviour came to apply the saving remedy by which sins are cured and happiness obtained, according as He says: [[Luke 19:10|the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost|Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]. For He instituted the sacrament of Baptism as the first plank after shipwreck, and the sacrament of Penance as the second plank after shipwreck. Again, the contrite of heart can be understood as those who truly repent, according to that saying, [[Ps 50:19|a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise|Cor contritum et humiliatum, Deus, non despicies]]: whom Christ came to heal by grace. For although, inasmuch as they are contrite, they are already healed of the wound of sin itself, that is, of the guilt, they still need to be cured of the effect and remnants of sin, which are proneness to evil and weakness toward relapse: and this is done above all through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which come down from Christ the head into His members. For as God, He gives them as efficient cause, creatively and with authority; but as man and mediator, He gives them as an instrumental cause, superabundantly meritorious.

paras.t: Et prædicare captivis, id est vinculis vitiorum implicatis, remissionem, id est indulgentiam, dummodo vere pœniteant. Hoc fecit Christus dicendo: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum. De hac captivitate in Proverbiis Salomon ait: Iniquitates suæ capient impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur. Fungitur enim peccatum tyrannide pessima, ad mala inducens, et acquiescentes confundens. Est autem et bona captivatio, de qua ait Apostolus: In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi. Theophilus per captivos intelligit in limbo detentos: qui Christo resurgente educti sunt pretio sanguinis ejus, remissionem a reatu originalis peccati adepti, quemadmodum in Zacharia dicitur Christo: Tu quoque, in sanguine testamenti tui, emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua. Prædicare etiam visum cæcis, id est spiritualem interioris visus illuminationem gentilibus, seu quibuscumque errore, ignorantia, aut vitiis, excæcatis. Unde Christus in Evangelio protestatur: Ego sum lux mundi; qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris. Cui per Isaiam Pater locutus est: Dedi te in fœdus populi, in lucem gentium, ut aperires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de conclusione vinctum, de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris.
paras.en: [[4:19|To preach|Et prædicare]] [[4:19|to the captives|captivis]], that is, to those entangled in the chains of vices, [[4:19|deliverance|remissionem]], that is, pardon, provided they truly repent. This Christ did, saying: [[Matt 4:17|Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum]]. Of this captivity Solomon says in Proverbs: [[Prov 5:22|His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins.|Iniquitates suæ capient impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur]]. For sin exercises the worst of tyrannies, leading into evils and confounding those who give in to it. But there is also a good captivity, of which the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 10:5|bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ|In captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi]]. Theophylact understands by the captives those held in limbo, who were led out when Christ rose, at the price of His blood, having obtained remission of the guilt of original sin: as it is said to Christ in Zacharias: [[Zach 9:11|Thou also by the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, wherein is no water.|Tu quoque, in sanguine testamenti tui, emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua]]. And to preach [[4:19|and sight to the blind|visum cæcis]], that is, the spiritual enlightening of inward sight to the Gentiles, or to any blinded by error, ignorance or vices. Hence Christ declares in the Gospel: [[John 8:12|I am the light of the world. He that followeth me walketh not in darkness|Ego sum lux mundi; qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris]]. To whom the Father spoke through Isaias: [[Is 42:6|I have given thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles|Dedi te in fœdus populi, in lucem gentium]]: [[Is 42:7|That thou mightest open the eyes of the blind, and bring forth the prisoner out of prison|ut aperires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de conclusione vinctum]], [[Is 42:7|them that sit in darkness out of the prison house|de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris]].

paras.t: Dimittere confractos, id est adversitatibus fatigatos, seu legalium observantiarum oneribus pressos, deducere, in remissionem, id est ad spiritualem consolationem ac relevamen. Christus namque nos ab observantia cærimonialium præceptorum legis per evangelicæ legis gratiam alleviavit, juxta illud: Quid tentatis imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus? Sed per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi credimus salvari. Hinc in Matthæo ait Salvator: Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos.
paras.en: [[4:19|to set at liberty them that are bruised|Dimittere confractos]], that is, to lead forth those wearied by adversities, or weighed down by the burdens of the legal observances, *into release* [the Vulgate adds *in remissionem*, which the Douay-Rheims does not render], that is, into spiritual consolation and relief. For Christ has lightened us of the observance of the ceremonial precepts of the law through the grace of the law of the Gospel, according to that saying: [[Acts 15:10|why tempt you|Quid tentatis]] [[Acts 15:10|to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear|imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus?]]? [[Acts 15:11|But by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, we believe to be saved|Sed per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi credimus salvari]]. Hence the Saviour says in Matthew: [[Matt 11:28|Come to me all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.|Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos]].

paras.t: Prædicare annum Domini acceptum, id est tempus gratiæ seu evangelicæ legis, in quo Deus benignissime se habuit ad genus humanum. De quo ait Apostolus: Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis; et Isaias, Tempore accepto exaudivi te. Quomodo autem Christus hoc egit, ostenditur in Marco, in quo legitur: Postquam traditus est Joannes, venit Jesus in Galilæam prædicans Evangelium regni Dei, et dicens, Quoniam impletum est tempus, et appropinquabit regnum Dei. De quo gratissimo tempore scribit Apostolus: Ecce jam venit plenitudo temporis, in quo Deus misit Filium suum; et in Actibus Petrus, Omnes Prophetæ a Samuel annuntiaverunt dies istos. Quidam per annum acceptum, intelligunt annum quo Christus prædicavit, præcipue in Judæa, vel annum dominicæ passionis, in quo generi humano placatus est Deus. Tempus quippe vocatur acceptum, propter gratiosa piaque opera quæ fiunt in ipso, sicut et dies mali dicuntur, propter mala quæ fiunt in eo. Et diem retributionis, id est extremi judicii, in quo unusquisque quod meruit, creditur recepturus, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi Judex asseruit: Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, reddere unicuique juxta opera sua. Hunc diem Christus frequenter denuntiavit, sicut in Joanne: Veniet hora in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus. Quidam per diem retributionis, intelligunt diem æternæ felicitatis electorum in patria. Præfata tamen expositio litteralior æstimatur, quia Hieronymus transtulit, Diem ultionis: quod tamen de tempore devastationis Judæorum (propter peccata in Christum commissa) accipi posset, de quo per Isaiam Christus fatetur: Dies ultionis in corde meo, annus retributionis meæ venit. Idem enim fuit tempus clementissimæ vocationis gentilium, atque justissimæ derelictionis vastitatisque Judæorum.
paras.en: [[4:19|to preach the acceptable year of the Lord|Prædicare annum Domini acceptum]], that is, the time of grace, or of the law of the Gospel, in which God dealt most kindly with the human race. Of which the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time: behold, now is the day of salvation|ecce nunc dies salutis]]; and Isaias: [[Is 49:8|In an acceptable time I have heard thee|Tempore accepto exaudivi te]]. How Christ did this is shown in Mark, where we read: [[Mark 1:14|after that John was delivered up, Jesus came in Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God|Postquam traditus est Joannes, venit Jesus in Galilæam prædicans Evangelium regni Dei]], [[Mark 1:15|And saying: The time is accomplished and the kingdom of God is at hand|et dicens, Quoniam impletum est tempus, et appropinquabit regnum Dei]]. Of this most gracious time the Apostle writes: [[Gal 4:4|when the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son|Ecce jam venit plenitudo temporis, in quo Deus misit Filium suum]] [Denis's wording: “Behold, now is come the fulness of time, in which God sent His Son”]; and Peter in the Acts: [[Acts 3:24|all the prophets, from Samuel|Omnes Prophetæ a Samuel]] … [[Acts 3:24|have told of these days|annuntiaverunt dies istos]]. Some understand by the acceptable year the year in which Christ preached, chiefly in Judæa, or the year of the Lord's passion, in which God was appeased toward the human race. For a time is called acceptable because of the gracious and holy works done in it, as days are also called evil because of the evils done in them. [[4:19|and the day of reward|Et diem retributionis]], that is, of the last judgment, in which each one, we believe, will receive what he has deserved, as the Judge declared in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:12|Behold, I come quickly: and my reward is with me, to render to every, man according to his works.|Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, reddere unicuique juxta opera sua]]. This day Christ often announced, as in John: [[John 5:28|the hour cometh wherein all that are in the graves shall hear the voice|Veniet hora in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus]]. Some understand by the day of reward the day of the everlasting happiness of the elect in the fatherland. The exposition given first, however, is thought more literal, because Jerome translated *the day of vengeance*: which could, however, be taken of the time of the laying waste of the Jews (for the sins committed against Christ), of which Christ says through Isaias: [[Is 63:4|the day of vengeance is in my heart|Dies ultionis in corde meo]], the year of my retribution is come [Denis's text has *retributionis*, where the Vulgate has *redemptionis*, “redemption”]. For the same time was that of the most merciful calling of the Gentiles and of the most just forsaking and desolation of the Jews.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod peccatum mala plurima infert hominibus: nam animam vulnerat, captivat, excæcat, a Deoque separat, et gratia et gloria privat. Ideo Christus contra prædicta mala venisse se perhibet. Unde Joannes inquit: In hoc apparuit Filius Dei, ut dissolvat opera diaboli.
paras.en: Note besides that sin brings very many evils upon men: for it wounds the soul, takes it captive, blinds it, separates it from God, and deprives it of grace and glory. Therefore Christ declares that He has come against these evils. Hence John says: [[1 John 3:8|For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil|In hoc apparuit Filius Dei, ut dissolvat opera diaboli]].

paras.t: Et quum plicuisset librum. Quo patet, quod librum sacræ Scripturæ reverenter tractavit, atque exemplum sic agendi nobis reliquit. Circa quod dicit Lyra: Judæi hanc reverentiam faciunt libris veteris Testamenti, quod nullo modo sederent juxta illos, sedendo tam alte ut illi sunt positi: quo constat, quod illi Christiani sunt valde reprehendendi, qui non solum libros veteris Testamenti, sed etiam novi, et sacra Evangelia tam irreverenter tractant, et irreverentius quam libros gentilium damnatorum; aliqui etiam theologi, dicta talium cum majori pondere et certiori quotatione allegant in scholis, quam dicta Christi et Apostolorum. Reddidit ministro: forte illi a quo librum accepit; et sedit, tanquam magister et doctor, ut quod legit, exponeret. Et omnium in synagoga oculi erant intendentes in eum: quia delectabilis fuit ad intuendum, tanquam speciosus forma præ filiis hominum, in cujus vultu fulgor quidam interioris perfectionis ac gratiæ resplendebat: sed et suavitate eloquentiæ suæ corda eorum attraxit. Mirabantur quoque rem novam, et quomodo legere scivit, qui ab homine illud non didicit. Talia autem nova, magna, mira et inopinata, homines diligenter concorditerque inspiciunt. Circa quod loquitur Origenes: Nunc etiam, si volumus, oculi nostri possunt intendere Salvatorem: quum enim principale cordis tui direxeris ad sapientiæ veritatem, Deique Unigenitum contemplandum, oculi tui intuentur Jesum.
paras.en: [[4:20|And when he had folded the book|Et quum plicuisset librum]]. From this it is plain that He handled the book of sacred Scripture reverently, and left us an example of doing so. On which Lyra says: “The Jews show this reverence to the books of the Old Testament, that they would on no account sit beside them, sitting as high as the books are placed.” From which it is clear that those Christians are much to be blamed who handle not only the books of the Old Testament, but also those of the New, and the holy Gospels, so irreverently, and more irreverently than the books of the damned heathen; and some theologians too, who cite the sayings of such men in the schools with greater weight and more exact quotation than the sayings of Christ and the Apostles. [[4:20|he restored it to the minister|Reddidit ministro]], perhaps the one from whom He had received the book; [[4:20|and sat down|et sedit]], as master and teacher, to expound what He had read. [[4:20|And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him|Et omnium in synagoga oculi erant intendentes in eum]]: because He was delightful to look upon, as one [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]], in whose face a certain brightness of inward perfection and grace shone out: and He also drew their hearts by the sweetness of His eloquence. They wondered too at the new thing, and how He knew how to read who had not learned it from man. And such things, new, great, wonderful and unexpected, men look at attentively and with one accord. On which Origen says: “Now too, if we will, our eyes can be fixed on the Saviour: for when you have turned the chief part of your heart to the truth of wisdom and to contemplating the Only-begotten of God, your eyes are looking on Jesus.”

paras.t: Cœpit autem dicere ad illos: Quia hodie impleta est scriptura hæc in auribus vestris, id est, per hoc quod audistis me Christum vobis evangelizantem, vestraque corda illuminantem, et gratiam benignitatis divinæ annuntiantem, impletum est aliqualiter quod in præfata prophetia fuit prædictum. Quo verbo docuit Christus, dicta atque promissa Prophetarum in Christi adventu spiritualiter debere intelligi, de spirituali videlicet liberatione a potestate diaboli et jugo peccati, non de corporali liberatione a captivitate exteriori et temporali, qua nunc tenentur Judæi: a qua se præstolantur in Christi adventu educendos, cunctisque gentibus dominaturos. Habent enim densissima errorum caligine intellectum cæcatum.
paras.en: [[4:21|And he began to say to them: This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears|Cœpit autem dicere ad illos: Quia hodie impleta est scriptura hæc in auribus vestris]], that is, in that you have heard me, the Christ, preaching the gospel to you, enlightening your hearts, and announcing the grace of the divine kindness, what was foretold in that prophecy has been in some measure fulfilled. By this word Christ taught that the sayings and promises of the Prophets about Christ's coming must be understood spiritually, namely of a spiritual deliverance from the power of the devil and the yoke of sin, not of a bodily deliverance from the outward and temporal captivity in which the Jews are now held: from which they expect to be led out at Christ's coming, and to rule over all nations. For they have their understanding blinded by the thickest fog of errors.

paras.t: Et omnes testimonium illi dabant: id est, plures de omnibus ibi præsentibus, protestabantur vera esse quæ protulit Jesus, quod scilicet scriptura Isaiæ inducta esset in ipso completa, et quod esset Christus in lege et Prophetis promissus, quamvis in illa notitia nondum essent firmati; vel testimonium illi dabant, id est, bonum de ipso testimonium proferebant, quod scilicet vere sapiens, gratiosus, virtuosus, magnusque esset, et quod Joannes Baptista de ipso affirmasset magnifica, jamque ipse Jesus mirabilia cœpisset peragere. Et mirabantur in verbis gratiæ, id est gratiosis, facundis, efficacissimis, sapientissimisque sermonibus, quæ procedebant de ore ejus ordinate et eloquenter, sicut prædixit Psalmista: Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis.
