Unde in Joanne adversarii ejus ipsa veritate compulsi sunt dicere: Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur. Denique bonus homo de bono cordis sui thesauro profert bona: idcirco, quo anima Christi gratia plenior fuit, eo gratiosiora verba deprompsit. Sicque verba Christi erant verba gratiæ: originaliter, quia manabant ex gratia; materialiter, quia tractabant de gratia; formaliter, quoniam gratiosa seu gratia eloquentiæ decorata; finaliter, quia tendebant ad gratiam; item causaliter, quia audientibus gratiam conferebant, eos ædificando. Ad quod imitandum hortatur nos Paulus: Omnis sermo malus ex ore vestro non procedat; sed qui bonus est, ad ædificationem fidei, ut det gratiam audientibus.
paras.en: [[4:22|And all gave testimony to him|Et omnes testimonium illi dabant]]: that is, many of all who were present there declared that what Jesus had said was true, namely that the scripture of Isaias He had brought forward was fulfilled in Him, and that He was the Christ promised in the law and the Prophets, though they were not yet settled in that knowledge; or, *gave testimony to him*, that is, bore good witness of Him: that He was truly wise, gracious, virtuous and great, and that John the Baptist had affirmed great things of Him, and that Jesus Himself had already begun to do wonders. [[4:22|And they wondered at the words of grace|Et mirabantur in verbis gratiæ]], that is, at the gracious, eloquent, most effective and most wise discourses [[4:22|that proceeded from his mouth|quæ procedebant de ore ejus]] in order and eloquently, as the Psalmist foretold: [[Ps 44:3|grace is poured abroad in thy lips|Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis]]. Hence in John His adversaries, compelled by the truth itself, were obliged to say: [[John 7:46|Never did man speak like this man|Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur]]. Further, [[Matt 12:35|A good man out of a good treasure bringeth forth good things|bonus homo de bono cordis sui thesauro profert bona]]: therefore, the fuller of grace Christ's soul was, the more gracious were the words He brought forth. And so Christ's words were words of grace: in their origin, because they flowed from grace; in their matter, because they treated of grace; in their form, because they were gracious, that is, adorned with the grace of eloquence; in their end, because they tended to grace; and also as causes, because they conferred grace on the hearers by edifying them. Paul exhorts us to imitate this: [[Eph 4:29|Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth: but that which is good, to the edification of faith: that it may administer grace to the hearers.|Omnis sermo malus ex ore vestro non procedat; sed qui bonus est, ad ædificationem fidei, ut det gratiam audientibus]].

paras.t: Et dicebant: Nonne hic est filius Joseph? Hoc aspernanter locuti sunt, tanquam dicerent: Quum sit filius simpliciani et pauperis fabri, non est verisimile quod tanta excellentia vere ei conveniat, aut Christus exsistat, aut prodigia operetur. Unde apud Matthæum et Marcum dixisse scribuntur: Nonne hic est fabri filius? Et hæc est mira excæcatio atque perversitas, despicere aliquem propter parentum inopiam, quasi gratia Dei divitibus potius quam pauperibus conferatur, et non potius vice versa.
paras.en: [[4:22|And they said: Is not this the son of Joseph?|Et dicebant: Nonne hic est filius Joseph?]] They said this scornfully, as though to say: Since He is the son of a simple man and a poor carpenter, it is not likely that such excellence truly belongs to Him, or that He is the Christ, or that He works wonders. Hence in Matthew and Mark they are recorded to have said: [[Matt 13:55|Is not this the carpenter's son?|Nonne hic est filius]][[Mark 6:3||]] And it is a strange blindness and perversity to despise anyone because of his parents' poverty, as though the grace of God were given to the rich rather than to the poor, and not rather the other way round.

paras.t: Quæritur, quum statim prædictum sit, Omnes testimonium illi dabant, quomodo de eisdem mox subditur, Nonne hic est filius Joseph? Qui enim testimonium ei dabant, eum reverebantur; hi vero eum spernebant. Ad hoc dupliciter respondetur: Primo, quod Scriptura loquitur de eisdem, videlicet habitatoribus Nazareth, et quod primo honoraverunt eum propter causas præfactas; sed post paululum, ex aliis considerationibus, scilicet ex attentione paupertatis matris ejus patrisque putativi, ad contemptum ejus invidiamque commoti sunt. Alii dicunt, quod Scriptura loquitur hic de diversis, quasi de eisdem, juxta unam septem regularum Tichonii valentium ad intelligendum Scripturas: quemadmodum et in Psalmo, Quum occideret eos, quærebant eum et revertebantur, etc.; qui enim occidebantur, non revertebantur diluculo. Zacharias quoque, Fugietis sicut fugistis in diebus Oziæ regis Juda. Certum est equidem, quod illi qui tempore Zachariæ prophetæ, unius duodecim Prophetarum, fuerunt, non fuerunt tempore Oziæ regis, qui tot annis ante Babylonicam captivitatem defunctus est. Itaque dicunt hæc verba a Scribis et Pharisæis invidia tactis prolata.
paras.en: It is asked: since it has just been said, [[4:22|all gave testimony to him|omnes testimonium illi dabant]], how is it presently added of the same people, [[4:22|Is not this the son of Joseph?|Nonne hic est filius Joseph]] For those who gave Him testimony revered Him; but these despised Him. To this a twofold answer is given. First, that Scripture speaks of the same people, namely the inhabitants of Nazareth, and that at first they honoured Him for the reasons given; but a little later, from other considerations, namely from attending to the poverty of His mother and His supposed father, they were moved to contempt and envy of Him. Others say that Scripture here speaks of different people as though of the same, according to one of the seven rules of Tichonius which are of use for understanding the Scriptures [the Rules of Tyconius, a fourth-century guide to interpreting Scripture, taken up by Augustine]: as also in the Psalm, [[Ps 77:34|When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned|Quum occideret eos, quærebant eum et revertebantur]], etc.; for those who were slain did not return early in the morning. And Zacharias: [[Zach 14:5|you shall flee as you fled|Fugietis sicut fugistis]] [[Zach 14:5|in the days of Ozias king of Juda|in diebus Oziæ regis Juda]]. For it is certain that those who lived in the time of the prophet Zacharias, one of the twelve Prophets, did not live in the time of King Ozias, who died so many years before the Babylonian captivity. So they say that these words were spoken by Scribes and Pharisees touched with envy.

paras.t: Et ait illis, ex caritate volens illorum emendare errorem: Utique dicetis mihi hanc similitudinem, id est, vulgare proverbium, seu metaphoricum et parabolicum verbum mihi objicietis, utpote istud, Medice, cura te ipsum: hoc est, objectionem a similitudine medici acceptam corporalis, mihi opponetis, ad me dicendo: O medice, qui extraneos curas, puta infirmos urbis Capharnaum, cura te ipsum, id est tuos concives ad te specialiter pertinentes, in Nazareth habitantes. Quasi dicant: Quum ita non agas, concluditur, quod vel insipienter vel inordinate te habes, vel quod tua miracula non sint vera miracula.
paras.en: [[4:23|And he said to them|Et ait illis]], wishing out of charity to correct their error: [[4:23|Doubtless you will say to me this similitude|Utique dicetis mihi hanc similitudinem]], that is, you will throw at me a common proverb, a metaphorical and parabolic saying, namely this: [[4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]]: that is, you will set against me an objection taken from the likeness of a bodily physician, saying to me: O physician, who cure strangers, say the sick of the city of Capharnaum, heal thyself, that is, your own fellow citizens who belong especially to you, the dwellers in Nazareth. As if they said: Since you do not do so, the conclusion is that you are acting either foolishly or wrongly, or that your miracles are not true miracles.

paras.t: Deinceps Christus, explanando parabolam introductam, ponit illorum tacitam objectionem: scivit enim quid cogitarent. Quanta, id est multa et magna miracula, audivimus facta a te in Capharnaum, fac et hic in patria tua, id est, in Nazareth ita in patria ubi conceptus atque nutritus es, fac tanta ac talia. Sed quum Lucas nulla Christi miracula usque ad hunc locum recitaverit in Capharnaum facta, cur ait Nazarenos verba hæc protulisse aut concepisse? Et respondendum, quod Lucas hæc refert per anticipationem. Propter quod asserit Augustinus: Quum Lucas jam magna a Christo facta fuisse commemorat, quæ se nondum narrasse cognoscit, quid evidentius quam eum hoc scienter præoccupasse narrandum? Itaque, quod hic scribitur ab illo loco inclusive, Et venit Nazareth, usque ad id quod infra in isto capitulo legitur, Et descendit Capharnaum, est interpositio quæ vocatur parenthesis (a para, quod est juxta, et thesis, positio, quasi positio juxta principale), nec continuatur immediate cum præcedentibus atque sequentibus secundum ordinem facti. Unde quod hic dictum a Christo et Nazarenis interponitur, non fuit statim dictum post præcedentia, scilicet post lectionem Christi in Isaia, sed postea diu, quum a Capharnaum in Nazareth advenisset. Ideo dicit Chrysostomus: Post multum tempus et signorum ostensionem, profectus est ad Nazarenos. Aliqui quoque affirmant, quod Christus frequenter venit a Capharnaum in Nazareth.
paras.en: Then Christ, explaining the parable He has brought in, sets out their unspoken objection: for He knew what they were thinking. [[4:23|As great things|Quanta]], that is, many and great miracles, [[4:23|as we have heard done in Capharnaum|audivimus facta a te in Capharnaum]] by you, [[4:23|do also here in thy own country|fac et hic in patria tua]], that is, in Nazareth, so in the country where you were conceived and brought up, do as great and as many. But since Luke has related no miracles of Christ done in Capharnaum up to this place, why does he say that the Nazarenes spoke or thought these words? The answer is that Luke relates this by anticipation. That is why Augustine says: “Since Luke records that great things had already been done by Christ, which he knows he has not yet narrated, what is clearer than that he has knowingly told it in advance?” So what is written here from the place, inclusive, [[4:16|And he came to Nazareth|Et venit Nazareth]], up to what we read below in this chapter, [[4:31|And he went down into Capharnaum|Et descendit Capharnaum]], is an insertion which is called a parenthesis (from *para*, which means “beside”, and *thesis*, “placing”, as it were a placing beside the main thing), and it does not run on directly with what goes before and after in the order of events. Hence what is here inserted as said by Christ and the Nazarenes was not said straight after what precedes, namely after Christ's reading from Isaias, but long afterwards, when He had come from Capharnaum to Nazareth. So Chrysostom says: “After a long time and the showing of signs, He set out to the Nazarenes.” Some also affirm that Christ often came from Capharnaum to Nazareth.

paras.t: Deinde Salvator ad tactam respondet instantiam. Ait enim: Amen, id est vere, dico vobis, quia nemo Propheta acceptus est in patria sua. — Contra hoc objici posset, quod Ezechias rex et populus ejus Isaiam prophetam in magno habebat honore, ut patet in libris Regum, obedivitque ei, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Fortiter ivit Ezechias in via David patris sui, quam mandavit illi Isaias propheta magnus. Denique David nonne sanctos prophetas Nathan et Gad, ceterosque sui regni ac temporis veneratus est vates? Sed et Josaphat rex devotus, suis loquens: Credite Prophetis Domini, et omnia prospere evenient. Postremo, paulo ante jam dictum est, quod omnes in Nazareth testimonium Christo dabant. Infra quoque habetur, quomodo omnis populus gaudebat in his quæ gloriose fiebant ab eo.
paras.en: Then the Saviour answers the objection He has touched on. For He says: [[4:24|Amen I say to you that no prophet is accepted in his own country|Amen, id est vere, dico vobis, quia nemo Propheta acceptus est in patria sua]]. (*Amen* means “truly”.) — Against this it could be objected that King Ezechias and his people held the prophet Isaias in great honour, as is plain in the books of Kings[[4 Kings 19:2||]], and obeyed him, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: Ezechias [[Ecclus 48:25|walked valiantly in the way of David his father, which Isaias, the great prophet|Fortiter ivit Ezechias in via David patris sui, quam mandavit illi Isaias propheta magnus]] commanded him. Further, did not David revere the holy prophets Nathan[[2 Kings 12:1||]] and Gad[[2 Kings 24:11||]], and the other seers of his kingdom and his time? And the devout King Josaphat, too, said to his people: [[2 Par 20:20|believe his prophets, and all things shall succeed well|Credite Prophetis Domini, et omnia prospere evenient]]. Lastly, it was said just before that all in Nazareth gave testimony to Christ. And below we read how [[Luke 13:17|all the people rejoiced for all the things that were gloriously done by him|omnis populus gaudebat in his quæ gloriose fiebant ab eo]].

paras.t: Et respondendum, quod Christus, magister veritatis ac pietatis, communitatis quoque amator, et singularitatis inordinatæ vitator, libenter verbis et factis se communitati conformavit in licitis et honestis. Unde proverbium istud inducit eo modo ac sensu, quo Salomon in libro Proverbiorum multa affirmat, non quia universaliter, ubique et semper, quantum ad singulos ita se habeat, sed quia frequenter sic accidit. Itaque Christus verba hæc protulit, quia communiter Prophetæ sancti apud compatriotas suos, aut contemnuntur, aut minus accepti sunt. Nam et cives civibus communiter invident. Homines etiam, ut frequenter, ægre ferunt dum compares sui ipsis præferuntur, et proni sunt considerare eum qui excellit, secundum id quod fuit dum eis similis videbatur. Rursus, excellentiam extraneorum non ita apprehendunt minorativam aut confusivam ipsorum, ut excellentiam intraneorum; imo erubescibile sibi arbitrantur, quod familiaris collega, concivis, in tantum eis præfulgeat. Et hoc verum est de hominibus nondum purgatis, in quibus superbia, invidia, passionesque ceteræ regnant. Porro, qui passionibus reformatis, caritate Dei ac proximi flagrat, de suorum profectu et eminentia spirituali lætatur; sed quoniam pauci sunt tales, ideo raro contingit hoc.
paras.en: The answer is that Christ, the master of truth and of godliness, a lover of the community and one who shunned disordered singularity, gladly conformed Himself to the community in words and deeds in things lawful and honest. So He brings in this proverb in the way and the sense in which Solomon in the book of Proverbs affirms many things: not because it is so universally, everywhere and always, with each individual, but because it frequently happens so. So Christ spoke these words because holy Prophets are commonly either despised by their fellow countrymen or less accepted. For citizens commonly envy citizens. Men too, as often happens, take it ill when their equals are preferred to them, and are inclined to regard the one who excels according to what he was when he seemed like them. Again, they do not take the excellence of strangers as lessening or shaming themselves as much as the excellence of those of their own; indeed they think it shameful to themselves that a familiar companion, a fellow citizen, should shine so far above them. And this is true of men not yet purified, in whom pride, envy and the other passions reign. But one whose passions have been set in order, and who burns with the love of God and neighbour, rejoices at the progress and spiritual eminence of his own people; but because such men are few, this happens rarely.

paras.t: Propter quod multi in terra aliena facilius promoventur, magisque honorantur ac reputantur quam in propria, ut patet de Joseph, Daniele, et Mardochæo. Ezechieli quoque Dominus ait: Si mittereris ad populum alienæ linguæ, ipsi audirent te; filii autem Israel nolunt audire te. Hinc ait Cyrillus: Quædam communis quasi cunctis accidit passio. Contemnuntur enim quodammodo semper etiam optima quæque, quando non raro contingunt alicui, sed ad velle suppetunt seu frequenter. Familiaris namque, quoniam semper præsto est, debita reverentia privatur a notis. Verumtamen, diligenter pensandum quod ait Ambrosius: Frustra opem misericordiæ cælestis exspectas, si alienis fructibus virtutis invideas. Aspernator est enim Dominus invidorum, et ab his qui divina beneficia in aliis persequuntur, miracula suæ potestatis avertit.
paras.en: That is why many are more easily advanced, and more honoured and esteemed, in a foreign land than in their own, as is plain in Joseph[[Gen 41:38||]], Daniel[[Dan 2:48||]][[Dan 5:29||]] and Mardochai[[Esth 8:2||]]. And the Lord said to Ezechiel: If thou wert sent to a people of a strange tongue, [[Ezech 3:6|they would hearken to thee|ipsi audirent te]]; [[Ezech 3:7|But the house of Israel will not hearken to thee|filii autem Israel nolunt audire te]] [Denis has “the children of Israel” for “the house of Israel”]. Hence Cyril says: “A certain common failing befalls almost everyone. For even the very best things are always in some way despised when they come to someone not rarely, but are at hand at will, that is, often. For one who is familiar, since he is always at hand, is deprived by those who know him of the reverence due to him.” Yet we must weigh carefully what Ambrose says: “In vain do you look for the help of heavenly mercy, if you envy others the fruits of virtue. For the Lord spurns the envious, and turns the miracles of His power away from those who persecute the divine benefits in others.”

paras.t: Itaque verbo inducto Christus se juste excusat, cur in Nazareth talia signa non egerit, utpote quia hoc accidit, non ex sua aversione a suis concivibus, sed propter eorum incredulitatem atque malitiam, quoniam Christum parvi pendebant, nec ei credebant. Unde in Matthæo et Marco habetur, quod non fecit ibi multa miracula, propter eorum incredulitatem. Et hoc Christus deinceps per duo ostendit exempla, quomodo scilicet compatriotæ privantur beneficiis Dei propter malitiam suam, quæ tamen extraneis communicantur.
paras.en: So by the saying He has brought in, Christ justly excuses Himself for not having done such signs in Nazareth: namely, because this happened not from any turning away of His from His fellow citizens, but because of their unbelief and malice, since they thought little of Christ and did not believe Him. Hence we have in Matthew and Mark that [[Matt 13:58|he wrought not many miracles there, because of their unbelief|non fecit ibi multa miracula, propter eorum incredulitatem]][[Mark 6:5||]][[Mark 6:6||]]. And Christ next shows this by two examples: how fellow countrymen are deprived of God's benefits because of their malice, while these are given to strangers.

paras.t: In veritate dico vobis: multæ viduæ erant in Israel, id est in regno et populo Israelitico, in diebus Eliæ, id est, tempore quo Elias in populo illo conversabatur ac operabatur. Tempus autem dicitur ipsius Dei, tanquam Domini ac creatoris ac moderatoris temporum universorum, dicente Boetio: Tempus ab ævo Ire jubes, stabilisque manens das cuncta moveri. Hominum vero dicitur esse dies vel tempus, tanquam eorum qui subjacent tempori, et tempore mensurantur in durando et operando. Specialiter tamen dicitur tempus aliquod esse illius qui in illo præclarioris fuit potestatis, operationis seu perfectionis. Unde prælatorum et principum tempora describuntur: imo juxta illorum successionem, temporum successio determinatur. Quando clausum, id est a solito suo effectu sive influxu prohibitum seu suspensum, est cælum, tam aerium quam stellatum seu orbis planetaris, annis tribus et mensibus sex. Tunc enim ad preces Eliæ intra tres annos atque sex menses pluvia de cælo aerio non descendit in terram Israel, nec in quædam loca vicina, cælum quoque stellatum modo solito ad pluviarum generationem influentiam non impendit, nec sol cursu consueto elevavit vapores, Deo omnipotente jubente. Quum facta esset fames in terra. Ex defectu siquidem pluviæ orta est sterilitas terræ, ad quam esuries est secuta. Unde in libris Regum legitur: Dixit Elias ad Achab: Vivit Dominus Deus Israel, in cujus conspectu sto, si erit annis his ros et pluvia, nisi juxta oris mei verbum. Quanta autem fuerit fames illa, in libris Regum describitur.
paras.en: [[4:25|In truth I say to You, there were many widows|In veritate dico vobis: multæ viduæ erant]] [[4:25|in Israel|in Israel]], that is, in the kingdom and people of Israel, [[4:25|in the days of Elias|in diebus Eliæ]], that is, in the time when Elias lived and worked among that people. Now time is said to belong to God Himself, as the Lord, creator and ruler of all times, as Boethius says: “Thou biddest time go forth from eternity, and, abiding unmoved, givest all things motion.” But a day or a time is said to be men's, as of those who are subject to time and are measured by time in lasting and working. In a special way, however, a time is said to be his who in it was of more eminent power, work or perfection. Hence the times of prelates and princes are recorded: indeed the succession of times is fixed by their succession. [[4:25|when heaven was shut up|Quando clausum]], that is, held back or suspended from its usual effect or influence, both the heaven of the air and the starry heaven, that is, the sphere of the planets, [[4:25|three years and six months|annis tribus et mensibus sex]]. For then, at the prayers of Elias, for three years and six months no rain came down from the heaven of the air on the land of Israel, nor on certain neighbouring places; the starry heaven, too, did not give its influence in the usual way for the forming of rain, nor did the sun draw up vapours in its accustomed course, at the bidding of almighty God. [[4:25|when there was a great famine throughout all the earth|Quum facta esset fames in terra]]. For from the lack of rain came barrenness of the land, and hunger followed it. Hence we read in the books of Kings: Elias [[3 Kings 17:1|said to Achab: As the Lord liveth, the God of Israel, in whose sight I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to the words of my mouth|Dixit Elias ad Achab: Vivit Dominus Deus Israel, in cujus conspectu sto, si erit annis his ros et pluvia, nisi juxta oris mei verbum]]. How great that famine was is described in the books of Kings[[3 Kings 18:2||]].

paras.t: Et ad nullam earum missus est Elias a Deo: quod fuit propter indignitatem et culpam earum, vel quia minus dignæ fuerunt quam vidua de qua subditur. Nisi in Sarepta Sidoniæ. Porro Sarepta urbs parva fuit inter Tyrum et Sidonem. Sidon vero urbs fuit a qua regio illa vocata fuit Sidonia. Ad mulierem viduam, quæ fuit paupercula, unicum habens filium, quem mortuum suscitavit Elias: asseruntque Hebræi, quod fuit Jonas propheta. Exceptio autem illa quæ designatur hoc loco per nisi, non est referenda ad viduas Israel, quasi vidua ista Sidonia fuerit de Israeliticarum numero viduarum, sed ad id quod dicitur, Missus est: ut sit sensus, quod non fuit missus nisi ad viduam Sareptanam, juxta illud: Factum est verbum Domini ad Eliam: Vade in Sarepta Sidoniorum, et manebis ibi, præcepi enim ibi mulieri viduæ ut pascat te. Denique, secundum Chrysostomum, Deus pia dispensatione fecit Eliam per tam longum pergere iter usque Sareptam, ut videns mundi pestem, peteret a Domino pluvias. Hujus quoque facti meminit Jacobus circa finem suæ Canonicæ, dicens: Multum valet deprecatio justi assidua. Elias homo similis erat nobis passibilis, et oratione oravit, ut non plueret super terram, et non pluit annos tres et menses sex; et rursum oravit, et cælum dedit pluviam. Hinc de Elia scribit Chrysostomus: Ipse quidem terrestris angelus et homo cælestis, qui nec tectum, nec mensam, nec amictum habebat; verumtamen clavem cælorum gessit in lingua.
paras.en: [[4:26|And to none of them was Elias sent|Et ad nullam earum missus est Elias]] by God: which was because of their unworthiness and fault, or because they were less worthy than the widow of whom it is added: [[4:26|but to Sarepta of Sidon|Nisi in Sarepta Sidoniæ]]. Now Sarepta was a small city between Tyre and Sidon; and Sidon was the city from which that region was called Sidonia. [[4:26|to a widow woman|Ad mulierem viduam]], who was very poor and had an only son, whom Elias raised from the dead[[3 Kings 17:22||]]: and the Hebrews assert that he was the prophet Jonas. The exception marked here by *but* is not to be referred to the widows of Israel, as though this Sidonian widow were of the number of the Israelite widows, but to what is said, *was sent*: so that the sense is that he was sent only to the widow of Sarepta, according to that saying: The word of the Lord came to Elias[[3 Kings 17:8||]]: [[3 Kings 17:9|go to Sarephta of the Sidonians, and dwell there: for I have commanded a widow woman there to feed thee|Vade in Sarepta Sidoniorum, et manebis ibi, præcepi enim ibi mulieri viduæ ut pascat te]]. Further, according to Chrysostom, God in His loving providence made Elias go so long a way, as far as Sarepta, so that seeing the plague upon the world he might ask the Lord for rain. James too recalls this deed near the end of his Canonical Epistle, saying: [[Jas 5:16|the continual prayer of a just man availeth much|Multum valet deprecatio justi assidua]]. [[Jas 5:17|Elias was a man passible like unto us: and with prayer he prayed that it might not rain upon the earth. And it rained not for three years and six months.|Elias homo similis erat nobis passibilis, et oratione oravit, ut non plueret super terram, et non pluit annos tres et menses sex]] [[Jas 5:18|And he prayed again. And the heaven gave rain|et rursum oravit, et cælum dedit pluviam]]. Hence Chrysostom writes of Elias: “He was an earthly angel and a heavenly man, who had neither roof, nor table, nor clothing; yet he carried the key of the heavens on his tongue.”

paras.t: Subinde ponit secundum exemplum. Et multi leprosi erant in Israel sub Eliseo propheta, id est tempore Elisei, imo tempore quo tanquam spiritualis pater, fuit præcipuus director Israeliticæ plebis. Propter quod morienti dixit rex Israel: Pater mi, pater mi, currus Israel et auriga ejus. Quod autem tempore Elisei fuerunt quatuor viri leprosi, qui etiam tempore noctis ingressi sunt castra Syrorum, legitur in libris Regum. Et nemo eorum mundatus est a lepra ab Eliseo, nisi Naaman Syrus: non quod Naaman fuerit unus leprosorum de Israel, sed quoniam ipse solus inter leprosos fuit ab Eliseo sanatus, ut scribitur in libris Regum. Fuitque Naaman princeps militiæ regis Syriæ, vir magnus ac honoratus apud dominum suum, dives et fortis: cujus bonitas claret ex hoc quod inductis verbis adjungitur, Per illum enim dedit Dominus salutem Syriæ. Præterea, quum referente parvula puella, audisset esse Prophetam in Israel, mox credidit se per preces Prophetæ a Deo Israel posse curari, imo et se curandum speravit. Unde quum Eliseus non egrederetur ad eum, indignatus est, dicens: Putabam quod egrederetur, et tangeret locum lepræ, et invocaret nomen Dei sui. Sicque videtur unius veri summique Dei tunc habuisse notitiam; et devote venit ad Eliseum, secundum Glossam. Curatus vero valde gratus fuit Deo et Eliseo, promittens se ultra soli Deo Israel sacrificaturum.
paras.en: Next He gives the second example. [[4:27|And there were many lepers in Israel|Et multi leprosi erant in Israel]] [[4:27|in the time of Eliseus the prophet|sub Eliseo propheta]], that is, in the time of Eliseus, indeed in the time when, as a spiritual father, he was the chief guide of the people of Israel. That is why the king of Israel said to him when he was dying: [[4 Kings 13:14|O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the guider thereof|pater mi, currus Israel et auriga ejus]]. That in the time of Eliseus there were four leprous men, who also went into the camp of the Syrians by night, we read in the books of Kings[[4 Kings 7:3||]]. [[4:27|and none of them was cleansed|Et nemo eorum mundatus est]] of leprosy by Eliseus, [[4:27|but Naaman the Syrian|nisi Naaman Syrus]]: not that Naaman was one of the lepers of Israel, but because he alone among lepers was healed by Eliseus, as is written in the books of Kings. And Naaman was the commander of the army of the king of Syria, a great man and honoured by his master, rich and valiant[[4 Kings 5:1||]]: whose goodness is plain from what is added to the words cited: [[4 Kings 5:1|for by him the Lord gave deliverance to Syria|Per illum enim dedit Dominus salutem Syriæ]]. Moreover, when he heard from a little girl that there was a Prophet in Israel[[4 Kings 5:3||]], he at once believed that he could be cured by the God of Israel through the Prophet's prayers, indeed he hoped to be cured. Hence when Eliseus did not come out to him he was angry, saying: [[4 Kings 5:11|I thought he would have come out|Putabam quod egrederetur]], and touched the place of the leprosy, and invoked the name of his God. And so he seems then to have had knowledge of the one true and supreme God; and he came to Eliseus devoutly, according to the Gloss. And when he was cured he was very grateful to God and to Eliseus, promising that from then on he would sacrifice to the God of Israel alone.

paras.t: Gorra hic quærit, cur Christus de Elia et Eliseo potius quam de aliis ponat exemplum. Ad quod respondet, quia hi soli inter Prophetas claruerunt miraculis. Cui responsioni objici posset: Primo, de Moyse, de cujus excellentia in gratia prophetiæ atque miraculis scriptum est in Deuteronomio: Non surrexit Propheta ultra in Israel sicut Moyses, quem nosset Dominus facie ad faciem, in omnibus signis et portentis quæ per illum fecit Dominus. Denique in libris Regum legitur, quomodo orante Samuele propheta Deus fecit rem grandem, dando voces, hoc est tonitrua, et pluvias tempore messis triticeæ: quod, ut ibi innuitur, valde magnum fuit miraculum. Insuper in libris Regum habetur, quemadmodum precante Propheta divinitus misso, Deus arefactam Jeroboam regis iniqui sanavit manum. Similiter in libris Regum describitur, quomodo invocante Dominum Isaia, sol miraculosissime rediit retro. Ipseque Ezechias a letali sanatus est morbo per Isaiam: unde in Ecclesiastico de Isaia asseritur, quod addidit regi vitam. Ezechiel quoque, quamvis non in Scriptura canonica, tamen in Scholastica historia legitur præclara fecisse miracula in Chaldæa; sicut et Jeremias in Ægypto mirabilia legitur perpetrasse. Hæc dixerim, non quasi Nicolao de Gorra derogare intendens, qui fuit magnus Scripturarum expositor, valdeque eruditus in eis, sed quia de solutione præfata admiror, et ut solutio illa caute legatur. Itaque puto aliam esse rationem quæsiti, videlicet, quod de Elia et Eliseo ideo Christus mentionem induxit, quoniam facta illorum præmemorata suo magis congruebant proposito, et quia valde excellentes fuerunt, imo in gestis præfatis Christi habuerunt figuram. Vidua vero et Naaman typum gerebant Ecclesiæ ex gentibus congregatæ, quam Christus per Spiritum Sanctum atque Apostolos, relictis ob suam perversitatem Judæis, visitare dignatus est.
paras.en: Gorra asks here why Christ takes His example from Elias and Eliseus rather than from others. To which he answers: because these alone among the Prophets were famous for miracles. Against this answer it could be objected: first, of Moses, of whose excellence in the grace of prophecy and in miracles it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 34:10|there arose no more a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face|Non surrexit Propheta ultra in Israel sicut Moyses, quem nosset Dominus facie ad faciem]], [[Deut 34:11|In all the signs and wonders|in omnibus signis et portentis]] which the Lord did through him. Again, we read in the books of Kings how, at the prayer of the prophet Samuel, God did a great thing, sending voices, that is, thunder, and rain in the time of the wheat harvest[[1 Kings 12:17||]]: which, as is there implied, was a very great miracle. Further, we have in the books of Kings how, at the prayer of a Prophet sent by God, God healed the withered hand of the wicked King Jeroboam[[3 Kings 13:6||]]. Likewise it is described in the books of Kings how, when Isaias called upon the Lord, the sun most miraculously went back[[4 Kings 20:11||]]. And Ezechias himself was healed of a deadly illness through Isaias[[4 Kings 20:7||]]: hence it is said of Isaias in Ecclesiasticus that [[Ecclus 48:26|he lengthened the king's life|addidit regi vitam]]. Ezechiel too, though not in canonical Scripture, yet in the *Scholastic History* [of Peter Comestor] is read to have done famous miracles in Chaldæa; as Jeremias also is read to have done wonders in Egypt. I would say this not as meaning to disparage Nicholas of Gorra, who was a great expositor of the Scriptures and very learned in them, but because I wonder at that solution, and so that it may be read with caution. So I think the reason for the question is another: namely, that Christ brought in mention of Elias and Eliseus because the deeds of theirs He recalled fitted His purpose better, and because they were very excellent men, and indeed in those deeds were a figure of Christ. The widow and Naaman bore the type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which Christ deigned to visit through the Holy Spirit and the Apostles, when the Jews had been left behind for their perversity[[Acts 13:46||]].

paras.t: Et repleti sunt omnes in synagoga ira per vitium, quæ est inordinatus appetitus vindictæ propter parvipensionem, hæc præinducta Christi eloquia audientes: quia ut eis apparuit, Christus eos superflue vilipendit, præferendo eis gentiles, quos Judæi contemnebant ut canes, et quia ipsos de ingratitudine aliisque peccatis notavit. Verumtamen Gregorius dicit eos commotos, quia Christus asseruit, Hodie scriptura hæc impleta est, etc., quasi se præsumptuose compararet Prophetis. In his Judæis sacrilegis, quorum insaniam, ingratitudinemque multi sectantur, illud Proverbiorum est impletum: Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit; illudque Amos, Odio habuerunt corripientem, et loquentem perfecte abominati sunt. Unde in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Stuppa collecta, synagoga peccantium, quæ statim igne iræ accenditur. Hinc et Terentius ait: Obsequium parit amicitiam, veritas odium.
paras.en: [[4:28|And all they in the synagogue|Et repleti sunt omnes in synagoga]] [[4:28|were filled with anger|ira]] (anger as a vice, which is a disordered desire for revenge on account of being slighted), [[4:28|hearing these things|hæc præinducta Christi eloquia audientes]], the words of Christ just given: because, as it seemed to them, Christ belittled them beyond measure by preferring to them the Gentiles, whom the Jews despised as dogs, and because He charged them with ingratitude and other sins. Gregory, however, says they were stirred up because Christ asserted, [[4:21|This day is fulfilled this scripture|Hodie scriptura hæc impleta est]], etc., as though He presumptuously compared Himself with the Prophets. In these sacrilegious Jews, whose madness and ingratitude many follow, that saying of Proverbs was fulfilled: [[Prov 15:12|A corrupt man loveth not one that reproveth him|Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit]]; and that of Amos: [[Amos 5:10|They have hated him that rebuketh in the gate: and have abhorred him that speaketh perfectly|Odio habuerunt corripientem, et loquentem perfecte abominati sunt]]. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 21:10|The congregation of sinners is like tow heaped together|Stuppa collecta, synagoga peccantium]], which is at once kindled by the fire of anger [the margin gives Ecclus. xxi, 10; Denis's last words are his own]. Hence Terence too says: “Compliance breeds friendship, truth hatred.”

paras.t: Et surrexerunt, ira eos bestialiter impellente, et ejecerunt, id est, tanquam reum mortis irreverenter expulerunt, illum extra civitatem suam Nazareth; et duxerunt illum usque ad supercilium montis, super quem civitas illorum erat ædificata, ut præcipitarent eum, et præcipitando occiderent illum: imitantes patrem suum diabolum, qui dixit ad Christum, Mitte te deorsum; imo quantum ad hoc illo pejores, quia quod ille suggessit, isti facere sunt moliti.
paras.en: [[4:29|And they rose up|Et surrexerunt]], their anger driving them like beasts, [[4:29|and thrust him out of the city|et ejecerunt]], that is, they drove Him out irreverently, as one guilty of death, outside their city of Nazareth; [[4:29|and they brought him to the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong|et duxerunt illum usque ad supercilium montis, super quem civitas illorum erat ædificata, ut præcipitarent eum]], and by casting Him down kill Him: imitating their father the devil, who said to Christ, *Cast thyself down*[[4:9||]]; indeed in this they were worse than he, because what he suggested they tried to do.

paras.t: Ipse autem transiens per medium illorum, ibat, id est, manus impiorum elapsus est et evasit, non volando aut currendo effugiens, sed per medium illorum pedester, potenter ac mire pertransiit. Quod tam increata potestate, quam virtute creata seu potestate humanitati collata, facere quivit. Per utramque etenim potuit mentem illorum subito immutare ac stupefactam seu stupidam reddere, sicut et tempore passionis prostravit sceleratos, dicendo, Ego sum: quando et dixit ad Patrem, Dedisti ei, videlicet mihi Filio tuo, potestatem omnis carnis. In templo quoque tot millium compescebat ingenia, quando negotiantes inde ejecit: quod secundum Origenem, fuit majus miraculum quam suscitatio mortuorum, vel saturatio quinque millium ex quinque panibus. Insuper, divina et increata virtute potuit se illis invisibilem reddere. Quod etiam per creatam sibi datam potentiam potuit, quia secundum superiorem animæ suæ portionem exstitit comprehensor: idcirco dum voluit, dotes corporis glorificati etiam ante passionem sæpe assumpsit, secundum Hugonem, corpusque suum animæ suæ perfecte obediens et subjectum erat in tantum, ut juxta Damascenum, omnia naturalia fuerint in Christo voluntaria: sicut et Thomas in tertia parte testatur. Ideo corpus Christi immutavit visum præsentium, secundum quod placuit animæ ejus, cujus potestate atque imperio suspendi poterat immutatio talis. Hinc aliqui asserunt, quod Christus reddidit se invisibilem illis, quemadmodum in Joanne inducitur: Jesus autem abscondit se et exivit de templo; itemque, Quærebant Jesum apprehendere, et exivit de manibus eorum.
paras.en: [[4:30|But he passing through the midst of them, went his way|Ipse autem transiens per medium illorum, ibat]], that is, He slipped out of the hands of the wicked and escaped, not fleeing by flying or running, but passing on foot through the midst of them, mightily and wonderfully. This He could do both by His uncreated power and by the created virtue or power bestowed on His humanity. For by either He could suddenly change their minds and make them stupefied or dull, as also at the time of the passion He threw the wicked to the ground by saying, [[John 18:5|I am he|Ego sum]]: when He also said to the Father, [[John 17:2|thou hast given him|Dedisti ei]], that is, me, Thy Son, [[John 17:2|power over all flesh|potestatem omnis carnis]]. In the temple too He held in check the minds of so many thousands when He cast out the traders from there[[John 2:15||]]: which, according to Origen, was a greater miracle than raising the dead or feeding five thousand with five loaves. Moreover, by His divine and uncreated power He could make Himself invisible to them. This He could also do by the created power given to Him, because according to the higher part of His soul He was a comprehensor [one already enjoying the vision of God]: therefore whenever He wished, He often took on the gifts of a glorified body even before the passion, according to Hugh, and His body was so perfectly obedient and subject to His soul that, as Damascene says, all natural things were voluntary in Christ: as Thomas too testifies in the third part. So Christ's body changed the sight of those present as it pleased His soul, by whose power and command such a change could be suspended. Hence some assert that Christ made Himself invisible to them, as is related in John: [[John 8:59|But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple|Jesus autem abscondit se et exivit de templo]]; and again, [[John 10:39|They sought therefore to take him: and he escaped out of their hands|Quærebant Jesum apprehendere, et exivit de manibus eorum]].

paras.t: Refert hic Beda, quod dum Dominus Christus de manibus illorum elapsus, de medio illorum de vertice rupis descenderet, ac sub rupe latere vellet, subito ad tactum vestis Christi, saxum illud subterfugit seu cessit, et instar ceræ solutum, quemdam sinum, hoc est concavitatem, fecit, in qua corpus dominicum susciperetur: in quo loco omnia lineamenta et rugæ vestis ac vestigia pedum in rupe apparent adhuc, sicut testantur qui viderunt. Sed et Joannes de Mandevilla in Itinerario suo scribit de hoc, adjiciens quod Christus tunc vehementer expavit. Hoc tamen credendum non reor, imo nequaquam tenendum, nisi dicatur quod sponte timorem illum assumpserit, quemadmodum tempore passionis. Alias, cur trepidasset qui universa futura tam perfecte præscivit, et tantæ potentiæ fuit, qui nec invitus ducebatur ab illis, sed sponte se duci permisit? Quod si voluisset, in quocumque viæ illius spatio omnes fecisset immobiles.
paras.en: Bede relates here that when the Lord Christ, having slipped out of their hands, was coming down from the midst of them from the top of the rock and wished to hide beneath the rock, suddenly at the touch of Christ's garment that stone gave way, that is, yielded, and, melted like wax, made a kind of hollow in which the Lord's body was received: and in that place all the lines and folds of the garment and the prints of the feet still appear in the rock, as those who have seen it testify. And John Mandeville too writes of this in his *Travels*, adding that Christ was then greatly afraid. This, however, I do not think is to be believed, indeed it is by no means to be held, unless it be said that He took on that fear of His own will, as at the time of the passion. Otherwise, why should He have trembled who so perfectly foreknew all things to come, and was of such power, who was not led by them against His will, but let Himself be led of His own accord? For had He wished, He would have made them all motionless at any point along that way.

paras.t: Noluit autem præcipitari: quoniam tempus passioni suæ divinitus præfixum nondum fuit impletum; et quoniam aliud genus mortis elegit, videlicet crucifixionem, ut impleretur quod scriptum est: Foderunt manus meas et pedes meos; et iterum, Dederunt in escam meam fel. Item, quia nondum implevit opera propter quæ missus fuit a Patre, videlicet prædicationem evangelicæ legis, institutionem sacramentorum, miraculosos effectus: de quibus omnibus passioni jam proximus dixit in Joanne: Pater, opus consummavi quod dedisti mihi ut facerem; nunc autem ad te venio.
paras.en: He did not wish to be cast down, because the time divinely fixed for His passion was not yet fulfilled; and because He chose another kind of death, namely crucifixion, that what was written might be fulfilled: [[Ps 21:17|They have dug my hands and feet|Foderunt manus meas et pedes meos]]; and again, [[Ps 68:22|they gave me gall for my food|Dederunt in escam meam fel]]. Also, because He had not yet fulfilled the works for which He had been sent by the Father, namely the preaching of the law of the Gospel, the institution of the sacraments, the miraculous works: of all of which He said in John, when already close to His passion: Father, [[John 17:4|I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do|opus consummavi quod dedisti mihi ut facerem]]; [[John 17:13|And now I come to thee|nunc autem ad te venio]].

paras.t: Et descendit in Capharnaum, quia relictis concivibus suis perfidis et ingratis, venit ad urbem Capharnaum. Verumtamen, ut ex præhabitis innotescit, istud, Et descendit in Capharnaum, usque ad finem capituli, non continuatur cum littera immediate præcedente, sed cum eo quod superius scriptum est: Regressus est Jesus in virtute Spiritus Sancti de Judæa in Galilæam. Venit ergo Capharnaum, civitatem Galilææ, ibique docebat illos, scilicet habitantes et præsentes ibidem, sabbatis, hoc est diebus sabbati, quando ut dictum est, Judæi copiosius ad loca divini obsequii confluebant.
paras.en: [[4:31|And he went down into Capharnaum|Et descendit in Capharnaum]], because, leaving His faithless and ungrateful fellow citizens, He came to the city of Capharnaum. Yet, as is known from what was said before, this, *And he went down into Capharnaum*, up to the end of the chapter, does not run on with the text immediately preceding, but with what was written above: *Jesus returned in the power of the Holy Spirit from Judæa into Galilee*[[4:14||]]. So He came to Capharnaum, [[4:31|a city of Galilee|civitatem Galilææ]], [[4:31|and there he taught them|ibique docebat illos]], namely those who lived and were present there, [[4:31|on the sabbath days|sabbatis]], when, as has been said, the Jews flocked in greater numbers to the places of divine worship.

paras.t: Et stupebant in doctrina ejus, id est, de excellentia documentorum prædicationisque Christi admirabantur. Cujus una causa subjungitur: quia in potestate erat sermo ipsius, id est, verba ejus efficacia valde et potentia erant: Primo, quia per miracula confirmabantur, atque divina et vera ostendebantur. Secundo, quia ea mox concomitabantur effectus. Statim enim ut jussit aliqua prodigia fieri, fiebant perfecte. Tertio, quoniam verba Christi habuerunt singularissimam atque fortissimam vim movendi audientium corda, utpote ea compungendo, inflammando, penetrando, terrendo. Ignea enim protulit verba sententiis plena; facundissimus quoque dulcissimusque fuit eloquio, et nihilominus terribilis, quando volebat. Unde illud Jeremiæ dicere potuit: Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis, et quasi malleus conterens petram? Nec mirum si in humanitate tam potestativi fuit sermonis, qui secundum divinitatem est Dei Patris sermo omnipotens, Verbum æternum, de quo ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Vivus est sermo Dei, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti. Quarto, quoniam habuit auctoritatem addendi ad verba legis, eam perficiendo et spiritualiter interpretando, imo finem eidem quantum ad præcepta cærimonialia imponendo, quum esset dator ac dominus legis. Quinto, quia quod docuit, opere adimplevit. Hinc Beda fatetur: Sermo (inquiens) prædicatoris in potestate est, dum ea quæ docet, operatur: qui enim facto destruit quod verbis prædicat, contemnitur.
paras.en: [[4:32|And they were astonished at his doctrine|Et stupebant in doctrina ejus]], that is, they marvelled at the excellence of Christ's teachings and preaching. One cause of this is added: [[4:32|for his speech was with power|quia in potestate erat sermo ipsius]], that is, His words were very effective and powerful. First, because they were confirmed by miracles and shown to be divine and true. Secondly, because the effects followed them at once: for as soon as He ordered any wonders to be done, they were done perfectly. Thirdly, because Christ's words had a most singular and most strong force for moving the hearts of the hearers, by pricking, inflaming, piercing and frightening them. For He uttered fiery words full of meaning; He was also most eloquent and most sweet in speech, and nonetheless terrible when He wished. Hence He could say that word of Jeremias: [[Jer 23:29|Are not my words as a fire|Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis]], [[Jer 23:29|and as a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces|et quasi malleus conterens petram?]]? Nor is it any wonder that in His humanity His speech had such power, who according to His divinity is the almighty speech of God the Father, the eternal Word, of whom the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living|Vivus est sermo Dei]], [[Heb 4:12|more piercing than any two edged sword|et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti]]. Fourthly, because He had authority to add to the words of the law, perfecting it and interpreting it spiritually, indeed putting an end to it as to the ceremonial precepts, since He was the giver and Lord of the law. Fifthly, because what He taught He fulfilled in deed. Hence Bede says: “The preacher's speech is with power when he does what he teaches: for one who destroys by his deeds what he preaches in words is despised.”

paras.t: Et in synagoga erat homo habens spiritum immundum, hoc est possessus a dæmone: qui immundus vocatur, quoniam in se ipso totus immundus seu vitiosus consistit, in omnibus quæ agit peccans, quia ad finem perversum omnia refert. Insuper immundus dicitur ab effectu, quoniam ad vitiorum impuritatem hominem tentando inducit: juxta quem modum etiam nominatur mutus et surdus, quia hominem possessum mutum facit et surdum. Et exclamavit voce magna, dicens. Aliqui dicunt, quod in Scripturis canonicis nullibi legitur vox magna, nisi in bono: cujus oppositum ex hoc loco probatur. Sine, id est, cessa nos dæmones affligere. Dolebat quippe diabolus de Christi præsentia, quem sibi maxime contrarium vidit; item de ejus salutari doctrina, quæ animarum exstitit medicina, sicque de hominum conversione potissimum tristabatur. Timuit quoque expelli ab homine, et ab hominum infestatione ac deceptione arceri, atque in loca pœnalia relegari. Ideo ait: Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu Nazarene? id est, quum nulla sit inter te et nos amicitia, societas, confœderatio, cur venisti ad nos? præsertim quum amor soleat esse ratio unionis: nam et Apostolus, Quæ, inquit, conventio Christi ad Belial? Sed Christus accessit diabolum, non sicut amicus amicum, sed ut judex reum, pugil adversarium, liberator raptorem. Quod et diabolus advertens, adjecit: Venisti perdere nos? Tanta est invidia impietasque diaboli, ut perdi se reputet, si ab hominibus expellatur, atque ab eorum nocumento frenetur. Itaque, Venisti perdere nos, id est vincere, spoliare, debilitare? Ad hoc utique Christus venit, ut vasa diaboli ei auferret, ejus tyrannidem refrenaret, ipsum comprimeret, suppeditaret, et tandem in infernum retruderet. Scio te, quia sis Sanctus Dei, hoc est Sanctus Sanctorum ad Deum specialissime pertinens, utpote Christus in lege promissus: de quo in Daniele habetur, Ungatur Sanctus Sanctorum; atque in Psalmo, Non dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem.
paras.en: [[4:33|And in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean devil|Et in synagoga erat homo habens spiritum immundum]] [Denis's text: “an unclean spirit”], that is, possessed by a devil: who is called unclean because in himself he is wholly unclean, that is, vicious, sinning in all that he does, since he refers everything to a perverse end. He is also called unclean from his effect, because by tempting he leads man into the impurity of vices: in the same way he is also called dumb and deaf, because he makes the man he possesses dumb and deaf[[Mark 9:16||]][[Mark 9:24||]][[Luke 11:14||]]. [[4:33|and he cried out with a loud voice|Et exclamavit voce magna]], [[4:34|Saying|dicens]]. Some say that in the canonical Scriptures a loud voice is nowhere read of except in a good sense: the opposite of which is proved from this place. [[4:34|Let us alone|Sine]], that is, cease afflicting us devils. For the devil grieved at the presence of Christ, whom he saw to be most contrary to himself; and also at His saving doctrine, which was the medicine of souls; and so he was saddened above all by the conversion of men. He feared too to be driven out of the man, and to be kept from harassing and deceiving men, and to be banished to places of punishment. So he says: [[4:34|What have we to do with thee, Jesus of Nazareth?|Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu Nazarene?]] that is, since there is no friendship, fellowship or alliance between you and us, why have you come to us? especially since love is wont to be the ground of union: for the Apostle too says, [[2 Cor 6:15|what concord hath Christ with Belial?|Quæ, inquit, conventio Christi ad Belial?]] But Christ came up to the devil not as a friend to a friend, but as a judge to the accused, a champion to his adversary, a deliverer to the robber. And the devil, noticing this, added: [[4:34|Art thou come to destroy us?|Venisti perdere nos]] So great is the envy and wickedness of the devil that he thinks himself destroyed if he is driven out of men and checked from harming them. So, *Art thou come to destroy us*, that is, to conquer, despoil and weaken us? Indeed Christ came for this: to take the devil's goods from him[[Mark 3:27||]], to curb his tyranny, to crush him, to trample on him, and at last to thrust him back into hell. [[4:34|I know thee who thou art, the holy one of God|Scio te, quia sis Sanctus Dei]], that is, the Holy of Holies, belonging most especially to God, namely the Christ promised in the law: of whom we have in Daniel, [[Dan 9:24|the Saint of saints may be anointed|Ungatur Sanctus Sanctorum]]; and in the Psalm, [[Ps 15:10|nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption|Non dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem]].

paras.t: Circa hoc quæritur, an dæmones cognoverunt Jesum esse Messiam. Et patet responsio ex dictis. Lyra autem circa hæc verba scribit super Marcum, quod dæmones sciebant Jesum esse Messiam in lege promissum; et intendit asserere, quod certitudinaliter hoc sciebant, utpote per prophetias de Christo prædictas, quæ determinant locum et tempus ac modum veniendi ipsius Christi. Verumtamen, ut affirmat, nesciebant eum esse Dei Filium per naturam Deo Patri æqualem, licet ad hunc finem tentaverit eum diabolus, quia si cognovissent eum esse Deum, nunquam induxissent Judæos ad ipsum crucifigendum.
paras.en: On this it is asked whether the devils knew that Jesus was the Messias. And the answer is plain from what has been said. Lyra, however, writes on these words on Mark[[Mark 1:34||]] that the devils knew that Jesus was the Messias promised in the law; and he means to assert that they knew this with certainty, namely through the prophecies foretold about Christ, which fix the place, the time and the manner of Christ's coming. Yet, as he affirms, they did not know that He was the Son of God by nature, equal to God the Father, although the devil tempted Him for this purpose; because if they had known He was God, they would never have led the Jews to crucify Him.

paras.t: Contra hæc objici posset, quia implicare videntur. Si enim diabolus scivit quod Jesus esset Messias, ex Prophetarum oraculis, consequens est quod pariformiter sciverit eum esse Unigenitum Dei, verumque Deum. Hoc enim ex scripturis Prophetarum patet, concluditur, et habetur, quod Christus in lege promissus, esset Unigenitus Dei, veram habens cum Patre divinitatem, Isaia dicente: Puer natus est nobis, et vocabitur nomen ejus Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis. Et Jeremias: Hoc est, inquit, nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster: loco cujus in Hebræo habetur nomen Domini tetragrammaton, quod non competit nisi vero summoque Deo, ut etiam Hebræorum magistri concorditer profitentur. Michæas quoque testatur: Egressus ejus sicut a principio, a diebus æternitatis. Et Daniel inquit: Potestas ejus potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur. Itemque Psalmista: Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi; et rursus, Concupiscet rex decorem tuum, quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus tuus, et adorabunt eum; et iterum, Sit nomen ejus benedictum in sæcula, ante solem permanet nomen ejus. Quod autem hic omnia ad litteram dicantur de Christo in lege promisso, dubitare non potest quisquis loca Scripturarum ubi ista habentur diligenter perspexerit, præcedentia et consequentia ibi pensando. Itaque ista esse de rege Messia prænuntiata certissime novit diabolus: idcirco, si ex Scripturis noverat Jesum esse Messiam, æque certitudinaliter scivit quod Filius Dei per naturam consisteret.
paras.en: Against this it could be objected that these statements seem to contradict each other. For if the devil knew from the oracles of the Prophets that Jesus was the Messias, it follows that he likewise knew Him to be the Only-begotten of God and true God. For from the scriptures of the Prophets it is plain, it is concluded and held, that the Christ promised in the law would be the Only-begotten of God, having true divinity with the Father; for Isaias says: [[Is 9:6|a child is born to us|Puer natus est nobis]], and [[Is 9:6|his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace|et vocabitur nomen ejus Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis]]. And Jeremias: [[Jer 23:6|this is the name that they shall call him: The Lord our just one|Hoc est, inquit, nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster]]: in place of which the Hebrew has the four-lettered name of the Lord [the Tetragrammaton], which belongs only to the true and supreme God, as the masters of the Hebrews too agree in professing. Micheas also testifies: [[Mich 5:2|his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity|Egressus ejus sicut a principio, a diebus æternitatis]]. And Daniel says: [[Dan 7:14|his power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away|potestas æterna, quæ non auferetur]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 44:7|Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever|Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi]]; and again, [[Ps 44:12|And the king shall greatly desire thy beauty; for he is the Lord thy God, and him they shall adore|Concupiscet rex decorem tuum, quoniam ipse est Dominus Deus tuus, et adorabunt eum]]; and again, [[Ps 71:17|Let his name be blessed for evermore: his name continueth before the sun|Sit nomen ejus]]. That all these things are said here literally of the Christ promised in the law, no one can doubt who has looked carefully at the places of Scripture where they are found, weighing what goes before and after there. So the devil knew most certainly that these things were foretold of the King Messias: therefore, if he knew from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Messias, he knew with equal certainty that He was the Son of God by nature.

paras.t: Insuper, non minus omisisset diabolus inducere Judæos ad occisionem Christi, si certitudinaliter agnovisset eum esse Messiam seu Christum, quam si scivisset eum Dei Filium naturalem. Causa enim quare non induxisset Judæos ad hoc, fuit, ne redimeretur genus humanum, quod scivit per Messiæ occisionem salvandum. Imo si certitudinaliter scivisset Jesum esse Dei Filium naturalem, plus odisset eum quam si putasset eum hominem purum. Quanto enim quis melior est, tanto plus odit eum: unde nec aliquem tantum odit, ut Deum. Itaque, si certe scivisset Jesum esse Dei Filium naturalem, non omisisset Judæos inducere ad crucifixionem ipsius ex aliqua dilectione vel reverentia ad ipsum: nec propter enormitatem peccati, quum quo quid iniquius fuerit, eo plus complaceat ei; nec ex timore suæ punitionis, quoniam tanta est ejus invidia contra Sanctos, quod eos tentare ac persequi non omittit propter augmentum suæ calamitatis vitandum: quemadmodum etiam tempore Antichristi non omittet Antichristum et ejus satellites inducere ad destruendum cultum, legem, fidemque Christi, quantum poterit; nec dubium quin et ad ipsam Christi interfectionem induceret Antichristum, si possibile esset Christum in propria persona ab Antichristo occidi, non obstante quod nunc utique noscit Jesum esse Deum et hominem. Denique dæmones omnesque damnati, in tantum invident gloriæ superbeatissimi Dei, quod vellent eum non esse, et si possent ipsam Divinitatem occiderent, patricidis ac matricidis similes exsistentes. Constat ergo, quod nulla sit ratio cur diabolus non induxisset ad Christi occisionem Judæos, si certe novisset Jesum esse Christum, nisi ne salvaretur genus humanum, cujus saluti ineffabiliter invident dæmones.
paras.en: Moreover, the devil would no less have refrained from leading the Jews to kill Christ if he had known with certainty that He was the Messias, that is, the Christ, than if he had known Him to be the natural Son of God. For the reason why he would not have led the Jews to this was so that the human race might not be redeemed, which he knew was to be saved by the killing of the Messias. Indeed, if he had known with certainty that Jesus was the natural Son of God, he would have hated Him more than if he had thought Him a mere man. For the better someone is, the more he hates him: hence he hates no one so much as God. So if he had known for certain that Jesus was the natural Son of God, he would not have refrained from leading the Jews to crucify Him out of any love or reverence toward Him; nor because of the enormity of the sin, since the more wicked a thing is, the more it pleases him; nor out of fear of his own punishment, since his envy against the Saints is so great that he does not cease to tempt and persecute them in order to avoid an increase of his own misery: as also in the time of Antichrist he will not fail to lead Antichrist and his henchmen to destroy the worship, law and faith of Christ as far as he can; and there is no doubt that he would lead Antichrist even to kill Christ, if it were possible for Christ in His own person to be killed by Antichrist, although he now certainly knows that Jesus is God and man. Lastly, the devils and all the damned so envy the glory of the more than most blessed God that they would wish Him not to be, and if they could they would kill the Godhead itself, being like parricides and matricides. It is clear, then, that there is no reason why the devil would not have led the Jews to kill Christ, if he had known for certain that Jesus was the Christ, except so that the human race might not be saved, whose salvation the devils envy beyond words.

paras.t: Postremo Glossa hoc loco sentit, quod dæmones non habuerunt certitudinalem, sed conjecturalem de Christo notitiam, quod scilicet Christus esset: nempe quod dictum est, Scio, exponit, Vehementer opinor. Itaque Christus est Sanctus Dei, quia ut Deus, est æqualis atque ejusdem sanctitatis cum Patre, et essentialiter et æternaliter infiniteque sanctus et sanctitas ipsa. Secundum humanitatem vero, est Sanctus Dei, tanquam sanctificatus a Deo ab incarnationis exordio: sanctificatus, inquam, non quasi ab aliqua labe purgatus, sed omni virtute, dono et gratia Spiritus Sancti repletus, et sanctior universis ac singulis, etiam simul sumptis. Unde in Joanne loquitur de se ipso: Quem Pater sanctificavit et misit in mundum.
paras.en: Lastly, the Gloss holds at this place that the devils had not a certain but a conjectural knowledge of Christ, namely that He was the Christ: for what is said, *I know*, it explains as, “I strongly suspect.” So Christ is [[4:34|the holy one of God|Sanctus Dei]]: because as God He is equal to the Father and of the same holiness with Him, and essentially, eternally and infinitely holy, and holiness itself. But according to His humanity He is the Holy One of God as sanctified by God from the first moment of the incarnation: sanctified, I say, not as cleansed from any stain, but as filled with every virtue, gift and grace of the Holy Spirit, and holier than each and all, even taken together. Hence in John He says of Himself: [[John 10:36|whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the world|Quem Pater sanctificavit et misit in mundum]].

paras.t: Et increpavit illum Jesus, dicens: Obmutesce, et exi ab eo. Quamvis quæ dixit diabolus, ad Christi pertinent præconium, nihilominus silentium illi Christus imposuit, quia ipse qui verus et veritas est, noluit testimonium ejus suscipere qui mendax est ab initio, et ne diabolus veris falsa misceret, item ut Christi exemplo doceamur dæmonum dicta contemnere. Dicit autem Cyrillus, quod dæmones putarent per hujusmodi laudem facere Jesum inanis gloriæ amatorem, ut ab eorum contrarietate cessaret, utpote gratiam pro gratia recompensans. Et quum projecisset illum hominem dæmoniacum, dæmonium quod fuit in eo, in medium, hoc est in terram coram præsentibus, exiit ab illo, nihilque illi nocuit. Quamvis enim ante egressionem affligeret hominem illum, juxta illud Marci, Discerpens eum spiritus immundus; tamen egresso dæmonio, prior illa afflictio divina virtute cessavit, et confortatus est homo.
paras.en: [[4:35|And Jesus rebuked him, saying: Hold thy peace and go out of him|Et increpavit illum Jesus, dicens: Obmutesce, et exi ab eo]]. Although what the devil said belonged to the praise of Christ, Christ nonetheless imposed silence on him: because He who is true and the truth itself[[John 14:6||]] would not accept the testimony of him who is a liar from the beginning[[John 8:44||]]; and lest the devil mix false things with true; and also so that by Christ's example we may be taught to despise what devils say. Cyril says that the devils thought by such praise to make Jesus a lover of vainglory, so that He would cease opposing them, repaying favour with favour. [[4:35|And when the devil had thrown him|Et quum projecisset illum]], the possessed man, that is, the devil who was in him, [[4:35|into the midst|in medium]], that is, onto the ground before those present, [[4:35|he went out of him|exiit ab illo]], [[4:35|and hurt him not at all|nihilque illi nocuit]]. For although before going out he afflicted that man, according to that saying of Mark, [[Mark 1:26|the unclean spirit, tearing him|Discerpens eum spiritus immundus]], yet when the devil had gone out, the former affliction ceased by divine power, and the man was strengthened.

paras.t: Et factus est pavor in omnibus, hoc est admiratio magna in omnibus qui istud viderunt. Admirabantur etenim potius modum agendi, quam factum in se, quum et exorcistæ eorum ejicere dæmones possent atque solerent. Porro naturale est homini, visis magnis et insolitis rebus timere, quamvis non omnes homines ideo æqualiter timeant. Boni enim et sapientes reverentialem timorem visis mirabilibus Dei concipiunt, alii sæpe aliter timent. Ex magnitudine quippe effectus, majestas causæ perpenditur, sicque timor reverentialis aut pœnalis innascitur; impia autem conscientia cito terretur, et ne quod meruit sibi contingat, veretur, præsertim dum divinæ potestatis advertit præsentiam. Unde et in Actibus Apostolorum habetur: Fiebat autem omni animæ timor, videlicet ex miraculis Apostolorum. Christus autem imperialiter fecit miracula: quod isti maxime mirabantur, ut subditur.
paras.en: [[4:36|And there came fear upon all|Et factus est pavor in omnibus]], that is, great wonder in all who saw this. For they wondered rather at the manner of acting than at the deed in itself, since their own exorcists too could and did cast out devils. Further, it is natural to man to fear when he sees great and unusual things, though not all men fear equally for this reason. For the good and wise conceive a reverential fear on seeing the wonders of God; others often fear otherwise. For from the greatness of the effect the majesty of the cause is weighed, and so a reverential or a penal fear arises [that is, the fear of reverence, or the fear of punishment]; but a wicked conscience is quickly terrified, and fears that what it has deserved may befall it, especially when it notices the presence of divine power. Hence too we have in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 2:43|And fear came upon every soul|Fiebat autem omni animæ timor]], namely from the miracles of the Apostles. But Christ worked miracles as a sovereign: and this is what these people wondered at most, as is added.

paras.t: Et colloquebantur ad invicem, dicentes: Quod est hoc verbum, hoc est, quid prætendit? aut quam potens est sermo istius! Vel verbum potest hic accipi pro re significata per verbum, sicut in Scripturis frequenter accipitur. Itaque dicunt: Quod est hoc verbum? id est, quam mirabile est opus istud! Quia in potestate, hoc est sermone auctoritativo ac imperioso, et virtute, id est per potentiam efficacem, ad quam quum voluerit mox concomitatur effectus. Potestas quoque ad increatam Christi potentiam, virtus vero ad creatam ejus potentiam potest referri, quamvis illi non intellexerint ita. Nondum enim innotuit eis Jesu divinitas. Iterum, virtus accipi potest pro sanctitate ac merito animæ Christi, per quam quodammodo egit miracula, præsertim quum et alii Sancti, suæ merito sanctitatis miracula operati scribantur. Imperat immundis spiritibus, hoc est dæmonibus maculosis, aliosque maculantibus, et exeunt ab obsessis, dum præcipit eis: non obstante quod de dæmonio scriptum sit in Job, Non est potestas super terram quæ comparetur ei: de naturali enim potestate terrenorum seu habitatorum terræ hoc dicitur. Christus autem divina, cælesti et supernaturali potestate hæc fecit: nam et creata Christi potestas tanta est, ut per eam summis angelis possit imperare, imperetque spiritibus, sicut et anima ejus illos illuminat, multo utique altius quam aliquis angelus superior inferiorem.
paras.en: [[4:36|and they talked among themselves, saying: What word is this|Et colloquebantur ad invicem, dicentes: Quod est hoc verbum]], that is, what does it mean? or, how powerful is this man's speech! Or *word* can be taken here for the thing signified by the word, as it often is in the Scriptures. So they say: *What word is this?* that is, how wonderful is this work! [[4:36|for with authority|Quia in potestate]], that is, with authoritative and commanding speech, [[4:36|and power|et virtute]], that is, by effective might, upon which, when He wills, the effect at once follows. *Authority* can also be referred to Christ's uncreated might, and *power* to His created might, though they did not understand it so: for the divinity of Jesus was not yet known to them. Again, *power* can be taken for the holiness and merit of Christ's soul, by which in some way He worked miracles, especially since other Saints too are written to have worked miracles by the merit of their holiness. [[4:36|he commandeth the unclean spirits, and they go out|Imperat immundis spiritibus]] from the possessed, when He commands them: although it is written of the devil in Job, [[Job 41:24|There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him|Non est potestas super terram quæ comparetur ei]]: for this is said of the natural power of earthly beings, that is, of the dwellers on earth. But Christ did these things by divine, heavenly and supernatural power: for even the created power of Christ is so great that by it He can command the highest angels, and He does command spirits, as His soul also enlightens them, far more highly than any higher angel enlightens a lower.

paras.t: Postremo, per dæmoniacum istum intelligi potest quicumque magnus peccator, dæmonum subditus voluntati et servituti peccati: quem Christus ingrediens synagogam, hoc est corda eorum qui per caritatem nectuntur in Deo, a dæmonio liberat, dum ei gratiam pœnitendi largitur, tuncque dæmonem egredi jubet, ingrediente talem animam Spiritu Sancto. Dæmon autem projicit hominem in medium, hoc est, ad medietatem, in qua virtus consistit, eum reducit, non effective, sed occasionaliter, in quantum suo recessu fit homini occasio redeundi ad medietatem virtutis, ad quam illo possidente seu inhabitante, homo redire nequivit: quemadmodum etiam Deus dicitur hominem indurare, in quantum gratiæ suæ subtractione hominem indurari permittit, qui sine gratiosa Dei præsentia ad pœnitentiam mollificari non valet.
paras.en: Lastly, by this possessed man can be understood any great sinner, subject to the will of the devils and to the slavery of sin: whom Christ, entering the synagogue, that is, the hearts of those who are bound together in God by charity, frees from the devil, when He grants him the grace of repentance, and then bids the devil go out, as the Holy Spirit enters such a soul. And the devil throws the man *into the midst*, that is, brings him back to the mean in which virtue consists: not as efficient cause, but as occasion, inasmuch as by his departure the man is given occasion to return to the mean of virtue, to which he could not return while the devil possessed or dwelt in him: as God too is said to harden a man, inasmuch as by withdrawing His grace He allows the man to be hardened, who without the gracious presence of God cannot be softened to repentance.

paras.t: Præterea quæritur, quum Christus non nisi unum obsessum curaverit, cur pluraliter loquebantur, Quia in potestate imperat spiritibus immundis. Ad quod dici potest, quod plurale pro singulari ponebant, ut sæpe fit in Scripturis, imo et in communi modo loquendi: præsertim quia tam magnifice Christus istum unum sanavit, quod videntes putabant eum eadem virtute posse et alios sic curare.
paras.en: It is asked besides: since Christ cured only one possessed man, why did they speak in the plural, *for with authority he commandeth the unclean spirits*? To this it can be said that they put the plural for the singular, as is often done in the Scriptures, and indeed in the common way of speaking: especially because Christ healed this one man so magnificently that those who saw it thought He could cure others in the same way by the same power.

paras.t: Et divulgabatur fama de illo, id est de Christo vel ejus miraculo, imo pariter de utroque, in omnem locum regionis Galilææ, juxta illud Marci: Processit rumor ejus in omnem regionem Galilææ.
paras.en: [[4:37|And the fame of him was published|Et divulgabatur fama de illo]], that is, of Christ or of His miracle, indeed of both alike, [[4:37|into every place of the country|in omnem locum regionis]] of Galilee, according to that saying of Mark: [[Mark 1:28|the fame of him was spread|Processit rumor ejus]] [[Mark 1:28|into all the country of Galilee|in omnem regionem Galilææ]].

paras.t: Consequenter aliud Christi recitatur miraculum. Surgens autem Jesus de synagoga urbis Capharnaum: in qua sedit docendo, quia sedere magistrorum ac judicum est; introivit in domum Simonis, id est Petri apostoli: qui primo vocatus est Simon, postea autem a Christo dictus est Petrus, ut infra dicetur. In Marco autem adjicitur, Et Andreæ: unde in domo illa Petrus et frater ejus Andreas aliquando pariter morabantur. Socrus autem, id est mater conjugis, Simonis, tenebatur magnis febribus: ita quod diu laboravit hac ægritudine; et Christo ingrediente actualiter vexabatur. Propter quod Marcus ait, Decumbebat febricitans. Habuit autem acutissimas febres, præsertim quia fuit annosa, et naturalis in ea calor defecit: unde in senibus febris solet mortem inducere. Et rogaverunt illum pro ea, id est, discipuli Christi et præsentes in domo Christum deprecabantur ut vetulam illam sanaret: quibus ipse tanquam piissimus mox consensit, ut subditur. Et stans super illam. Accessit enim ad locum quo jacuit illa, et sic situ altior fuit: et forte faciem suam inclinavit ad decumbentem ægrotam, agens quod sequitur, imperavit febri. Auctoritatem enim, potestatem, atque dominium habuit super omnem entitatem creatam. Itaque, Imperavit febri, id est, jussit eam cessare, et dimisit illam, id est, febris statim a vetula illa recessit. Et continuo surgens, ministrabat illis, id est Christo et commensalibus ejus, tanquam grata de beneficio sanitatis sibi tam miraculose collato, et valde læta; eos quoque quibus ministrabat, spectaculo lætificans tam jucundo.
paras.en: Next another miracle of Christ is related. [[4:38|And Jesus rising up out of the synagogue|Surgens autem Jesus de synagoga]] of the city of Capharnaum, in which He had sat teaching, for sitting belongs to masters and judges, [[4:38|went into Simon's house|introivit in domum Simonis]], that is, of the apostle Peter, who was first called Simon and afterwards named Peter by Christ, as will be said below. In Mark it is added, [[Mark 1:29|and Andrew|Et Andreæ]]: so Peter and his brother Andrew sometimes lived together in that house. [[4:38|And Simon's wife's mother|Socrus autem]] (that is, the mother of his wife) [[4:38|was taken with a great fever|tenebatur magnis febribus]], so that she had long suffered from this sickness; and as Christ came in she was actually in its grip. That is why Mark says, she [[Mark 1:30|lay in a fit of a fever|Decumbebat febricitans]]. And she had very sharp fevers, especially because she was old and her natural heat had failed: hence in the old a fever is wont to bring on death. [[4:38|and they besought him for her|Et rogaverunt illum pro ea]], that is, Christ's disciples and those present in the house begged Christ to heal that old woman: to whom He, most loving as He is, at once consented, as is added. [[4:39|And standing over her|Et stans super illam]]. For He came to the place where she lay, and so was higher in position: and perhaps He bent His face toward the sick woman lying there, doing what follows: [[4:39|he commanded the fever|imperavit febri]]. For He had authority, power and dominion over every created being. So, *he commanded the fever*, that is, ordered it to cease, [[4:39|and it left her|et dimisit illam]], that is, the fever at once went away from that old woman. [[4:39|And immediately rising, she ministered to them|Et continuo surgens, ministrabat illis]], that is, to Christ and those at table with Him, as one grateful for the benefit of health so miraculously bestowed on her, and very glad; gladdening too those she served by so happy a sight.

paras.t: In quibus multa miranda sunt contemplanda, quia modus agendi gloriosior fuit quam opus in se, quum et naturaliter quis posset curari a febre; sed tam imperialiter et repente gravibus febribus laborantem curare, ita ut febre cessante plena sanitas et corporis robur pariter mox reverterentur, omnino divinum miraculosumque fuit: potissimum, quoniam febricitantes, febre cessante, valde lassi sunt corpore, incipienteque sanitate, pristinæ ægritudinis sentiunt mala, paulatim quoque vires recipiunt. Constat autem quia potestas, quo major est, eo celerius operatur. Potestas autem Christi secundum quod Deus est, infinita consistit, sed et creata ejus potestas, omnium creaturarum potestatem excedit: ideo potuit in instanti atque celerrime miracula operari; et si aliqua fecit protractius, non ex defectu potestatis hoc fuit, sed propter mysterium.
paras.en: In these things there are many wonderful things to contemplate, because the manner of acting was more glorious than the work in itself, since one could also be cured of a fever naturally; but to cure one suffering from heavy fevers so sovereignly and suddenly that, as the fever ceased, full health and bodily strength at once returned together, was wholly divine and miraculous: above all because those who have had a fever are very weary in body when the fever ceases, and as health begins they feel the ill effects of the former sickness, and recover their strength little by little. Now it is certain that the greater a power is, the more quickly it works. And Christ's power, as He is God, is infinite; and even His created power exceeds the power of all creatures: so He could work miracles in an instant and most quickly; and if He did some more slowly, this was not from any lack of power, but for the sake of a mystery.

paras.t: Denique juxta Glossam, Christus interdum rogatus, interdum non rogatus, fecit miracula, ad insinuandum quod aliquando orantibus peccata relaxat, aliquando non recordantibus gratis indulget, quando videlicet ita dispositi sunt, quod si recordarentur vitiorum suorum oblitorum, dimitterent ea, et veniam precarentur.
