Tunc enim dimittit ea, aut certe revelat ea, ut recordans pœniteat et exoret. — Insuper, Christi dignatio atque humilitas sunt pensandæ: qui apud Petrum virum inopem manere elegit, ut discamus, sicut ait Cyrillus, cum pauperibus conversari, nec depressos inopesque spernamus.
paras.en: Further, according to the Gloss, Christ worked miracles sometimes when asked, sometimes when not asked, to intimate that sometimes He forgives sins to those who pray, and sometimes freely pardons those who do not remember them: namely when they are so disposed that, if they remembered their forgotten vices, they would give them up and ask for pardon. For then He forgives them, or else reveals them, so that remembering, the man may repent and pray. — Moreover, Christ's condescension and humility are to be weighed: who chose to stay with Peter, a poor man, so that we may learn, as Cyril says, to keep company with the poor, and not to despise the lowly and needy.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per vetulam febricitantem, designatur quæcumque anima vitiis et passionibus, quæ animarum gravissimæ febres sunt, inveterata: ad quam quum Christus per pietatis suæ opem, seu gratiæ infusionem accesserit, mox curatur, et Christo ejusque servis obsequitur, sicut ait Apostolus: Per caritatem servite in invicem. Si autem discipuli, visa corporali ægritudine vetulæ, compassi sunt, et Christum pro illius curatione deprecabantur, quanto magis quum viderimus alicujus animam vitiis et passionibus superatam, læsam atque squalentem, mox caritative humiliterque condolere debemus, et Christum pro illius cura ac reformatione cordialiter exorare? Sed multi sunt indiscreti, ad indignationem et ultionem proniores quam ad compassionem atque subsidium; quum tamen dicat Apostolus, Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi; imo Christo testante, eadem mensura qua mensi fuerimus, remetietur et nobis.
paras.en: Spiritually, by the fevered old woman is signified any soul grown old in vices and passions, which are the heaviest fevers of souls: when Christ comes to it with the help of His loving-kindness, that is, with the infusion of grace, it is at once cured, and serves Christ and His servants, as the Apostle says: [[Gal 5:13|by charity|Per caritatem]] … [[Gal 5:13|serve one another|servite in invicem]]. And if the disciples, seeing the old woman's bodily sickness, had compassion and begged Christ to cure her, how much more, when we see someone's soul overcome by vices and passions, wounded and squalid, ought we at once to grieve with it in charity and humility, and heartily beg Christ for its cure and renewal? But many are indiscreet, more inclined to indignation and revenge than to compassion and help; though the Apostle says, [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens: and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.|Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi]]; indeed, as Christ testifies, [[Luke 6:38|with the same measure that you shall mete withal, it shall be measured to you again|eadem mensura qua mensi fuerimus, remetietur et nobis]][[Matt 7:2||]].

paras.t: Verum, quia innumerabilia fuerunt Christi miracula, sicut et ejus potestas incomparabilis exstitit, idcirco post particularem duorum narrationem signorum, plura generaliter referuntur. Quum autem sol occidisset, omnes qui habebant infirmos variis languoribus, ducebant illos ad eum. Omnes itaque in Capharnaum, cognatos, domesticos, familiares, seu caros, variis infirmitatibus tabefactos, quorum multi per se ire non poterant, duxerunt ad Christum, cognitis præfatis duobus miraculis. Ita et Christiani, præsertim prælati et patres, infirmos suos, id est vitiis languidos, Christo adducere debent, eos ad pœnitentiam inducendo. At ille singulis infirmis manus imponens, curavit omnes: quos utique solo imperio sine contactu, quivit curare; sed singulis manus imposuit, ut dignationem suam, caritatem, et compassionem ad languidos et egenos ostenderet, item ad demonstrandum quod corpus suum divinæ potestatis instrumentum esset et organum, per quod Deus genus humanum in corpore et anima reformare decrevit. Quemadmodum autem Christus illos manum imponendo sanavit, ita et omnes qui per veram contritionem ad ipsum accedunt, vel saltem quod in ipsis est faciunt, spiritualiter curat, gratia et virtutibus firmat: quibus et manum, id est pietatis suæ opem, imponit, juxta illud de electo conscriptum in Psalmo: Quum ceciderit non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam.
paras.en: But since Christ's miracles were countless, as His power too was beyond compare, after the particular account of two signs many more are related in general. [[4:40|And when the sun was down, all they that had any sick with divers diseases brought them to him|Quum autem sol occidisset, omnes qui habebant infirmos variis languoribus, ducebant illos ad eum]]. So all in Capharnaum brought to Christ their kinsfolk, household, friends or dear ones, wasted with various infirmities, many of whom could not go by themselves, once those two miracles were known. So too Christians, above all prelates and fathers, ought to bring their sick, that is, those languishing in vices, to Christ, by leading them to repentance. [[4:40|But he, laying his hands on every one of them, healed them|At ille singulis infirmis manus imponens, curavit omnes]]: whom He could certainly have cured by command alone, without touching them; but He laid His hands on each to show His condescension, charity and compassion toward the sick and needy, and also to show that His body was the instrument and organ of the divine power, through which God had decreed to renew the human race in body and soul. And as Christ healed them by laying on His hand, so He spiritually cures all who come to Him through true contrition, or at least do what lies in them, and strengthens them with grace and the virtues: on whom He also lays His hand, that is, the help of His loving-kindness, according to what is written of the elect man in the Psalm: [[Ps 36:24|When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, for the Lord putteth his hand under him|Quum ceciderit non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam]].

paras.t: Quæritur, cur præfati adduxerunt infirmos suos de sero ad Christum, et non in die. Ad quod Origenes respondet, quod verecundabantur, vel Pharisæos timebant, vel quia putabant non licere sanare in sabbato, vel quia in die circa alia erant intenti.
paras.en: It is asked why those people brought their sick to Christ in the evening and not in the day. To which Origen answers: because they were ashamed, or feared the Pharisees; or because they thought it was not lawful to heal on the sabbath; or because in the day they were busy with other things.

paras.t: Exibant autem dæmonia a multis, clamantia. Ex quo apparet, quod multi de numero infirmorum illorum fuerunt obsessi, ex quibus ejecit dæmones, exeundo clamantes: Quia tu es Filius Dei. Circa quod asserit Gorra, quod et paulo ante jam affirmavi, quod dæmones noverant per Scripturas Dei Filium incarnandum, ideo eo modo noverant Jesum esse Dei Filium, quo noverant eum esse Christum. Et increpans ea: non quia falsum dixerant, sed quia verum mala intentione locuta sunt, et quia eorum confessio fuit extorta, ex servili procedens timore: quia metu gravioris supplicii ista dixerunt, sicut et servus iniquus ac fugitivus a domino deprehensus, metu verberum veritatem fatetur et dominum laudat; non sinebat ea loqui quia sciebant eum esse Christum, hoc est, non permisit dæmones amplius prosequi aut resumere verba prædicta, et quod scirent eum esse Messiam. Cur autem prohibuit dæmones sibi testimonium dare, jam dictum est; et addi nunc potest, quod etiam ideo ne sua passio impediretur. Si enim Judæi certitudinaliter atque stabiliter agnovissent eum esse Christum, nunquam eum crucifixissent, nec occidissent. Unde et Beda ait: Ipsi quoque Apostoli præcipiuntur a Christo reticere de ipso, ne divina majestate prædicata, passionis dispensatio differretur. Postremo, non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris, nec decuit purissima Christi mysteria fœdissimis dæmonum pandi linguis, ut Theophilus atque Chrysostomus protestantur. Quomodo autem sciebant Jesum esse Christum, præhabitum est, utpote scientia conjecturali, non certa et stabili.
paras.en: [[4:41|And devils went out from many, crying out|Exibant autem dæmonia a multis, clamantia]]. From which it appears that many of the number of those sick were possessed, from whom He cast out the devils, who cried as they went out: [[4:41|Thou art the son of God|Quia tu es Filius Dei]]. On which Gorra asserts, what I too affirmed a little before, that the devils knew from the Scriptures that the Son of God was to become incarnate, and so they knew that Jesus was the Son of God in the same way as they knew Him to be the Christ. [[4:41|And rebuking them|Et increpans ea]]: not because they had said what was false, but because they spoke the truth with an evil intention, and because their confession was forced out of them, coming from servile fear: for they said this from fear of a heavier punishment, as a wicked and runaway slave, caught by his master, confesses the truth and praises his master from fear of the lash; [[4:41|he suffered them not to speak|non sinebat ea loqui]] [[4:41|for they knew that he was Christ|quia sciebant eum esse Christum]], that is, He did not allow the devils to go on or to take up again the words they had spoken, and that they knew Him to be the Messias. Why He forbade the devils to bear Him witness has already been said; and it can now be added that it was also so that His passion should not be hindered. For if the Jews had known with certainty and firmly that He was the Christ, they would never have crucified or killed Him[[1 Cor 2:8||]]. Hence Bede too says: “The Apostles themselves are commanded by Christ to keep silent about Him, lest, if His divine majesty were preached, the dispensation of the passion should be put off.” Lastly, [[Ecclus 15:9|Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner|non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris]], nor was it fitting that the most pure mysteries of Christ should be laid open by the foulest tongues of devils, as Theophylact and Chrysostom declare. How they knew that Jesus was the Christ has been said before: namely by conjectural knowledge, not certain and firm.

paras.t: Facta autem die, id est die immediate sequenti de mane, egressus urbem Capharnaum ibat in desertum locum, scilicet in solitudinem: primo, ut doceret nos fugere laudem gloriamque humanam, tunc maxime quum aliquid magnificum egerimus, et magis a cunctis adspicimur et reputamur; secundo, ad instituendum, commendandum, ac confirmandum solitariæ ac eremiticæ vitæ secretum; tertio, ut doceret aliorum prælatos ac prædicatores, imo et omnes fideles, ut post occupationem externam, hominumque tumultum, ad secretum confugiant locum, ubi orando ac meditando, cor suum recolligant, ac Deo sincerius atque stabilius vacent. Et turbæ requirebant eum. Populares etenim Christo magis adhæserunt, quam primates Judæorum, ac Scribæ et Pharisæi, quorum vel pauci, vel nulli, eum secuti dicuntur hac vice. Et venerunt usque ad ipsum; et detinebant illum, ne discederet ab eis. Delectabantur enim in eloquentia, sapientia, virtutibus, ac miraculis ejus.
paras.en: [[4:42|And when it was day|Facta autem die]], that is, early in the morning of the day immediately following, [[4:42|going out he went into a desert place|egressus urbem Capharnaum ibat in desertum locum]], going out of the city of Capharnaum into a solitary place: first, to teach us to flee human praise and glory, above all when we have done something great and are the more looked at and esteemed by all; secondly, to institute, commend and confirm the retirement of the solitary and hermit life; thirdly, to teach the prelates and preachers of others, indeed all the faithful, that after outward work and the tumult of men they should take refuge in a secret place, where by praying and meditating they may gather their hearts again and give themselves to God more purely and steadily. [[4:42|and the multitudes sought him|Et turbæ requirebant eum]]. For the common people clung to Christ more than the chief men of the Jews, and the Scribes and Pharisees, few or none of whom are said to have followed Him on this occasion. [[4:42|and came unto him|Et venerunt usque ad ipsum]]; [[4:42|And they stayed him that should not depart from them|et detinebant illum, ne discederet ab eis]]. For they delighted in His eloquence, wisdom, virtues and miracles.

paras.t: Quibus ille ait: Quia et aliis civitatibus oportet, id est, expedit, hominumque saluti opportunum est, imo et ex suppositione oportuit, quia ita præordinavit Deus, me evangelizare regnum Dei, hoc est prædicare beatitudinem paradisi cælestis, et qualiter ad illud venitur. Regnum quoque Dei potest intelligi status Ecclesiæ militantis vel sacra Scriptura. Quia ideo missus sum a Patre æterno per incarnationis mysterium, item per jussionem qua Pater seu Trinitas tota Christo secundum naturam assumptam officium istud præcepit, quemadmodum in Joanne loquitur: Sicut mandatum, inquiens, dedit mihi Pater, sic facio. Ex quo patet, quam divinum ac præclarissimum sit prædicationis officium, quum Unigenitus Dei propter illud exercendum se perhibeat missum. Et iterum patet ex hoc, quam cæci damnabilesque consistant pastores sive prælati, qui ex superbia quadam, vel negligentia, seu alia insufficienti causa, illud omittunt, quum illud ad eos præsertim pertineat, et taliter vivere teneantur, ut sint ad prædicandum idonei. Aliqui quoque insufficientissime se excusant, ut quod sint malæ memoriæ: quibus salubrius esset et tutius, sermones in libro legere (quod et Gregorius Papa sæpe peregit) quam prædicationem omittere.
paras.en: [[4:43|To whom he said: To other cities also I must|Quibus ille ait: Quia et aliis civitatibus oportet]], that is, it is expedient and fitting for the salvation of men, indeed it was necessary on a supposition, because God had so preordained [that is, necessary not absolutely but given God's decree], [[4:43|preach the kingdom of God|evangelizare regnum Dei]], that is, preach the beatitude of the heavenly paradise and how one comes to it. The kingdom of God can also be understood as the state of the Church militant, or as sacred Scripture. [[4:43|for therefore am I sent|Quia ideo missus sum]] by the eternal Father through the mystery of the incarnation, and also by the command by which the Father, or the whole Trinity, laid this office on Christ according to the nature He assumed; as He says in John: [[John 14:31|as the Father hath given me commandments, so do I|Sicut mandatum, inquiens, dedit mihi Pater, sic facio]]. From this it is plain how divine and how glorious is the office of preaching, since the Only-begotten of God declares that He was sent to exercise it. And again it is plain from this how blind and damnable are those pastors or prelates who, out of a kind of pride, or negligence, or some other insufficient cause, leave it undone, since it belongs to them above all, and they are bound to live in such a way as to be fit for preaching. Some too excuse themselves most insufficiently, as by saying that they have a bad memory: for whom it would be more wholesome and safer to read sermons from a book (as Pope Gregory too often did) than to leave off preaching.

paras.t: Et erat prædicans in synagogis Galilææ. In synagogis equidem docuit, ubi populus amplius confluebat. Veritas enim non appetit angulum, sicut et Christus in Joanne protestatur: Omnis qui facit veritatem venit ad lucem, ut manifestentur opera ejus. Unde et tempore passionis dixit pontifici: Ego semper docui in synagogis, ubi omnes Judæi conveniunt; et in occulto locutus sum nihil.
paras.en: [[4:44|And he was preaching in the synagogues of Galilee|Et erat prædicans in synagogis Galilææ]]. He taught in the synagogues because there the people flocked together in greater numbers. For truth does not seek a corner, as Christ too declares in John: [[John 3:21|he that doth truth cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest|Omnis qui facit veritatem venit ad lucem, ut manifestentur opera ejus]]. Hence also at the time of His passion He said to the high priest: [[John 18:20|I have always taught in the synagogue|Ego semper docui in synagogis]], [[John 18:20|whither all the Jews resort|ubi omnes Judæi conveniunt]]; [[John 18:20|and in secret I have spoken nothing|et in occulto locutus sum nihil]].

5.title: Elucidatio capituli quinti: Factum est autem, quum turbæ irruerent in eum, ut audirent verbum Dei
5.title_en: Explanation of the fifth chapter: “And it came to pass, that when the multitudes pressed upon him to hear the word of God”

paras.t: Factum est autem, quum turbæ, de quibus in fine præcedentis capituli dictum est, irruerent, id est, cum magno fervore et copiose accederent, in eum, ut audirent verbum Dei, scilicet Christum, qui est verum et æternum Patris Verbum, ejus quoque sermonem. Desiderabant enim non solum eum adspicere et audire, sed etiam tangere, et posteriores impellebant priores, ita ut cum impetu quodam irruerent ad eum. Quis enim bonæ mentis non appeteret tam dulcem et pulchrum adspicere, tam sapientem et eloquentem audire, tam virtuosum et sanctum attingere, tot et tantorum mirabilium operatori adstare, præsertim quia gratiosissimum habebat delectabilissimumque adspectum? Imo in Revelationibus sacratissimæ Brigittæ credibiliter legitur dignissima virgo Maria loqui ad Brigittam, quod quicumque desolatus seu tristis vultum Filii sui adspexerat, mox relevamen consolatorium sensit, ita quod adversitatibus aut mœstitudine pressi, dicere consueverunt: Eamus ad Filium Mariæ, ut ex ejus consolemur adspectu. Nec mirum: ipse est enim de quo Psalmista prædixit, Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum. Denique multi Sanctorum tantæ leguntur sanctitatis et gratiæ exstitisse, quod quasi angelicum vultum habebant, resplendentibus in eorum facie mirabili serenitate atque fulgore: quanto magis hoc ita fuisse credendum in eo, in quo omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter inhabitavit, non solum per gratiam sicut in ceteris, sed et per hypostaticam unionem, cujus et anima Deo beatifice fruebatur, in quo tanta gratia erat quantam capere mens valet creata?
paras.en: [[5:1|And it came to pass, that when the multitudes|Factum est autem, quum turbæ]], of whom it was spoken at the end of the preceding chapter, [[5:1|pressed upon him|irruerent, id est, cum magno fervore et copiose accederent, in eum]], that is, came to Him with great fervour and in great numbers, [[5:1|to hear the word of God|ut audirent verbum Dei]], namely Christ, who is the true and eternal Word of the Father, and also His speech. For they desired not only to see and hear Him, but also to touch Him, and those behind pushed those in front, so that they pressed upon Him with a kind of rush. For who of good mind would not long to look on one so sweet and beautiful, to hear one so wise and eloquent, to touch one so virtuous and holy, to stand near the worker of so many and such great wonders, especially since He had a most gracious and most delightful countenance? Indeed, in the *Revelations* of the most holy Bridget we read, credibly, that the most worthy Virgin Mary told Bridget that whoever, desolate or sad, had looked upon the face of her Son at once felt consoling relief, so that those weighed down by adversities or sorrow used to say: “Let us go to the Son of Mary, that we may be consoled by the sight of Him.” Nor is it any wonder: for He is the one of whom the Psalmist foretold, [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]]. Further, many of the Saints are read to have been of such holiness and grace that they had almost an angelic face, a wonderful serenity and brightness shining in their faces: how much more must this be believed to have been so in Him in whom dwelt [[Col 2:9|all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally|omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter]], not only by grace as in the others, but also by hypostatic union, whose soul too was enjoying God in beatitude, in whom there was as much grace as a created mind can hold?

paras.t: Et ipse stabat juxta stagnum Genesareth: quod alio nomine dicitur mare Galilææ, a provincia in qua est; et mare Tiberiadis, a civitate Tiberiade sibi vicina. Et vidit duas naves stantes secus stagnum, videlicet prope littus lacus illius, ut moris est. Piscatores autem, videlicet Petrus et Joannes et Jacobus, ut infra habetur, et si qui forte eis associati fuerunt, descenderant, id est, ex navibus egrediendo, aquam circa littus intraverant, et lavabant, id est purgabant, retia sua, ut purgata plicarent, quia nil ceperant, et volebant ad tempus a piscatione cessare. Ascendens autem in unam navim, quæ erat Simonis, scilicet Petri, et fratris ejus Andreæ, ut aliqui dicunt: unde in Matthæo et Marco habetur quod Jesus invenit Petrum Andreamque simul piscationi intentos; rogavit eum a terra reducere pusillum, hoc est navim ad modicum spatium in aquam dirigere, ut esset separata et distans a ripa, non tantum quin Christus posset ex ea audiri convenienter a populo stante in littore. Ideo quoque navim intravit, quia turbæ cœperunt eum comprimere, et in terra cum eis stans, non poterat ab omnibus tam congruenter adspici et audiri sicut in navi stans, ubi et nemini dorsum vertit in faciem, atque in omnium stetit adspectu.
paras.en: [[5:1|he stood by the lake of Genesareth|Et ipse stabat juxta stagnum Genesareth]], which by another name is called the sea of Galilee, from the province in which it lies, and the sea of Tiberias, from the city of Tiberias near it[[John 6:1||]]. [[5:2|And saw two ships standing by the lake|Et vidit duas naves stantes secus stagnum]], that is, near the shore of that lake, as is the custom. [[5:2|but the fishermen|Piscatores autem]], namely Peter and John and James, as we have below, and any who were perhaps their companions, [[5:2|were gone out of them|descenderant]], that is, getting out of the ships, had gone into the water near the shore, [[5:2|and were washing|et lavabant]], that is, cleaning, [[5:2|their nets|retia]], so as to fold them up clean, since they had caught nothing and wished to stop fishing for a while. [[5:3|And going into one of the ships that was Simon's|Ascendens autem in unam navim, quæ erat Simonis]], that is, Peter's, and his brother Andrew's, as some say: hence in Matthew and Mark we have that Jesus found Peter and Andrew busy fishing together[[Matt 4:18||]][[Mark 1:16||]]; [[5:3|he desired him to draw back a little from the land|rogavit eum a terra reducere pusillum]], that is, to steer the ship a short distance into the water, so that it would be apart and away from the bank, yet not so far that Christ could not be heard from it fittingly by the people standing on the shore. He went into the ship also because the crowds began to press upon Him, and standing on land with them He could not be seen and heard by all as fittingly as standing in the ship, where He turned His back to no one's face and stood in sight of all.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod Lucas non servat hic ordinem rei gestæ describendo historiam, ita quod littera ista non continuatur ad litteram immediate præcedentem, in qua prædicta ibi signa narrantur: nam socrus Petri, quæ ibi sanata describitur, fuit curata post vocationem Petri et Andreæ ad Christi apostolatum, ut ex Matthæo et Marco monstratur. In illa autem vocatione Petrus navim omnino reliquit, nunc vero in isto capitulo post verba inducta recitatur vocatio Petri, Joannis, et Jacobi ad Christi apostolatum, ut aliqui dicunt, vel ad ejus familiaritatem, et quemdam discipulatum, ut alii potius arbitrantur. — Porro ex hoc ostenditur maxima Christi dignatio, mansuetudo et pietas, quod Petrum pro tam parva re, tam modeste humiliterque rogavit, cui præcipere habuit: docens prælatos, ut proniores sint ad monendum quam ad præcipiendum, magisque cupiant diligi quam timeri. Sed econtrario agunt stulti ad præcipiendum proclives, et gladium sine causa idonea extrahentes: quibus per Ezechielem Deus improperat, Cum austeritate imperabatis ovibus meis et cum potentia.
paras.en: Note besides that Luke does not keep here the order of events in describing the history, so that this text does not follow literally on the text immediately preceding, in which the signs mentioned there are narrated: for Peter's mother-in-law, who is described there as healed, was cured after the calling of Peter and Andrew to Christ's apostleship, as is shown from Matthew and Mark[[Matt 8:14||]][[Mark 1:16||]]. And in that calling Peter left his ship altogether, whereas now in this chapter, after the words cited, the calling of Peter, John and James is related: to Christ's apostleship, as some say, or to His familiar company and a kind of discipleship, as others rather think. — Further, this shows the very great condescension, gentleness and kindness of Christ, that for so small a thing He asked Peter so modestly and humbly, whom He had the right to command: teaching prelates to be readier to advise than to command, and to wish rather to be loved than feared. But fools do the opposite, quick to command and drawing the sword without fit cause: whom God reproaches through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 34:4|you ruled over them with rigour, and with a high hand|Cum austeritate imperabatis ovibus meis et cum potentia]] [Denis's text: “you ruled over my sheep”].

paras.t: Et sedens in navi, docebat de navicula turbas. Navim nunc vocat naviculam, quoniam parva erat, et navigium egenorum. Verba autem prædicationis Christi Evangelista non exprimit, sicut nec omnia ejus prodigia aliquis Evangelistarum in particulari prosequitur. Tanta vero de ejus documentis atque miraculis Evangelistæ scripserunt, quantum ad ædificationem Ecclesiæ, ad fidei confirmationem, ad salutem fidelium sufficere noverant, inspirante ac moderante Spiritu Sancto. Hinc est quod sæpe de observatione ordinis in historica recitatione gestorum signorumque Christi non curant, quia ad prædicta agenda, nil referat quid in re ipsa præcesserit, aut quid primo narretur.
paras.en: [[5:3|And sitting, he taught the multitudes out of the ship|Et sedens in navi, docebat de navicula turbas]]. He now calls the ship a little ship, because it was small, the boat of poor men. The Evangelist does not give the words of Christ's preaching, as none of the Evangelists follows out all His wonders in detail either. The Evangelists wrote as much of His teachings and miracles as they knew to be enough for the building up of the Church, the strengthening of faith and the salvation of the faithful, under the inspiration and guidance of the Holy Spirit. That is why they often do not take care to keep the order in their historical account of Christ's deeds and signs: because for the purposes just named it matters nothing what came first in the event itself, or what is narrated first.

paras.t: Ut autem cessavit loqui, volens pauperem naviculæ dominum præmiare pro obsequio jam narrato, dixit ad Simonem: Duc in altum, id est, navem remotius amove a littore ad profundiora aquæ loca: sicque altum, pro profundo accipitur, sicut in Joanne, Puteus altus est; atque in Psalmo, Veni in altitudinem maris. Vel ideo ait, In altum, quoniam aqua plus distans a littore altior est quam quæ ripæ propinquior est, ut in libro de Sphæra ostenditur. Et laxate retia vestra in capturam, id est, ad capiendos pisces ea explicate. Ait autem singulariter Petro, Duc, quia hoc ab eo solo fieri quivit; pluraliterque adjungit, Laxate, quia hoc a pluribus fieri aptius potuit. — Mystice autem, per Petrum perfectiores signantur, ad quos præcipue pertinet in altum ducere, id est profunda scrutari mysteria. Per adjutores Petri signantur inferiores prælati, ad quos retia spectat laxare, id est connexa ordinate verba ad aliorum conversionem extendere.
paras.en: [[5:4|Now when he had ceased to speak|Ut autem cessavit loqui]], wishing to reward the poor owner of the little ship for the service just related, [[5:4|he said to Simon|dixit ad Simonem]]: [[5:4|Launch out into the deep|Duc in altum]], that is, move the ship farther from the shore to deeper places of the water: and so *altum* is taken for “deep” [*altus* means both “high” and “deep”], as in John, [[John 4:11|the well is deep|Puteus altus est]]; and in the Psalm, [[Ps 68:3|I am come into the depth of the sea|Veni in altitudinem maris]]. Or He says *into the deep* [*in altum*, “into the high”] because water farther from the shore is higher than water nearer the bank, as is shown in the book *On the Sphere* [the medieval astronomical textbook of Sacrobosco, which teaches that the surface of the sea curves with the earth]. [[5:4|and let down your nets for a draught|Et laxate retia vestra in capturam]], that is, spread them out to catch fish. He says to Peter in the singular, *Launch*, because he alone could do this; and adds in the plural, *let down*, because this could more fittingly be done by several. — Mystically, by Peter are signified the more perfect, to whom it belongs especially to launch into the deep, that is, to search out deep mysteries. By Peter's helpers are signified the lower prelates, to whom it belongs to let down the nets, that is, to spread out words joined in due order for the conversion of others.

paras.t: Et respondens Simon, dixit illi: Præceptor, id est tu, o Domine, qui tantæ es auctoritatis ut merito appelleris Præceptor, cui et protinus est parendum, per totam noctem laborantes ad pisces capiendos, nihil, id est nullum piscem, cepimus. Quod quamvis naturaliter accidere potuerat, sicut et sæpe fit, divina tamen tunc dispensatione sic evenisse apparet, ut Christi potestas per sequens miraculum clarius emicaret, et alii magis confirmarentur ad fidem. In verbo autem tuo, id est propter tuum præceptum; vel, In verbo tuo, id est ex spe adimpletionis jussionis tuæ; laxabo rete cum adjutoribus meis similiter agentibus. In quo promptitudo obedientiæ S. Petri probatur, præsertim quia secundum naturam videbatur infructuosum retia laxare, quum non appareret spes naturaliter capiendi pisces.
paras.en: [[5:5|And Simon answering said to him: Master|Et respondens Simon, dixit illi: Præceptor]], that is, you, O Lord, who are of such authority that you are rightly called Master [*Præceptor*, literally “one who commands”], and must be obeyed at once, [[5:5|we have laboured all the night|per totam noctem laborantes]] to catch fish, [[5:5|and have taken nothing|nihil]], that is, no fish. Though this could have happened naturally, as it often does, yet it appears to have turned out so then by divine dispensation, so that Christ's power might shine out more clearly through the miracle that followed, and the others might be more strengthened in faith. [[5:5|but at thy word|In verbo autem tuo]], that is, because of your command; or, *at thy word*, that is, in the hope of carrying out your bidding; [[5:5|I will let down the net|laxabo rete]], with my helpers doing the same. In this the readiness of St Peter's obedience is proved, especially since according to nature it seemed fruitless to let down the nets, there being no apparent hope of catching fish naturally.

paras.t: Et quum hoc fecissent, concluserunt Simon et socii ejus, piscium multitudinem copiosam. In quo docemur, quam fructuosum sit obedire. Quemadmodum etiam Petrus laxavit rete ad piscandum, Christo jubente, non obstante quod ante in tanto conatu ac tempore nil cepisset; sic prælati, doctores et prædicatores, juxta sacræ Scripturæ præceptum seu exhortationem laxare debent spirituale rete, hoc est coordinatas documentorum propositiones ad aliorum instructionem, profectum, seu conversionem proponere, cum fiducia gratiæ atque auxilii Dei; sicque sæpe Deo agente multos convertent, in quibus ante nil profecerunt. Rumpebatur autem rete eorum, hoc est, partim rumpi cœpit. Non tamen aliquis excidit piscis: quod etiam miraculum fuit.
paras.en: [[5:6|And when they had done this, they enclosed|Et quum hoc fecissent, concluserunt]], Simon and his companions, [[5:6|a very great multitude of fishes|piscium multitudinem copiosam]]. In this we are taught how fruitful it is to obey. And as Peter let down the net to fish at Christ's bidding, although before, with so much effort and time, he had caught nothing; so prelates, teachers and preachers, according to the precept or exhortation of sacred Scripture, ought to let down the spiritual net, that is, to set forth well-ordered statements of teaching for the instruction, progress or conversion of others, trusting in the grace and help of God; and so, God working, they will often convert many in whom before they had made no progress. [[5:6|and their net broke|Rumpebatur autem rete eorum]], that is, began to break in part. Yet not a single fish fell out: which was also a miracle.

paras.t: Et annuerunt sociis qui erant in alia navi, videlicet Jacobo et Joanni, ut venirent ad eos navigio, et adjuvarent eos. Annuerunt autem, id est, nutu vel signo, non verbis, insinuaverunt eis ut subvenirent, quia præ admirationis magnitudine loqui vix poterant, et præ Jesu reverentia vix loqui audebant. Sic et spirituales pastores, videlicet prælati et prædicatores, quum se viderint omnes ad portum securitatis ac finem beatum non posse perducere, quos de hoc sæculo nequam velut ex procellosissimo mari jam aliqualiter abstraxerunt, atque ad pœnitentiam induxerunt, alios viros idoneos debent in adjutores quærere, invitare, assumere, ut conversos et pœnitentes custodiant, inflamment, perficiant. Sed quidam præsumptuosi et superbi sunt nimis, atque de propriis viribus et virtutibus fatue confidentes, aliorum auxilium sibi necessarium non arbitrantes, quum tamen se ipsos regere insufficientes probentur.
paras.en: [[5:7|And they beckoned to their partners that were in the other ship|Et annuerunt sociis qui erant in alia navi]], namely James and John, [[5:7|that they should come|ut venirent]] to them by boat [[5:7|and help them|et adjuvarent eos]]. They beckoned, that is, by a nod or sign, not by words, they made known to them that they should come to their aid: because for the greatness of their wonder they could scarcely speak, and for reverence of Jesus they scarcely dared to speak. So too spiritual pastors, namely prelates and preachers, when they see that they cannot bring to the harbour of safety and the blessed end all those whom they have already in some measure drawn out of this wicked world as out of a most stormy sea and led to repentance, ought to seek, invite and take on other fit men as helpers, to guard, inflame and perfect the converted and penitent. But some are too presumptuous and proud, foolishly trusting in their own strength and virtues, and thinking they need no help from others, though they are proved unable to rule even themselves.

paras.t: Et venerunt socii illi, et impleverunt, non illi soli, sed simul cum Petro ac suis, ambas naviculas, ita ut pene mergerentur. Quo patet, quod valde onerosa et copiosa piscium multitudo simul exstitit capta. Sic pluribus verbum Dei concorditer prædicantibus, et juxta propria verba viventibus, plurimi convertuntur. Propter quod Salomon ait: Frater qui adjuvatur a fratre, quasi civitas munita. Porro, naviculæ sunt particulares Ecclesiæ, quæ plurimis conversis pene merguntur, dum in ipsis recenter conversis manent quædam priorum vitiorum reliquiæ et pronitates ad malum ac passiones: in quibus et alii sæpe periclitantur, qui nondum ita perfecti sunt ut illorum imbecillitates æquanimiter valeant tolerare.
paras.en: [[5:7|And they came|Et venerunt]], those partners, [[5:7|and filled|et impleverunt]], not they alone, but together with Peter and his men, [[5:7|both the ships, so that they were almost sinking|ambas naviculas, ita ut pene mergerentur]]. From which it is plain that a very heavy and great multitude of fishes was caught at once. So when several preach the word of God in concord, and live according to their own words, very many are converted. That is why Solomon says: [[Prov 18:19|A brother that is helped by his brother, is like a strong city|Frater qui adjuvatur a fratre, quasi civitas munita]]. Further, the little ships are the particular Churches, which almost sink when very many are converted, as long as there remain in the newly converted some remnants of their former vices, and leanings to evil, and passions: in which others too are often endangered, who are not yet so perfect that they can bear their weaknesses with equanimity.

paras.t: Quod quum videret Simon Petrus, procidit ad genua Jesu, dicens. Honor enim virtuoso debetur: ideo sicut censuit Jesum esse maximæ virtutis ac sanctitatis, sic exhibuit ei reverentiam grandem. Nam et ante istud miraculum credidit Jesum esse Christum, quando videlicet Andreas dixit ad eum, Invenimus Messiam qui dicitur Christus, adduxitque eum ad Jesum, ut in Joanne habetur: unde et viso isto miraculo, aucta fuit in eo hæc fides. Exi a me, quia homo peccator sum, Domine, id est, tibi adsistere, adesse, cohabitare, indignus sum, quia homo fragilis ac peccator, ac servus inutilis, tu autem tam potens, tam sanctus, ac Dominus. Itaque ex magnitudine miraculosi effectus, majestatem causæ pensavit; et quia opposita juxta se posita clarius innotescunt, quo Petrus Christi virtutem excellentiamque magis attendit, eo propriam culpam ac parvitatem evidentius intellexit, atque humilius fassus est. Hinc Christum a se exire rogavit, non eum indignanter repellens, sed ex profundissima humilitate honorans; nec tamen spiritualem ejus præsentiam seu gratiæ opem a se abesse optavit. Unde in isto similis fuit centurioni dicenti: Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum; sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur puer meus. De hac quoque spirituali præsentia semper optanda ait Gregorius: Si te peccatorem consideras, necesse est ut a te Dominum non repellas.
paras.en: [[5:8|Which when Simon Peter saw, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying|Quod quum videret Simon Petrus, procidit ad genua Jesu, dicens]]. For honour is owed to the virtuous: so, as he judged Jesus to be of the greatest virtue and holiness, he showed Him great reverence. For even before this miracle he believed Jesus to be the Christ, namely when Andrew said to him, [[John 1:41|We have found the Messias|Invenimus Messiam]], who is called Christ, and brought him to Jesus[[John 1:42||]], as we have in John: and so, when he saw this miracle, this faith was increased in him. [[5:8|Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord|Exi a me, quia homo peccator sum, Domine]], that is, I am unworthy to stand by you, to be near you, to dwell with you, because I am a frail and sinful man and an unprofitable servant, while you are so mighty, so holy, and the Lord. So from the greatness of the miraculous effect he weighed the majesty of the cause; and since opposites placed side by side are more clearly known, the more Peter considered Christ's power and excellence, the more plainly he understood his own guilt and littleness, and the more humbly he confessed it. Hence he asked Christ to go away from him, not rejecting Him with displeasure, but honouring Him out of the deepest humility; yet he did not wish His spiritual presence, that is, the help of His grace, to be away from him. So in this he was like the centurion who said: [[Matt 8:8|Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed|Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum; sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur puer meus]]. Of this spiritual presence, always to be desired, Gregory too says: “If you consider yourself a sinner, you must not drive the Lord away from you.”

paras.t: At vero, sicut Petrus viso hoc signo, nihil meritis suis adscripsit, neque inaniter gloriatus est, sed totum se humiliavit, et Christo grates rependit, ejusque præsentia se fatebatur indignum; ita dum prælatus, aut prædicator, seu exhortator, multos aut quosdam converterit, totum divinæ pietati attribuat, et gratias agens nullatenus extollatur, imo se indignissimum arbitretur ut per eum Spiritus Sanctus talia operetur, et Domino se prosternat. Ex hoc quoque ostenditur magnitudo devotionis fervorisque Petri, quod ipse solus ad genua Jesu prolapsus sit, quum tamen aliis senior esset.
paras.en: But as Peter, seeing this sign, ascribed nothing to his own merits and did not glory vainly, but humbled himself wholly, gave thanks to Christ, and confessed himself unworthy of His presence; so when a prelate, preacher or exhorter has converted many or some, let him ascribe it all to the divine goodness, and giving thanks let him in no way be puffed up, but rather think himself most unworthy that the Holy Spirit should work such things through him, and prostrate himself before the Lord. This also shows the greatness of Peter's devotion and fervour, that he alone fell down at Jesus' knees, though he was older than the others.

paras.t: Stupor enim circumdederat eum, et omnes qui cum illo erant, in captura piscium quam ceperant, hoc est, vehemens admiratio ex omni parte atque totaliter occupavit corda istorum, ex consideratione tanti prodigii: cujus admirabilitatem tanto certius noverant, quo in arte piscatoria exercitatiores fuerunt. Unde et Christus eorum infirmitati condescendens, per tale miraculum voluit eos allicere, quod ad eorum officium magis spectabat quantum ad actus materiam: sicut et Magos astronomiæ intentos, per stellam apparentem adduxit. Denique tam repentina piscium tot innumerabilium captio, fuit prorsus mirabilis. Quæri quoque potest, quomodo tot pisces ibi adunati exstiterint. Ad quod facile respondetur, quod Christus divina sua potestate pisces subito et de novo creare, seu ex diversis locis colligere potuit, quos item angelico ministerio potuit illico adunare. Similiter autem Jacobum et Joannem, filios Zebedæi, qui erant socii Simonis in piscando, circumdedit stupor: non tamen corruerunt ad genua Jesu, quamvis ipsius essent cognati. Sic quoque omnem rite pensantem merito admirationis stupor adimplet, dum ab ipsis Christi Apostolis, viris idiotis atque simplicibus, considerat totum quodammodo mundum tam cito conversum ad tam arduam legem, tamque incomprehensibilem fidem, quod omni pene miraculo majus reputatur miraculum: in quo et facta olim miracula, quasi in suo relucent effectu. Unde nec opus est ea frequentius iterari, quamvis Deus ex sua superimmensa clementia multoties iteraverit ea, ad excitandam hominum tarditatem, qui præterita non advertunt, nec inchoationem et processum Ecclesiæ subtiliter intuentur, atque ad confutandam hæreticorum infideliumque aliorum insaniam.
paras.en: [[5:9|For he was wholly astonished, and all that were with him, at the draught of the fishes which they had taken.|Stupor enim circumdederat eum, et omnes qui cum illo erant, in captura piscium quam ceperant]], that is, a vehement wonder seized the hearts of these men from every side and wholly, from considering so great a prodigy: whose wonderfulness they knew the more surely, the more practised they were in the fisherman's craft. Hence Christ, condescending to their weakness, wished to draw them by such a miracle as belonged more to their own trade as to the matter of the act: as He also drew the Magi, who were given to astronomy, by a star that appeared[[Matt 2:2||]]. Further, so sudden a catch of so countless a number of fishes was altogether wonderful. It may also be asked how so many fishes came to be gathered there. To which the easy answer is that Christ by His divine power could create fishes suddenly and anew, or gather them from various places, and could likewise bring them together at once by the ministry of angels. [[5:10|And so were also James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were Simon's partners|Similiter autem Jacobum et Joannem, filios Zebedæi, qui erant socii Simonis]] in fishing: wonder seized them, yet they did not fall down at Jesus' knees, though they were His kinsmen. So too wonder rightly fills everyone who weighs the matter duly, when he considers that by Christ's Apostles themselves, unlettered and simple men, the whole world, so to speak, was so quickly converted to so hard a law and so incomprehensible a faith: which is reckoned a miracle greater than almost any miracle; in which the miracles done of old also shine out, as in their effect. Hence there is no need for them to be repeated often, though God in His more than boundless clemency has repeated them many times, to rouse the sluggishness of men, who do not notice the past nor look closely at the beginning and progress of the Church, and to confute the madness of heretics and other unbelievers.

paras.t: Et ait ad Simonem Jesus: qui sicut se Christo singulariter humiliavit, sic meruit singulariter consolari ab eo. Cor enim contritum et humiliatum Deus non despicit, sed exhilarat, et confortat. Noli timere, immoderato timore, ex consideratione tuæ parvitatis et culpæ, ex contemplatione quoque signi hujus et excellentiæ meæ, ut ideo petas me exire a te; sed in consideratione pietatis et gratiæ meæ respira et gaude. Hoc etiam omnibus nobis implendum est. Ex hoc enim, id est cito post tempus istud; vel, Ex hoc, id est post istud piscationis officium; rursus, Ex hoc, id est hujus tuæ obedientiæ ac reverentiæ mihi exhibitæ, stuporis humilitatisque merito: homines eris capiens, id est, prædicator et apostolus efficieris, ita quod exemplo, sermone, miraculis, orationibus, multos convertes, et intra Ecclesiam colliges, sicut intra sagenam colliguntur detinenturque pisces. Nam et ipsa Ecclesia comparatur sagenæ, Christo dicente: Simile est regnum cælorum sagenæ missæ in mare, et ex omni genere piscium congreganti. Retia autem Apostolorum et prædicatorum, fuerunt instrumenta ac media quibus homines converterunt, videlicet exemplaris vita, miracula, prædicationes et preces. Juxta hanc similitudinem Dominus in Jeremia loquitur: Ecce ego mittam piscatores multos, et piscabuntur eos.
paras.en: [[5:10|And Jesus saith to Simon|Et ait ad Simonem Jesus]]: who, as he had humbled himself before Christ in a singular way, so deserved to be consoled by Him in a singular way. For God does not despise [[Ps 50:19|a contrite and humbled heart|contritum et humiliatum]], but gladdens and strengthens it. [[5:10|Fear not|Noli timere]] with immoderate fear, from considering your littleness and guilt, and from contemplating this sign and my excellence, so as to ask me for that reason to go away from you; but in considering my kindness and grace, breathe again and rejoice. This we must all carry out too. [[5:10|from henceforth|Ex hoc]], that is, soon after this time; or, *from this*, that is, after this work of fishing; or again, *from this*, that is, by the merit of this obedience and reverence you have shown me, of your wonder and humility: [[5:10|thou shalt catch men|homines eris capiens]], that is, you will be made a preacher and apostle, so that by example, word, miracles and prayers you will convert many and gather them into the Church, as fishes are gathered and held in a net. For the Church itself is compared to a net, as Christ says: [[Matt 13:47|the kingdom of heaven is like to a net cast into the sea, and gathering together of all kinds of fishes|Simile est regnum cælorum sagenæ missæ in mare, et ex omni genere piscium congreganti]]. And the nets of the Apostles and preachers were the instruments and means by which they converted men, namely an exemplary life, miracles, preaching and prayers. According to this likeness the Lord speaks in Jeremias: [[Jer 16:16|Behold I will send many fishers|Ecce ego mittam piscatores multos]], [[Jer 16:16|and they shall fish them|et piscabuntur eos]].

paras.t: Et subductis ad terram navibus suis duabus prædictis, relictis omnibus, quæ ibi habebant, videlicet navibus et navium instrumentis, captisque piscibus; vel, Relictis omnibus hominibus qui ibi tunc aderant; secuti sunt eum. Corporaliter enim comitati sunt Christum, et mente devota ei adhæserunt.
paras.en: [[5:11|And having brought their ships to land|Et subductis ad terram navibus]], their two ships already mentioned, [[5:11|leaving all things|relictis omnibus]] that they had there, namely the ships, the ships' tackle, and the fish they had caught; or, leaving all the people who were then present there; [[5:11|they followed him|secuti sunt eum]]. For they went with Christ in body, and cleaved to Him with devout mind.

paras.t: Sed si soli Petro dictum est, Eris homines capiens, cur Joannes quoque et Jacobus secuti sunt Christum? Insuper, hoc loco non scribitur quod Christus vocaverit eos ad sequendum se. Itaque advertendum quod triplex fuit discipulorum istorum vocatio: una et prima, ad solam Christi notitiam, quæ per Joannem describitur; secunda fuit ad Christi familiaritatem; tertia, ad apostolatum, quæ per Matthæum et Marcum refertur. De secunda autem jam mentio facta est. Aliqui tamen dicunt, quod ista de qua nunc Lucas scribit, sit eadem cum illa quam Matthæus et Marcus enarrant. Sed Glossa aperte hic contradicit: Nondum (inquit) Petrus ad apostolatum eligitur, sed ei prædicitur quod aliquando sit eligendus. Et istud verius reor, quia ut dixi, hoc loco non legitur Christus alicui discipulorum istorum dixisse ut se sequeretur. Præterea in Matthæo et Marco habetur, quod primo invenit Petrum et Andream, quibus et dixit: Venite post me. Deinde progressus pusillum, invenit Jacobum et Joannem cum patre eorum in navi, vocavitque eos. Hic vero habetur, quod Joanne et Jacobo ingressis ad Petri navigium, locutus sit Petro hæc verba, et tunc pariter iverunt cum Christo; sed et infra loquitur Lucas de illius vocatione, de qua Matthæus et Marcus. Unde, quod hoc loco dicitur, Omnibus relictis Christum secuti sunt, intelligendum est, quod ex reverentia Christi ad spatium iverunt cum eo: nam et ideo, secundum quosdam, naves reduxerunt ad terram, quoniam ad eas intendebant reverti. Porro Augustinus in libro de Consensu Evangelistarum, tangit utrumque modum dicendi, nullum determinans.
paras.en: But if it was said to Peter alone, *thou shalt catch men*, why did John and James also follow Christ? Moreover, it is not written at this place that Christ called them to follow Him. So it must be noted that the calling of these disciples was threefold: one, the first, to the mere knowledge of Christ, which is described by John[[John 1:37||]]; the second was to Christ's familiar company; the third, to the apostleship, which is related by Matthew[[Matt 4:18||]] and Mark[[Mark 1:16||]]. Of the second mention has now been made. Some, however, say that the calling of which Luke now writes is the same as that which Matthew and Mark relate. But the Gloss here openly contradicts this: “Peter (it says) is not yet chosen for the apostleship, but it is foretold to him that he will one day be chosen.” And I think this truer, because, as I said, we do not read at this place that Christ told any of these disciples to follow Him. Besides, in Matthew and Mark we have that He first found Peter and Andrew, to whom He also said: [[Mark 1:17|Come after me|Venite post me]]. Then, going on a little, He found James and John with their father in the ship, and called them. But here we have that when John and James had come to Peter's boat, He spoke these words to Peter, and then they went together with Christ; and Luke speaks below of that calling of which Matthew and Mark speak. Hence what is said at this place, *leaving all things they followed Christ*, is to be understood to mean that out of reverence for Christ they went with Him for a while: and that is why, according to some, they brought the ships back to land, because they meant to return to them. Augustine, in the book *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, touches on both ways of putting it, deciding for neither.

paras.t: Sciendum quoque, quod in Joanne aliquid huic miraculo simile scriptum est, quomodo scilicet discipuli isti post Christi resurrectionem uno impetu concluserunt centum quinquaginta tres magnos pisces; et ibi pro miraculo additur, quod quum tanti essent, non est scissum rete. Hic vero, ad insinuandum aliud miraculum, fertur quod rete rumpebatur, et naviculæ pene demergebantur, quum tamen pisces non elaberentur. Unde per piscationem de qua ait Joannes, signatur collectio electorum intra triumphantem Ecclesiam, in qua nulla scissura est, nullumque periculum; per istam vero, collectio credentium intra Ecclesiam militantem, in qua boni malis miscentur, atque diversa occurrunt pericula, hæreses et schismata.
paras.en: It is to be known also that in John something like this miracle is written: how these disciples, after Christ's resurrection, enclosed at one cast a hundred and fifty-three great fishes; and there it is added as a miracle that, though they were so many, the net was not broken[[John 21:11||]]. But here, to intimate another miracle, it is said that the net was breaking and the little ships were almost sinking, and yet the fishes did not slip away. Hence by the fishing of which John speaks is signified the gathering of the elect into the Church triumphant, in which there is no rending and no danger; but by this one, the gathering of believers into the Church militant, in which the good are mixed with the wicked, and various dangers occur, heresies and schisms.

paras.t: Deinceps narratur leprosi curatio. Et factum est, quum esset in una civitatum, videlicet in Capharnaum, et ecce vir plenus lepra, id est multum leprosus, ita quod lepra toto corpore fuit diffusa ac patens, et videns Jesum oculis exterioribus, et internis, quia majestatem et sanctitatem ejus credidit ac pensavit oculo mentis, qui est intellectus seu ratio: de cujus visu loquitur Christus Philippo, Qui videt me, videt et Patrem; et alibi, Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt; et procidens in faciem, id est, solo tenus se prosternens, tam propter Christi dignitatem, quam propter curationis affectum ferventem, magnamque suam indigentiam, sperans se tanto celerius exaudiendum atque curandum, quo humilius sinceriusque rogaret; rogavit eum, dicens. Apud Matthæum habetur, quod adoravit eum: quod Athanasius de adoratione latriæ exponit, dicendo quod leprosus credidit Jesum esse Unigenitum Dei, non creaturam, sed Deum verum. Secundum Ambrosium vero, quod in faciem corruit, humilitatis exstitit ac pudoris. Domine, si vis, potes me mundare, id est, de potestate tua non dubito quin curare me possis, si velis. Nec exprimit clarius quid affectet, quia ex sua prostratione satis innotuit, et quoniam coram Christo plura loqui in conspectu turbæ erubuit. Rursus, quoniam corporalis infirmitas saluti animæ non repugnat, quemadmodum culpa, imo frequenter salubris est: ideo ejus medela non est multum importune et absolute quærenda; sed beneplacito dispositionis divinæ totum est committendum, cum humili propriæ affectionis interpretatione, ut sic curari quæramus, dummodo sit ad Dei honorem et nostram salutem, et quidquid fecerit Deus, complaceat nobis.
paras.en: Next the healing of a leper is narrated. [[5:12|And it came to pass, when he was in a certain city|Et factum est, quum esset in una civitatum]], namely in Capharnaum, [[5:12|behold a man full of leprosy|et ecce vir plenus lepra]], that is, very leprous, so that the leprosy was spread and showing over his whole body, [[5:12|who, seeing Jesus|et videns Jesum]] with his outward eyes, and with the inward ones too, because he believed and weighed His majesty and holiness with the eye of the mind, which is the understanding or reason: of which sight Christ speaks to Philip, [[John 14:9|he that seeth me seeth the Father also|Qui videt me, videt et Patrem]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart: they shall see God|Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt]]; [[5:12|and falling on his face|et procidens in faciem]], that is, throwing himself down to the ground, both because of Christ's dignity and because of his fervent desire to be cured and his great need, hoping to be heard and cured the more quickly, the more humbly and sincerely he asked; [[5:12|besought him saying|rogavit eum, dicens]]. In Matthew we have that he adored Him[[Matt 8:2||]]: which Athanasius explains of the adoration of latria [the worship due to God alone], saying that the leper believed Jesus to be the Only-begotten of God, not a creature but true God. According to Ambrose, however, his falling on his face was a sign of humility and shame. [[5:12|Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean|Domine, si vis, potes me mundare]], that is, I do not doubt your power, that you can cure me if you will. He does not say more plainly what he wants, because it was clear enough from his prostration, and because he was ashamed to say more before Christ in sight of the crowd. Again, since bodily sickness is not opposed to the soul's salvation, as sin is, but is often wholesome: its cure is not to be sought very importunately and absolutely; but all is to be committed to the good pleasure of the divine disposition, with a humble declaration of our own desire, so that we ask to be cured on condition that it be for God's honour and our salvation, and that whatever God does may please us.

paras.t: Et extendens Jesus manum, tetigit eum dicens. Sicut enim pro nostra salute corpus assumpsit, ita per illud nostram est salutem operatus. Unde quem sine attactu curare potuit, tetigit: primo, ad suæ pietatis, humilitatis, ac dignationis magnitudinem ostendendam, quia hominem solo adspectu horrendum non abhorruit tangere; secundo, ad nostram instructionem, videlicet ne corporaliter languidos et deformes spernamus, imo si opus est, foveamus, portemus, tangamus, cum omni compassionis affectu; tertio, ut per corporalem contactum, spiritualem designaret attactum, videlicet quod illi vere ab omni culpa mundantur, quos ipse per dona et gratiam suæ caritatis tangit ac visitat; quarto, ut se verum assumpsisse corpus ostenderet, ad confutationem perfidiæ impurissimi Manichæi. Volo. Et quod subditur, passive legendum est, scilicet, Mundare, hoc est, præcipio ut a lepra munderis. Denique Christus voluit, jussit et fecit hoc signum divina et increata voluntate ac potestate, tanquam per causam simpliciter primam, principalem et auctoritativam. Voluntate quoque humana ac potestate creata et supernaturali voluit, jussit et fecit hoc tanquam per causam secundariam, instrumentalem et subauctoritativam, seu minus principalem: cui conveniebat præcipiendo operari miracula, non eo modo ut voluntati ac potestati divinæ, imo quoad illam fuit instrumentalis; sed quia omnis creatura fuit subjecta etiam voluntati ac potestati Christi creatæ, et quia Deus per illam taliter instituit operari. Unde et aliqui Sancti leguntur quasi jubendo fecisse miracula, non quod sua, sed divina hoc agebant virtute.
paras.en: [[5:13|And stretching forth his hand, he touched him, saying|Et extendens Jesus manum, tetigit eum dicens]]. For as He took a body for our salvation, so through it He worked our salvation. Hence He touched the man whom He could have cured without touching: first, to show the greatness of His kindness, humility and condescension, since He did not shrink from touching a man horrible merely to look at; secondly, for our instruction, namely that we should not despise those who are sick and disfigured in body, but rather, if need be, cherish them, carry them and touch them with every feeling of compassion; thirdly, to signify by bodily touch a spiritual touch, namely that those are truly cleansed from all guilt whom He touches and visits by the gifts and grace of His charity; fourthly, to show that He had taken a true body, to confute the faithlessness of the most impure Manichæus [Mani, whose followers held that Christ's body was not real]. [[5:13|I will|Volo]]. And what follows is to be read as passive, namely [[5:13|Be thou cleansed|Mundare]], that is, I command that you be cleansed of leprosy. Further, Christ willed, commanded and did this sign by the divine and uncreated will and power, as by a cause simply first, principal and with authority. And by His human will and created and supernatural power He willed, commanded and did it as by a secondary, instrumental and subordinate cause, that is, a less principal one: to which it belonged to work miracles by commanding, not in the same way as to the divine will and power, for with respect to that it was instrumental; but because every creature was subject also to the created will and power of Christ, and because God ordained to work in such a way through it. Hence some Saints too are read to have worked miracles as if by commanding, not by their own power, but doing it by divine power.

paras.t: Et confestim lepra discessit ab illo, id est, in momento seu instantanee periit et cessavit. Divinæ etenim potestati, quum sit infinita, competit agere in instanti, quum placet; et dicere Christi efficax fuit. Augustino quoque testante, idem est rem fieri Deo volente et agente.
paras.en: [[5:13|And immediately the leprosy departed from him|Et confestim lepra discessit ab illo]], that is, in a moment, instantly, it perished and ceased. For to divine power, since it is infinite, it belongs to act in an instant when it pleases; and Christ's saying was effective. As Augustine also testifies, for God to will and act is the same as for the thing to be done.

paras.t: Quæritur, quomodo dicat Lucas factum hoc signum in urbe, quum Matthæus scribat, quemadmodum Christo descendente de monte, leprosus iste ipsum accesserit, sitque sanatus, et postea legitur Christus ibi introisse Capharnaum. Ad quod aliqui dicunt, quod leprosus iste cœpit in via accedere, ut refert Matthæus, sed in urbe curatus est. Matthæus tamen propter compendium, prosequitur ejus curationem antequam Christi ingressum in Capharnaum narret. Non enim Evangelistæ in omnibus semper ordinem loci ac temporis determinate observant, recitando quæ gesta sunt, sed quod principale est promunt, et id de quo vis non est, determinare non curant.
paras.en: It is asked how Luke says this sign was done in a city, when Matthew writes how this leper came to Christ as He came down from the mountain and was healed, and afterwards we read that Christ then went into Capharnaum[[Matt 8:1||]][[Matt 8:5||]]. To this some say that this leper began to approach on the way, as Matthew relates, but was cured in the city. Matthew, however, for brevity follows out his healing before he narrates Christ's entry into Capharnaum. For the Evangelists do not always keep definitely to the order of place and time in everything when relating what was done, but bring out what is principal, and do not take care to settle that which is of no importance.

paras.t: Et præcepit illi ut nemini diceret. Non absolute prohibuit leproso beneficium sibi impensum manifestare ac dicere: nam subditur, Sed vade, ostende te sacerdoti. Voluit ergo ut primo sacerdoti se præsentaret, ne si sacerdotes ante illius adventum perciperent eum a Jesu curatum, ex invidia recusarent eum tanquam curatum admittere, ut dicit Chrysostomus; item, ut doceret Salvator vanam laudem esse vitandam, nec ea jactemus quæ tamen aliunde satis apparent, quemadmodum istud factum se ipsum declaravit, et coram multis fuerat factum. Sed vade, ostende te sacerdoti, et offer, Deo gratias referendo, pro emundatione tua, tibi exhibita, sicut præcepit Moyses in testimonium illis, id est, quemadmodum Moyses jussit curatis a lepra, ut sacerdotibus se præsentarent in testimonium illis, hoc est, quatenus sacerdotes testarentur ac judicarent illos vere esse mundatos, et posse inter homines conversari. Jussit equidem Deus per Moysen ut curatus a lepra, tortam panis duosque turtures, olei quoque sextarium Deo offerret, juxta ritum ibidem descriptum.
paras.en: [[5:14|And he charged him that he should tell no man|Et præcepit illi ut nemini diceret]]. He did not absolutely forbid the leper to make known and tell of the benefit done him: for it is added, [[5:14|but: Go, shew thyself to the priest|Sed vade, ostende te sacerdoti]]. So He wished him first to present himself to the priest, lest, if the priests learned before his coming that he had been cured by Jesus, they should out of envy refuse to admit him as cured, as Chrysostom says; and also so that the Saviour might teach that vain praise is to be avoided, and that we should not boast of things which are plain enough in other ways, as this deed declared itself and had been done before many. *But go, shew thyself to the priest*, [[5:14|and offer|et offer]], giving thanks to God, [[5:14|for thy cleansing|pro emundatione tua]] granted you, [[5:14|according as Moses commanded|sicut præcepit Moyses]], [[5:14|for a testimony to them|in testimonium illis]], that is, as Moses ordered those cured of leprosy to present themselves to the priests for a testimony to them, that is, so that the priests might testify and judge that they were truly cleansed and could live among men. For God commanded through Moses that one cured of leprosy should offer to God a cake of bread and two turtledoves, and also a sextary of oil, according to the rite described there[[Lev 14:2||]].

paras.t: Denique Christus tanquam novæ et evangelicæ legislator ac veteris legis perfector et consummator, sæpe legem dignanter implevit, ostendens legem sanctam atque divinam fuisse; sæpenumero eam ad litteram non servat, sed auctoritative transcendit. Unde et leprosum hunc tetigit, quum tamen in Levitico tangere leprosum esset prohibitum: quamvis illud præceptum daretur secundum communem statum ac cursum hominum, obligaretque eos qui a leprosis poterant maculari magis quam eos mundare, nec obligaret eos qui ex singulari gratiæ dono leprosos possent sanare: quemadmodum et tangere mortuum fuit prohibitum, et nihilominus Elias ac Eliseus super mortuos incubuerunt, quos suscitaverunt, ut liber Regum testatur.
paras.en: Further, Christ, as the lawgiver of the new law of the Gospel and the perfecter and fulfiller of the old law, often graciously fulfilled the law, showing that the law was holy and divine; and very often He does not keep it to the letter, but goes beyond it with authority. Hence He also touched this leper, though in Leviticus it was forbidden to touch a leper[[Lev 13:46||]][[Num 19:22||]]: although that precept was given according to the common state and course of men, and bound those who could be defiled by lepers rather than cleanse them, and did not bind those who by a singular gift of grace could heal lepers: as it was also forbidden to touch a dead man[[Num 19:11||]], and nevertheless Elias and Eliseus stretched themselves upon the dead whom they raised, as the book of Kings testifies[[3 Kings 17:21||]][[4 Kings 4:34||]].

paras.t: Insuper, Christus misit leprosum hunc post curationem ad sacerdotem, ne sacerdotibus occasionem contra se irrationabiliter daret, et sacerdotibus propter honorem Ordinis deferendum doceret, item ut eis causam credendi in ipsum offerret. — Mystice vero hoc egit, ad insinuandum quod in evangelica lege quicumque a lepra animæ, id est peccato, per contritionem curatus est, nihilominus debeat sacerdoti confiteri, et ejus judicio stare tempore opportuno, si poterit. Postremo, si iste leprosus pro corporalis lepræ emundatione Christo tam humiliter se prostravit, quanto magis nos pro spiritualium nostrarum purgatione leprarum, videlicet passionum et vitiorum expulsione, Christo nos prosternere atque humillime supplicare debemus, quum lepra hæc spiritualis, incomparabiliter pejor nocentiorque exsistat, quam corporalis?
paras.en: Moreover, Christ sent this leper to the priest after his cure so as not to give the priests an unreasonable occasion against Himself, and to teach that deference is due to priests for the honour of their Order, and also to offer them a reason for believing in Him. — Mystically, He did this to intimate that under the law of the Gospel whoever has been cured of the leprosy of the soul, that is, of sin, through contrition must nonetheless confess to the priest and abide by his judgment at a suitable time, if he can. Lastly, if this leper prostrated himself so humbly before Christ for the cleansing of a bodily leprosy, how much more ought we to prostrate ourselves before Christ and beseech Him most humbly for the cleansing of our spiritual leprosies, that is, for the driving out of our passions and vices, since this spiritual leprosy is incomparably worse and more harmful than the bodily?

paras.t: Perambulabat autem magis sermo de illo, id est, fama virtutum ac sapientiæ Christi quotidie latius diffundebatur, uno alteri referente quid viderit, et Christo quotidie plura prodigia operante, atque in omnibus irreprehensibiliter se habente, ac sapientissime prædicante facundissima venustate. Ideo factum est quod subditur: Et conveniebant turbæ multæ, ut audirent eum, informari salubriter cupientes, et curarentur ab infirmitatibus suis corporalibus: non quod omnes illi fuerunt corporaliter ægri, sed quoniam inter eos multi tales fuerunt. Sed et plures eorum devote ad Christum profecti sunt, ut ejus sermonibus ad emendationem vitæ perducerentur, sicque a spiritualibus curarentur languoribus. Ipse autem secedebat in desertum, et orabat: non quod frequentia tumultusque hominum, eum in aliquo a Dei contemplatione, interiorique exercitio impedirent; sed ad nostram instructionem hoc fecit, ut post occupationes vitæ activæ, post exercitia exteriora, hominumque frequentiam, ad secretiora loca confugiamus, in quibus contemplativæ exercitiis vitæ liberius atque stabilius intendamus, animas nostras discutiamus, et quidquid culpæ incurrerit defleamus; ibi quoque in abscondito a pietate obtineamus divina gratiarum charismata ampliora, quæ redeuntes ad publicum aliis communicemus, sicut Petrus loquitur: Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes. Christus quoque tam activam quam contemplativam vitam verbo et factis docere, fundare et approbare volebat; et præfato suo abscessu docuit prædicatores, imo et omnes, devitare hominum applausus ac adulationes.
paras.en: [[5:15|But the fame of him went abroad the more|Perambulabat autem magis sermo de illo]], that is, the fame of Christ's virtues and wisdom spread daily more widely, one telling another what he had seen, while Christ daily worked more wonders, behaved blamelessly in all things, and preached most wisely with the most eloquent grace. So what follows came about: [[5:15|and great multitudes came together to hear|Et conveniebant turbæ multæ, ut audirent]] Him, desiring to be instructed for their salvation, [[5:15|and to be healed by him of their infirmities|et curarentur ab infirmitatibus suis]] of body: not that all of them were sick in body, but because many among them were. But many of them also went devoutly to Christ to be led by His words to amend their lives, and so to be cured of their spiritual sicknesses. [[5:16|And he retired into the desert; and prayed|Ipse autem secedebat in desertum, et orabat]]: not that the throng and tumult of men hindered Him in any way from the contemplation of God and inward exercise; but He did this for our instruction, so that after the occupations of the active life, after outward exercises and the company of men, we may take refuge in more secret places, where we may give ourselves more freely and steadily to the exercises of the contemplative life, examine our souls, and weep for whatever fault they have incurred; and there too, in secret, may obtain from the divine goodness larger gifts of graces, which we may share with others when we return to public life, as Peter says: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes]]. Christ also wished to teach, found and approve both the active and the contemplative life by word and deed; and by this withdrawal of His He taught preachers, indeed everyone, to shun the applause and flattery of men.
